“As we saw,” Mydei agrees. “Enough, then. Bathe and come to bed. The hour grows late, and I’m weary.”

Phainon’s expression goes shuttered and wary.

“The tiny bed in the closet.”

Mydei scoffs. “No. No, I wouldn’t put my worst enemy in that claustrophobic closet. And we must convince my mother that you’re doing your job.”

“I suppose we must,” Phainon says, though he doesn’t sound happy about it. He pushes away from the table, his expression still shuttered. “I’ll take that bath, then.”

Mydei gestures to indicate the way to the bathroom, which is unnecessary, really. Phainon already knows where it is because he was quite literally right there earlier. Something like shame, like self-loathing, burns its way through Mydei as Phainon ducks into Mydei’s bedroom. He stares at the empty plate, inhaling deeply, fighting off the guilt. He did what he had to do to maintain the charade, and Phainon had been apparently amenable. Phainon is too new a slave. Surely, he would have fought back if he felt the need.

Disgust tightens Mydei’s stomach, and he shoves himself away from the table. Dwelling on his past actions won’t help him. He can’t afford to be mired in regret when he has to try, somehow, to outsmart his mother.

For now, though, he needs a distraction. Any will do. He wanders over to a shelf of scrolls and selects from his collection a treatise on the Chrysos Wars. It’s been decades since the Chrysos Heirs warred with each other to obtain the powers of their respective Titans, too busy fighting off the inevitability of Castrum Kremnos. Eurypon’s accession as Strife, succeeding Nikador, had been violent and bloody thing decades ago, and it had changed the face of Amphoreus, uniting and stabilizing the Chrysos Heirs against a common foe. A foe they have been unable to turn back.

Mydei’s jaw clenches, and he takes the scroll away from the shelf, opening it as he goes. Considerable military wisdom came out of the Chrysos Wars, and while Eurypon rarely seeks Mydei’s counsel, Mydei refuses to go into battle ill-prepared. His education on combat and strategy was considerable, yes, but the wisdom of the ages should always be studied. And, if nothing else, the treatise will occupy his mind.

Settling on his bed with the scroll in hand, Mydei kicks off his sandals and reclines, propping himself on one elbow as he reads the same line of the scroll over and over and over. The splashing from the bathroom is a terrible distraction. Every five words, his mind helpfully provides him with a mental image of Phainon’s naked chest, dripping with water, and he has to bite the inside of his cheek viciously to drag his attention back to the treatise in his hands.

He’s read the same sentence of the same paragraph at least five times when Phainon emerges from the bath, wrapped only in a scrap of linen, his skin still damp. Mydei’s mouth goes dry. Though he’s had years of practice hiding his expression, he doesn’t do a good job of it now. Phainon’s lips twist.

“Would you like me to prepare myself for you, Your Highness?” he asks with a mocking half bow.

“Don’t be crass,” Mydei says, refusing to rise to Phainon’s obvious bait. “I’ve told you already I have no intention of actually fucking you.”

“Then why are you staring?”

Mydei despises himself more in that moment than he has in his entire life. He looks away from Phainon and makes a show of returning his attention to his scroll. “It is not my intention. There are clothes in the adjacent room.”

“I know.”

“Then dress,” Mydei snaps.

“And here I thought you liked the look of me.”

Infuriating man. Mydei refuses to dignify the comment with a response, rereading the same damn sentence yet again.

But Phainon drifts into his closest, rummaging noisily through the trunks of clothing, and when he emerges, he has a proper skirt wrapped around his waist and his chest is less damp if still, unfortunately, on prominent display. Mydei is no beast. He’s been around handsome, half-naked men for much of his life. Phainon, he tells himself, is no different than them. Can’t be any different than them.

Mydei picks up his scroll, laying it across his legs as Phainon approaches the bed. Outside, beyond the open windows, the sun kisses the horizon. The light will be gone soon, and wise men will find their rest. “There’s room,” he says, trying to sound disinterested.

With clear reluctance, Phainon eases onto the bed and beneath the thin blanket atop it. “Are you not going to sleep?”

“Not yet,” Mydei replies, attention fixed on the scroll. He doesn’t see a single word written on the papyrus.

Phainon grunts, rolling to his side with his back to Mydei, but even then, Mydei can’t relax. Phainon’s presence is too much, too new, too overwhelming and strange, and he’ll have to adjust to this, to having someone in his bed every night, sharing his space. Breathing his air.

Unlike his friends—unlike Hephaestion—he’s not particularly worried about a knife in his back. Certainly, a knife in a very particular place in his back would be wildly inconvenient, but knives in general aren’t much of a bother. No weapons are. Phainon can do him no harm except as an inconvenience. He’s a complication Mydei doesn’t want, and he only wishes he could make sense of Gorgo’s machinations. But such musings are useless. Trying to unravel Gorgo’s motivations never ends well—he’s tried, and the results rarely fall in his favor.

He forces himself to read, making his way slowly through the scroll as the sun sinks into the cradle of the earth’s embrace. By the time he reaches the end of the long-dead general’s musings, he’s squinting to make out the

words on the papyrus—and Phainon is still awake, his breathing even but not deep with slumber.

There’s nothing to be done about it, so Mydei rolls up his scroll and sets it on a nearby table before stripping off his chiton. He tosses the cloth on a settee before returning to his bed.

“You’re really going to sleep next to me,” Phainon says abruptly, looking over his shoulder.

With a quiet laugh, Mydei slips beneath the sheet. “And what will do you, Phainon of Nowhere? Kill a man who cannot be killed?” He settles against his pillows on his back, tucking his arms behind his head.

Phainon makes a quiet sound, something like an acknowledgement, as if he’s accepting all the many rumors that swirl around Mydei’s immortality.

The night deepens around them.

Mydei remains on his back, staring at the ceiling, acutely aware of how the bed dips around him, the weight of another person at his side. Even though he can’t be killed, the idea of rolling to his side and giving Phainon his back makes his skin itch—and he usually sleeps on his side. How inconvenient.

“Why are you keeping me if you know I’m a spy?” Phainon’s question is quiet, as though Phainon fears breaking the darkness surrounding them.

Mydei considers all the answers to that question, the truths and the lies. Gorgo would spin a pretty tale for Phainon, something reassuring and comforting, but Mydei is not a liar. Not like that. “If I refused you, it’s more likely that you would go to the general slave quarters rather than back to my mother,” Mydei says. “Periander is not a kind master.”

“And you are?”

“Phainon, not only are you my first and only bed slave, you are my first and only slave.”

There’s a sharp inhalation from the other side of the bed.

“I don’t put much stock in the institution. I don’t own slaves.”

“But you permit them to exist.”

Mydei grinds his fingers into his eyes. “I permit nothing.” He has no power, no influence over his father or Castrum Kremnos. “I wouldn’t expect an Okheman to understand.”

“What’s there to understand?”

To be fair, it’s a question Mydei has asked himself on numerous occasions. If Okhema can manage without slaves, surely the far superior Castrum Kremnos can do the same. “I will not abandon you to a cruel fate,” Mydei says.

“How noble.”

Mydei drags a hand down his face, recognizing the losing battle before him. “Go to sleep,” he says, finally turning to his side, as much to dismiss Phainon as to end the conversation.

“I don’t need your protection.” How unsurprising that Phainon won’t relent.

“And yet you have it,” Mydei says, closing his eyes. He expects to lie there for hours, disquieted by the other man’s presence, hyperaware of the sound of his breathing. Instead, Mydei is asleep in minutes.

“Be silent. You must always be silent, even if someone speaks to you. Do not respond. Do not look anyone in the eye. Stay in my shadow,”

“Because you’re the newest addition to the royal court,” Mydeimos says once they’ve passed the guard, “you’ll be subjected to additional scrutiny. You will be mocked and insulted. You must not react.”

“I—”

Mydeimos draws up and turns, his expression so serious that it’s frightening. “What part of be silent did you not understand?”

Phainon presses his lips together, his fingers twitching not with irritation but with the kind of anxiety that only comes over him before stepping into a fight. Grinding his teeth together, he gives Mydeimos a clipped nod. Mydeimos understands this world, he does not, and Mydeimos is giving him every impression that failure to adhere to the rules will have serious consequences. Life and death consequences.

“Good.” Mydeimos relaxes, but only the slightest bit, as if he’s accepting that he won’t have to be uncertain of Phainon at his back. “My last bit of advice to you.” He reaches out, catching Phainon’s chin.

Heat jolts down Phainon’s spine.

“No matter what happens, no matter what you see or hear or what is said to you, you must not react.”

He wants to speak. Wants to protest that this is a party. The severity of Mydeimos’s expression stays his tongue as his unease grows. He nods once, sharply, and uses the gesture to pull his chin free of Mydeimos’s grasp.

Mydeimos drops his hand. “Good.” He resumes his brisk walk, and Phainon follows, two steps behind, his fingers curling. He wants a sword, a dagger, a knife, but all he has is fine linen, a fibula at his shoulder, and a belt around his waist. The pin on the fibula might be long enough to—to what? Put out someone’s eye?

Phainon smothers a laugh and grinds his teeth together. Right, exactly what he wants to do: put a pin through someone’s eye. He’s a slave now. He needs to think like one.

Mydei steps through the grand doors to the great hall and knows this is going to be bad. At a glance, he sees all his father’s generals, all the citizens of standing and the senators—for what good they are. Braziers line the walls, and a haze of smoke crowds out the high ceiling. In the center of the hall, half-naked slave girls dance around a central pyre, their skirts swirling around them, the bangles on their wrists and ankles jingling in time to the musicians’ music. Among the players, Mydei spies Peucesta, and their eyes meet briefly, but Peucesta is, as always, too focused on his music to communicate anything of value in that glance.

Phainon crowds his back, and Mydei hisses. Phainon’s too close, but Mydei can’t acknowledge that without breaking several rules of etiquette, and while he’s fine flaunting many traditions, he’s not stupid enough to flaunt them in front of his father.

Eurypon sits above them all on a throne atop an elevated dais that overlooks the banquet hall and the dancers, and a brazier at the center of everything.

Stomach turning, Mydei waits for his father to notice him before giving a little bow. Eurypon looks away, and Mydei closes his eyes, his only outward show of relief. That’s one blade dodged.

Trusting Phainon to stay close—which is perhaps more trust than Phainon deserves—Mydei makes his way through the crowd. While he would prefer to find an empty table and take up residence there for the evening, a prince is expected to play a certain part at these events. He’ll start with—

“Mydeimos.”

—his mother.

She steps smoothly from the crowd, flanked by her two closest slaves, and she looks beautiful in the warm light from the braziers, her skin cast in bronze. Like Mydeimos, she wears red, and it suits her, suits the copper of her hair and the blazing amber of her eyes. Unlike Mydeimos, she wears sleeves tied to her chiton, and they drape long down her arms, far past her wrists. Her slaves hold her goblet of wine and a plate of foods easily fed to her—dolmas, fritters, and spanakopita.

A wide smile blooms across her weathered face, and he knows her well enough to see that it doesn’t quite reach her eyes. She, too, is wary of this sudden feast. Her smile grows, though, when her gaze slides over his shoulder. “I see you’re taking good care of my gift,” she says.

Mydeimos can feel the way Phainon prickles, and he offers a prayer to any Titan that may care to listen that Phainon holds his tongue. “He is easy to care for,” he replies.

“How wonderful to hear that.” She steps around Mydei, and he makes room for her, allowing her to approach Phainon.

Now, he prays that she doesn’t touch the man; he can’t imagine Phainon tolerating that, and then there will be a scene, and he’ll have to whip Phainon in public. Which he doesn’t want to do for a whole host of reasons he’s not particularly interested in reflecting on.

The gods must hear him, for Phainon remains still as Gorgo leans toward him, canting her head to inspect him. “Your color remains good. And there’s still meat on your bones.”

Oh, but there’s an obvious tension to the way Phainon smiles at the Queen of Castrum Kremnos. Miraculously, he remains silent.

“My son isn’t neglecting you then,” Gorgo says, and Mydeimos could sink into the ground and die.

“Mother.”

She rolls her shoulder, her way of dismissing him. “Allow a mother her affectations. I am happy that you seem so content with my gift. He is a fine specimen, isn’t he?” At last, she pulls away from Phainon and turns back to Mydei, who really could perish on the spot. “You are enjoying him?”

His own smile grows tense, fragile. “I am sure you know.”

She doesn’t even look offended. “It’s different to hear from your own child rather than through the lines of palace gossip.”

“Forgive me if I prefer not to have this discussion with my mother.”

She laughs, the sound rich and throaty. “I have given you exactly what you enjoy most. The finest specimen of a man—”

“Mother.”

“—who is tall and well-muscled—”

“Mother.” Mydei sends a terrified glance at Phainon, but the tension has eased from Phainon’s mouth. Or, rather, now the tension stems from holding back laughter. His pale eyes sparkle with mirth. Their eyes meet, briefly, and Mydei knows he’s enjoying Gorgo’s teasing.

Gorgo is carrying on. “—firm of body and certainly of—”

“Enough,” Mydei says, mortified, his face burning. “This is hardly appropriate for a feast.” Or anywhere, really.

Gorgo merely laughs again. “It is my hope that you are truly enjoying the gift I’ve given you,” she says.

She knows, then, that while they share a bed, they’re not sleeping with each other. She knows her gift isn’t being used in the way he’s meant to be used, and Mydei wonders which of his servants she’s paying behind his back.

Phainon snorts.

Neither Mydei nor Gorgo acknowledge him.

“I find Phainon very pleasing, Mother, thank you,” Mydei says. “Your insight is, as always, sharper than any blade.”

Her lips curl, and she turns to her slave. The slave lifts the goblet to her lips, and Mydei marvels, as he always does, at how she can maintain her dignity being thus fed. Gorgo is a stronger woman than he a man. But she is also terrifying, and the longer he spends talking to her, the more of his secrets— what few remain his—will unravel for her.

“Forgive me,” he says, “but I see Hephaestion, and I—”

“Go to your friend,” she says, stepping away from the goblet. “Can’t be seen too long with your mother, after all.”

He gives her a small smile. “You know that’s not the case.”

Her gaze is sharp, wickedly so. “Do I?” she asks dryly.

And because he is too afraid to answer that question, he steps around her and moves away. Phainon follows, shaking, and Mydei glances over his shoulder. Low enough so that he can’t be overheard, he says, “React to nothing.”

Before he swings back around, he catches the roll of Phainon’s eyes, and he could kill the man. At least he’s managed to stay silent; there are small mercies from the Titans after all.

He wasn’t lying to his mother about Hephaestion. Mydei cuts a direct path to his friend even as he reflects that this is probably a bad idea. Hephaestion has made nothing but denigrating comments about Phainon, as many deserved as not, and bringing the two men together certainly promises conflict—or at least more of Hephaestion’s derision. Unfortunately, Hephaestion navigates the court in a way that Mydei can’t. He’ll have a deeper knowledge of what’s going on that Mydei does, and Mydei needs that knowledge.

He just doesn’t expect Hephaestion to lead with, “I hope you’ve adequately prepared your newest acquisition for tonight’s festivities.”

Mydei fully expects Phainon to react poorly. He’s neither subdued nor broken, and he doesn’t have any understanding of what it means to be a slave in Castrum Kremnos. But he’s taken Mydei’s warnings and instructions to heart: while his jaw flexes, he remains silent in Mydei’s shadow.

Relieved, Mydei sighs heavily, a little too heavily, but he’s trying to make a point to Phainon as much as to Hephaestion. “Can we not begin this way?”

Hephaestion regards Mydei, crossing his arms and paying Phainon no further mind. Just as the silence between them grows uncomfortable, he lowers his voice and asks, “Have you heard about the mercenaries?”

Cold dread crystallizes in Mydei’s stomach. “You’ll need to be more specific.” There are always mercenaries coming and going from Castrum Kremnos, supplements to Eurypon’s armies of conquest, but he can already guess where this conversation is headed. Eurypon only throws feasts like this for a specific set of reasons, but he’d hoped, perhaps, not this time.

“They’ve come back from a village near the Grove of Epiphany,” Hephaestion says. “And they didn’t return emptyhanded.”

“How many?” Mydei asks, that dread climbing into his chest, his throat. It strangles him.

“Five.” Hephaestion glances toward the head of the banquet hall, toward a doorway to the left of the base of Eurypon’s elevated dais. “There are children, Mydei.”

Mydei’s vision tunnels, and he has to remind himself of his instructions to Phainon. React to nothing. Not even this. He cannot show weakness. “There have been children before.” Oh, but this will be so much worse than he expected. Bad enough to have one of these feasts, but for Phainon’s first of these ordeals to feature children is even worse.

Hephaestion grimaces, too much emotion on display, and Mydei instinctively shifts to block Hephaestion from Eurypon’s line of sight. No one is allowed to have anything less than a wonderful time at these feasts. “There are at least two,” he says.

At Mydei’s back, Phainon shifts restlessly, and Mydei can all but feel his frustration over their opaque conversation. But he doesn’t demand clarity. He doesn’t interrupt.

“Mydei, this is getting worse.”

“I know.” Mydei reaches out, picking up a goblet from a nearby table, unconcerned with who it might belong to, the picture of a spoiled prince. He waves it in front of Phainon’s face, and though Phainon takes two seconds too long to get the message, he does as he should and picks up the pitcher on the table. He pours while Mydei continues. “But what are we to do?”

“There’s nothing… I just wish…” His lips pull in a grimace. “There’s nothing that can be done.”

There isn’t, but somewhere in the most secret corners of his heart, Mydei wishes something could be done. That, unfortunately, would mean treason, and Eurypon is terrifyingly good at sniffing out even the smallest hint of treason.

Mydei places his hand on Hephaestion’s shoulder, ignoring the way Hephaestion’s eyes light too much. “Find the others. If nothing else, we can…” He sighs. “We can be together for whatever comes next.” Hephaestion reaches for Mydei’s hand, but Mydei pulls away before they can touch. He shouldn’t have reached out at all.

Hephaestion’s expression hardens. “Of course, Your Highness,” he says.

Mydei doesn’t have the energy to take offense to the cold tone. He waves Hephaestion away as Phainon crowds close with his pitcher. “Don’t,” he warns Phainon.

“What was all that about?” Phainon asks in what he must think is a whisper but is much too loud.

Narrowing his eyes, Mydei gives Phainon a withering look. “Be silent,” he hisses, “and react to nothing.”

“Not even—”

“Not even this.” He turns his eyes heavenward, wondering why Strife has seen fit to curse him in this way, and then decides to throw Phainon a bone. “Later,” he says, trying to laden the word with meaning.

Phainon withdraws, but his expression is barely concealed frustration and anger. Wonderful. The court will see Mydei trailed by an angry new slave. Exactly the image he needs to project. He—

“How refreshing to see Your Highness here with a slave in attendance!”

Mydei plasters a pleasant expression on his face as quickly as he can, turning to face the man who has approached them from the side. Themistocles is the greatest of Eurypon’s generals, a brilliant tactician and charismatic leader, but he’s also a carousing drunkard, and Mydei wants Phainon nowhere near him. For no particular reason.

“Themistocles,” he says, trying to inject some measure of warmth into his voice. “How good of you to notice.” Fuck, but he hates politics. Kremnoans aren’t above political maneuvering even though they like to pretend they are. They’re just usually more cutthroat and direct than their Okheman adversaries. “A gift from my mother.” He gestures to Phainon with his goblet and prays—remarkably—for peace instead of Strife.

He all but feels the loathing radiating off Phainon and hopes desperately that Phainon is keeping his expression at least neutral.

“Well,” Themistocles says, “you mustn’t let such things distract you, eh?” He lifts his brows. Mydei considers putting a fist through Themistocles’s face, but that’s too direct, even for a Kremnoan. “Not when our victories are so close at hand.”

Mydei shifts his weight to subtly insert himself between his Okheman slave and the general in front of them. “I assure you: I am committed to my father’s cause.”

“As you should be.” Themistocles tosses back a generous mouthful of his wine, splashing some of it on his chiton, and Mydei pretends not to notice. “Okhema is on its last legs. Soon the entire continent will belong to Strife— to our god and king.” He lifts his goblet in salute toward Eurypon.

Eurypon, engaged in a conversation with another general, doesn’t even acknowledge Themistocles, forcing him to hang his hand in the air for a lengthy and awkward moment. Finally, realizing he’s not going to get anything out of the king, Themistocles lowers his hand and returns his attention to Mydei.

“The Okheman scourge will be destroyed.” He flicks a disparaging look Phainon’s way, a pitying look. “Gutless cowards will be better served as our slaves than managing a city-state of their own.”

Phainon shifts forward, and Mydei grabs his wrist with his free hand, squeezing hard enough that bones grind together. “Excuse me, General,” Mydei says, already starting to drag Phainon away. “There’s something that requires my attention.” It’s not a graceful exit but it’ll do, and Mydei hauls Phainon after him, setting his wine aside as he passes a table.

“You—”

“Shut. Up,” Mydei snarls over his shoulder, pulling Phainon through the crowd of guests, ignoring their gawking looks. There’s a small nook at the back of the banquet hall that is usually occupied by trysting citizens, but it’s empty at the moment, and Mydei all but throws Phainon into its shadowy depths. “How many times do I have to make it clear to you that you can’t react to any of their goading? How many times do I have to remind you to stay quiet?”

In the darkness, Phainon scoffs. “Do you really expect me to take that many blows to my pride?”

“Yes.” Mydei crowds Phainon, pushing him deeper into the nook. “Yes, I do. I expect you to be silent when I tell you to be silent and to school your expressions and to listen to me because I’m not telling you any of this for my own health. Do you understand me, Phainon of—” He pauses. “Where are you really from?”

“Okhema,” Phainon replies too quickly.

“Liar. Where?”

“I—”

“I cannot protect you if you aren’t honest with me.”

That causes Phainon to jerk back. The darkness doesn’t do enough to hide his surprise. He regards Mydei before turning away. “Aedes Elysiae,” he says.

Mydei groans. He knows the name of every city-state Eurypon has absorbed into his empire, every town and village he’s sacked and razed in pursuit of his conquest, and Aedes Elysiae is one of them. He wasn’t there —was too young for the conflict—but he’s heard plenty of stories of a brutal, bloody campaign that ended with more bodies in pieces than whole, with more dead than enslaved. That Phainon hails from Aedes Elysiae complicates things enough, but more complicated still is that can only mean he’s an Okheman refugee. His mother sent Phainon to him knowing he’s an Okheman refugee from Aedes Elysiae.

There’s a play there, but he can’t see it, not yet.

“And you’ve been in Okhema all this—” There comes a mighty clanging, the sound of spears hitting shields, and Mydei yanks himself away from Phainon. “Fuck,” he mutters, too off balance to moderate his language. “This conversation isn’t over. Follow me—and remember what I’ve said.”

He spins around and vacates the nook, not pausing to ensure Phainon is behind him. Phainon isn’t stupid; he’ll follow.

The banquet tables aren’t arranged in any particular order, but everyone knows Gorgo sits opposite Eurypon and Mydei takes the table to her immediate right. They settle in their places, Mydei giving his mother a brief nod of acknowledgement, and he’s relieved when Phainon leans over his shoulder to pour him another goblet of wine. Before Mydei can drink from it, though, Phainon lifts it to his own lips, taking a sip—just as he should to test for poison. Only then does he set it in front of Mydei.

And Mydei hates it. Hates the subservience of it, hates the necessity of it. Poison can’t kill him anymore than a blade can, but Phainon is supposed to risk his life for Mydei’s own immortal one because of all the rules surrounding slaves in Castrum Kremnos. Phainon was right to cut into him that first night.

There’s little time to reflect on his own moral shortcomings, however. Eurypon rises from his throne, stepping forward to the edge of his dais. He lifts his hands, and music and conversation ceases. Everyone in the room, from senator to general to slave, turns their attention to the King of Castrum Kremnos, bearer of the coreflame of Strife, Titan of Strife, god of war. He’s old, nearing sixty, but still possesses a striking gravitas that draws everyone in the room to him. Even in anonymity, Mydei supposes, Eurypon’s magnetism would capture the attention of the masses.

“My friends,” he says, his voice booming through the banquet hall. A broad smile cuts across his handsome face, a face that informs Mydei’s own. He has his mother’s coloring but his father’s features. “My friends, we are standing on the precipice of a new age. The Chrysos Wars, that time of turmoil as men vied to become gods, are a century behind us and now at last we can see the future forming ahead of us. A time of unity, of peace—”

It takes all of Mydei’s self-control not to snort.

“—where our daughters grow fat on the riches of our harvests and our sons no longer go to war to defend our very way of life,” Eurypon continues. “That time is coming. Soon, Castrum Kremnos will bring all of Amphoreus into this bold new future.” There is roar of approval from the audience, the generals and senators cheering. Mydei lifts his goblet in deference to the occasion, but the sentiment is hollow. “Our enemies retreat further every

day, crumbling beneath the lines of our legions. Their borders shrink, their refuges fall alongside their villages and their towns. Soon, we will stand before the Holy City—” He scoffs. “—and we will take it as we have taken all the others.” Another roar of approval, another half-hearted salute of Mydei’s cup as he watches his father and prepares for the inevitable turn in this pretty speech. “And yet we must acknowledge the insidious forces working against us.”

There it is. Mydei rolls the goblet around its base, maintaining the perfect picture of indolence. A shame there’s no preparing Phainon more than he has. He can only hope Phainon maintains his own emotionless façade.

Eurypon gestures toward the doorway to the side of his dais. Rough-hewn mercenaries tumble through it, dragging with them a young man, bound and gagged. The young man is complacent only long enough for the realization of his location to register, and then he struggles, kicking his feet against the marble ground and making desperate, urgent sounds muffled by the gag.

Mydei’s stomach churns.

“We have conquered Amphoreus through our force of will and the strength of our determination, yes,” Eurypon says as the young man is thrown to his knees at the front of the dais. “But also because we suffer no threats to our empire. Threats like these.”

One of the mercenaries steps forward. He tears the young man’s chiton from his chest as another unsheathes his blade. This farce is practiced; Eurypon has done this enough times for everyone to know the steps in the dance, and yet the onlookers are as riveted as if this is the first time, as if they’ve never seen these events unfold before. The second mercenary slashes across the young man’s chest, his cry of terror and pain smothered, and steps aside.

Gold blood pours from the young man’s chest.

“The Chrysos Heirs are as much a plague on the world as the Okhemans,” Eurypon declares. “At every turn, they threaten the stability of our empire.”

Every Chrysos Heir is an existential threat, an heir apparent to Strife himself. Even Mydei, especially Mydei, who occupies a precarious niche in the royal household.

He sees his own face reflected in that of the young man’s.

Behind him, Phainon has gone preternaturally still. Mydei can’t offer him any reassurance; to act would draw attention to them both, and neither of them can afford the court’s attention. But he understands. Long have the Okhemans placed their faith in the Chrysos Heirs, certain one of them will somehow overthrow Eurypon’s reign in accordance with prophecy. None has, and Eurypon has done everything in his power to purge the Chrysos Heirs from his conquered lands.

“Let us suffer no Chrysos Heir to live,” Eurypon says.

The young man makes a shrill, terrified sound from behind his gag as the mercenaries grab him, as they drag him toward that central brazier. He grows more hysterical, fighting wildly against them, but they are too many and too strong.

Phainon’s breathing is hard, is loud enough for Mydei to hear it.

Mydei studies his goblet, doing everything he can to appear utterly disinterested. The senators and generals are, of course, riveted, but they’re not the primary audience for this show.

The mercenaries pull the young man into the brazier, chaining him with bronze in its center as he flails and sobs, as golden blood drips down his chest.

Eurypon descends his dais, fixing his gaze on Mydei.

Mydei debates yawning. No, that would be too much. This is a delicate balance. Any interest, any fear, and Eurypon will draw this out as much as he can—but he’s just as likely to do the same in an attempt to make his point if Mydei looks too bored.

“My son,” he says without a drop of parental warmth. “Had you not been so otherwise occupied this past week, this glory could have been yours.”

Sighing, Mydei runs his finger around the edge of his goblet. “The queen’s gift is far more interesting than the conquest of yet another Chrysos Heir,” he says.

Phainon hisses, and Mydei burns with the knowledge that his expression is a far cry from neutral.

“Such an attitude doesn’t commend you,” Eurypon says easily. He paces the length of the banquet hall, approaching Mydei with a congenial smile that doesn’t reach his eyes. “If we are to ensure peace and prosperity, we must purge Amphoreus of the Chrysos Heirs. There is no greater calling.”

“My king needs only make the request of me.” Mydei leans to the side in his chair, closer to Phainon, trying to put himself between the Okheman and his father. “I would, of course, find it in me to pull myself away from the queen’s gift.”

The words are carefully crafted. He’ll do only what’s asked of him, not anything more, but Eurypon craves initiative from his vassals. With two sentences, he has reminded Eurypon that he doesn’t care for the murder of the Chrysos Heirs and that he’ll only participate when he’s ordered to take action against his own kin. It’s enough to make Eurypon’s pleasant expression turn cruel.

Good.

“Let us remind our beloved son the cost of being a Chrysos Heir within our empire,” Eurypon says, as though he is amused instead of infuriated, but Mydei can read the tightness around Eurypon’s eyes and the flare of his nostrils. Turning, the king makes his way back toward his dais as the half-naked slave girls wend through the gathered attendees, torches in their hands.

The young man on the brazier screams and thrashes, but his chains hold. They always do.

As the first torch touches the kindling at the young man’s feet, Mydei gives an affected sigh.

“This is madness,” Phainon whispers, hoarse. Mydei flicks a glance at him as he falls to his knees, his expression stark and horrified. “How can you sit here and—”

“Be silent,” Mydei reminds him.

As he gains the steps to the dais, Eurypon flings his wine-dark cloak behind him and faces his rapt audience. “My people, fear not! Though my son is often errant, the soldiers of Castrum Kremnos do their duty.” How insulting, calling barbarian mercenaries soldiers of Castrum Kremnos. Mydei’s lip curls. “I will purge Amphoreus of the taint of the Chrysos Heirs.” He tips his face toward Mydei—and then toward Phainon.

Mydei freezes.

“Do you not agree?” the king asks Phainon. “Is this not the most noble of callings?”

The young man screams through his gag. Heat wafts over Mydei’s face accompanied by the sweet stench of burning flesh, and Mydei clutches his goblet to hide the shaking of his hand, offering prayers to all the Titans—all except Strife—that Phainon doesn’t fuck this up. Phainon is Gorgo’s agent. Surely, surely, he isn’t a complete fool.

“As you say, Your Majesty,” Phainon says, with surprising clarity. With surprising conviction.

The tension drains out of Mydei, and he downs a generous mouthful of wine.

But Eurypon isn’t done yet. “So little to say? Surely you have an opinion, Okheman slave.”

All the tension comes back. Mydei forces himself to lounge in his chair, to remain boneless and unaffected. He can play this game. His mother can,

too. Even his friends can. But Phainon is too new, too unbroken.

“My opinion is my master’s,” Phainon replies.

Mydei could weep with relief.

“And what is his opinion?” Eurypon asks. He holds up a hand, forestalling Mydei. “No. You answer me, slave. Not him.”

At last, Mydei turns to Phainon, who remains kneeling beside the table, his eyes downcast, his head bowed. He is the picture of a contrite man, a broken slave. “That the mighty King Eurypon deals out only justice to the people he rules.”

A terrifying smile cuts across Eurypon’s face. “Even Okhema’s snakes can acknowledge the truth!” he declares, and a cheer goes up from the crowd. “Do you hear that, HKS?” he asks, turning to the Chrysos Heir burning alive in the center of the room. “This is justice.” Eurypon’s smile stretches wider.

The scent of cooking flesh fills the room alongside the young man’s hysterical, agonized cries. Mydei’s grip tightens on his goblet as he watches the young man die for the uncontrollable sin of his birth, keenly aware of how easily he could find himself on that same pyre. One misstep, and Eurypon won’t hesitate to burn him, either, won’t hesitate to kill his son and heir—and the only credible threat to his godhood.

Forcing himself to sigh, Mydei takes a sip of his wine and turns his attention to the ceiling, as though he can’t be bothered with the horrors before him. Eurypon wants his fear, so Mydei refuses to give it.

Eurypon’s patience is, thankfully, a threadbare thing. Perhaps a minute passes, marked by the snapping of wood and the screams of the young man, before Eurypon gestures irritably to one of the mercenaries. The man steps forward, angles his spear, and plunges it into the young man’s chest. Golden blood spills down his front, sizzling when it hits flame.

Beside the table, Phainon shudders. His hands curl into fists against his thighs, but he doesn’t give any other reaction. Mydei could weep with relief, but he takes another sip of his wine before picking through a plate of grapes despite a complete lack of appetite. His stomach heaves in protest— both of the wine and the grapes—but he eats a few anyway, forcing himself to remain utterly disengaged.

Eurypon turns toward a much more receptive audience, his senators and generals hanging on his every word as he says, “This, then, is the price of disobedience, of harboring a criminal.”

One the generals, almost certainly Themistocles, bangs his fist on his banquet table. The others pick up the rhythm of it, beating their fists on their own tables. Mydei finally allows himself a yawn, using it to hide his horror when another cadre of mercenaries march in four more people.

Five. Hephaestion had warned him there were five.

A mother, a father. A teenaged girl. A young boy. The mother and daughter weep openly, the father is stone-faced, the boy confused but clearly afraid.

They are forced to their knees at the foot of Eurypon’s dais, the mercenaries holding blades to their throats. The young boy at last comprehends the truth of what’s about to happen to him, and he begins begging for his father and mother’s help.

Mydei doesn’t look away from them. His stomach churns, his chest aches, and a cold sweat covers his skin; no matter how many times his father has done this, he can’t grow used to it. He will never grow used to it.

“What fate is there for such treasonous scum except death?” Eurypon asks the assembly, raising his voice to be heard over the pounding of their fists. “We will not suffer them.”

The mercenaries pull their blades across four throats. Blood gushes down their fronts, spilling down their chests, and the mercenaries release them. The little boy falls immediately, twitching on the marble floor as he bleeds out. The father remains upright the longest, his eyes upturned, his lips

moving, but the Titans are uncaring creatures. They don’t answer his pleas. He dies alongside his family in a mixed pool of their blood as the senators and generals cheer for their king.

Mydei swallows his gorge, setting his wine aside.

“These rodents were found just outside of the Grove,” Eurypon says. “And where there is one rat, there is always another.”

Breathing through his mouth, ignoring the growing scent of charred flesh and the coppery tang of blood, Mydei meets his father’s eyes. He knows exactly what Eurypon is about to say.

“Since my son is so eager for my command, he will lead a force to the Grove and unearth any other traitors.” Eurypon’s smile is cold. “Go forth, my son, and root out the corruption in our empire.”

As soon as they return to Mydeimos’s suite, Phainon shoves past the prince. He rushes to the bathroom, heedless of anything or anyone in his path, finds a bucket, and vomits bile into it. His stomach clenches, twists, and heaves again.

Cold sweat coats his skin. He shudders as he vomits a third time. Only then does his stomach settle, and he sinks even lower on the floor, pressing his forehead against cold tile despite his shivering. The room tunnels around him, his vision speckling with black dots, and he sucks in desperate mouthfuls of air to keep from passing out.

But he’s not so disoriented that he doesn’t hear Mydeimos’s footsteps.

“Are you well?” Mydeimos asks, so softly that it’s an insult.

Phainon shudders once more and then shoves himself to his feet. The world spins as he does, whirling around him as he faces the crown prince. “How could you just sit there?” he demands. “How could you just let all that happen?”

There isn’t an ounce of contrition on the prince’s arrogant face, not a drop of compassion. “We were lucky,” he says.

“Lucky?” Phainon laughs, wild and disbelieving. “Lucky to watch five people die in front of us like it was some amphitheater tragedy?”

“Yes.” Mydeimos leans against the wall and has the gall meet Phainon’s gaze without any shame. “We were lucky it was that fast, that my father got bored of the Chrysos Heir’s screaming and ended him quickly. That he had the family’s throats slit instead of torturing them for weeks in an attempt to get more information about their neighbors out of them. You think my dispassion is disregard, but it’s not.” He shoves away from the wall, advancing on Phainon.

Phainon doesn’t move, holding his ground. “Then what is it?”

“Armor,” Mydeimos snaps. He touches the side of his throat. “I bleed gold. Do you not understand that every last one of those killings is a message to me? One misstep, one whiff of treason, and my father will bind me to that same pyre and burn me alive over and over and over.”

“So you’re just a self-serving bastard,” Phainon snarls back.

Mydeimos’s lips curl with disdain. “I am keeping myself safe.”

“To what end? To serve your father’s murderous whims? To—”

Mydeimos lunges forward. Phainon swings out of his way quickly—too quickly—he’s betraying himself with that reaction, he knows it, but he won’t take the hit that Mydeimos clearly had planned. But Mydeimos isn’t trying to strike him.

“Shut up, you utter fool,” Mydeimos hisses, grabbing him by the shoulders and slamming him hard enough against the wall that the wind gets knocked out of him. Wheezing, Phainon struggles for breath. “Do you think I can protect you if anyone hears you speaking like that?”

“Why would you bother?”

“Because you’re an innocent man.”

What an ignorant thing to say, but Mydeimos’s ignorance is Phainon’s salvation. He inhales as deeply as he can, reminding himself that he’s here to play a part. He’ll never be the sulking, well-behaved slave, but Mydeimos isn’t wrong. Speaking out so boldly will get him killed, and his death will betray why he’s here at all.

He looks away from Mydeimos.

“Understand,” Mydeimos says, “that the more uncomfortable an audience he has, the longer my father will draw out someone’s death. If you can feign disinterest, if you can pretend what you’re seeing doesn’t affect you at all, he’ll end it faster.”

“You could do something. Help them,” Phainon says, but even as he speaks, he knows he’s wrong.

“No. I can’t.” There’s pain in Mydeimos’s voice. Regret. It’s enough to make Phainon wonder if he hasn’t somehow misjudged the prince. “You did well,” Mydeimos says, releasing Phainon’s shoulders and stepping back. “In the end, you did very well.”

Hollow, empty, meaningless praise. Phainon says nothing.

“It’s late. Come to bed, Phainon.”

More bile climbs Phainon’s throat. He doesn’t move away from the wall.

Mydeimos lingers for only a moment before exhaling heavily and leaving Phainon in the bathroom.

Alone, Phainon slides down the wall, collapsing onto the floor and drawing up his legs. He rests his forehead against his knees, covering his head with his hands. The razing of Aedes Elysiae was a terrible thing to survive, but he’s had years to distance himself from the bloody violence. Those murders —he’s never seen anyone so calmly execute another human being, so casually take away someone else’s life.

All at once, the clothing and jewelry he’s wearing become too much. He rocks forward, onto his knees, and yanks off the bangles, the necklace. He almost dashes them to the ground, but he hesitates. If he breaks something, his flesh will pay the price, and that’s not a price he can afford to pay. He drops the jewelry to the tiled floor and carefully unpins his chiton, shouldering out of it. The fabric pools around his hips until he stands, shuffling out of it.

Naked, he stares at the inset pool nearby. Dirty. He feels so dirty.

And helpless. Titans, he’s so utterly helpless.

He steps into the bath, sinking into it up to his shoulders, but water can’t wash away this kind of pain, this kind of disgust. The murders cling to him, staining his soul like blood on fresh linen. He’s not responsible for them, but he did nothing to stop them.

Laughing mirthlessly, he splashes water on his face.

Doing anything to stop those deaths would compromise him. He’s no better than Mydeimos, in the end, chained by duty and regret—and the reality of appearances. He realizes now how tenuous his position is in Castrum Kremnos. One misstep, one angered nobleman, and he’ll be exposed.

He’ll be dead.

He takes his time washing himself, scrubbing away invisible splatters of blood and the scent of charred flesh, numb. When he closes his eyes, he sees the screaming youth writhing on the pyre, and he knows he won’t cleanse his mind of that vision for months. He knew this would be dangerous, but tonight’s feast has made all that theoretical danger very, very tangible.

Swallowing, he leaves the bath and towels himself dry, standing before a mirror of beaten copper and regarding his reflection. A man beautiful enough, strong enough, to tempt the prince of Castrum Kremnos, to get close to him. He drags a hand over his mouth. Rubs it over his chest.

He chose this.

He goes to bed with Mydeimos.

Chapter End Notes
