chapters.title: Chapter 4
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Mydei is exhausted. He stands at the heart of the Grove of Epiphany with Hephaestion, overseeing the kind of work that leaves him ill at ease. His legionnaires have been raiding homes since dawn, barreling through doors to ransack houses in search of trapdoors and hidden rooms where Chrysos Heirs have been hidden away. They haven’t found any. He doesn’t expect them to find any.

He does expect this to sour the citizens of the Grove on the empire as a whole, however, and even now a family regards him and Hephaestion with hurt expressions as their home is turned upside down in search of what certainly isn’t there. These are citizens, and they should be better treated, but Eurypon’s paranoia knows no end.

All it takes is one well-placed Chrysos Heir assassin to end his long reign.

The Sages observe, too, watching from a distance, as if distance will somehow save them. If a Chrysos Heir is by some twist of fate discovered in any home within the Grove, the Sages’s lives will be forfeit, too. Eurypon is merciless: he will blame their weak leadership for allowing someone to harbor an enemy of the state.

A legionnaire approaches him and Hephaestion, offering a quick salute. “Your Highness,” he says, addressing Mydei before turning to Hephaestion. “All clear on the east. Nothing to report.” He hands a scrap of papyrus to Hephaestion, who glances over it to note the completed raids on his own scroll.

“Thank you, legionnaire.”

The man salutes once more and backs away.

“This is a waste of time,” Mydei mutters.

Hephaestion shoots him a warning look.

“Am I wrong? How many houses have we done?”

“Most of them,” Hephaestion admits.

“And what have we found? Nothing.” He tips his head back, letting cool air wash over him.

Phainon stands slightly behind him, fan in hand. He didn’t fight the job when given it. Since the feast, he’s been far more biddable, which Mydei finds worrisome, but he hasn’t had the time to deal with it. The morning after the feast, Mydei assembled his century and his somatophylakes and began the three-day march to the Grove. Since then, he’s been consumed by the march, too tired at the end of each day to have more than a passing conversation with Phainon, and they’ve fallen into Mydei’s bed without speaking. Phainon has been withdrawn and contemplative on the march, resulting in his lingering silence—and Mydei can’t complain about that. Mydei is, frankly, relieved about that. If Phainon is silent, he can’t get himself into trouble.

“Go check in with Leonnius,” Mydei says to Hephaestion. “See if his region is clear as well.”

Hephaestion gives him a clipped nod and trots off, trailed by an aide.

He’s more alone with Phainon now than he’s been in the past three days, even in his own tent, and he turns toward the man. Phainon wears a bored expression as he moves the fan mechanically up and down, as if he’s not mentally present. His eyes take too long to focus on Mydei.

“Deep in thought?” Mydei asks, amused.

Phainon’s lips quirk in a frown, there and gone. He’s taken Mydei’s advice almost too well since the feast, barely emoting at all. “Merely doing as my prince commands,” he replies.

He’s been more obedient, too. He hasn’t pushed back against a single command, acting dutifully when requests have been made of him, and Mydei doesn’t like it. He’s always been bothered by subservience in slaves especially, but this makes him even more uncomfortable.

“I find it hard to believe you don’t have an opinion on what we’re doing here,” Mydei says, not entirely sure why he’s trying to tease this out of Phainon but dogged in his pursuit of conversation.

Phainon flicks his eyes toward the nearest cohort of legionnaires, far enough away that their conversation won’t be overheard, and turns a bland expression on Mydei. “I wasn’t under the impression that the empire treats its citizens so poorly.”

With that simple statement, Mydei finds himself curiously inclined to defend an act he doesn’t agree with. Wrestling down that strange instinct, he shakes his head. “Not something you should say in public.”

“You invited commentary. I gave it. I wouldn’t want to disappoint my prince.”

Mydei frowns. “Phainon,” he begins.

A nearby commotion cuts him off, and he turns. His legionnaires have surrounded a tall man with greenish hair, a man Mydei recognizes at once. Anaxagoras, founder of the Nousporists, a man who walks the knife-edge of treason with a casual disregard for his own life at every opportunity. He weaves his seditions into pretty words, disguising them in metaphor, and has thus far managed to keep himself alive, but everyone in Castrum Kremnos knows it’s only a matter of time before he walks into his own grave at Eurypon’s behest.

The legionnaires crowd him back, holding him at bay.

Mydei resists the urge to pinch the bridge of his nose. “Let him through,” he says, loudly enough to be heard. He steps away from Phainon only to pause, glancing back. “Put down the fan and follow me.”

With a little shrug, Phainon obeys, passing the fan to another servant. He falls into step two paces behind Mydei, not that they go very far.

Anaxagoras meets them. “Since when does the empire violate the rights of its citizens?” he demands.

Delightful. “Since the citizens of the empire have made themselves complicit in treason,” Mydei replies. The words sound hollow even to him.

“And what proof do you have?” Anaxagoras presses.

“The tanner’s family from Orini harbored a Chrysos Heir in secret.” Mydei plumbs the depths of his patience. Anaxagoras should know better than to fire these questions at him in public. “The empire has reason to believe—”

“The actions of one man hardly reflect on his family, his village, or the neighboring city state.”

Scholars. They’re all so Titansdamned argumentative, and Mydei has no interest in defending his father to even one of the Sages—especially when he agrees. There was no reason for Eurypon to order this raid on the Grove except to exert his control and soothe his paranoia. “A man is a product of the environment that raised him,” Mydei says.

Anaxagoras snorts. “So, you did pay attention to your tutors.”

“Some of them.”

“You’re wasting your time here, Your Highness.” Anaxagoras manages to make the title a sneer without actually sneering, which is impressive, really. No one has ever so openly disdained Mydei, and while it’s irritating, it’s also refreshing. This is why he likes Phainon so much. “You will find nothing but loyal citizens. The true concern is beyond the city.”

“Does an army of barbarians lie in wait?” Mydei asks dryly.

Anaxagoras fixes him with a look that would flay the skin off most men’s bones. “The black tide encroaches.”

Mydei’s stomach drops. The black tide, that inexorable and ancient enemy of Strife, the one his father has neglected for nearly a century. Every inch of land Eurypon claims for Castrum Kremnos at the frontlines, the black tide erodes at the far edge of their borders. “The danger of the black tide is overstated,” he says, parroting the tract favored by his father’s politicians.

Now, Anaxagoras does sneer, and Mydei knows whatever regard the man might have held for him as dropped considerably. “I was under the impression you were smarter than that.”

“It is the position of Castrum Kremnos that—”

“The position of Castrum Kremnos is ill-conceived and misinformed.”

Mydei lifts a brow. The first interruption he could ignore. This one, he cannot. “Interrupt me again, scholar, and you will not live long enough to regret it.” His men look on, silent and still, but he can’t let one man undercut his authority in front of them. It’s taxing. It’s annoying. It’s frustrating, and he hates this game more than most others.

“Then do not be—”

“Mind your tongue,” Mydei says, ignoring the fury that flashes over Anaxagoras’s face. “You speak to your prince. And while I am not as quick to anger as some, my patience has limits.”

In silence, Anaxagoras regards him. Certainly, he’s smart enough to understand the warning Mydei is giving him. Indeed, instead of snapping back, Anaxagoras smooths out his expression. “If Your Highness has the time, I would show you the real danger.”

They’ve danced around each other long enough for politics and pride. “Very well.” Mydei turns to the legionnaires. “Fetch me Hephaestion, Leonnius, and Perdikkas.”

The men salute, two heading in search of Hephaestion and Leonnius and the other for Perdikkas.

“A prince without his somatophylakes is as good as naked,” Anaxagoras observes.

From another man, that would be a threat. “If the prince is mortal, perhaps.” Mydei shrugs. “I am not. My friends are a formality.”

“Friends. How interesting.”

Mydei doesn’t dignify that with a response, allowing an awkward silence to fester between them and keenly aware of the weight of Phainon’s gaze on his back. Anaxagoras shared Phainon’s question, and Mydei finds himself caring more that his answers satisfied his slave than the Sage. He wants a genuine moment alone with Phainon in a place where there are thick walls instead of the thin fabric barrier of a tent. Perhaps tonight he’ll have an opportunity to press Phainon. They’ll stay overnight at the Grove to be feted by the Sages, no matter that it’s for show. The rooms in the Grove have real walls, if walls made of trees, and while Mydei has no doubt Cerces will listen through her many branches, they can at least speak in vagaries.

At last, his three friends return, approaching at a brisk jog, the legionnaires who summoned them directed to other work.

“The Sage believes the black tide encroaches too closely on the Grove,” he says with a nod toward Anaxagoras. “I believe it’s in our best interests to investigate his claims.”

Leonnius grins, punching his fist into his palm. “It’s been too long since I’ve had a good fight.”

Perdikkas rolls his eyes. “All you think about is fighting.”

“Because it’s fun.” Leonnius drops his arm on Perdikkas’s shoulder, leaning heavily on him even when Perdikkas attempts to shake him off.

“We’re investigating,” Hephaestion says. “Not necessarily taking action.”

“But we’re not necessarily not taking action,” Leonnius replies as Perdikkas shoves him. Hard. He doesn’t budge.

Mydei allows a faint smile, a brief show of humor. “We’re investigating,” he says, echoing Hephaestion, “and we’ll see what actions might be necessary.”

Hephaestion grins, and for a second, everything is the way it was a year ago: they’re in lockstep with each other, in perfect sync. Then Hephaestion’s eyes flicker to Phainon, and his grin falls. “You should send the slave to your quarters.”

If Hephaestion hadn’t spoken, Mydei almost certainly would’ve sent Phainon to their room in the Grove, but the presumption is one Mydei can’t leave unanswered. “No,” he says, stomping down his weariness. “No, he comes with us.”

“Your Highness,” Hephaestion begins.

“He comes with us,” Mydei says again, tone brooking no argument.

Thankfully, Hephaestion relents—Mydei has no desire to take action against his oldest friend.

Hephaestion turns away from Mydei and toward Anaxagoras. “Where is this, then? And how do we know you’re not leading our prince into a trap?”

“Trapping the immortal prince of Castrum Kremnos would only put the Grove—and by extension my research—in danger. I would do no such thing,” Anaxagoras replies, clearly offended. “The practicality of springing a trap that could hold him—tch.” He clicks his tongue. “Who are you? Who taught you?”

Hephaestion pulls himself up to his full height, just as offended.

“The black tide,” Mydei reminds them both. “If it is such an emergency, we shouldn’t wait.”

Mydei expects the black tide to be a few miles off from the Grove. But when Anaxagoras takes them to the hills beyond the city state, it’s closer than he imagined, all but licking at the roots of Cerces’s tree. He stands a few paces from the boundary, keenly aware of the monsters roaming the desiccated remains of the land, keenly aware that they’ve noticed him and his companions. There are far too many of those misshapen creatures approaching the boundary and on it in either direction, lingering there as though uncertain they can walk on fresh grass. But then they do, and the black tide creeps after them, a slow and inexorable wave of destruction.

“If the tide isn’t pushed back,” Anaxagoras says, “it will consume the Grove within a week.”

Mydei has no reason to mistrust that calculation, and it carves cold horror through him. The black tide has wiped out countless villages in its approach. Even from where he stands, he can see their distant remains. Worse, the black tide has destroyed fertile farmland and the people who can till it.

“We must call for the king,” Hephaestion says. “Urgently. He will need to push back the tide.”

Perdikkas steps forward. “I’ll go.”

But even Perdikkas can’t run the distance he needs to cover fast enough. The march that took them three days will take Perdikkas two, yes, except the greatest trial won’t be racing back to Castrum Kremnos. It will be convincing Eurypon to act. It will be convincing Eurypon to turn away from the front lines of his war with Okhema to view the second front of this conflict that he so stubbornly ignores.

Mydei rakes a hand through his hair.

“The monsters already test our defenses,” Anaxagoras says. “The tide may consume the Grove in a week, but the monsters at our walls will take us much sooner.”

“Do you have no warriors to defend you?” Leonnius asks.

A foolish question.

“All the able-bodied young men are on the frontlines,” Anaxagoras says in a tone as close to mockery as possible without crossing the line into outright treason.

“What about you?” Leonnius pushes.

Anaxagoras laughs. “I am but a feeble scholar.”

Mydei has his doubts about that. Anaxagoras doesn’t carry himself like a so-called feeble scholar.

“Why have you not evacuated?” Hephaestion demands. “Why stay here? And for that matter, why not send an emissary to Castrum Kremnos?”

“They did,” Mydei says. He looks over his shoulder where the others stand several feet back, as though even this is too close to the black tide. “The king ignored them.”

Hephaestion bristles. “How do you know?”

“I was there,” Mydei says, “when my father laughed the first one out of the room and jailed the second.” This is a battle his father isn’t interested in fighting. He chokes those words down; that’s a line he cannot cross. “The Grove didn’t send a third.”

“Not after we lost two of our best minds,” Anaxagoras agrees. He thinks better of this. “Perhaps two of our most adequate minds. In a time of intellectual drought, one takes what one can get.”

They have to take what they can get, too. Mydei regards the tide, far too close for comfort, and the monsters advancing on them at a slow, shuffling pace. “Hephaestion was right to ask. Why didn’t you evacuate?”

“And leave our research and all our knowledge behind?” Anaxagoras sounds aghast, as though Mydei has asked him to amputate his own hand.

“Surely you can take some of it,” Perdikkas says.

Anaxagoras scoffs. “Spoken like a man who doesn’t value the completeness of a thing. You ask us to pick and choose between our insights? What good is incomplete knowledge?”

“What good is the destruction of all knowledge?” Hephaestion fires back. “Take the most important pieces—”

“As if importance can be ascribed—”

“Enough,” Mydei says. “The black tide can be pushed back enough now that we can buy time for the Grove.” He turns to Anaxagoras. “In that time, you and the other Sages will organize your people to evacuate.”

“But—”

“Do you gainsay your prince?” Mydei asks, crossing his arms and dropping his voice. He doubts the threatening tone will have all that much impact on Anaxagoras, but it does shut him up for a moment. “The knowledge of the Grove will survive. The black tide corrupts people, not codices and scrolls, but without your people to interpret that information, it’s as good as useless. You will leave, you will flee to Castrum Kremnos, and I will make my father see reason and address the black tide here. For now, I can buy you time.”

All three of his somatophylakes speak at once, voices tumbling over each other in a harmony of protests. Phainon remains too quiet behind them all, his eyes focused with surprising intensity on Mydei.

Mydei holds up a gauntleted hand. “I am the only Chrysos Heir among us. My blood is enough to push the tide back, to buy you extra time.” He turns his attention back to Anaxagoras. “You will use it.”

Anaxagoras returns his gaze, his own thoughtful. He is, blissfully, silent, but his expression is otherwise inscrutable.

“Leonnius.”

Leonnius snaps a brisk salute. “My prince.”

“Left flank. Hephaestion, right. Perdikkas, return to the Grove and bring Peucesta and Ptolemy in case any of us are injured.” Neither are known for their battlefield prowess but underestimating them for their ancillary skills would be a mistake.

Perdikkas gives a quick salute before turning and racing away, his speed a truly remarkable thing.

“And me?” Anaxagoras asks.

“Stay out of the way,” Mydei replies, quite seriously, very certain that the so-called feeble scholar will almost certainly find a way to get himself involved in the fight. Only a fool wouldn’t have noticed the weapons concealed beneath his chiton, and Mydei isn’t a fool. “Keep an eye on my slave and ensure he comes to no harm.”

Phainon chokes, and it’s the most noise he’s made since they’ve exited the Grove.

Anaxagoras reels back. “Am I his master? Am I—”

“His keeper,” Mydei says. “Because I decree it, yes. You are.”

Anaxagoras looks furious. Phainon remains quiet, his expression still thoughtful, which disturbs Mydei on some fundamental level. Phainon has been too docile lately, too reserved. For now, though, that’s a boon.

“Stay here,” he tells them both, and he turns away.

The monsters have come closer, drawn by their conversation. Though not particularly quick, they are relentless things, driven by some strange urge to infect others as they have been infected. Already, Hephaestion and Leonnius have engaged the creatures on either flank, pushing them back with brutal cuts of their blades.

There is no glory in this. There is no honor. Mydei could twist the story and make it about protecting the people of the Grove, but that only puts in sharper relief the terrible truth: Castrum Kremnos failed the outlying

villages. Since the black tide’s first appearance, it has been Strife’s holy duty and most noble calling to beat it back, often aided by Chrysos Heirs vying to be Strife’s successor. Eurypon’s ascension changed all that.

Now, the black tide erodes everything that Eurypon gains, eating away at the back of their empire as he expands it at the front lines. Now, the black tide consumes their people, their farmlands. Mydei clenches his jaw. They can’t afford to lose more of their farmlands.

If there was a way to purify the people, perhaps this wouldn’t be so terrible. Oh, there would surely be a moral and ethical critique to be had, letting the citizens of the empire fall beneath the tide, but if they could be saved at a later date, maybe immediate sacrifices could be allowed. But they can’t. Once taken by the tide, a human is forever consumed, freed only, one hopes, in death. Thanatos has been silent on the subject.

Mydei draws his sword and steps forward, onto the surface of the black tide.

While his friends must fight at the borders of it, minding their feet so they don’t make contact with the reddish black substance, Mydei—and all the Chrysos Heirs—has no such concern. Whatever the black tide is, it can’t corrupt them the way it can the common man.

Turning his hand palm up, he draws his blade across his forearm just beneath the bend of his elbow and above the line of his gauntlet. Immortality hasn’t dulled pain for him. He hasn’t grown used to it. But he is better at hiding his discomfort than most men. Years of practice hiding his disdain for his father has, perhaps, sharpened the talent.

His blood drips from his arm and onto the surface of the black tide. Immediately, the monsters engaging his friends surge toward him.

Hephaestion and Leonnius are too good at what they do to let all the monsters escape them, but some do, and Mydei steps deeper onto the black tide to engage these strays. In the distance, other monsters howl with rage, and they begin racing toward Mydei as well, as though he is a disease that must be eradicated. Perhaps, to them, he is. Perhaps all Chrysos Heirs are.

The first creature to engage him loses its head. The second creature is gutted—or it would have been, had it had anything left in it resembling guts. It disintegrates despite the lack, dissolving into red and black nothingness.

As is always the case with the black tide’s monsters, the more he cuts down, the more appear before him. The death of their kin summons them, the destruction calling them from vast distances. Soon, he is surrounded on all sides, the monsters ignoring his friends to come for him. His blood is as much a lure as the death he deals out.

They reach for him without coordination, jamming their hands together as they grab at his wrists. He cuts through their limbs and then removes their heads, but he’s losing his maneuverability. More and more cluster around him, pressing in, pressing close, and though they don’t wield blades and can’t corrupt him, they have their own dangers. One gets its hand on his shoulder, and a strange buzzing vibrates through his brain. Another gouges its nails down his back. The first is trouble, the second a mere nuisance. His blood splatters on the ground, the black tide receding even more, and the creatures hiss and wail, dancing back with it.

Driving his elbow backwards, he dislodges the creature clinging to him. He whips around, slicing through the monster’s neck, and barely has the time to duck away from another that leaps for him.

Hephaestion and Leonnius call out code words that tell him they’re advancing in his direction. Good. He needs the support.

He grabs another creature by the face and throws it backwards into another large pack, causing them to stumble and buying himself some time.

Beneath his feet, the black tide retreats faster, as if desperate to escape his blood. And then the ground begins to shake.

Shit.

“Clear the rabble,” he shouts to his friends, and they do what they can on the border of the black tide, but the trouble is that Mydei has the attention

of every monster within half a mile. They converge on him as a hulking behemoth appears on the horizon, barreling toward him at an alarming speed.

Mydei cuts a path through the monsters even though that means putting them at his back. He trusts Hephaestion and Leonnius to defend him— though not even they know how dangerous a maneuver this is.

Racing ahead of the black tide’s retreat, Mydei readies his sword.

The behemoth roars, its form massive even at a distance. As it closes on him, it grows only larger, but he’s not particularly worried. Its legs carry it quickly, but it lacks agility. He drops, sliding across the slick, red surface of the tide as it brings down a meaty hand, pummeling the ground where he just stood.

Twisting to his feet, he launches himself forward, cutting his blade across the behemoth’s side. At the same time, he hazards a glance over its shoulder. A line of monsters has followed him, stranding Hephaestion and Leonnius at the edge of the tide. They’ve switched from swords to bows, and they’re picking off the stragglers with arrows through throats, but they’re not fast enough to make much of a difference.

Muttering an oath, Mydei swings around the behemoth as it twists, flailing to strike him. This has to be quick. Too long, and the other monsters will be on him, and then he’ll have too many battles to fight. With a twist of his blade, he ducks under a fist the size of a wine barrel. His sword meets the behemoth’s wrist, cutting deep—but not deep enough. While it roars with pain, its hand remains attached to its arm. Enraged, the behemoth sweeps both arms toward Mydei, stomping after him as he dances backwards, trying to lead it further away from his friends.

“Mydei!” Hephaestion shouts, frustration coloring his cry.

He hasn’t led the monsters out of bow range, so he ignores his friend. Hephaestion and Leonnius continue to pick off the more humanoid creatures, taking potshots where they can, as he weaves around the behemoth. It crashes after him, rushing toward him with a speed that

catches him by surprise. It’s all he can do to lift his sword as a makeshift shield. The behemoth crashes into it, driving Mydei backwards, toward the edge of the tide.

Better to be closer to the boundary, where his friends can use their swords if necessary.

Planting his left heel, Mydei swings around. The behemoth stumbles forward, losing its balance, and Mydei drives his blade into its side. Using his sword as a fulcrum, he launches himself up and onto its back, drawing a dagger from the sheath on his thigh. He drives the dagger into the behemoth’s back, anchoring himself, and yanks at his sword.

It sticks in the creature’s side.

Mydei clings to the dagger as the behemoth flails, reaching up to pound at its back, forcing Mydei to roll across it and dodge its gargantuan fists. One crashes down directly next to his head, and his heart hammers, chest hollowing. For a brief moment, he can’t breathe. But he doesn’t have time to panic or even feel relief that he’s not inconveniently dead. He throws himself across the creature’s back, grabs the hilt of his sword, and yanks.

The blade comes free with a shrill scream. Mydei hauls himself up, bracing one foot on his dagger. His balance is precarious, but he only needs one good hit—and he finds it, swinging his sword across the behemoth’s neck.

Its head tumbles from its shoulders, and then he’s falling the six feet to the ground to land awkwardly on his ankle. Pain reverberates through him, but not enough to suggest he’s broken anything. It’ll heal, anyway.

With the behemoth gone, the monsters break. They flee in every direction but toward the Grove, and Mydei turns his back to them once more, approaching his friends with an irritating limp but a smile on his face.

“And so we meet with success,” he says, sheathing his blade and spreading his arms wide.

Anaxagoras studies him, but Hephaestion has one hand over his face and Leonnius has dropped to lay on the ground, staring upward.

“Next time,” Hephaestion says, “don’t run where we can’t—”

There’s a hideous screech from behind him.

Mydei goes for his sword. Hephaestion slings his bow back around, Leonnius rocks to his feet, but it’s Phainon who moves fastest. He has one of Anaxagoras’s knives in his hand, is yanking Mydei forward, is driving the dagger’s blade into the monster’s chest, right where its heart should be.

Everything hangs, suspended in a strange, liminal moment.

And then Mydei’s sword finishes the job Phainon began, cutting across the monster’s neck to sever its head. The creature pulses with red light as it crumbles in blackish cubes, disappearing into so much aether.

Phainon drops the knife and all but leaps back from it, his hands raised. Leonnius is already on him, grabbing his wrists, yanking them back. “I just reacted,” Phainon says, a wild look on his face.

Mydei lowers his sword, sheathing it as he and Hephaestion trade a knowing look. That was a swordsman’s speed and instinct.

“He saved my life,” Mydei says to Leonnius.

Hephaestion retrieves Anaxagoras’s knife, handing it back to the scholar, who takes it with a strange expression on his face, as though he can’t quite believe any of what he just saw.

There’s no resistance in Phainon as Leonnius pulls his arms behind his back. “A slave who wields a blade should be put to death,” Leonnius says.

Phainon’s wild look grows wilder, almost terrified. “I didn’t know,” he rasps.

“Did he wield a blade?” Mydei asks Leonnius. “I saw only my sword in the monster’s neck.” He is asking Leonnius to lie for him—asking every man

present to agree to his lie—but he is the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos.

Hephaestion doesn’t hesitate. He bows his head. “I saw only our prince’s strike,” he says, though his tone is tight, begrudging.

Leonnius looks from Mydei to Hephaestion and back again, bewildered for only a moment before understanding what Mydei is intimating. He presses his lips together in a thin line. Of all Mydei’s somatophylakes, he is most likely to refuse to accept the lie. But he, too, inclines his head. “It is as my prince says.” He releases Phainon and steps back. “No slave could move so quickly or strike so true.”

That’s a warning, and Mydei would be a fool not to hear it. He gives Leonnius a nod of acknowledgement before turning to Anaxagoras.

Anaxagoras sweeps his eyes over all of them. “Interesting.” He tucks his blade back into his chiton. “You are an interesting man, Your Highness.”

That’s a warning, too, though Mydei doesn’t understand it quite as well. “Am I?”

“A prince of Castrum Kremnos who defends a slave, who fights back the black tide with his own blood.” Anaxagoras makes a thoughtful sound. “How uncommon.”

Mydei’s lips twitch. “Anyone would have done the same.”

“No,” Anaxagoras drawls. “No, anyone would not have, as we discussed earlier.” Mydei stiffens. “And if Chrysos Heirs alone could push back the black tide, perhaps we would not be in so much danger.”

“Are you suggesting there are Chrysos Heirs secreted away in the Grove?” Mydei asks sharply, eager to change the course of the conversation.

Anaxagoras’s smile is almost feral. “Of course not, Your Highness. Harboring Chrysos Heirs would be treasonous, and we are, all of us, loyal citizens.”

Anxiety claws through Phainon as he and Mydeimos make their way back to the prince’s apartment in the Grove, flanked by a pair of legionnaires and those two somatophylakes, Hephaestion and Leonnius. Both regard him with outright suspicion.

He really did fuck up earlier, and he can’t figure out why Mydeimos didn’t kill him on the spot. Leonnius’s words—a slave who wields a blade should be put to death—circle in Phainon’s mind, a song trapped in the cage of his skull, relentlessly badgering him with the stark truth. He’s going to die. Mydeimos has to kill him. There’s no way Leonnius and Hephaestion will stay silent. Rumors will circulate, and they’ll force Mydeimos’s hand, and then Phainon will have failed.

But when Mydeimos reaches the door to his apartment, neither somatophylax says anything about Mydeimos keeping a dangerous slave with him when he’s alone. They salute him alongside the legionnaires and depart, leaving Phainon and Mydeimos alone.

Mydeimos shuts the apartment’s door behind them both.

Expectation weighs heavily on Phainon’s shoulders. He should speak. Should defend himself. But what is there to say? He betrayed his skill to save Mydeimos’s life, and he still doesn’t know why he did it. Ultimately, Mydeimos wouldn’t have stayed dead. But he saw a man in peril, and he simply reacted. He followed his instinct to protect. And that instinct will surely see him dead.

“I…” He turns to Mydeimos.

“Death is unpleasant to recover from,” Mydeimos says, stepping away from the door and into the apartment. It’s warm and cozy, much smaller than his suite in Castrum Kremnos, with walls made of wood. So late after the feast the Sages prepared for them, darkness blots out the details of Mydeimos’s face and blurs the edges of the room.

Candles aren’t permitted in the Grove.

“So, in that way, I owe you my life,” Mydeimos continues. “Which makes you profoundly lucky.” Phainon pulls a hand over his face, still certain that Mydeimos is about to name him a dead man. “A life for a life, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

His legs feel like water. Feeling blindly behind him, he finds a kline, and he sinks onto it. He’s shaking and lightheaded, his vision, what little he has, tunneling in the darkness of the room. “You’re not going to kill me?”

“No.”

“Because I saved… Because I prevented you from having to come back from death.” This feels surreal.

“Because I saw your feet, Phainon,” Mydeimos says.

Oh. Oh, fuck, that’s even worse. He hasn’t betrayed his skill with a sword and marked himself a dangerous man, he’s betrayed his identity.

“I saw where you stood.”

He remembers his stance with frightening clarity, one sandaled foot on soft grass, one on the slick, red-black substance of the black tide.

Phainon has been through hell. He watched his friends and family cut down and slaughtered by Eurypon’s army, heard the screams of the dying left in the streets, saw heads trampled beneath horse’s hooves. And yet the terror of that day has faded so much that it cannot compare to his fear in this moment.

“Killing you would be a tremendous inconvenience,” Mydeimos says.

“Your father.” Phainon clasps his trembling hands. “He’ll kill you if you kill me.” Phainon’s blood will mark Mydeimos a traitor.

“Yes.”

“You’d come back.”

Mydeimos tips his head to the side. “Have you ever drowned, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae?” he asks softly. Phainon’s eyes widen. “I have. Ten times, chained to a boulder beneath the water of a palace pond. I was five.”

Phainon shudders, unable to imagine it. The horror of his life leaving him. The terrifying knowledge he’d come back to same, miserable extinction. “Then this is self-serving.” He’s never been so grateful for someone else’s sense of self-preservation.

Mydeimos exhales. “Not entirely.” He stands in front of Phainon, close enough that Phainon can make out his features but not his expression. “I am tired of death.”

How telling. Mydeimos isn’t tired of dying. He’s tired of death.

“Two counts of treason,” Phainon says quietly.

“It could just be one. The forests to the south are dense and dangerous, but someone like you…” Mydeimos trails off.

Someone like Phainon, a trained fighter and a Chrysos Heir, wouldn’t struggle to survive. He could slink off in the night, find a way to remove the torc from his throat, or even make his way back to Okhema. But to leave would be to betray his people and the memory of Aedes Elysiae. “The black tide,” Phainon offers in meager protest. “It’s in the forest, too.”

“By virtue of your blood, you will be fine.”

Phainon isn’t so sure of that. He’s bled all over the black tide before, and it’s never retreated for him the way it did for Mydeimos. “Do you really believe that, son of Strife?”

Even in the darkness, Phainon sees the grimace twist Mydeimos’s lips. “Strife’s meager protection isn’t all that holds back the black tide.”

Another thing Phainon isn’t sure of. From all the stories he’s heard, of all the Titans, only Strife is strong enough to stand against the tide. “Leaving would condemn me,” Phainon says, almost reluctantly. “I can’t go.”

Mydeimos’s lips twist even more, sardonic but not cruel. “Because of what my mother has you up to.”

Shaking his head, Phainon looks away. “It’s not that.” And then he huffs out a dry sort of laugh. “I’d like to see the world one day, you know. Explore what’s beyond the city states of Amphoreus. Supposedly, there are other continents. It’d be nice to see them. But…” He looks at his hands. “I can’t.”

“You’re not alone in that,” Mydeimos says softly, like he’s giving up a secret. “There is a whole world beyond us, and what we see, what we live in, is only a small part of it.” What an unexpected sentiment from the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos. “Watching the whole of our world crumble into Castrum Kremnos’s shadow…” Regret tinges his voice.

They’ve come close to treason several times already, but this is the closest brush, and it catches Phainon by surprise. “You,” he says, lifting his face to regard Mydeimos in the darkness, “aren’t what I expected.”

Mydeimos snorts. “A brute?”

“Something like that.” Telling Mydeimos what he really expected probably won’t get him killed, especially based on the conversation they just had, but Phainon doesn’t want to risk his current good favor. A brute, a tyrant like his father, a bloodthirsty madman. Okhema has many rumors about Mydeimos, and all of them are wildly misinformed.

“Not everyone agrees with what Castrum Kremnos has become,” Mydeimos says. “But to discuss such things outright would be to court treason.”

Phainon swallows. Eurypon’s message to his son was couched in theatrics, but Phainon understands it now. Understands Mydeimos better now. “You’re a better person when you do,” Phainon says carefully.

Mydeimos inhales sharply. He’s so close, having drifted into Phainon’s space as they’ve talked, that Phainon can feel the warmth of him. “A strange sentiment from you,” Mydeimos says, lifting his hand. His fingers ghost along Phainon’s jaw, and Phainon shivers with heat.

“An honest one.” He forces himself to stay relaxed, fighting not to turn his head into Mydeimos’s touch.

“Have you been dishonest with me?” Mydeimos asks.

Yes. Titans, yes, he’s been so dishonest. But there’s only one safe answer to that question. “I’ve never lied to you,” Phainon replies, and he hasn’t. He just hasn’t always told the truth, either.

Mydeimos’s hand smooths over Phainon’s jaw, and Phainon doesn’t pull away. Mydeimos is trapped, playing a political game with his father that runs counter to his nature just to survive. “You truly are my mother’s creature,” Mydeimos says with a quiet laugh, but he doesn’t sound angry or upset.

Slowly, Mydeimos leans toward Phainon, and Phainon, despite himself, doesn’t pull away. He tips his head up, anticipation a sweet drug curling through his veins.

Mydeimos kisses him, a barely there touching of their lips, their eyes open and fixed on each other. Staring someone down like this should be strange and awkward, but it’s not. Phainon shifts forward, pressing his mouth firmly against Mydeimos’s own.

The Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos isn’t a brute, isn’t a mindless soldier, isn’t his father’s loyal lackey. He is trapped, as Phainon is trapped.

Mydeimos’s fingers slide deeper into Phainon’s hair. His eyes drift shut, and his mouth moves against Phainon’s own, a lingering but hesitant caress. And then he’s drawing back, dropping his hand and stepping away, his face turned to the side.

“Forgive me,” Mydeimos says. “I should not have forced myself on you.”

Dazed, confused, Phainon stares up at him. “You—”

“Good night, Phainon,” Mydeimos says, and he hurries away, deeper into the apartment, leaving Phainon sitting on the kline, shaken.

He didn’t dislike that kiss. He doesn’t dislike Mydeimos. He—he drags a hand down his face. He can’t let Mydeimos be too human, too real, too relatable. Phainon has a purpose here, and it isn’t to lust after his captor.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 5
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

“No Chrysos Heirs?”

There’s nothing good about that question, nothing good about the disbelief in Eurypon’s tone.

Mydei remains expressionless, a soldier reporting to his commanding officer, not a son speaking to his father. “Not a single one, Your Majesty.” He stands at the far end of a long table in Eurypon’s council room, meeting his father’s gaze and ignoring those of his father’s generals. The generals share glances between them, most echoing Eurypon’s disbelief, not a single original thought among them. But it’s better to fall in line with the king.

“I find that hard to believe,” Eurypon says, folding his hands together. He leans forward. “Did you check every home?”

Mydei knows better than to vociferously defend his men against the implied slight. “We did.” He extends one hand, and Hephaestion steps forward, laying a scroll across his palm. “The details are here, should Your Majesty wish to review them.” Eurypon will. He’ll pour over the scroll for hours, will probably summon Mydei back to him in private and berate him for not finding what Eurypon expected him to find.

“Themistocles,” Eurypon says, and Mydei passes the scroll to the nearest general, who in turn passes it up the table to Themistocles.

Sober, the man is canny and terrifying, crafting the strategies that have seen Castrum Kremnos crush Amphoreus beneath the gears of its war machine. Themistocles opens the scroll, eyes scanning back and forth across it.

“Rats,” Eurypon says, his gaze fixed on Mydei, “are insidious. They breed ceaselessly and infect every home with their presence. How did you find

nothing, boy?”

Mydei keeps his expression as neutral as he can. “The people of the Grove are far more concerned with the approach of the black tide.”

A groan goes up from the table, the generals rolling their eyes and scoffing —and throwing quick glances at the king to ensure their reaction is the correct one. Eurypon snorts, chuckles, and then outright laughs, leaning back in his kline.

“The black tide? A passing distraction,” Eurypon declares. His generals agree with him.

Mydei remains where he is, still and disaffected by their laughter, sorting through the various arguments he can present to his father. None of them are particularly promising, but he gave Anaxagoras and the other Sages his word. He will try to sway his father’s opinion.

“When we arrived, it was licking at the Grove’s walls,” Mydei says. Facts won’t matter. He needs to appeal to Eurypon’s paranoia without suggesting the Grove may be hiding Chrysos Heirs capable of pushing back the black tide.

Strange, though, that Phainon behaved as if such a thing isn’t possible.

“Monsters prowled the fields beyond the Grove,” Mydei continues. “According to the Sages, they make regular incursions against the city state.”

Eurypon waves a dismissive hand before reaching for his wine. “This is a problem for the Grove to solve,” he says.

Until Eurypon ascended to Titanhood and took up Strife’s coreflame, the histories are quite clear: Nikador regularly battered the black tide back from civilization.

“If the Grove falls to the black tide, we will lose our most brilliant minds,” Mydei says, testing one of his arguments.

“As if we need an educated citizenry,” Themistocles says, and the generals rumble their agreement.

Eurypon pushes himself upright and leans to the side, slapping Themistocles on the shoulder.

That had always been a losing argument, but Mydei had wanted to start with it in some vain hope that, perhaps, his father would understand the dangers of an ignorant citizenry. But for a country at war, smart men are an inconvenience. Smart men question their leaders while fools fall in line.

He tries again. “With the fields subsumed by the tide, our food stores are decreasing. If we wish to keep our troops fed, we should not overlook the damage the tide is doing.”

Again, Eurypon waves him off. “The black tide is nothing more than Okheman trickery,” he says.

Mydei takes a deep, calming breath and says nothing.

“They have used it—Kephale has used it—throughout time to occupy the kings and Titans of Castrum Kremnos, forcing us to play defense on their behalf. When they are gone,” Eurypon says, “the black tide will go with them.”

It is an alarming thing when the king of an empire believes his own propaganda so thoroughly. Perhaps if his generals weren’t seated with him, Eurypon would be more honest, but Mydei doubts that. Eurypon has always sought refuge in his own lies. This lie, however, will lead to too many deaths, will see not just the farmlands destroyed and the farmers transformed into monsters, but Castrum Kremnos’s army starved.

“The writings of Herodotus tell us the tide existed before Okhema was founded,” Mydei says, keeping his tone neutral.

Eurypon slams his goblet on the table, spilling wine over his scrolls and his maps. The generals all fall silent, recoiling. Mydei has pushed his father too far, even though he has barely pushed at all.

He bows his head. “Forgive me, Father, I—”

“Do you think me an ignorant fool?” Eurypon demands. “Do you think I don’t see what you’re trying to do, boy?”

Dread curls down Mydei’s spine, puncturing him with icy fingers. Eurypon’s temper is always mercurial. He should have kept silent.

“You are no better than the Okhemans, are you?” Eurypon rises to his feet, bracing his hands against the table and leaning over it. His blood-red wine pools at his fingertips, staining them. “I will not have my attentions split between the front lines and an old wives’ tale used to scare children into behaving.” Eurypon laughs, cruelly.

A few of the generals laugh, too.

“The black tide’s monsters will steal you away if you don’t behave.” Eurypon’s voice drips with mocking derision. “Are you so terrified of legends?”

Mydei says nothing. Feels nothing. Not even the earlier dread remains. He is empty, a void, and his father’s mockery washes over him without affecting him. But Eurypon demands a reaction.

“Did I raise a coward?” the king demands. “Did I raise a son who is afraid of his own shadow? Did I allow you to be coddled by that insubordinate creature the lot of you dare to call my queen?” The room is completely silent as Eurypon leans over the table, snarling at Mydei.

Though Mydei’s heart hammers, he remains outwardly calm and keeps himself that empty void. He allows himself no rage, no fury on his mother’s behalf. “No, Your Majesty,” he says, keenly aware that failure to manage his father here will see him tied to a stake in the great hall. Some would think Eurypon’s threats empty, but Mydei isn’t a fool. Eurypon will wring every drop of use out of Mydei and then, when Mydei is more a danger than useful boon, Eurypon will find a way to kill him, immortality be damned. He prefers not to hasten his own end—or to experience it over and over as Eurypon tries and fails.

“Then why do you waste my time with legends?” Eurypon demands. “Why do you bother my generals with such preposterous drivel when we are at war? Do you mean to undermine us, to split our forces?” Eurypon points at him, finger shaking. “Is my own son a traitor in my home?”

A cold sweat gathers on Mydei’s skin. “I am loyal to the crown and Castrum Kremnos,” Mydei says. “And I obey my king in all things.”

“And yet you fail to bring me the Chrysos Heirs hidden in the Grove!” Spittle flies from Eurypon’s mouth. “A disgrace! My own son is a disgrace!” Those words no longer hurt him. Mydei bows his head lower and says nothing. “A failure.” Eurypon sucks his teeth, derisive. “Get out.”

Mydei does not hesitate. He bows, deeply respectful, and flees the room, Hephaestion wisely close behind.

As soon as the door to the war council closes, Hephaestion reaches for him. “Your Highness—”

But there are guards outside the doors, and Mydei will show the court nothing of weakness or affection, whatever lingers between him and Hephaestion still. “No,” he says, cutting Hephaestion a warning look. Hephaestion should know better.

Chastened, Hephaestion drops his hands.

They begin down the hall, side by side, and Hephaestion drops his voice. “That could have gone much better.”

“We could be dead,” Mydei says. “But, yes, it could have.” Eurypon rarely descends into a rage so terrible he blackens Gorgo’s name. When he does, the situation is dire. Mydei rubs a hand over his chest.

“Even Ptolemy has said it,” Hephaestion murmurs. “Statistically, there should have been several Chrysos Heirs. That there wasn’t even one…”

Mydei grimaces. He isn’t a fool, he understands Ptolemy’s numbers well enough, but what frightens him most is that there was a Chrysos Heir. They

are, all of them, lucky that no one else noticed Phainon’s status as one. “And are we to condemn men for the status of their birth?” Mydei asks.

Hephaestion grimaces. “I understand this is a sensitive thing for you.”

“Sensitive. Yes. You might say that.”

“You are different,” Hephaestion says.

Revulsion heaves in Mydei’s belly. “Enough, Hephaestion. We survived my father, and I upheld my oath to Anaxagoras.” He sighs, weary. “I would like to rest.” He is drained and exhausted.

Hephaestion smiles broadly. “Come rest with me.” Mydei’s expression must slip, because he adds, quickly, “And the others. Peucesta can play something to calm your nerves. We can enjoy wine, and—”

“I would like to be alone,” Mydei says, turning away from Hephaestion at the intersection that will bring Mydei to his rooms. “Understand this.” He draws away from Hephaestion, and Hephaestion, thank the Titans, does not follow. Mydei doesn’t look back, doesn’t want to see the grief on Hephaestion’s face. Doesn’t want to be the reason for it yet again.

Something on his face must turn away his own servants. They don’t approach him when he enters his suite. He spares a glance for Phainon and eventually spies him beyond a window, in the shade of the courtyard’s strawberry trees. If Phainon were truly his bed slave, Mydei might call him in. Might lose himself in the pleasure of someone else’s body. But Mydei wasn’t lying to Hephaestion. He doesn’t want to trouble himself with complicated company.

He sinks onto his bed, bundling a pillow in his arms and pressing his face into it.

There’s only so long Phainon can avoid Mydeimos’s bedroom. He’s done his best to occupy himself in the courtyard, but now the sun is low on the horizon, and he’s not just tired, he’s hungry. The servants in Mydeimos’s

household can eat whenever they want, but he’s only afforded the scraps from Mydeimos’s plate. Whatever supposed benefits come with being a bed slave are surely offset by all these terrible, humiliating rules.

At last, with a gnawing pain in his stomach, Phainon climbs the three steps into Mydeimos’s bedroom.

A low groan issues from Mydeimos’s bed. Phainon stills, peering through the growing darkness, wondering if Mydeimos is, perhaps, not alone. But no, there’s only one Mydeimos-shaped lump on the bed, and that groan isn’t a pleasurable one. It’s distress.

Phainon crosses the room without any attempt at stealth. His sandaled feet slap against the marbled floor, but Mydeimos doesn’t stir, not even when Phainon sits on the edge of the bed. He hesitates and then touches Mydeimos’s shoulder.

Mydeimos surges upward, one hand wrapped around Phainon’s throat. Phainon gasps, grabbing at Mydeimos’s wrist, and finds himself on his back before he can react any further.

“Phainon?”

“Yes,” he gasps out, squeezing Mydeimos’s wrist.

Mydeimos releases him and pulls away, pressing his face into his hand. “I don’t do well when startled awake,” he says.

“Obviously.” Phainon pushes himself up, folding his legs to sit across from Mydeimos on the bed, and he wonders at how Mydeimos has lived to react so violently to someone waking him. An immortal man need fear no assassin, but Phainon supposes pain is still unpleasant and assassins remain an inconvenience. “You were having a nightmare.”

“Yes.” Mydeimos lowers his hand. In the darkness, his expression is impossible to discern. “I…” He shudders.

Phainon leans toward him. “I’ve always found talking about it helps.”

“I am not a child in need of comfort.”

And Phainon leans back. “Never said you were,” he says, rebuffed.

Exhaling heavily, Mydeimos tips his head to the side, regarding Phainon. “It was the black tide.” He falls silent, and Phainon realizes he’s expecting mockery, derision, contempt. This is a man who has learned that any vulnerability is met with cruelty.

Phainon stays quiet, expecting that any comforting gesture will shut Mydeimos down.

Abruptly, Mydeimos continues. “I was drowning in it.” He turns his face to the bed, staring at the sheets. “It was all around me, a living thing, consuming me. A lake of it, an ocean of it.” He shudders. “When I kicked toward the surface, the monsters pulled me back down. I couldn’t breathe.” Absently, he rubs his chest. “It was just like…” His voice trembles. “It was so real.” He sags. “Even now, my chest burns.”

They’re not close enough for this. Mydeimos knows one of Phainon’s secrets, but they’re not intimate. They’re not even friends. “Your somatophylakes,” he begins.

“No,” Mydeimos says, and then he laughs bitterly. “Such friends as those will only poke fun at my weakness. The mighty crown prince of Castrum Kremnos, disturbed by a mere dream of drowning?” He shakes his head.

“Here,” Phainon says, setting the towel on Mydeimos’s stomach and rubbing him clean. “Maybe now Your Highness will sleep soundly.”

Mydeimos makes an irritated little sound. “My prince,” he says. “Your Highness.” He drops his arm, and the clouds outside part, allowing a sliver of silver moonlight to spill across his face. “When we are alone, you should call me Mydeimos.”

“Mydeimos,” Phainon says, and this, he thinks, is the better prize than the prince’s body. This is the prince’s trust.
