Chapter Notes

as in chapter 3, this chapter features some potentially triggering, but not graphically described, violence. if you're worried and want more details, click the additional warning below

additional warning

Sweat drips down Mydei’s back. Above him, the sun hammers down mercilessly, but heat isn’t a reason to forgo practice. He’s on the training pitch with his century, working with one of his centurions, a back-and-forth dance of spears. They circle each other carefully, each studying the other, looking for openings. Mydei has gone out of his way to ensure his century is home to some of the best men in his father’s army, which certainly hasn’t gone unnoticed. No, it’s another reason for Eurypon’s unrelenting suspicions.

Mydei feints right, lunging forward. The centurion, a young man named Drakon, ignores the feint and meets him blow for blow. They dance across the training field, testing each other rather than trying to launch believable attacks; this is more about reaction times than it is trying to win the bout.

A flurry of activity to the side of the pitch draws Mydei’s attention, and he just barely steps out of the way of a brutal thrust. Knocking the spear tip away from his throat, he sidesteps and holds up a hand. “Hold,” he says, and Drakon immediately bows back.

Leonnius stands on the side of the pitch, engaged in quiet but furious conversation with Hephaestion, whose stormy expression threatens thunderous wrath.

An uneasy feeling crawls across Mydei’s back. He trots over to them as Hephaestion says, “His Highness needn’t be bothered with—Mydei. This

isn’t important.” Unfortunately, those words betray Hephaestion. Whatever’s going on is almost certainly important.

“I can judge that for myself,” Mydei says, turning to Leonnius. “What tidings, then?”

“Phainon,” Leonnius says, and the ground beneath Mydei’s feet rolls. There are precious few reasons Leonnius would come running about Phainon, and none of them are good. His mother must have— “Krateros found him trying to escape over one of the back walls.”

Mydei’s blood runs cold. He isn’t surprised, though he is a little annoyed. Mostly, though, he is afraid. “Periander?” he asks.

“Mydei,” Hephaestion says as Leonnius nods. “Mydei, he’s a slave and your mother’s spy. There’s no reason—”

But Mydei has already tossed his spear to the quartermaster and set off at a brisk pace. Sweat drips down his skin and sand cakes his frame. He probably looks frightful. Good. He’ll need all the presence he can muster to cow Periander before the slave master brings his whip down on Phainon’s back. And then he will need to understand why Phainon was trying to sneak over the back of the palace instead of simply arranging a meeting with one of Gorgo’s contacts inside the walls.

Scrubbing a hand over his face, he hurries through the palace’s halls, vaguely aware of Hephaestion and Leonnius at his back. Hephaestion has given up calling for his attention; Leonnius, meanwhile, is a quiet shadow trailing behind him. An ache grows behind his eyes, a throbbing that zings along his scalp to the base of his skull. Trouble. Gorgo’s agents are always so much trouble, and he wouldn’t be so bothered if Phainon wasn’t also a Chrysos Heir. No one deserves to die the way Eurypon executes Chrysos Heirs. No one.

Mydei is so tired of watching people die.

The slave quarters open onto a large, sandy courtyard, and it’s there that Mydei goes. He steps onto the sand, unsurprised to find Phainon bound to a

whipping post already. There’s a small crowd, because of course there is, a smattering of citizens and senators, a general. His own father. Eurypon stands at the edge of a covered balcony, looking down from the second story of the palace, his expression shadowed. There’s no sign of Gorgo. Unsurprising. She’s never tolerated mistakes from her agents, instead choosing to let the Titans decide their fates.

With Eurypon overlooking the courtyard, there’s no way this won’t be a spectacle. A muscle twitches in Mydei’s jaw, an irritating flex.

Periander stands over Phainon, a scourge in hand. He is a thick man, with broad shoulders and a full beard, handsome and, generally, congenial— except when it comes to his slaves. There, his humor dies, and he is a heartless, ruthless master, quick to punish with the most brutal tools.

Mydei spares a quick glance for Phainon, who has a white-knuckled grip on his restraints. He stares ahead of himself, jaw set, and doesn’t acknowledge Mydei at all.

“Periander,” Mydei says, quickly organizing his thoughts. Periander is never swayed by emotion, only by practicality; the law is his most powerful weapon. “What right have you to harm my property?” His stomach curdles with disgust.

Phainon doesn’t move, doesn’t turn his head, barely even breathes.

Periander turns toward Mydei with a sweeping bow, perfectly polite in every way. “Your Highness!” His dark eyes flick to Leonnius over Mydei’s shoulder, and his expression falters if only for a moment.

Oh, but he’s been waiting for an opportunity like this, a chance to exert his power of Mydei’s household, but Mydei has never owned a slave and so Periander has never had the chance.

A charming smile pulls across Periander’s face as he rises from his bow. “I mean only to assist Your Highness,” he says, “as it has never been the prince’s pleasure to punish an errant slave. Perhaps his arm would grow tired before the required fifty strikes.”

Fifty? Hell. “It is mine and my household’s business,” Mydei says, casting a brief glance toward his father. “Not yours.”

Periander taps the scourge into his open palm. “An escaping slave is certainly my business,” he says cheerfully. “We must laud Krateros for his keen eyes, no?”

“Of course,” Mydei says, his expression tight but pleasantly polite. “I would still manage my slave and my household.”

“It would not do,” Periander all but purrs, “if the prince were to do nothing.” They all know Mydei is a soft touch with his staff. They all know he abhors the practice of slavery. They all know he’s maneuvering to get Phainon released without punishment at all. Even one strike of a Kremnoan scourge is too many. “If a slave attempts escape and is not reprimanded, others may mistake us as soft. Weak.” His congenial smile turns sharp, malicious. “But our prince is not weak.”

The vultures in the open halls surrounding the courtyard lean in.

Hell. Any other slaveowner would take the whip from Periander’s hand and mete out punishment himself, but if Mydei does that, Phainon burns. There is the principle of the thing—Phainon doesn’t deserve to burn, not even if he was attempting to escape—and something deeper that Mydei doesn’t have the time to examine closer.

Phainon cannot, should not burn. Not for this.

He must think like his mother. Gorgo would come at this from the side, stepping around the issue of punishing her slave entirely, nimbly twisting the situation to her advantage while maintaining her position. But Gorgo is cleverer than Mydei; he may be her son, but he doesn’t see the world the way she does. He suppresses a grimace. He sees one path forward where his mother would surely see several. It’s an unpleasant path, but he has no time to outsmart the whole of society.

“No,” Mydei agrees. “No, I am not.” At least this path will reinforce that truth: that Mydei isn’t weak. “A slave is a reflection of his master, isn’t he?”

Periander chuckles. “Are we to engage in philosophy, Your Highness?”

“When a slave acts, he does so on his master’s behalf,” Mydei continues, ignoring the question. “He acts with his master’s authority. His mistakes are his master’s.” A few of the vultures have drifted closer still. Eurypon himself leans over the balustrade, still in too much shadow for Mydei to make out his expression. He’s sure it’s feral with delight. Eurypon isn’t stupid; he’s almost certainly realized what the other vultures have. “Is that not true, Periander? Are a slave’s actions not a proxy for his master?”

Periander’s smile has slipped. “This is true,” he says slowly. He hasn’t caught up to Mydei’s circuitous logic.

A sharp inhalation from behind tells him that Hephaestion has, but Hephaestion is, in this at least, too smart to speak.

“Then I am guilty of my slave’s mistakes, and it is as fitting to punish me,” Mydei says, closing his trap around Periander, “as it is to punish him.”

The courtyard is hushed, and Periander is no longer smiling. He glances toward Eurypon, clearly ill at ease, before saying, “Certainly, I could not punish the crown prince for a slave’s indiscretion.”

But he could. There is precedent for it. “Has my mother not taken blows meant for me?” Mydei asks softly. Periander’s face pales. “Did Homeros not accept strikes meant for Kyrillos?” The two are borderline mythical, heroes from an age long past. Homeros took a beating meant for his slave, and his slave won a major battle in one of the myriad Chrysos Wars.

“I would not presume—”

Eurypon lifts his hand, and the entire courtyard’s attention shifts to him. Mydei, too, studies his father, his face lit just enough for his expression to be clear. Amusement. Delight. “Who are you, Periander, to argue with the Crown Prince?” Eurypon asks mildly.

That’s all it takes for the tenor in the courtyard to change. Periander is all smiles once more, and the onlookers buzz with excitement.

“As the king says.” Periander gives Mydei a mocking bow.

Many times throughout his life, Mydei has mocked Periander in turn. His staunch refusal to accept slaves from beneath Periander’s thumb has destroyed any equanimity between them. Periander has loathed Mydei for a decade.

Ignoring Periander, Mydei turns to a pair of nearby slaves. “Free my slave,” he says. He ignores Phainon, too, who is now staring at him with a mix of disbelief and horror—and bald understanding. Mydei has no idea if Phainon had reckoned with his own death, but he can only imagine the sudden change in outlook has shaken him.

As soon as Phainon is freed, Mydei beckons Leonnius forward. “Take him back to my rooms.”

Leonnius gives a curt nod.

Phainon, of course, doesn’t intuit the unspoken command. “What are you doing?” he hisses, approaching Mydei directly.

This man. This impossible man will get himself killed. “You walk a dangerous line,” Mydei replies, taking Phainon by the upper arm and yanking him close. Quieter, in his ear, he murmurs, “Do not make this worse for me. I have saved your life as you did mine. Go with Leonnius. Behave, just this once, for both our sakes.” He squeezes hard on Phainon’s bicep.

Phainon meets his eyes, but, thankfully, only briefly. He bows his head. “Yes, my prince.”

Mydei releases him, giving Leonnius a meaningful look.

Irritation and disdain flicker across Leonnius’s face as he places his hand between Phainon’s shoulder blades and shoves. “Move, slave,” he says.

“No.” Once more, every head in the courtyard turns to Eurypon. “How will the slave learn his lesson if he doesn’t watch?” Eurypon gestures Leonnius

and Phainon toward the side of the courtyard. “He stays.”

This isn’t ideal. Mydei doesn’t want Phainon anywhere near his father. Doesn’t want Phainon anywhere near the courtyard. The longer Phainon is here, the more likely he is to make a mistake, and then all of this will be for nothing. But no one will gainsay the king.

Leonnius jerks Phainon to the side of the courtyard, taking up a post there, holding Phainon by the upper arm. Hephaestion joins them, stone-faced. Disappointment flashes in his eyes when he looks on Mydei, but it barely matters. Mydei cares about Hephaestion, yes, but his ego is independent of Hephaestion’s judgement. It has been for months, now.

Rolling his shoulders back, Mydei approaches the post meant for Phainon. Fifty strokes. He’ll probably die once. “Get on with it, then,” he says, gripping the circumference of it. He forces himself to relax, and he waits.

This is a farce. It has to be. There’s no way the slave master of Castrum Kremnos will whip his crown prince in a public courtyard while the king watches. And Mydeimos—sure, Phainon saved his life in the Grove, but Mydeimos allowing himself to be whipped in Phainon’s place is almost unthinkable. Phainon understands the alternative. He understands that if Periander whips him, his gold blood will give him away and then he’ll burn. But Mydeimos can’t possibly value him so much to take these hits on Phainon’s behalf.

At any moment, this whole circus will surely collapse in on itself, and Phainon, standing between Hephaestion and Leonnius, waits for it.

Periander turns to Mydeimos as Phainon waits.

Periander raises his whip as Phainon waits—and a chill goes down Phainon’s spine.

No one has bound Mydeimos to the whipping post. No one has moved. The king leans over the balustrade casually. The citizens stand in the shadows, still and silent. Someone, he thinks, will say something.

Periander’s arm is fully raised. He stands ready for one second, two.

Someone will say something. These two somatophylakes on either side of him. The one who caught him, who brought him here, who all but worships the ground Mydeimos walks on. Hell, the king himself. Surely the king will burst out laughing and declare this all a joke at—

The whip cracks across Mydeimos’s back.

Now. Now someone will speak up. Surely this is all for show and the actors have all played their parts.

Again, the whip cracks across Mydeimos’s back, and the metal bits on the end of the leather tassels draw golden blood.

“Periander,” the king says, and Phainon sags with relief as the slave master turns toward Eurypon. “Put your back into it.”

Bile rises in the back of Phainon’s throat. His head jerks from Eurypon to Leonnius and then Hephaestion, but their faces are blank. They stare straight ahead, neither looking at either their king or their prince. They are —they cannot be cowards, not if they’re the prince’s somatophylakes, but Phainon can’t help but think them so.

Another crack of the whip, and Phainon forces his eyes back to Mydeimos, who clings to the whipping post but has yet to make a single noise.

He can’t do anything. He’s powerless. He has been powerless for weeks, yes, but standing to the side as Periander strips the skin off Mydeimos’s back drives that home for him. There’s nothing he can do—there’s nothing Mydeimos can do—they’re both trapped, they’re both under the thumb of a half-mad tyrant, and that half-mad tyrant knows it.

Eurypon has a goblet in his hands. He’s drinking wine as he watches a slave master whip his own son, his crown prince.

None of the onlookers do anything. They don’t speak. They don’t move. They watch with fixed interest, as though all the blood pouring down

Mydeimos’s back is more palatable for its golden hue.

A Chrysos’s Heir’s muscle, it turns out, is as red as a normal human’s.

And Mydeimos is doing this for him, to pay back his life, surely, so that Phainon doesn’t burn.

Mydeimos slips to his knees but doesn’t make a sound. When he begins to list to one side, Periander pauses, ordering him tied to the post. He’s only delivered eighteen strikes, and Phainon isn’t sure he can watch any more of this even though he knows he has to. This, like the banquet, is a test from Eurypon, and if he doesn’t perform his part, he’ll burn anyway, and Mydeimos’s sacrifice here will mean nothing.

A prince allowing himself to be whipped in place of a slave. Of course Eurypon wouldn’t end this after one strike. This kind of sacrificial nobility undermines everything he stands for. Now, he has to make a point.

But Phainon won’t burn. Mydeimos will probably die, but Phainon won’t burn. He can’t decide if that’s a good trade off, even if Mydeimos is immortal. Immortality doesn’t prevent pain.

He chances a quick glance at Hephaestion. Hephaestion still faces forward, expression blank, but he trembles. When he, too, turns his eyes toward Phainon, there’s rage in them. Phainon did this. Phainon’s the reason Mydeimos’s back is a morass of gold and red.

He hopes Eurypon will lose interest like he did at the banquet, but hope is a fool’s errand. The king watches as he drinks his wine, seated on the balustrade with his back against a mighty column. No one leaves the courtyard. The slaves and servants and citizens alike watch their crown prince’s silent torture.

It only lasts ten minutes.

When Periander lowers his arm for the last time and steps back, slick with sweat and red of face, Mydeimos kneels, unmoving, in a pool of gold.

Phainon moves first. Perhaps he shouldn’t. Perhaps this will make everything worse for him and Mydeimos both, but to remain still would be to minimize Mydeimos’s sacrifice.

He goes to the prince’s side, kneeling in Mydeimos’s blood to free his wrists. The rough rope has rubbed them raw and golden. Mydeimos is breathing, somehow, shallow and rasping, but his eyes are closed and his body is limp. He lists to the side, and Phainon catches him about the waist, carefully slipping beneath one of his arms. He has no idea how he’s going to get Mydeimos to his bed, not with his back shredded, but he’ll be Titan damned if he doesn’t try.

Staggering to his feet, he pulls Mydeimos’s arm firmly over his shoulder. The agonized sound that comes from Mydeimos wounds Phainon’s soul.

And then Hephaestion is there, ducking under Mydeimos’s other arm. He says nothing, doesn’t even look at Phainon, but they don’t need to look at each other. They carry Mydeimos from the courtyard, leaving streaks of golden blood behind them. Leonnius silently leads the way.

“You,” Periander snaps. “Clean this up. And you, clean up after them before the blood stains the marble.”

How vile and utterly unsurprising.

Laboring under Mydeimos’s weight, even with Hephaestion’s assistance, is no easy thing. They’re both breathing heavily when they reach Mydeimos’s room. The servants there have already heard the news, clearly: there is a basin of fresh water and several piles of clean, folded linen strips waiting for them in the bedroom.

With great care, they maneuver Mydeimos onto his bed, and Phainon is grateful he’s unconscious. He can’t imagine the pain Mydeimos would otherwise be in.

“I know what to do,” Phainon says, reaching for the linens.

Hephaestion grabs him by the upper arm, and he reacts without thinking, breaking the hold and retaliating with a strike of his own. But Hephaestion is agile. He dodges, knocks Phainon off balance with a well-placed kick to Phainon’s knee, and then slams him into the nearby wall, knocking all the wind out of him. “You,” he snarls.

Phainon’s head rings, his chest caves, and he gasps valiantly for breath.

“Hephaestion—” Leonnius grabs Hephaestion’s shoulder, but Hephaestion won’t be moved.

“Who the fuck are you?” Hephaestion demands, his face a mask of rage. “Who are you that Mydei would take that on your behalf?”

There’s no way to safely answer that question, and even if he wanted to, he can’t; he’s still sucking in desperate gasps of air.

“Hephaestion!”

Hephaestion shakes Leonnius off, takes Phainon by the throat and the shoulder, and slams him against the wall a second time. “Why would he do that for you?”

Sure, there’s no safe answer to that question, but the wild emotion in Hephaestion’s eyes makes one thing very clear: he won’t relent until he gets an answer that satisfies him. And for all Phainon knows, Hephaestion will kill him in an attempt to get that answer. He can’t die. Not yet. Not when Mydeimos has just saved him.

He needs a good lie, but as he struggles to breathe, only one comes to mind. “I love him,” he gasps, grabbing Hephaestion’s wrist.

The fury drains out of Hephaestion’s face, replaced by stark horror and utter bewilderment. “You—you what?”

“I love him,” he says again, wheezing, scratching Hephaestion’s skin. Hephaestion’s grip doesn’t relent. “We’re in love.”

Hephaestion squeezes harder, snarling. “You don’t know him. He doesn’t know you. You are a conniving, deceitful, traitorous sack of shit. You—”

Leonnius comes between them, driving his elbow into the bend of Hephaestion’s arm, breaking Hephaestion’s hold on Phainon’s throat. “Enough,” he says, bullying Hephaestion back.

“He’s lying,” Hephaestion howls, throwing himself against Leonnius as Phainon sags against the wall, gulping down precious air.

“So what if he is?” Leonnius asks, driving Hephaestion further back, more than likely sparing Phainon’s life.

Phainon touches his throat, wincing, certain it will bruise. Leonnius, he decides, is a good man. Or at least a more levelheaded one. Straightening, one hand on the wall for grounding support, he studies Hephaestion and his rage.

“So what if he’s lying?” Leonnius says again. “Mydei chose to take that whipping for him, sparing his life. It doesn’t matter what he says to you. Mydei’s actions say more.”

Hephaestion’s sneer is terrible and ugly, the loathing in his expression would kill lesser men. “He should be executed.”

“That would undo everything Mydei just fought for.” Leonnius shoves Hephaestion again. “Get out of here,” he says. “Get out and cool your head. Your anger doesn’t belong in this room.”

“My anger—”

“Get out, Hephaestion, or I will drag you out myself.”

Hephaestion sobers, staring Leonnius down, and Phainon tries to decipher whatever else is passing unsaid between them. Unfortunately, for all his weeks here, he has spent little enough time with Mydeimos’s somatophylakes, and he can’t read anything beyond Hephaestion’s anger.

With a disgusted sound, Hephaestion relents. He steps back, both hands upraised. “I’ll go,” he says, but not before turning a murderous look on Phainon. “Don’t mistake me, slave. I will come for you for what you’ve cost him.”

Phainon swallows back the desire for a witty retort, having no interest in suffering Hephaestion’s touch again. In his silence, Hephaestion departs, leaving him alone with Leonnius. The servants, it seems, have all fled.

Heaving a sigh, Leonnius turns to him. Studies him. Phainon lets him, peeling away from the wall and approaching the linens and the basin.

“Do you know how to care for these wounds?” Leonnius asks.

“Yes.” Phainon takes a long strip of linen and lays it across Mydeimos’s ruined back. Already, the skin on the edges is beginning to repair itself. “Will his quick healing change anything?”

“No,” Leonnius says. “He’ll need the same care as anyone else who survives Periander’s whip, it just won’t take as long for him to recover. But he’s still vulnerable to blood rot.”

Phainon trades the strip of linen for another, mopping up the blood, trying not to see too clearly what remains of Mydeimos’s back. He did this. “Has that ever killed him before?”

“Once,” Leonnius says. “Gut wounds are a bitch.” He hovers near the bed. “I can still send for a physician.”

Phainon replaces the strip of linen. “If the servants keep bringing me what I need, I’ll be able to manage.” He doesn’t look at Leonnius. “He saved my life today.”

“He did. And you probably took his at least once. You might’ve prevented a death in the Grove, but this math doesn’t balance out,” Leonnius says, and Phainon realizes that Leonnius doesn’t much like him, either, but his hatred isn’t as virulent as Hephaestion’s. “Maybe he does love you, maybe you’re not a liar, but best you even out all these scales.”

Not just the ones between him and Mydeimos but the ones between him and Leonnius, too. “I understand,” he says.

“Good. I’ll keep Hephaestion off your back, but Ptolemy will want to come by. Don’t piss him off.” Leonnius doesn’t wait for Phainon’s response. Warning and advice dispensed, he leaves.

Phainon sits on the edge of Mydeimos’s bed, sopping up his blood, and staring sightlessly over Mydeimos’s shoulder.

Love.

It had seemed, in the moment, the best lie. The most believable lie. Why else would a man take fifty lashes meant for a slave if not for love? Surely, Phainon’s own life is not worth so much. Surely, his saving Mydeimos’s life as he did could not require such a steep price in return. He isn’t familiar with Castrum Kremnos and its laws and traditions, but there must have been some other path than Mydei putting himself on the sacrificial pyre for Phainon’s sake.

A shudder rolls through him. Perhaps that’s not the best metaphor when Eurypon quite literally has a pyre in his banquet hall.

“Why?” he asks Mydeimos’s unconscious body. “How do you value my life to make this cost worth it?” He trades out the bloodied linen for another clean sheet, moving mechanically. When he looks too long at Mydeimos’s back, his stomach heaves, and he swallows his gorge as he turns away.

He did this. He’s the reason Mydeimos is barely clinging to life, the reason Mydeimos certainly died once in that courtyard. Mydeimos traded his life and well-being for Phainon, and while maybe Mydeimos views his life as cheap, he still suffered.

Mydeimos is a good man.

Mydeimos is a better man than Phainon is; Phainon would not have made that sacrifice. In Mydeimos’s position, to save his own skin, he would have let himself die.

Maybe the comparison is unfair. He has to stay alive. He has things yet to do, and Mydeimos has made that possible. Leonnius is more right than he knows about the balance between Phainon and Mydeimos.

Gold blood soaks the linen in his hands.

He changes it out again.

Fire. He’s on fire. He burns.

Pain blazes through his body. Every breath is a new and unique agony.

His limbs are heavy, his brain foggy except where pain breaks through in staticky bursts and renders coherent thought impossible.

A broken sound spills from his lips.

Cool hands touch his arm, his hip.

A voice speaks, the words distant and distorted. There’s an ocean of space between him and—and that’s not Hephaestion speaking. Those hands aren’t Hephaestion’s.

The hands pull back. Something ceramic touches his lips, and he parts them. Bitter liquid floods his mouth. He coughs, and agony razes all conscious thought until there’s nothing but numbness.

Not Hephaestion. If not Hephaestion, then…

The pain dims. The fog returns, blessed relief, but for one thought, one name.

Phainon.

“Come back to us.”

Sleep and pain cling to the edges of his blurred awareness. He can’t open his eyes. Doesn’t want to. Morpheus sings sweet lullabies to him.

“Come back to me.” Ah. Hephaestion. “I miss you so much.”

His tongue is too thick, his pain too intense, his dreams too strong. He cannot manage a reply, and he doesn’t want to. They’ve had this conversation before.

“Won’t you come back for me?”

He slips away.

Once more, he drifts from sweet unconsciousness to the reality of a body on fire with pain. He doesn’t whimper, doesn’t groan, doesn’t make any noise to betray himself. He can’t. If anyone knows his weakness, he will surely be destroyed.

Phainon.

Phainon knows. But Phainon is caring for him. Phainon is—

“—not what was agreed to,” a woman’s voice says. Familiar. He knows that voice, struggles to place that voice, wrestles with his own memories until a sun-worn face coalesces in his mind. Mother. That’s his mother.

“I can’t stay trapped here when there is more to do,” a man’s voice replies. Phainon. He recognizes Phainon immediately.

“So you put my son in danger?” Gorgo demands. She is angry, so angry. He has rarely ever heard her this angry. He can’t remember the last time she was so angry on his behalf. Anger is deadly in Castrum Kremnos. Only Strife, Eurypon, Father, is allowed to be angry. “Do you truly expect me to believe that you are the best she could send me?”

The pain grows. It radiates across his back, and at last he makes a noise of discomfort.

“Mydeimos,” Gorgo says, her voice breaking. She kneels beside him, and he turns his head to look at her, trying to focus his blurry vision. “My precious son. Why have you done this thing?”

She doesn’t know. If Gorgo doesn’t know, then no one knows. Phainon is safe.

“More poppy milk,” Phainon says.

Chapter Notes

Fury doesn’t come easy to Mydei. He doesn’t lose his temper quickly, doesn’t lash out the way his father does. He refuses to be like Eurypon, tamping down on his anger until he has no choice but to utilize it as a blade against his enemies. He wields it now as he drags Phainon out of the tree, heedless of the damage he does to Phainon’s skin.

Phainon falls out of the tree with a quiet shout, and Mydei yanks him to his feet, shaking him by the shoulders. “This is how you repay me?” Mydei demands. “I take fifty lashes for you, and you try to escape again?”

Phainon finally reacts, knocking Mydei’s hands away, but Mydei is ready for this. He’s seen Phainon move once already, knows he’s a warrior trained, and so he anticipates Phainon’s actions. He grabs Phainon by the wrists as Phainon hisses at him, both of them trying to keep quiet—though why he doesn’t wake the whole fucking palace, Mydei doesn’t know. Betrayal cuts so deep, deeper than the bite of the scourge’s tassels.

“It’s not—”

“Don’t you dare try to defend yourself,” Mydei snarls. Phainon, for all his dreams of being a warrior, was a farm boy first. While he tilled the fields and played at swordsmanship, Mydei received training from the best teachers in the empire. It is no great struggle to get Phainon’s arms behind him, held in Mydei’s unrelenting grip. He shoves Phainon forward, steering him back into the bedroom.

Servants cluster in the doorway, staring, as Mydei shoves Phainon inside. “Out,” Mydei says, and when they don’t respond immediately, he shouts the command. “All of you, out.” He drags Phainon after him, all but chasing his servants out of his suite, and he bolts the main door behind them. They’ve fled to their own quarters, but this should buy him a minute of peace.

Not that Phainon is peaceable. No, Phainon struggles wildly in his hold, attempting to break it, but Mydei has years of training on Phainon and is more equipped to deal with a squirming fool. He shoves Phainon back into the bedroom, tossing him onto the bed.

Phainon scrambles across it, a wild look on his face. “Mydei—”

The nickname is a brutal strike. “Do not call me that.” Mydei stalks toward the foot of the bed, trying to climb on top of his fury, his betrayal. “Fifty strikes, Phainon. I died for you on that sand, and this is how you repay me?”

“I can explain.”

“Can you?” Mydei demands. “Do you truly think you can justify this? That I could—that I would—protect you a second time for the same stupid, asinine behavior? If you need to meet my mother or even one of her agents —”

“It’s not your mother!” Phainon exclaims.

Mydei throws himself onto the bed, onto Phainon, slapping his hand over Phainon’s mouth. He bears down on Phainon, pinning him beneath his own weight. “If you are going to give up your secrets, don’t be so loud about them,” he hisses. “Even with my servants gone, the walls have ears.” He presses his hand harder to Phainon’s mouth, ignoring the way Phainon struggles and flails beneath him. “You will tell me what you mean. You owe this to me. Fifty lashes, Phainon. You owe me the truth.”

Phainon abruptly goes slack beneath Mydei, his eyes closing. Mydei doesn’t relent, doesn’t let Phainon up. He does, however, remove his hand from Phainon’s mouth.

“Explain,” Mydei says, “or I will turn you over to Periander myself.”

Phainon tries to free his arms from beneath Mydei’s knees, but Mydei doesn’t give him an inch. Warm hands curve over Mydei’s legs, and Mydei sneers.

“Do you think to distract me with your touch this time?”

“No,” Phainon says, defeated. He opens his eyes, and they are resigned. “It’s not entirely your mother. It’s Aglaea.”

Mydei stares at him, dumbfounded, but only for a moment. So much suddenly becomes clear to him. “Your Aglaea is working with my mother. This is why she made you my bed slave. The men who captured you didn’t know who you are, but my mother knew you were Aglaea’s agent.”

Phainon looks away, and Mydei knows he’s right.

A sneer pulls across Mydei’s lips again. “Do you think yourself some savior?” he demands. “Some deliverer for all of Okhema and the rest of Amphoreus?”

Phainon’s face snaps back to Mydei’s, and he bares his teeth in a snarl. “Someone has to stop your father. He’s a monster, and you know that, Mydei.”

The nickname breaks his heart. “Don’t call me that.”

“You know that,” Phainon says again, ignoring him. “You’ve all but said it yourself! Someone has to do something to put a stop to Eurypon’s advance. We aren’t winning. Every time we meet your father in combat, he pushes us back further. So, yes, I thought I could deliver—” He spits the word. “—my people from your father and—well. Aglaea sent me into the woods to be captured, and your mother picked me for this purpose specifically.”

Mydei reels back, sitting on Phainon’s hips, pressing a hand to his forehead. His mother. His mother has orchestrated all of this. His mother is acting against Eurypon in the shadows, and now he knows, unequivocally, and he realizes he stands at a crossroads. She has maneuvered him into this choice with masterful strokes, pushing him to this place without him even realizing it. He has never felt as though he could act against Eurypon, too afraid of the tortures his father could visit on him. But now, with Phainon, with a man connected to the Goldweaver herself…

“Will you turn me into him?” Phainon demands. “You who claim to be so tired of death? Will you—”

“Shut up,” Mydei says, hanging his head between his shoulders. He grabs the pillow to either side of Phainon’s head, trying to breathe, trying to ground himself. He is at a crossroads, yes, but there is only one choice. There has only ever been one choice, but he’s been standing here for so long, so capable of making the choice but unable to commit to it.

He is so tired of death. He is so tired. But not so tired that he cannot act.

Lifting his head, Mydei meets Phainon’s gaze. “You want to save the world, Deliverer?” Mydei asks, weary. “Then I will help you.”

Phainon jerks beneath Mydei, his ire transforming into the surprise of a man who has never had anyone’s support. “What?”

“I will help you,” Mydei says again.

“Why?”

Mydei laughs, mirthless. “I protect you from my somatophylakes, I tell you my feelings about the empire, I allow myself to be whipped in your place, and you ask me why?”

“You didn’t have to do any of that.”

“No, but I did,” Mydei says. He sits back, shifting his knees off Phainon’s shoulders. He lowers his voice. “I will admit to you that I am… I am very afraid of my father.”

Phainon’s fingers tighten on Mydei’s calves. “He can’t kill you,” Phainon reminds him, softly, gently.

“No, but he can hurt me. And he can hurt the people I care about.” Mydei exhales heavily. “He has already hurt my mother, and he wouldn’t hesitate to hurt…” He trails off, looking away from Phainon, gazing over the dark courtyard beyond his room. “He wouldn’t hesitate to hurt anyone else. Nor would he hesitate to chain me at the bottom of another lake for the rest of

my life.” His lips twist in a wry smile. “No blade nor poison, but I age. Perhaps Thanatos will find me in my old age, after I’ve drowned hundreds of thousands of times.” He shakes his head. “I’m afraid of my father, Phainon, but I will help you.”

Phainon pulls his tongue across his lips and says nothing. Good. Mydei could not bear to reveal more of himself right now. This is enough.

With a heavy sigh of his own, Phainon rubs his thumbs against Mydei’s calves, soothing strokes. “I’ve been trying to reach a contact in the city,” he admits. “I haven’t been able to establish any communication yet. I’d hoped to sneak out. Obviously.” He snorts. “That didn’t work for me.”

“Either time,” Mydei agrees, and Phainon has the grace to look chagrined. “Where in the city to you need to go?”

“The agora. My contact is a merchant in the agora. I don’t want to reveal much else. You understand.”

Mydei nods. “The less I know, the less someone can torture out of me if we are discovered.”

With a grimace, Phainon says, “Yeah. That.” Though Mydei thinks there’s more to it. Phainon’s trust is not easily won. Clearly.

Mydei studies him in the darkness, the world-weary wariness to him, the haunted look of a man who has seen too much, and considers their options. Neither of them are prisoners in the palace—technically—though it often feels that way. “We will go to the agora then,” Mydei declares, and he slides off Phainon’s hips.

Letting him go, Phainon levers himself up. “Are you—you’re serious? That easily?”

“That easily,” Mydei says with a shrug. “I wish to go shopping, and it’s only right for you to accompany me. We will have to go with my full somatophylakes, so you will need to be careful.” He pauses. “And smart,” he adds, meaningfully.

Phainon bristles. “I—”

“Have not been smart about this,” Mydei says. “Twice, you have tried. Twice, you have been caught. Which increases the danger.” And he does wonder why Phainon is so cavalier with his own life—and the lives of others. Phainon isn’t the kind of man who would think so little of life, Mydei is sure of that. Phainon saved him in the Grove. He can’t make sense of the inconsistencies. Not yet.

“My contact won’t meet me if you’re there. If the whole group of you is there.”

Mydei shrugs again. “This is the best I can do for you.”

“If your somatophylakes realize…”

“Then we should make sure the risk to you is worth it.” Mydei has no idea what information Phainon already has, but it certainly won’t be enough to justify all the time he’s missed connecting with this contact. “And you will endeavor not to be so Titans-damn stupid.”

Phainon splutters. “I haven’t been stupid!”

“No, it wasn’t your stupidity that got my skin stripped from my back,” Mydei replies dryly. It might be a low strike, a dirty one, but it makes his point.

The horror and regret in Phainon’s eyes speaks volumes. “Fine,” he says, looking away, at least a little ashamed. “A little stupid.”

“Profoundly.”

Phainon’s eyes narrow.

Mydei smiles faintly. “Now, let us make a mess of my room and half the rest of the suite so my servants believe we were particularly passionate tonight.”

“And they say Kremnoans can’t be sneaky and duplicitous,” Phainon says, venturing a tentative laugh, a hopeful expression on his face.

Mydei lifts a brow, reaching behind Phainon’s head. He pulls Phainon close. “There will be no sneaking about this,” he says, sealing his mouth to Phainon’s.

“The Okhemans are reinforcing their lines along the Acheron,” Themistocles says, pushing pieces across the war map. “They are gathering additional forces here, here, and here, shoring up their defenses. Breaking them here will send them back to the Holy City itself.” He leans back, crossing his arms. “And they know it. This is the last place they can stand against us before we turn to siege warfare.”

Mydei watches his father from the opposite end of the war table, studying Eurypon’s fixed expression. He is calmer today, his father, intent on the map before him. These days of terrifying clarity are worse than the others, when Eurypon is paranoid and barely lucid. Days like these, Eurypon condemns men to die in strokes of tactical brilliance.

“Then we must meet them,” Eurypon says. “This will be our most decisive battle yet.”

“If he wishes for decisiveness,” Hephaestion murmurs, “then he should deploy you.”

Mydei hisses, turning his face toward Hephaestion but keeping his eyes on his father and the map. “And make me Castrum Kremnos’s hero? No, he would never.”

“He—”

“Be silent,” Mydei says, ignoring the way Hephaestion stiffens and shifts his weight to lean away. Let Hephaestion be angry; it is his default state of late, and Mydei finds Hephaestion’s anger more tolerable than his affection.

At the head of the table, Eurypon is speaking again. “They are afraid,” he says, and here he falls prey to his own propaganda. “They know if we push them back to the city, they will break.”

That isn’t true, but Mydei bites his tongue. Siege warfare is the worst kind.

“We won’t even need to take it,” Eurypon continues, a wild glint in his eyes. “Not if we break them at the Acheron.” He laughs. “Yes, Themistocles, do you see? If we shatter their forces at the Acheron, if only their citizens await in the Goldweaver’s city, then we shall have them.” A manic smile stretches across Eurypon’s face. “We have already won.” He spins out the fantasy in real time, and it is an uncomfortable thing to witness his delusional madness. “We have destroyed them, crushed them already. They are broken.”

A murmur of assent goes up from the generals—but not, Mydei notices, from Themistocles. The generals offer their congratulations to Eurypon, and Eurypon basks in their adoration.

Mydei leans forward, resting his fingertips on the table. “If Okhema is broken,” Mydei says, “then we need not deploy any forces at all.”

The room goes silent. The generals look everywhere but at him. Themistocles meets his eyes and gives a minute shake of his head.

And Eurypon, his smile suddenly fragile, turns his face slowly toward Mydei. “I cannot have heard my son correctly,” he says, low and dangerous.

Mydei considers the map in front of him. With the knowledge that Eurypon will deploy forces to the Acheron with the intent to break Okhema—for that is the heart of this discussion, no matter what Eurypon believes now—he has enough to give to Phainon to pass on to his contact. But it’s not enough, not for him. Not anymore, now that he’s turned from the crossroads and started down his own path to either decades of torture or, perhaps, salvation.

“If Okhema is already broken, then why deploy your forces at all?” Mydei asks. “Are they not better spent tilling the fields? Our people are starving. The black tide licks at our borders.”

Beside him, Hephaestion sucks in a sharp breath. Softly, he says Mydei’s name in warning.

Mydei ignores him. “Perhaps the king should consider building the empire up, if his enemies have been so soundly defeated already,” he says.

“Unfilial,” one of the generals says abruptly, his lips curling with disdain. “Unfilial and treasonous.” There’s a round of affirmations. Themistocles remains silent.

“Is it unfilial and treasonous to inform the king that Castrum Kremnos stands on the brink of starvation?” Mydei asks, his gaze fixed on his father.

Eurypon’s expression is unmoving, a rictus grin.

“All the wealth we’ve stripped from Okhema in the face of their endless retreats, from the city states we’ve conquered, it’s all gone back into our war machine,” Mydei continues. “Our farmlands either lie fallow or consumed by the black tide, and we have taken much of Okhema’s farmland, too.”

“Then let them starve when we lay siege to them,” a second general declares, glancing nervously at Eurypon.

Mydei’s expression is tight. “Then we will starve, too. We cannot afford a lengthy siege of the Holy City.”

“So we will break them on the banks of the Acheron,” says the first general, gesturing broadly to the table.

“I thought we did not need to do that,” Mydei says softly. “Winter will come down from the north soon enough, and it will end not just Okhema, but us, too, if we stretch ourselves as thin as this campaign.”

It happens in an instant, before Mydei can react. One moment, he’s leaning over the table. The next, his father has him against the wall, impacting it so hard all the breath knocks out of him, a blade at his throat. Red crystal bursts from Eurypon’s arms, his face, forming a glittering chrysalis of

armor. “Betrayal,” Eurypon snarls, pressing the blade hard enough to Mydei’s throat that skin parts and golden blood drips down his skin. “My own son, turning against me and the empire he stands to inherit!”

Mydei has no doubts that he will never inherit Eurypon’s empire. The Titanblessed live until they are killed. Mydei is a comfort to the people but doesn’t factor into Eurypon’s reign. He never has. “I do not want our empire to fall, Father,” he says, his throat scraping against Eurypon’s blade with each word.

“You would have me pull back,” Eurypon hisses. “You would have Okhema walk all over us, destroy us, strip us of our very way of life. They are vermin, demanding everyone bow to their laws, their whims, their rules.”

The irony is not lost on Mydei. “They do not deserve to live,” Mydei agrees, placating. “But will you sacrifice your empire for their decline?”

Eurypon reels away from him. “I am the chosen child of Strife,” he snarls, whipping his blade through the air to fling Mydei’s blood off it. He smears it against his hip, wiping what remains of golden blood on his chiton, on the heavy fall of his robes. “I will have the entire continent, the entire world, as is my right, and you would tell me to stand down! To let the Okhemans take back what is rightfully ours!” He brandishes his blade at Mydei once more, and then spins about, pointing his sword at his generals. “And there are those among you who agree with him.” The words emerge a hiss.

The generals react as one mass, protesting in increasingly hysterical tones.

Themistocles alone remains silent, his lips pressed together in a fine line. And yet Eurypon is clear minded enough not to round on Themistocles. No, he grabs one of the generals near the end of the table by the arm, the glittering red crystals extending from Eurypon’s shoulder to his wrist. The general stares at them with utter terror in his eyes.

“You have always held my son in high regard, Stasanor,” Eurypon says, far too calm.

Heart pounding, Mydei peels himself away from the wall. “Father,” he begins. This cannot be allowed to go on.

“Do you, perhaps, agree with him now?” Eurypon asks.

Stasanor, his eyes fixed on the crystals sprouting from the back of Eurypon’s hand, shakes his head. “No, my king. I am with you! I believe we must crush the Okhemans completely. I believe—”

“You do not think they are already broken?” Eurypon demands.

“No!” Stasanor’s eyes are so wide there’s white all around his irises. “I mean—that is—I believe my king when he says—”

Eurypon snarls, animalistic, a virulent red energy wafting from his body.

“Father,” Mydei says again, urgently, reaching for Eurypon’s shoulder. “Father, Stasanor is—”

Strasanor is a shower of blood. The crystals move too quickly to be seen, exploding out of him, tearing him apart, popping him like an overfilled waterskin. Mydei turns away, closing his eyes against the gruesome sight. He has wondered many times if Eurypon’s crystals could truly end him, and there is a part of him terrified to find out. But he should have done more to prevent Strasanor’s death. The old general didn’t deserve it; he held no great regard for Mydei, no matter what Eurypon said.

“This,” Eurypon says, his voice shaking with fury. “This will be you.”

Mydei opens his eyes and turns to face his blood-spattered father, aghast. He did this. Pressing Eurypon killed a man who didn’t deserve it. Not like this. Strasanor’s actions have killed so many people, but he didn’t deserve to go like that, torn to pieces by crystal. “Father,” he says, imploring.

“I will do this to you, you insolent child, if you think you can turn my men against me.”

He holds up both hands, tense to keep from shaking. “I don’t,” he says. “I won’t.”

“I should have thrown you back into the Sea of Souls after that whore you call a mother saved you from it,” Eurypon snarls. “I have fed you, clothed you, taught you, raised you—” He has done none of those things, except, perhaps, for allowing them to happen. “—and this is how you repay me!” He lunges for Mydei, and Mydei, keenly aware of the crystals pulsating on Eurypon’s hand, ducks away, his hands still upraised. “If you are so ready to end this war,” Eurypon continues, “you can do so. It will be you on the frontline in ten days’ time.”

Cold dread grips Mydei’s spine, but he immediately drops to his knees. “Yes,” he says, acquiescing and hoping this will defuse his father. “As my king commands.”

A scalding hot hand descends on his shoulder, but when he glances at it, he is relieved beyond measure to find only human flesh there. Burning flesh, flesh that makes Mydei’s own scream with pain, but a human hand nonetheless. “That is the son I raised. Obedient.”

There must be more to this. Even in his madness, Eurypon wouldn’t put Mydei in a position to help him win the war. Eurypon must be the hero that Castrum Kremnos wants, Eurypon demands the adulation, the adoration. Now, it will fall to Mydei, if he is successful.

Perhaps Eurypon knows something Mydei does not, something that will see him fail.

Eurypon turns his hand, patting his scorching hot palm against Mydei’s cheek. He pulls away, tottering back to his kline, and he sinks into it. “Wine,” he says.

Wasting no time, Mydei rocks to his feet. He bows to his distracted father and turns, all but fleeing the war room.

Hephaestion is on his heels. “What was that?” he demands as the doors close behind them.

Mydei presses thumb and forefinger to his eyes, digging deep, trying to ignore the unimaginable pain from his burned shoulder.

“Why did you provoke him like that?”

Weary, Mydei drops his hand. He doesn’t even care that there are guards behind them that might overhear this conversation. “I have been thinking about things differently, lately,” he admits, extending an olive branch to Hephaestion and hoping Hephaestion will take it in the way it’s meant.

Hephaestion steps in front of him, taking him by the arms, only then noticing the burn across his shoulder. But that doesn’t stop him from saying, “This is your bed slave’s doing. He is Okheman, we all know it. He—”

“He isn’t to blame,” Mydei says, gently brushing aside Hephaestion’s hands.

Hephaestion hisses. “He said you love him.”

Mydei stills and then slumps just the slightest bit. Of course this is about Hephaestion’s jealousy, his desire to still be in Mydei’s bed, his anger that he isn’t. He doesn’t understand—has struggled to understand—that Mydei never loved him the same way. Could never give him what he wanted. But there’s a profound sadness in Hephaestion’s face that softens Mydei. He is afraid, Mydei thinks, that he’ll be replaced. Even by a slave.

“You’re the one who ended our relationship,” Mydei reminds him. “So, don’t use Phainon as a weapon against me now.”

Hephaestion reels back. “If you could only try,” he says, his expression breaking. “If you would give me another opportunity to prove to you my ardor.”

“It was never you, Hephaestion,” Mydei says, still so very weary. “Please. Leave me in peace. I have much to think about.”

“Will there ever be enough room in your life for me?” Hephaestion asks.

Mydei gives him a sad smile and pulls away, leaving Hephaestion in the hall.

“Your shoulder,” Phainon says. “What the fuck happened to your shoulder?” Mydei sags in the doorway to his bedroom as Phainon lurches out of the bed. “How did this happen?”

“My father,” Mydei says, half collapsing against Phainon.

Phainon catches him, holding him, wrestling with the sudden fury that courses through him. His hatred for Eurypon is an old, comfortable thing, but it burns brighter, now. Chapter Notes

Phainon breathes in the air of the agora and realizes it’s not all that different from the air in the palace. It’s fragrant with spices and human bodies, but the palace smells like that, too: smells like oregano and basil, though the palace also has the sweet-smelling strawberry and olive trees. He’d expected the agora to feel like freedom, to taste like it. It doesn’t. Maybe that’s because Mydei’s somatophylakes have fallen in around them, a barrier between him and Mydei and the rest of the world. It seems silly, the way they protect Mydei, but appearances go a long way, he supposes. Can’t have the crown prince running amok in the city unguarded and looking vulnerable.

The agora itself disquiets him, too much like Okhema’s own agora to provide much comfort. Vendors hawk their wares, aggressively shoving goods at the men surrounding him and Mydei. Children run underfoot, their fingers wily and clever, and Phainon isn’t surprised when Peucesta catches one trying to take his coin purse. He’s not surprised, either, when Peucesta lets the child go with enough coin to buy food; Mydei’s friends don’t like him, but they don’t seem like bad people. Bright colors slash across dull limestone walls, strips of fabric for decoration and sale, and Leonnius wraps himself in one of these lengths of fabric, wearing it as a skirt, while the others laugh at him.

Even the smithies, laboring to create weapons for Castrum Kremnos’s war machine, are familiar to him. Many are closed, their owners behind the frontline, but the ones that are open serve up blades for cooking and for farming. It all feels too normal, too much like home. He wants to hate the agora, but he can’t. The people here are innocent of Eurypon’s decisions, caught up in a mad king’s paranoias and fantasies.

“Phylo’s!” Leonnius calls, disentangling himself from the slash of bright red fabric. He bullies the group of them across the thoroughfare, to a restaurant with seating around the front of it. “Ho, Phylo!”

Even Hephaestion, usually so surly, is smiling, and he claps a hand to Leonnius’s shoulder, leaning over his back and into the restaurant to speak with the proprietor. “How goes it, friend?”

They know people here. They are friendly with people here. They, too, Phainon hates to admit, are people trapped in Eurypon’s schemes. So many of them must obey Eurypon out of the same fear Mydei possesses.

“Wine skins,” Mydei says, slapping Leonnius and Hephaestion on the back. He doesn’t try to push forward, staying behind them as the other three form a barrier at his sides and back, Phainon close to his flank.

Ptolemy makes a disdainful little noise, and Perdikkas says, “We shouldn’t while we’re at our work.”

“What work?” Mydei asks, laughing. He gives Perdikkas and Ptolemy both light shoves, dislodging them from their formation. “You all know I’m more than capable of protecting myself. Let’s enjoy ourselves. A bit of drink won’t see me dead, and even if it did, what harm is that?”

“You are too glib,” Ptolemy says, sighing heavily. “Your mother would see us destroyed if you died on our watch.”

Phainon startles at that, surprised Gorgo would respond so viciously to Mydei’s meaningless deaths, but he supposes he has his protections from Gorgo’s wrath.

“Never mind my mother,” Mydei says, reaching between Leonnius and Hephaestion to take a wine skin in hand. “Enjoy.” He presses the skin on Ptolemy, who glares half-heartedly but takes a sip regardless.

How curious, then, that Mydei passes wine to everyone and saves none for himself.

“Is my prince not thirsty?” Phainon asks, lowering his voice and arching his brow.

Mydei smiles at him, a rakish grin that has his heart stuttering in his chest. “Not for wine,” he says, and Phainon’s heart hammers at the warmth in Mydei’s voice, in his eyes. This is a game, surely. They have to look like a besotted master and slave in public.

“He blushes!” Leonnius crows, pointing at Phainon with both hands before taking a swig of his own wine skin. “Behold!”

Phainon scowls, but Mydei—and his friends, even Hephaestion—laughs.

“Not used to being teased?” Perdikkas asks from Phainon’s side.

“Is that what this is?” Phainon returns dryly. “Teasing?”

“From Leonnius, certainly.”

Scoffing, Phainon crosses his arms, acutely aware of the torc tight around his throat. “I can’t imagine why. Unless it’s because I’m an easy target.”

The other somatophylakes close around Mydei as Phainon pulls away, attended by Perdikkas, and he makes a great show of examining the jewelry on display. Thick cuffs and heavy bracelets for men, delicate necklaces dripping with gemstones for women. He lets his fingers wander over several different pieces before holding one up, turning it into the sunlight so he can look past it and study the other vendors.

“Can you afford that?” Perdikkas asks, but with a grin so charming that Phainon can’t be offended.

Briefly, bitterly, he wonders if he’s ever been in control. “Why does he care?” Phainon rakes both hands through his hair, driving it away from his face. “Why would Mydei be so swayed?”

Hephaestion laughs, but it’s not cruel, it’s as sad as his smile. “We both know you’re smarter than that.”

“He has no reason to care about me,” Phainon insists, dropping the back of one hand into his palm. “No reason.”

“According to the philosophers, love precludes reason.” Hephaestion’s expression is so shattered, so sad, so resigned, that it catches Phainon utterly by surprise.

“No,” he says. “No, that’s…”

“Phainon,” Hephaestion says, gentle like a parent to a child. “I remember how Mydei looked at me when he thought he loved me.”

“No,” Phainon says again, watching everything he’s worked so hard for fall through his fingers. It wasn’t supposed to go like this.

“His regard for you is so much more tender than it ever was for me.”

Chapter End Notes
