Chapter Notes

please mind the tags for this one, and remember that "happy ending" is among them. the more tenderhearted among you may want to wait until next week to read this chapter

The journey to the frontline doesn’t take long, even for Mydei and his century. They march too well, too efficiently, and the weather is good and clear. He resents their swiftness, wishing for more time to mull over his own potential demise, to cajole Phainon into opening up to him, but they accomplish the march in a little under two days.

Phainon rides with him at the center of his somatophylakes, at the head of the century, but refuses to give more than clipped responses or quiet grunts, leaving Mydei baffled. Phainon’s uncharacteristic silence is inscrutable, and he doesn’t know how to coax Phainon out of it. In the end, he decides it’s not his place. They can playact at being lovers, but the truth is that they aren’t. They never will be. They are master and slave, coconspirators in treason, and their personal feelings—for surely this has more to do with their personal relationship—matters so much less than everything else. How strange it is to find himself with such a relationship, one he craves, only to learn he can’t prioritize it above all things.

When they reach the frontline, Mydei’s century makes camp under the watchful eyes of his somatophylakes, and he retreats into the command tent with Phainon, even though Phainon’s company is poor at best. The silence between them is uncomfortable as they eat, as they prepare for bed—Mydei has already been briefed. He will go to the field in the morning and wait for Castorice there, as she has been waiting for him each morning.

More than just the silence, Mydei himself is uncomfortable. Death isn’t something he’s ever had to fear. Dying, yes, but death, no. Now, he not only faces the prospect of a gruesome death, but the prospect of staying dead,

and he wants. There’s a yearning inside him, though he doesn’t know what for.

It’s only after their dinner is cleared and Mydei has washed his face and hands, after they’ve stripped to their loincloths and are well and truly alone —and Mydei feels so very alone—that Phainon speaks.

“I could go. In the middle of the night, I could simply leave.”

Mydei startles, looking away from his mirror to study Phainon. He sits on the edge of the palette they’re to share, his arms draped over his knees, his eyes fixed on the floor between his feet. “To what end?” Mydei asks.

Phainon doesn’t look at him. “If your father has no leverage, you don’t have to test Castorice in the morning.”

They’ve seen the blackened field, the corpses of birds that flew too close overhead, pulled down by the wafting of Castorice’s deadly miasma.

Frowning, Mydei sets his basin aside and goes to his knees in front of Phainon. Phainon’s eyes remain downturned. “Would you really abandon your mission?”

Phainon’s hands curl into fists. “There are other ways to accomplish it,” he says, and there’s something there, something Mydei should understand but doesn’t. Phainon is still hiding things from him, and Mydei wishes he wouldn’t but knows why he does. Some secrets must remain between them. They are not true allies—and his heart doesn’t grieve that. “And if you really die tomorrow, that…”

“That will deal a deadly blow to Kremnoan morale,” Mydei says, not hoping that Phainon trails off for another reason. “That will give Okhema the advantage. That will give your people a chance to strike deeper into the heart of the Empire, Phainon, and you, perhaps, the opening we both know your people need.” Mydei isn’t a fool. This isn’t just about defeating the army. There is only one way to end this war. “But more likely, I’ll be fine. Nothing has been able to keep me down yet.”

“There’s a first time for everything,” Phainon says, his fists curling so tight his knuckles pop.

Mydei won’t let himself believe Phainon is afraid for him. That would be too much. “Your concern is appreciated but likely misplaced.”

At last, Phainon looks at him. “Mydei—”

“All the odds suggest I’ll be fine. Nothing has killed me yet. Why should we believe Castorice will?”

“She’s Thanatos’s heir,” Phainon says. “Handpicked and blessed. If anything—if anyone—is going to end your life, it’s her.”

A sad smile pulls at Mydei’s lips. “Why do you care so much?”

Phainon looks away. “We’re allies.”

“We’re enemies with a common goal,” Mydei reminds him, but he doesn’t know that’s true. Enemies don’t fuck each other the way Phainon fucks him. Enemies aren’t distressed about the prospect of losing a convenient ally, and Phainon is so clearly distressed. “Don’t worry for me, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon scoffs. “As you say.”

“I would go into battle forearmed and forewarned,” Mydei says, shifting to sit beside Phainon. “What do you know of Castorice?”

Exhaling heavily, Phainon tips his head back, staring at the top of the tent. “She’s from Aidonia.”

“Ah.” So she, too, has personal reasons to hate Mydei, Eurypon, and all of Castrum Kremnos, for the sack of Aidonia wasn’t a pleasant thing. “That’s… unfortunate.”

Phainon makes a quiet sound of agreement. “She was there during the sacking, already chosen by Thanatos. When the soldiers returned too maimed to survive, she was their Holy Maiden who took them into the

afterlife. But even before that, it was Castorice who released the dying from the shackles of mortal life.” Phainon turns his hands palm up, staring at them. “With a touch, she took their lives. She’s always lived apart, a harbinger for the end.”

“Interesting,” Mydei says. “You knew her in Okhema?”

“You could say that.” Phainon flexes his fingers. “She’s always been alone, set apart. She’s desperate for human connection. She—” He laughs. “This won’t help you fight her.”

No. It won’t. “Knowing her state of mind could be useful.”

“Maybe. Probably not.” Rubbing his jaw, Phainon stares into the distance, thoughtful. “In Okhema, wrapped in Aglaea’s threads, she was less dangerous, and less potent. You could get close to her, but never more than five paces. No one ever sparred with her, that’d require getting too close, but I saw her learning ranged weapons. Throwing knives, slings, archery. The masters stood at a distance and gave her instruction.”

“Then she’ll come armed?”

“Doubt it. I expect she’ll show up in a breastband and a loincloth and try to physically touch you. The miasma will confound you, slow you down, strangle you, but it’s her touch that’s deadliest.” Phainon turns toward him, concern in his drawn brows. “You can’t let her touch you. You have to stay at range.”

“One-on-one combat with a bow won’t be particularly effective,” Mydei says dryly, “but I take your meaning. I’ll bring my spear.”

“Even that—” Phainon cuts himself off, looking away. “The spear is your best bet, if you’re to engage her at all.”

“I have no choice.” Mydei says.

Phainon closes his eyes. “You do.”

“I don’t,” he insists softly, hoping Phainon understands. “Do you think she will believe me a traitor if I tell her I’m on her side?”

Phainon flinches.

“Do you think she’ll play at killing me—or let me play at killing her? No, this will be to the death for one of us,” Mydei says. “There is no other way.”

They settle on opposite sides of the small pallet, backs touching, and Mydei presses his face into his hand. He doesn’t believe he’ll die, but the smallest kernel of fear kindles within him. There are so many things he hasn’t done, so many things he hasn’t prepared for. If he does die on the morrow—

But then Phainon rolls over, Phainon takes him into his arms and presses his face into Mydei’s neck, and Mydei relaxes. Phainon curls around him as though a shield, as though he can ward off the entire world.

At least for the night, Mydei will let himself imagine something more: a world where they weren’t born on opposite sides of a terrible conflict, where he wasn’t born a prince and Phainon the son of a farmer. He presses a kiss to Phainon’s knuckles, and Phainon rests his lips on the curve of Mydei’s shoulder, and Mydei pretends they aren’t on the front at all.

There is no pretending in the morning. In the morning, he rises with the sun, and his somatophylakes arrive to help him armor himself. They laugh and slap him on the back, the shoulders as they strap him into his tassets, his chest plate, his bracers. Leonnius speaks of Phylo’s and the agora; Peucesta, a newly composed song he thinks Phainon will enjoy; Ptolemy, a story he thinks Mydei should read. Their words betray them. Every last one of them is afraid this will be the last morning they see him alive, but they shouldn’t fear.

Nothing has killed Mydei yet. Castorice will be no different.

Only Hephaestion is silent, standing surprisingly close to Phainon. They don’t speak, but there’s some strange difference in the way they occupy such proximity. No one else remarks on it, and Mydei, uninterested in

sparking conflict, keeps his own counsel as anticipation for the battle flutters in his stomach.

This, at least, is a familiar feeling: the tightening of his muscles, the need to get a weapon in his hands, the excitement and thrill of oncoming combat. He has always enjoyed testing himself against new trials, and this won’t be any different. The rules will be, certainly—this won’t be armed combat against an opponent trying to gut him but rather him attempting to fend off someone who wants to touch him. A new and interesting challenge.

When he emerges from the tent, flanked by his somatophylakes, with Phainon trailing behind, the air in the camp is hums with a strange tension. His centurions are all waiting for him, armored and ready to observe the battle, but their helms can’t hide their mixed emotions. Some are clearly jubilant, expecting this, as Mydei must, to be the final confrontation between Castrum Kremnos and Okhema. Their immortal prince will end Castorice and the war in one stroke. But there are those who are somber, those who, as Phainon, are possessed of a deep fear that Mydei’s immortality won’t extend to Thanatos’s right hand.

Leonnius presents his spear to him, and Mydei takes it, hefting it high. “Today,” he calls out over the hushed crowd, reflecting a little idly that this is better delivered to the entire army, “we put an end to Okhema’s tyranny! Today, I meet the Hand of Shadow on the field of battle, and I will cast her down for the glory of Castrum Kremnos!” The words threaten to stick in his throat. He doesn’t want this. He doesn’t want any of this. “You, my century, are witness to our greatness, to the righteousness of our course. We defend the Titan of Strife and his mastery of all lands and peoples, his right to rule us under the banners of Reason, Tenacity, Sacrifice, Honor, and Courage. We bring these edicts to the barbarians, the outsiders, and show them the strength of our convictions. And with the strength of our convictions, of your convictions, I will crush the Hand of Shadow beneath my feet!”

The century roars with approval as nausea churns in Mydei’s stomach. He doesn’t believe any of what he’s just said, and he fears a population that does. Castrum Kremnos is on the road to ruin, and there are no hands to steer it aside, none who can stand up to Strife.

He leads his century to the rest of the Kremnoan army, already gathered on the banks of the Acheron. Both armies are camped east of the river and just south of the nearby and very much destroyed city state of Ioannina. Here, a large bridge crosses the Acheron’s depths, and the Okhemans control it. The bridge is broad enough to facilitate a retreat if necessary, but it will be a bloodbath if that’s how this conflict ends. It’s clear to Mydei—and likely the other generals at the front—that Okhema is betting on breaking the Kremnoan troops by killing their prince and routing them beyond the ruined city state.

Mydei grips his spear. He wants none of this, not to see his troops die or routed, nor to see the Okhemans slaughtered in a mad retreat across the bridge.

Hephaestion approaches him as he surveys the dead field before him. Beyond the field, across the river, is another line of death: Castorice’s progress. She stands in the field already, all lavender hair and pale pink skin. Phainon was right.

“You have the blessings of Strife upon you,” Hephaestion says with the tone of a man who might no longer believe in his gods.

“Let us hope,” Mydei says, glancing back. Phainon stands with Mydei’s other somatophylakes, his expression unreadable. Mydei turns back to Hephaestion. “Hephaestion.”

Hephaestion doesn’t look at him. He surveys the field, too, his hands clasped loosely behind his back. “Mydeimos.” His voice is tight.

“I know things aren’t well between us,” Mydei says softly. He hesitates for just a moment and then sets his hand on Hephaestion’s shoulder. Hephaestion stiffens beneath the touch. “I… I don’t know how to fix any of it.” He isn’t sure he can. “But I want you to know that I’m sorry. For the pain.”

“Put this ridiculous sentimentality behind you,” Hephaestion says, shaking Mydei’s hand off his shoulder. “You’re not going to die today.”

Mydei huffs a quiet laugh. “No. No, I’m not going to die today,” he says, trying to believe it beyond any doubt, but that little kernel of fear has grown roots in his gut. “All will be well, won’t it?”

“Of course it will. Even if we must suffer your mother’s spy among us.” Hephaestion’s words lack their usual bite.

“He’s a good man, you know. Phainon.”

Hephaestion presses his lips into a thin line. Finally, he says, “I’m not sure that I would classify any spy a good man by nature of their duties and deceptions. But you’ve always been a decent judge of character.” He snorts. “With one exception. Or, perhaps, two.”

Now, Mydei laughs. He releases Hephaestion’s shoulder with a squeeze. “Well. There’s no accounting for taste, is there?”

“There isn’t,” is Hephaestion’s dry reply. He sobers. “Kill her, Mydeimos. Kill her, protect what you love, and put an end to this.”

Mydei tightens his grip on his spear. “I will.” He hesitates, suddenly keenly aware of how much he wants to go to Phainon, to… he doesn’t know what he’d do. Accepting or giving any show of affection from or to his bed slave would be wildly inappropriate. He should’ve said something—anything— before his somatophylakes entered this morning. Should have taken the opportunity to say a goodbye, just in case, perhaps.

But he’s not going to die today.

Under the eyes of the Kremnoan legions, Mydei strides forward. The weight and hope of a nation settles across his shoulders as he makes his long, lonely journey, as he approaches Castorice. She’s younger than he expected, barely out of her adolescence, her face guileless and innocent despite the lives she’s surely taken. The corpses of birds litter the field around her, the grasses withered to nothing, the dirt soft beneath his feet. A purple miasma rolls across the earth like so much fog, billowing out from her feet. Where it passes over him, his skin prickles with faint irritation.

He stops five paces from her, setting the butt of his spear against the ground. “Daughter of the River of Souls,” he greets her.

“Mydeimos the Undying,” she replies, her voice soft and mellifluous. “I am very sorry.”

That irritates him, and he lifts his chin. “Presumptuous,” he says. “Your Titan has no hold on me.”

“Death is the one inevitability of our world. Even for you, Thanatos counts your days.” She speaks like his death is a foregone conclusion, and that irritates him more.

But briefly, he entertains the thought of extending an alliance to her. Perhaps they truly could play at one of their own deaths long enough to satisfy the opposing side. Perhaps they could work together as allies, as he and Phainon have. Gorgo would know how to manipulate this situation as she has manipulated him, but he isn’t his mother’s son. He’s Eurypon’s child.

He lowers his spear, shifting into an offensive stance.

Castorice remains where she stands, the wind catching her hair and lifting it from her mostly naked body. There’s a sorrow about her that only infuriates him. She closes her eyes and bows her head—and if she’s going to be so foolish, so be it.

He lunges forward.

She whips to one side, stepping around him, and he turns with her, pivoting on the ball of one foot. He expects her to dance away from him. Instead, she ducks around the thrust of his spear and launches herself at him with a wild, reckless abandon.

Castorice is no wrestler. She clearly has no idea how to brawl. But she doesn’t need to. If one touch from her is the sweet promise of oblivion, he can’t risk letting her anywhere near him. His men might trust his immortality—he trusts his immortality—but he isn’t much of a gambler, nor

is he particularly reckless. A deathblow will slow him down even if he doesn’t kill him, and Castorice, while not a fighter, is quick. Extremely quick.

Ducking and weaving around him, she reaches for his back. He twists around and leaps back, putting space between them once again, but she pursues.

The more they move, the more the miasma pouring off her wafts around them. It swirls up from the ground, a translucent cloud. When he inhales, he breathes it in, and his lungs begin to burn—too soon for the pain to be exhaustion. The more of it he breathes in, the more his vision begins to swim and his chest ache. His legs tingle unpleasantly, and he almost loses his footing as he dodges her yet again.

Dread curls around his spine.

In any fight against her, were she a normal person, he would have killed her by now. But he can’t take risky strikes, can’t overextend, can’t leave himself exposed to the possibility of her touch. And she is more than a little wild in her own attacks, unpredictable and hard to read. There’s no fluidity to her movement, and while her own lack of experience should make her telegraph every move, he finds he mistakes her more often than not. An armed opponent shifting like that would have him moving toward her, and if he moves toward her, she will be able to grab him by the wrist, the arm, so he stays at a greater distance.

His spear swipes across her cheek, her shoulder, her side. He leaves lines of golden blood to drip down her skin but never manages to pierce her in any meaningful way. Miasma continues swirling around them, thicker and thicker, as though she’s deliberately churning out more of it. Maybe she is. It chokes him, burning his lungs and stinging his eyes. His grip on his spear weakens, and he realizes whatever resistance he might have to it as another Chrysos Heir is minor. If the miasma kills small land animals, given enough time, it will kill him as well.

This fight has a timer on it, but he won’t let himself become desperate.

He’s becoming desperate.

Sweat slicks down his back. His lungs labor heavily. His limbs grow sluggish, and his reaction time slows. He narrowly pulls away from Castorice’s grasping hands, panting hard. Stumbling back, he shakes his head, trying to focus.

More dread creeps through him, overwhelming in a way he’s unaccustomed to. A little anxiety about a fight is normal, but this is something else entirely, something all-consuming. It chokes him as much as the miasma.

Is it worth an attempt at telling her they are allies? Is now the moment he should speak? “Castorice,” he begins, but she lungs for him, and he twists away, raking the point of his spear across her belly.

A good hit, forcing her back. She gasps, clearly unused to the pain, and he throws himself forward. This is his opportunity to end their conflict, and he takes it, rushing in, gripping his spear in his weakening hands. He lunges forward, angling his spear to the side, with the intent to graze her ribs, to make this look like a death blow. To get in close and in that moment betray his people. He can’t betray his people. There is no honor in that, and he is nothing if not honorable. He—

Castorice’s eyes meet his.

He mistook her stumble as truth; it was an act. Victory lights her eyes as she steps to the side, as he overextends, as her hands wrap around his wrist and his forearm.

Cold. She’s so cold, icier than death, like the depths of a mountain river, and the cold spreads through him like a wave. It seizes his heart, his lungs. It chokes his throat, fills his mouth. He watches purple light ripple consume his arm, watches the limb disappear as the light travels up, up, up, until it’s eating his shoulder, his chest, his neck.

How surprising.

It doesn’t hurt.

There are two people on the battlefield below Phainon. There are two people, and then, in a ripple of violet light, there is one. There is Castorice.

A second passes. Two. He can’t comprehend what he’s seeing until the Okheman war horns sound, and then he’s moving forward, is shrugging past Mydei’s stunned somatophylakes, is reaching for Hephaestion’s hip for his blade, is on his way to—to what? Kill Castorice? To assassinate a woman who is and has been his ally?

Hephaestion grabs his wrist before Phainon can draw his sword, rounding on him with a look of fractured and broken despair.

Kremnoan war horns answer and echo Okhema’s, more like mourners’ wails than calls to battle.

He’s done this. Phainon has done this, has killed the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, and, now, as he stands facing Hephaestion’s grief, which can only eclipse his own, he faces his own death, too. Twisting his wrist in Hephaestion’s grip, he pulls Hephaestion forward, toward him. “Kill me,” he says as the war horns blare again, as the sound of marching fills the air. “You have to kill me.”

Hephaestion stares at him with red-rimmed eyes bright and full of unshed tears. “This is impossible,” he says, as if he hasn’t heard Phainon at all. Maybe he hasn’t.

Again, Phainon reaches for Hephaestion’s blade, this time with his other hand, and that snaps Hephaestion out of his daze. He grabs that wrist, too, bearing down on Phainon with tremendous strength, until Phainon, gasping, sinks to his knees.

“You have to kill me,” he says. “I have to—this isn’t—”

Hephaestion goes with him, releasing him, embracing him, and Phainon freezes. Hephaestion embraces him, clutches at him, and Phainon holds his arms wide to either size, utterly stymied. “You are the last thing he loved,”

Hephaestion says, grasping Phainon’s chiton in his fists and resting his forehead on Phainon’s shoulder. “I cannot—will not—end your life.”

Panic wells in Phainon’s throat. “I’m the reason he’s dead,” he says, shoving at Hephaestion’s shoulders. “Where is your hatred?” He has to die. Hephaestion has to understand that Phainon has to die.

“Dead with him,” Hephaestion says, gripping Phainon harder, and Phainon can’t comprehend this. He struggles against Hephaestion’s hold, only for Hephaestion to wrap one hand around the back of Phainon’s heads and bring their foreheads together. “He would choose you,” Hephaestion says. “Every time, he would choose you.”

“I don’t deserve that,” Phainon insists.

“You don’t.” He absolutely deserves that disdain. “But he would.” Hephaestion releases Phainon and pulls back, clasping Phainon’s right forearm with his hand.

Beyond them, the legions of two armies march onto the field where Mydei —where—

Eyes glittering, Hephaestion squeezes Phainon’s forearm. “On Strife’s own rock, this I swear.”

Phainon’s own eyes go wide. “No,” he says. “No, don’t you dare—”

“That your life is as my own, that I will bear your burdens as my own, that I will make your load lighter with my back.”

“Shut up,” Phainon hisses.

Hephaestion squeezes harder. “My blade is your blade. My breath is your breath.” His eyes burn. “On Strife’s own Honor, you are my brother, and I am yours.”

Horrified, Phainon tries to shake Hephaestion off him, but there’s nowhere for him to go. The other somatophylakes are there, surrounding them, and

Hephaestion drags Phainon up from the ground, forcing him to his feet. “I can’t accept—”

“It’s not yours to accept,” Leonnius says, taking Phainon’s arm from Hephaestion’s hand, his grip stronger still. He, too, is fierce as he recites the same oath, fingers digging into Phainon’s flesh.

This is the worst possible scenario, the worst possible outcome, as each of them swears to protect the life that Phainon needs desperately to discard. He is a dead man walking without Mydei, and their oaths mark them, too.

“The lot of you don’t even know,” he begins as Peucesta, the last to make his oath, releases him.

“That you’re a Chrysos Heir?” Leonnius asks. He snorts. “I’m not that stupid.”

Hephaestion slugs his shoulder. “I’m the one who told you.” He turns to Phainon. “You were extremely obvious at the Grove.”

Bewildered, Phainon drives both his hands into his hair. He’s surrounded by Mydei’s—by his own somatophylakes. Him. A slave. This is— “Surely you understand this will destroy your positions at court,” he says, desperate.

“Mydei loves you,” Hephaestion says sharply. “And we will honor his memory by honoring you. Let us deal with the court.”

Ptolemy clears his throat. “On the topic of the court,” he says, lifting a finger. “Who owns your slave contact, Phainon?”

Phainon, who has never once thought of a slave contract, who has no idea what a slave contract is, can only say, “What slave contract?” And he watches each of their faces crumble with horror.

“We need to find out. Immediately,” Ptolemy says, directing that to Hephaestion.

“Find out what?” Phainon asks.

They ignore him.

Hephaestion sets one hand on the hilt of his sword. “We’ll put the century under Drakon’s command with the order they stay with the main army. Ptolemy.” He inclines his head. “You’ll return to the palace as quickly as possible. Use whatever means necessary to quietly find out if the queen still owns the contract or if she turned it over to—” His voice catches. “—to Mydei. Bring word to us in Oleinus.”

“Why does it matter?” Phainon asks as Ptolemy nods again and retreats in the direction of the camp.

“Leonnius,” Hephaestion says. “Go to Drakon. Don’t waste time.”

Leonnius nods and trots off, too, leaving Phainon with Hephaestion, Peucesta, and Perdikkas. Perdikkas’s expression is drawn and nervous, and he fidgets, his fingers twisting together.

“We can’t stay here,” Perdikkas says. “Nor can we return to the palace without this information.”

Hephaestion grimaces. “If we don’t go back, our families…” He swallows hard. “The king will brand us traitors, and he will kill them.”

Peucesta swears and rubs his hand over his face.

“Would someone please tell me why my slave contract is so fucking important?” Phainon says, finally losing his patience.

Hephaestion turns to him, grave and somber. “When a member of the royal family dies, their slaves are put to death with them.”

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 12
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

They’re gone from the camp in an hour, taking only what they can carry.

“Aren’t you deserting?” Phainon asks as they ride for Oleinus. Hephaestion rides beside him, and the others surround them in a protective diamond.

Hephaestion’s expression isn’t reassuring. “Not technically. The five of us serve—served Mydei.” His throat works. “We didn’t have official positions within the army, and we’re not running away from Castrum Kremnos.” The yet goes unspoken. “But how the king sees it…”

“I still don’t get it,” Phainon says. “You hate me.”

“Yes,” Hephaestion agrees.

Phainon makes a frustrated gesture with one hand. “Then why?”

“Because I love him more than I hate you, and he would be furious if you died after everything he’s done to protect you,” Hephaestion snaps back. “It’s not that complicated, but you are extremely stupid, aren’t you?”

The smile that pulls across Phainon’s lips is frigid. “You have no idea.”

He waits the whole day for a moment alone, but even when they arrive at Oleinus, he doesn’t get one. They buy a single room and pile into it, ordering a bath. Hephaestion insists Phainon go first, and Phainon, realizing the only privacy he gets is the screen in front of the tub, doesn’t protest. He’d rather the clean water as he scrubs the dust from his skin. When he’s finished, the others cycle through. Hephaestion goes after him and then vanishes to collect food from the kitchens with Peucesta’s help, leaving him with Perdikkas and Leonnius.

Leonnius watches him as he sharpens his blade, and Phainon grimaces.

“Hephaestion I get,” Phainon says. “The others—no offense.” He nods to Perdikkas, but Perdikkas waves him off. “I get the others, too. But not you. Not considering the scales.”

Leonnius slides his whetstone across his blade, the sound of it awful in the otherwise quiet room. “Sometimes,” he says at last, “shit balances in ways we don’t understand. Sometimes, we leave it to Thanatos to take a pound of flesh from someone.”

“I didn’t realize you were a devotee.”

“I’m not,” Leonnius says. “But you get real friendly with death when you’re a somatophylax.”

Phainon takes a minute to digest that. “You’re not the only one.” He pinches the bridge of his nose. “You’ll kill me one day, won’t you?”

“Probably.”

“Why not now?”

Leonnius snorts. “That’d just devastate Hephaestion, and I don’t want to pick his ass up again. Your life gives him purpose.” His tone makes it clear what he thinks of Hephaestion’s newfound and certainly misplaced tolerance for Phainon.

Dropping his hands between his legs, Phainon stares at them. There was no way Leonnius would do him the courtesy of death, especially not with Perdikkas in the room, but it’d been worth a shot.

They hunker down in Oleinus, doing what they can to avoid attention. The rumors about Mydei’s death at Castorice’s hands arrive the next morning, bright and early, as they take breakfast. By early evening, the entire city sate knows the Kremnoan lines broke for Okhema’s forces and that Castorice marches ahead of the now-advancing Okheman army.

Instead of feeling relief, Phainon is terrified. The somatophylakes discuss what the advance means quietly, describing more city states that will be sacked and burned, more destruction, more death. Phainon wants to think better of the Okheman army, but he can’t defend them. They will do as all armies are wont.

He should have anticipated something like this. Aglaea always has plans within plans, but he assumed she’d been honest with him, and she wasn’t. She’s marching on Castrum Kremnos with Castorice at the front of her armies, and Castorice will do the same work as the black tide.

Ptolemy returns the next day, exhausted, horse run ragged, but with news: the queen still owns Phainon’s slave contract.

“We’ll have to return you to her,” Hephaestion says. They’re all in the tiny room they’re renting, crowded onto the too few beds. “Ptolemy? What can we do from there?”

Ptolemy shakes his head, spreading his hands wide. “Not much, I’m afraid. The queen isn’t sentimental, so it’s unlikely you could beg for Phainon’s contract,” he says to Hephaestion, who makes a face Phainon isn’t sure how to read. To the group, Ptolemy adds, “We’d need to buy Phainon through manumission or buy his contract from her. Both will be a hefty expense.”

“We could cobble it together,” Peucesta says. “Surely. We are all of us wealthy men.”

“But that wealthy?” Ptolemy asks. “Phainon is the queen’s slave.”

And Phainon is the queen’s slave due to an agreement with Aglaea. He can only hope that Aglaea may have voided that agreement by marching her army on Castrum Kremnos, but for all he knows, Gorgo knows this part of this alternative plan.

“There are standard prices for manumission, aren’t there?” Hephaestion asks.

“I doubt Her Majesty is going to be that generous with us,” Leonnius says. “The minute we express interest, she’s going to fuck with us. Especially if she still wants him for something.”

All five men turn to Phainon, who refuses to shrivel under the weight of their gazes. He sits a little taller, rolling his shoulders back.

“You wanna tell us why you were spying for her?” Leonnius drawls.

“Not particularly,” Phainon says.

Leonnius narrows his eyes, but it’s Hephaestion who speaks. “Surely, whatever you were doing for Her Majesty no longer matters in light of Mydei’s—Mydei’s death.”

Sighing, Phainon says, “She was worried about him after the two of you—”

“That’s a lie,” Ptolemy says, studying Phainon closely. “The queen has always used her interest in Mydei’s affections as a disguise for other motivations.” He lowers his voice, and it’s not a threat, but it’s close to one when he says, “Perhaps you should reconsider your allies and allegiances.”

Phainon laces his fingers together, gripping his hands. He’s reconsidered so much already, but there’s no way to explain that Ptolemy, to any of them, and he knows better than to try. He needs to get back to the palace, to get back to Gorgo, and he needs to finish what he came here to do. He needs to kill Eurypon. But, maybe, he doesn’t need Gorgo or her resources to do it. And if she was as unaware of Aglaea’s plan to march on Castrum Kremnos with Castorice as he was, she might view him as a traitor.

“Phainon of Okhema,” Ptolemy says thoughtfully, like he’s tasting the name, like he’s putting something together slowly in his head, and Phainon is sure he is. “Phainon of Okhema.” He cocks his head to the side. “Were you ever the queen’s spy?”

Leonnius scowls. “The fuck’s that mean?”

But Hephaestion has already figured it out and so have Peucesta and Perdikkas. Realization washes across their faces, and Phainon knows he’s out of places to hide.

“Inasmuch as there’s an alliance between Gorgo and Aglaea,” Phainon says softly, meeting each of their eyes in turn.

“The truth,” Ptolemy says, and Phainon could curse the man even as he’s impressed.

Leonnius mutters an oath as Peucesta and Perdikkas both sit back, stunned looks on their faces. Hephaestion leans forward, a sharp look in his eyes.

“You’re Aglaea’s creature, then,” Hephaestion says.

Phainon shakes his head. “It’s more complicated than that. But I was working with her, yes.”

“You were?”

“The current march on Castrum Kremnos wasn’t part of the plan we agreed on,” Phainon says. “I should’ve realized she’d have plans within plans, certainly ones I wasn’t privy to, but I—” He rakes a hand through his hair, frustrated. “I trusted her when I shouldn’t have.”

Leonnius holds up a hand. “So, you’re telling us—” He points at Phainon and Ptolemy. “—you’re telling us that the queen is working with the Goldweaver? To what end?” He scoffs. “To kill the king?”

The entire room is silent, at least until Perdikkas rolls his eyes and says, “Leonnius, really?”

Leonnius’s expression goes stark. “You’re serious? You’re all—you’re serious.” He leans back. “Shit. Shit. So, we are committing treason.”

“Are you?” Phainon asks, strangled.

“That’s your purpose, isn’t it?” Ptolemy asks. “Chrysos Heir and spy sent by the Goldweaver. Get close to the prince, and use him to get close to the

king?”

“But what does that have to do with any of you?” Phainon asks in return.

Leonnius scoffs and Peucesta murmurs with laughter.

“Perhaps Okhemans forget their oaths,” Hephaestion says, “but Kremnoans don’t.”

And Phainon realizes all at once that he’s not alone in this anymore, and that, perhaps, he never had to be. If he’d just been direct and honest with Mydei, they wouldn’t be here. He lowers his head in shame and regret, closes his eyes, and wonders if he could get his hands on a sword fast enough. Unlikely with all of them watching him.

It doesn’t have to be this way. It doesn’t have to go this way.

He lifts his face, surveying them. “Get me back to the palace, return me to Gorgo. Let’s…” His voice catches, and something horrible that he’s been ignoring the past few days wells up within him. “Let’s grieve.” That hits all of them, their expressions faltering, falling, blanching. “And then decide what to do. An army marches slowly, and Aglaea will almost certainly loot and pillage the city states in her way. Your own legions will regroup to hold her back, too. We have time. We have time for this.”

They return to the palace a day later, riding up the main thoroughfare to the gates as the common people of the city part before them, as they emerge from their homes, as they stare after them, whispers following close behind and spreading like wildfire ahead. The crown prince’s somatophylakes ride without him. There’s only one reason they would do such a thing.

Phainon rides at the center of the somatophylakes, mostly alone, hating what this says about him, too. Hating the message he’s afraid it sends. His torc has never felt tighter around his throat.

Throughout the journey to palace, they haven’t left him alone, his new guardians. At first, he figured it was because of their oaths. Now, he’s not

so sure. They watch him carefully, and if they’re all as clever as Ptolemy and Hephaestion, he’s sure it’s because they all saw him reaching for Hephaestion’s sword. He’s sure they heard him beg Hephaestion to kill him. And earlier that very day, Peucesta pulled his horse beside Phainon’s to offer him a word of comfort and to assure him that he won’t die, that he’ll be safe with Gorgo. It’d come out more like an awkward threat, and Peucesta had maneuvered his horse away a minute later.

They think he’s going to kill himself. They think he loves Mydei, especially Hephaestion, and he—he doesn’t know what he feels. Not anymore. He’s so tired as he dismounts the horse, as he slides to the dusty ground, as two palace guards flanked by four men wearing torcs approach in chitons too fine for most slaves. These must be the queen’s own men, sent to retrieve what belongs to her.

Hephaestion grips his shoulder. “Be smart for once,” he says softly.

Phainon rolls his eyes. “You—” He catches himself. Forces a small, sad smile. “I’ll do my best.”

One of the slaves steps forward. “Phainon. You are to come with us.” He is cold, distant, expression imperious, and he even manages to flick a disdainful look at Hephaestion, as though he is above the other man. Phainon regrets never learning anything about the Kremnoan rules surrounding slavery, but certainly a citizen like Hephaestion outranks even the queen’s slaves.

Still, he’s not in the mood to make trouble. “Of course,” he says, drifting out from under Hephaestion’s hand and away from the rest of the somatophylakes.

Hephaestion takes a single step forward but catches himself. He says nothing more, and neither do the others, but there’s nothing for them to say. They can’t declare Phainon their charge, not without causing too many issues for everyone. Slaves aren’t given guardians like them.

Phainon follows the queen’s slaves, the guards falling into step behind him, cutting off any thought of escape. But if he’d wanted to escape, he

would’ve done it on the journey back. Maybe he should’ve. Maybe he should goad these men into slicing his throat, if that’s even possible. Kremnoan guards are notoriously unflappable.

They keep to the servants’ passages, out of sight of the court, passages Phainon doesn’t know particularly well. Part of him wonders if they’re taking him to the queen at all. Maybe this will be the end for him, too.

Titans. There’s that ache in his chest, that hollow pain carving through him. He’s been doing so well ignoring it, but now it throbs and pounds in time with his heartbeat, and he wants to lean over and vomit. He wants to rip something, someone, to pieces with his naked hands until his flesh is torn and bleeding. He wants to make someone else bleed, the desire directionless, untargeted. It’s not rage, it’s something else, something he doesn’t want to contemplate.

One of the slaves opens a door ahead of them, and they emerge into a splendid, gilded hallway, with murals alternating between carved reliefs of the Titans. No, not the Titans. Just Strife. This hall is a homage to Strife, is thick with his power, and at the end of it are two doors, one twice as large and ornate as the other. It’s the other, smaller door he’s led to.

“Thank you, Iason,” a woman’s voice says as Phainon passes through the door and into a lavish, open-air room that looks onto a broad courtyard.

“Your Majesty.” Iason, the slave at the head of the entourage, bows deeply. With a gesture to the other three slaves and the two guards, they all depart.

Phainon is, after all this time, alone with the Queen of Castrum Kremnos, and he doesn’t know what to say to her.

She is as he remembers: red of hair, like her son, with flashing golden eyes and handsome features. Pins of golden laurels hold her hair in elaborate twists around her head. As at the party, the tied-on sleeves of her chiton fall well past her wrists.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” she says, rising from her kline.

He should bow. He doesn’t. He’s too tired. “Your Majesty,” he says with as much deference as he can muster. It’s not much.

Stoic, expression neutral, she approaches him. He expects her to touch him, to grab him, to slap him. She folds her arms before her, craning her head to look up at him, and she says, “You killed my son,” with so little feeling, as though she can’t bear to feel anything, that it breaks him.

His heart cracks open, his grief pouring through him, a legion of men swarming a battlefield wielding his own emotions as a weapon. They stab him through the heart, stab into his guts. Eviscerated by his own grief, he swallows once, hard, and locks every muscle in his body to keep from trembling in front of her. Tears threaten his eyes, so he tips back his head and gazes upward, at the marble ceiling painted with yet another mural of Strife.

Anger replaces grief, a violent bubbling of it. It burns through him, a blazing wall of fire, evaporating his tears and leaving nothing but cold fury.

Phainon meets the Queen of Castrum Kremnos’s eyes. “Eurypon killed your son,” he says.

“Fool boy,” she says gently. “Would my husband have orchestrated such machinations as these, would he have forced Mydei onto the battlefield, were you not here?”

“And you?” Phainon demands. “Are you not equally responsible, by that measure? Did you not put me in Mydei’s household?” He doesn’t miss the faint widening of her eyes at his use of the nickname.

“Yes,” Gorgo says. “A move carefully calculated to put you close to my husband so you could do what no other Chrysos Heir has yet to manage. But you were too busy—” She breaks off, her lips pressing into a thin line. “What have you to show for my generosity? My husband still lives and yet my son, my only son, is dead. You have failed your mission, and your mistress has betrayed me. You should not have come back. You should have run.”

“My mission isn’t over. Not yet.”

Her mouth twists. “Oh? And what do you hope to gain now? Do you think I will protect you as Mydeimos did? Do you think I will step beneath Periander’s lash when you have done me so great a wrong? What mother wants to bury her only child—her only immortal child?” Each word lands like the crack of a whip, one after another, and he can only imagine this is a fraction of the pain that killed Mydei.

Phainon can’t deny the truth of her words. He cannot refute her. She is one of the Moirae, casting judgement on him. No one is more deserving of a mother’s disdain than he is. His choices, his actions, drove Mydei to a true grave, leaving nothing, not even a body to bury.

“He could still come back,” he says, and then he flinches back from her, expecting a strike.

But all Gorgo does is jerk back as though he struck her. “Could still—could still come back?” she asks, her voice sharp with her disbelief. “We have heard the rumors. Your Goldweaver’s Maiden of War didn’t just kill him. She erased his physical form from existence. She unmade him. And you would dare to suggest he might come back?”

“Then why are you here with me?” Phainon demands, his anger overflowing, turning sharp and acrid. This woman is right. She is right about everything. He is a murderer; he murdered her son. He may not have landed the final blow, but his every action drove Mydei to that battlefield with Castorice, and now he is full of loathing. For her, for himself. Oh, how he hates himself. “It’s been days, Your Majesty. Days, and you’re here instead of weaving his shroud and—”

She moves so fast he doesn’t register that she’s kicked his knees out from under him until his back hits the floor, until his head cracks against marble, until all the air is knocked out of him and he can only wheeze desperately. She’s on him a second later, her knees pinning his arms to the floor by his elbows, all her weight bearing down. Seething, she leans over him, stray hairs floating around her head like a flaming halo.

“Weaving his shroud?” she asks with a laugh. “Weaving his shroud. Do you know how Mydeimos came by his immortality, you fool child?”

Phainon gasps for air, trying to fix his interrupted breathing, trying to fill his lungs. Speckles of color cloud his vision, and his head throbs. Distantly, he wonders if he’s bleeding.

“The Oracle at Delphi prophesied that Eurypon’s line would end with him, so my husband threw Mydei into the Sea of Souls.” One of her forearms presses against his throat as he finally catches his breath only for her to threaten it again. “I begged him not to. On my knees, I pleaded with him to spare our child. He spat on me and then threw him into the Sea of Souls despite my pleas. And as soon as his back was turned, I reached into that Sea to save my boy.”

She removes her weight from Phainon’s throat, and Phainon, wheezing, draws in a full breath. His lungs burn, but his tunneling vision corrects itself in time for Gorgo to hold up her arms, for her sleeves to fall back, for him to see stumps at the ends of her wrists.

“This was the price of my love,” she says. “My husband took my hands, and you wish for me to weave my son’s shroud.” She presses one of her wrists to Phainon’s jugular, and he tries to buck her off him. But Gorgo is a warrior queen, and she moves with him, throwing her weight against him, and he can’t dislodge her. “All men do is take. I should have expected nothing less. I should not have trusted your mistress. For here I am, without even a body to bury while my husband yet draws breath.”

And then she’s off him, standing to the side of him as if she never kicked into the ground.

He rolls to his side, grasping at his throat as he sucks in great mouthfuls of air, as he looks up at her, radiant and terrible.

“You will serve me,” she says, shaking her arms until her sleeves fall over her wrists. “You will do my bidding, do you understand me?”

Dropping his hand, he pushes himself to his knees. She thinks he’s a pawn —first Aglaea’s, then Mydei’s, and now hers in truth. But of course she does. She has no idea how many times he’s played these games. “I understand,” he says.

“I will use you for your intended purpose, Chrysos Heir,” she says, and he understands that for the threat it is, but he doesn’t care. Not anymore. “With you, I will tear down my husband.”

He gives her a bow, fluid and practiced. “I am yours to command,” he says, the lie coming easily. He has become such a good liar.

Gorgo smiles at him. “It is such a shame,” she says, suddenly gentle again. “With you, I could have had two sons.”

Though he’s played these kinds of games so many times before, she elegantly guts him with those words, leaving him reeling. He lives an entire life in her words, a life where he wasn’t a bed slave to a prince, where he and Mydei didn’t meet this way, where—but that life is as much a lie as his words. No matter how much he wants it, it’s a lie. There is no version of reality in which he and Mydei could ever be happy together.

He bows lower. “When do we begin?”

And then she’s a woman again, a mother instead of a terrifying queen. “Allow me to mourn.” She waves him aside. “The prothesis is tomorrow.” She turns cold, disdainful. “At least those rites, I can perform. Iason!”

Phainon straightens as the slave enters, and he wonders how much the other slave overheard.

“Iason,” she says, gentling. “Take Phainon to his room.”

His room is small, smaller than the closet that should have been his in Mydei’s suite, barely big enough to contain the hard palette that will be his bed. Iason bars him in the room with a bucket for his piss and shit. There’s no death waiting for him here, only misery, only his own grief.

Sitting on the palette, he brings his knees to his chest.

This has all gone so very wrong. Mydei is dead, and for the first time in three days, he lets that reality wash over him. Grief, despair. Rage and fury. He wants to wrap his hands around Aglaea’s throat and choke the life out of her with such visceral need that it frightens him. He imagines killing Eurypon, too—on his throne, by condemning him to the pyre, by slitting his throat like he slit the throats of that family. He detests them, loathes them. Every fiber of his being despises them so much he’s surprised his own hatred doesn’t somehow rewrite the fabric of reality, bending time and space to the force of his will.

Digging his fingers into his hair, he pulls at it until his scalp burns and his knuckles ache, until he’s surely bruised himself. He wants to scream, but he won’t give Gorgo or any of her slaves and servants the satisfaction of his breakdown.

Mydei is dead, and Phainon was the instrument of his destruction. Gorgo was right. Everything Phainon did, every action he took, sent Mydei onto that battlefield with Castorice. He drove Mydei to his own end, to dissolution.

There’s no way for even an immortal body to come back from such a thing as that. Mydei is truly gone, and Phainon has never been so lost.

He doesn’t understand why he’s so lost. Mydei was—Mydei was—Mydei was, and that cuts through him, tears through him, rips him apart until he’s nothing but a sieve for the hatred coursing through him. Mydei was, and he hates himself as much as he hates Aglaea and Eurypon and even Gorgo, because her machinations, too, put them in this place. She could have kept Phainon in her own household, could have found some other way to put him in proximity to Eurypon, but she gave him to Mydei. Mydei who was and will never be again.

There’s a small, square window high on the wall of his cell, and through it, he’s able to measure time. Another slave comes when the room purples with evening light, trading his slop bucket for a new one and leaving a tray of

meager food. Phainon forces himself to eat it, wondering if these are Gorgo’s leavings and wishing, yearning for them to be Mydei’s.

Darkness crawls across the cell, and he eventually lays down on the pallet. Eventually closes his eyes. Eventually dreams of the moment when Castorice must have killed Mydei, when she touched him, her hands on his arms, his face, his chest, melting him away into nothing over and over, and no matter how Phainon tries to run to Mydei, his feet never move from the hilly rise he stood on.

He wakes with the sun and the sound of women wailing. Wakes to more of an overwhelming grief that he can’t possibly cope with, and so he seeks refuge in the hatred burning within him. No one brings him food, but he supposes the entire palace must be at Mydei’s prothesis except for Strife, for even the Titans can be corrupted by death, and so have no place near it, excepting Thanatos. Nothing perverts the holy and divine like death. Phainon stares at one forearm, wondering if he’d bleed gold or black if he tore himself open.

The cell brightens. The wailing diminishes, and he wonders where the mourners will go, wonders if they’ll pretend to cremate a body they’ll never have.

He closes his eyes, resting his head against the cool wall of his cell, wondering when he’ll be fed. It’s almost noon, now, and there’s a strange swelling of distant noise. His eyes still closed, he tries to focus on it, but it’s too far away for him to make sense of it. He puts it from his mind and rises.

That distant noise grows louder, louder. He’s in the middle of doing pushups off the wall when he realizes it’s the sound of cheering.

Footsteps fill the hall, urgent and quick, slapping against the stone floor.

Phainon turns toward his door, a strange anticipation churning low in his gut.

Wood clatters against stone, the door’s bar tossed aside, the door itself opened. Hephaestion stands there, a wild look on his face. “You must

come,” he says before Phainon can even react to his presence. “It’s—it’s Mydei.”

Chapter End Notes
