chapters.title: Chapter 13
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Phainon and Hephaestion race through the palace, Phainon so close that his toes rake down the backs of Hephaestion’s ankles once, twice. Hephaestion doesn’t complain. He leads Phainon through the myriad and vaguely familiar hallways, taking him toward the front entrance. As they run past guards and duck around members of the court, those rich citizens Eurypon deems worth of his attention, the distant cheering grows louder, louder. Rumbling turns into thunderous cheering, loud enough as they approach the front gates that Phainon can finally make out the words of the rhythmic chant.

Son of Gorgo, crowned in blood.

Hope swells in his chest, choking his throat. Something warm grips his heart, something so much more than mere hope, effulgent and effervescent.

They round a corner, and Leonnius peels away from the wall to join them. “Perdikkas is already at the gates with Ptolemy and Peucesta,” he says, and Hephaestion gives him a clipped nod. “The queen’s there, too.”

But not, Phainon knows, Eurypon, who as a god must be sequestered from death.

They clear the inner gates, rushing into the courtyard. Mydei’s own funerary procession is there, led by Gorgo, gowned in wine-dark robes. She is still at the head of the procession, her attention on the main gates.

“Shit,” Hephaestion says, drawing to a stop. Phainon halts at his side, head cocked to the side. “Galenos is at the gates.”

“I’ll handle it,” Leonnius says, striding forward. He beckons for Phainon to follow, and Phainon, frustrated by his own uselessness, does so. There’s

nothing he can do here. He’s a slave to every person in this courtyard, to every person in this city state. He has no sway with anyone except Mydei.

Beyond the front gates, the chanting is thunderous. Son of Gorgo, crowned in blood. Gorgo herself, closer now as Phainon and Leonnius approach the gates and the guard captain on duty, is bloodless with shock, one covered wrist at her throat. The wind catches the folds of her chiton, and it ripples in the breeze, snapping like a bloody herald.

“Captain,” Leonnius says. He doesn’t bother with a salute, but Phainon supposes he doesn’t need to. He’s separate from the guard and military structure of Castrum Kremnos. “Why are the gates closed?”

Captain Galenos, however, does salute, crisp and practiced. “It’s against procedure to open the gates to a rioting crowd,” he says with the patience of a man who thinks he’s talking to an idiot.

“That’s a welcome party, not a riot,” Leonnius says. “And your men on the walls can confirm it. Our prince has returned.”

Phainon’s heart lurches.

The captain’s eyes flick briefly toward the palace. “The prince is dead,” he says, though his voice wavers with uncertainty.

A guard approaches with Perdikkas at his back, Perdikkas’s expression grim and the guard clearly pressed beneath his helm. He, too, salutes both his captain and Leonnius. To the captain, he says, “Sir, there’s a man—”

“Mydeimos,” Perdikkas says, crossing his arms.

“—approaching through the crowd.” The guard doesn’t acknowledge Perdikkas. “He has the bearing of the crown prince.”

“Open the gates,” Leonnius says.

“We cannot allow a mob into the palace,” the captain says, staring straight ahead, his posture set.

Leonnius steps closer to him. “You’d deny the crown prince entry into his own home?” he asks, voice low and threatening. “I can’t have heard you right.”

A wordless roar goes up from beyond the gates.

The captain flinches. “I—”

“Do you think the king will be pleased that you’ve refused entry not just to the crown prince but to the hero of Castrum Kremnos? The man who defeated death?” Leonnius presses.

The captain swallows.

“Open the gates,” Leonnius says again.

The captain continues to stare straight ahead, and he says nothing.

“Then order your men not to interfere,” Leonnius says, peeling away. “Phainon, with me. Perdikkas, to Hephaestion and the others at the gate.”

Phainon gives the guard captain a final look before following Leonnius. “Why wouldn’t he listen?”

“Loyal to the king,” Leonnius replies. “Like the vast majority of everyone here. And everyone knows that Eurypon doesn’t want an heir.” His lips twist in a snarl. “The sun will never set on Eurypon’s empire.” They reach the portcullis, surrounded by guards who take menacing steps forward at their approach. Leonnius glances over his shoulder, and Phainon does, too.

The guard captain is there behind them, staring past them still to his men. He gives a minute shake of his head. Whatever else can be said about Eurypon’s men, they are well trained. The guards stand down, stepping aside, and Leonnius and Phainon are on the winch, throwing their weight against it to turn it. The winch gives beneath their combined strength, but it’s meant for four men, not two, so they struggle, their feet digging into the ground as they labor to open the portcullis. The chains scream in protest,

pulling taut, but the portcullis lifts, and the roaring of the crowd grows louder still.

“To the gate,” the guard captain commands, and his men leave Leonnius and Phainon to their work.

“You really think it’s him?” Phainon asks as he struggles with the winch.

Leonnius grunts. “No one would chant these words for anyone else.”

Phainon’s heart lurches. “A pretender, though.”

“Would be put to death immediately. No one’s that stupid.”

The winch jerks to a stop, at its limit, and Leonnius holds it while Phainon secures it, and then they’re out of the gatehouse, they’re in the courtyard, and the palace guards are holding back a throng of people with the help of Mydei’s somatophylakes. The crowd’s chanting is deafening, but Phainon barely hears them.

His world narrows to the parting of bodies at the front of the crowd, people peeling back to reveal a narrow path and a man at the heart of the crowd with red-gold hair and leonine eyes, a man wearing a tattered chiton, bare-chested except for his tattoos.

Mydei.

Phainon shoves forward, through the line of guards, pushing them aside until he’s beside Hephaestion. Hephaestion who salutes his prince and joins the chanting of the crowd: Son of Gorgo, crowned in blood.

The other somatophylakes, too, have taken up the call. The guards say nothing as they form a barrier against the pulsating crowd, but their silence couldn’t matter less.

And Mydei. Mydei meets Phainon’s gaze, and Phainon’s lips part and his heart pounds, and he wants to go to his knees at Mydei’s feet. He wants to beg for forgiveness, but this isn’t the moment. It’s not his moment. It’s Mydei’s, and Mydei is resplendent in the afternoon sunlight, haloed and

golden and perfect, the warrior prince who defeated the Servant of Death’s deadly touch.

“Phainon,” he says, pressing his hand to Phainon’s face. Lightning ricochets through Phainon’s veins. Mydei’s touch burns, and he grips Mydei’s wrist with his own hand, caught in Mydei’s arresting gaze, drowning in it.

“You’re alive,” he says, half expecting Mydei to condemn him, because Mydei wouldn’t have died if not for Phainon’s presence.

Mydei laughs. “My deaths are cheap,” he says, and Phainon’s stomach turns. Releasing Phainon’s face, he turns to Hephaestion, clapping him on the shoulder. Hephaestion gives him a nod but doesn’t stop his chanting until Mydei, ducking through the line of guards, ascends the steps to the palace’s inner gates.

Gorgo separates from her fellow mourners, one arm lifted to her face.

The people surge against the line of guards with such force that Phainon expects them to break. They don’t, but Phainon stumbles back beyond the line of men, caught between the people and Mydei on the steps.

Mydei raises both his hands, and the chanting comes to a slow, echoing halt.

The silence is somehow louder, the world holding its breath, and Phainon thinks the man on the palace steps isn’t a prince. Mydei is a king.

“Castrum Kremnos,” Mydei calls, his voice carrying like thunder through the courtyard.

Shouts from the crowd, a raucous cheer. Men and women raise their fists and shout, “Castrum Kremnos!” in echo. Only when their cries have died does Mydei continue.

“Castrum Kremnos,” he calls again, “I stand before you having truly defeated death. The Daughter of the River of Souls took my form from me,

but I have returned from the depths of the underworld, escaping from beneath the thumb of Thanatos themself to stand before you.”

Another cheer from the crowd, booming like thunder. The guards strain against the pressure of so many people, caging them in the threshold of the courtyard, and a strange anxiety curls in Phainon’s stomach, a fear the crowd might surge forward and overwhelm them, might rush into the courtyard like a flood. And, too, there is the fear of where this speech might go, that Mydei, having been killed by Castorice, might not side with his father, no, but might still stand against Aglaea and Okhema and all she embodies.

Mydei lifts his hands again, calling for quiet, and he gets it except for the low murmur of people passing his words through the crowd.

“I come to you a changed man,” he says, “having put on my flesh anew, traversing the Acheron itself from the depths of Tartarus to return to you. I have come to you in this time of endless war, where peace seems so distant, to ask you this: have you not paid enough?”

Relief washes through Phainon, so profound that his knees nearly give out. Fear chases in relief’s wake, cold and cruel, and he shifts his stance so he can watch Mydei and the crowd and Mydei’s mother, too. Gorgo remains stricken, pale against her dark robes, and the crowd has gone strangely still, as though they can’t make sense of what Mydei has just said.

“Have you not paid enough in bread gone not to your tables but to the front?” Mydei asks. “Have you not paid enough in the limbs of your husbands and your sons, in children who will never come home, in empty bellies and barren fields?”

The only sound now is the murmur of people passing back Mydei’s words. Tension fills Phainon’s limbs, and he clenches his right hand in a fist, wishing he had a blade at his side. He stands alone between the crowd and Mydei, opposite Gorgo and her mourners, set apart, and he has no recourse, no way to defend himself—or anyone else—if the crowd decides it doesn’t like Mydei’s speech.

“Are you not tired?” Mydei demands. A ripple goes through the crowd. Unease, uncertainty. “Are you not exhausted, sick to death of hunger and loss?” Another ripple, this time of quiet agreement, and the guards are not so well trained that they disguise their own disquiet as they set their shields more firmly before them and reach for their blades. “I ask you, the people of Castrum Kremnos, is there no other way the world may live? Must we sacrifice our children to endless wars that see us maimed and broken and driven to the brink of starvation?”

Phainon’s breath trembles, shuddering as he inhales. Mydei has come back from death not to exhort the people to violence but to call for peace, and he could weep even as the fear remains—no longer that Mydei will incite more violence but rather that the people might turn on him. That the guards might turn on him.

“In this restored life, I seek to breathe new vitality into the empire of Castrum Kremnos, but we cannot have lives if we mire ourselves in death. We cannot pursue knowledge, cannot create, cannot renew, if we consign ourselves to death on the field of battle. Where is the honor in destroying ourselves for land the black tide consumes? Where is the reason in our repeated, endless sacrifice?” Mydei shouts each word, each question, and the crowd is silent except to relay his words, those at the front enraptured.

Only Gorgo is not fixed on Mydei, her eyes lifted to the second, interior wall, to the balustrade, and Phainon raises his gaze, too. There above them, above Mydei, stands a god who should be in seclusion, protected from the funerary rites of his own son.

Mydei raises his fist. “Castrum Kremnos, if we wish to see the rebirth of our own nation as a place of prosperity, we must find our way to peace!”

Phainon is moving before he has a chance to think, is rushing the steps of the inner courtyard. He slams into Mydei, yanking him to the side, as stone explodes where Mydei once stood, fractured by the tremendous force of a single, golden lance.

Mydei hits the stone, sliding across it. The pain registers distantly, the body on top of his much more presently, and the lance embedded in the stone where he just stood quite immediately. Screams erupt from the crowd as Phainon peels off him, as both of them watch Eurypon, wearing little more than a chiton of his own, alight on the ground beside his lance.

“Death has made you bold, Mydeimos,” Eurypon says, his lips stretching into a broad smile that doesn’t reach his eyes. His eyes are cold and dead, utterly lacking in humanity.

With Phainon’s help, Mydei rises. “Father.”

“Am I?” Eurypon asks. “Am I your father or your god?”

Mydei shifts his gaze beyond Eurypon’s shoulder, to where the guards keep back the press of people—who have, of course, opted not to flee—and to where his mother stands with the other mourners, expression inscrutable at such a distance. “Can you not be both?” he asks, meeting Eurypon’s flat eyes once more.

It’s a child’s question, one last plea from a boy loved only by his mother, a child cast aside and abused by his father, the final curl of smoke from the hope of a dying candle.

“No,” Eurypon says, gripping his lance and yanking its point from the stone.

And there it is, the last of whatever affection Mydei might harbor for the man who helped create him evaporating like so much dew on a hot morning. “You are mad,” he says, stepping forward, putting himself between Eurypon and Phainon. “And you aren’t fit to rule Castrum Kremnos.”

“I am your god,” Eurypon roars, echoing across the courtyard.

“Where is your honor?” Mydei demands. “Where is your reason? You are a defiled god, unworthy to lead our people.” He shifts his feet, bracing himself, but the impact of Eurypon’s attack still knocks him off his feet.

Air bursts from his lungs as he collides with a nearby column. His vision clouds over. He gasps for breath as his knees hit the floor, but he has no time to stay there. Eurypon is too fast for him to linger. Mydei rolls to the side before he’s caught his breath, his back aching, as Eurypon drives his lance clear through the column, punching a hole through it.

Distant shouts fill the air; he recognizes Hephaestion and Leonnius’s voices, but he has no time to wonder what they’re doing. He hopes they’re crowding the people, his mother, the mourners out of the courtyard, because this is not a place for humanity.

Eurypon wrenches his lance free of the column and rounds on Mydei. He’s fucked. Without a weapon—maybe there are blades in the guard tower beside the portcullis, but that’s so far—he has only his body to use against Eurypon, and there’s no way he can hold up. Deaths rendered by blade rarely incapacitate him for long, but that period will be long enough for Eurypon to turn on his somatophylakes. On whoever’s still in the courtyard. On Phainon.

Mydei crouches low as Eurypon rushes him. They collide, Mydei slapping aside the tip of the lance, letting it cut across his palm and shoulder. He slides backward, using his own momentum to twist away from Eurypon and drive an elbow into his back, into his kidneys. But Eurypon is a Titan, and Mydei only half a god, the promise of one. Instead of stumbling with pain, Eurypon releases a furious roar and rounds on Mydei, driving him back with wild thrusts of his lance.

The blade is barely visible as it punches through the air, whispering across Mydei’s cheek, his ear, his arms. He dodges each strike instinctively; though he’s not familiar with Eurypon’s particular style, he knows these forms, has trained in them since childhood, and reading them isn’t so difficult. This long-ingrained knowledge keeps him alive as he dances out of reach of Eurypon’s lance.

How strange that he’s not afraid. The lance blade slides across his side, and it hurts, but Mydei feels no fear, only a cool, dispassionate anger. This is the man who has held Mydei and the whole of Castrum Kremnos under his thumb for decades, who has tormented Mydei personally, who created an

empire only to drive it to the brink of ruin. Pathetic. This is a man who lacks all reason, all honor, and if he is allowed to persist, he will destroy the whole of the world.

Someone must put him down. Aside from Aglaea—and perhaps Thanatos —the other Titans have turned a blind eye to Strife’s advancement across Amphoreus. They have been content to let city state after city state fall, doing nothing to turn Strife’s blade and army aside.

Let it be Mydei, then, who will battle endlessly to his own death, who will turn the entirety of the palace into a battlefield if he must, who puts an end to this.

Sunlight glints off a blade, and Mydei lunges to the side. He catches Hephaestion’s gladius just above the hilt, grimacing as it cuts into the fingers of his left hand. Tossing it into the palm of his right, he whirls to face Eurypon, knocking aside the blade of the mad god’s lance just before it can pierce through his stomach.

“Do you think a blade will save you, boy?” Eurypon demands, bearing down on him with a wild flurry of blows Mydei can barely fend off. “Do you think you, a mere child, can defeat a Titan?”

He has to.

Sweat drips into his eyes and down his back. One of his borrowed sandals, poorly made, snaps, so he kicks both off his feet as he twists away from Eurypon’s strikes. He dances across the packed earth of the courtyard, desperately trying to do too many things at once.

Protect his mother and the mourners. Keep Eurypon distracted from the people, now well on their way out of the gate. Deflect attention from Phainon, who—who is no longer on the steps.

There’s no time to determine where Phainon has gone, not as Eurypon’s lance strikes faster, faster. Mydei pants heavily, muscles burning as he strains to keep up with the mad god’s terrible speed, as he barely manages to fend off hit after hit.

He misses, taking a nasty thrust between two ribs. He gasps, choking on the pain, as Eurypon tears the blade out of him sideways, ripping through his skin. He can’t falter. Doesn’t let himself give over to the blazing pain. He lunges into the space Eurypon has created, swiping his blade up, up, up, and the tip of his gladius cuts across Eurypon’s chest.

Gold blood pours from the mark, and Eurypon stands there, stunned.

Mydei doesn’t waste the opportunity. He lashes out again, thrusting his blade toward Eurypon’s soft belly.

Eurypon grabs the blade, ripping it from Mydei’s hands, and throwing it aside. He snarls, the sound barely human, reaching with gold-streaked fingers for Mydei’s throat, only to whip around at the last possible moment and duck beneath the flight of a javelin. The javelin soars over Mydei’s shoulder as he stands panting, as he stares past Eurypon to Phainon. Phainon who runs toward them, pulling a gladius from its scabbard.

He engages Eurypon, and they don’t fight, they dance. Mydei staggers back, one eye on the fight, disbelieving, as he searches for another blade.

Phainon moves with liquid grace, with the fluidity of a man who lives and breathes with his sword, not a farmer’s pitchfork. His footwork is quick, nimble, as he glides from one strike to the next, meeting Eurypon’s fevered attacks with measured ones of his own.

“Mydei.” He looks away long enough to accept the blade Hephaestion offers, his somatophylakes falling in around him. Hephaestion gives him a crisp nod. “We’re with you,” Hephaestion says.

And while that means the world to him, he shakes his head. “Not against a Titan.”

Leonnius watches the fight beyond them, watches Eurypon throw Phainon into a wall and Phainon recover with a speed that borders on inhuman. “No,” he says, expression fierce. “This a rebellion for men.” He grabs Mydei’s upper arm. “The gods should fear us. All of us.”

“We’ve got your back,” Hephaestion says. “Yours and his.” Mydei’s eyes widen, and he wonders what has changed in these three days he’s been dead that Hephaestion would willingly defend Phainon. “Command us.”

Mydei turns back to Phainon and Eurypon, watching with an even more critical eye as Phainon weaves between Eurypon’s strikes with the air of someone who knows this fighting style intimately. Perhaps defectors from Kremnos taught Phainon, but Mydei doesn’t have the time to play at analysis. He gestures his friends forward. “Leonnius, Hephaestion, shields.”

The two step forward, flanking him, holding their shields steady.

“Perdikkas. Peucesta.” They step up behind Leonnius and Hephaestion respectively, spears at the ready. It’s not an ideal, or even decent, shield wall, but it will have to do. He glances over his shoulder at Ptolemy, who stands unarmed. “Get my mother and the mourners out of the courtyard, then find your bow and take whatever shots you can.”

Ptolemy gives him a quick salute and hurries away.

“Harry right and left flanks,” Mydei tells his men, and they advance. “Break to protect yourselves, and if he uses the crystals to attack, get out.”

They’re too well trained to gainsay him, even though he knows they want to. He won’t risk their lives. Not for this. Not for Eurypon. And maybe a selfish part of him wants Eurypon for himself—for the lake, for Gorgo, for men like Strasanor.

Across the courtyard, Phainon has noticed them, and he has begun to do what Mydei can only think is impossible: he’s pushing Eurypon back. Phainon fights with a graceful fury that Mydei has never seen before, not from Phainon himself or any of Mydei’s own trainers. Not even Krateros is as fluidly beautiful, and Krateros is one of the best swordsmen Mydei has ever worked with, surpassed only by god-king Eurypon himself. But there is Phainon, beating down on Eurypon, driving him backwards one step at a time, until Mydei’s somatophylakes flank him and Mydei is at his back.

They harry Eurypon with their strikes, forcing him to fend off attacks from every angle. Perdikkas and Peucesta manage to land blows as Leonnius and Hephaestion ward off Eurypon’s strikes, but they are only men. They groan under Eurypon’s return attacks, staggering back, until Eurypon drives the point of his lance through Hephaestion’s shield and tears it from Hephaestion’s hands.

Hephaestion shoves Peucesta back, but the movement costs him. Mydei watches, one step too far, as Eurypon reaches out with an arm glowing virulent red with glittering crystal—only for Phainon to lunge forward and swipe his blade through the joint of Eurypon’s wrist.

Eurypon staggers, howling, as golden blood pours from his wrist. His lance clatters to the ground.

If they weren’t fighting a god, Mydei might call his men off. A man without a hand is surely defeated. But Eurypon is a god, and they must take every opportunity they can muster. While Phainon yanks a fallen Hephaestion to his feet and snaps, “Go, get out!” at him, Mydei leaps forward, gripping his blade overhead with both hands. He drives the point down, down, aiming for the soft hollow of Eurypon’s collarbone. This is his moment, their moment. He tastes victory.

Eurypon surges upward, grabbing Mydei by the wrists with his good hand, and his strength is great and terrible. His fingers grind Mydei’s bones together with such force that he drops his blade as pain claws up his forearms and into his shoulders. Grinning savagely, Eurypon’s stump still dripping blood, he steps into Mydei.

“Fool boy,” he hisses, and red crystal spears through the ragged flesh at the end of Eurypon’s arm, forming into a new hand. “Did you think—”

Phainon drives his blade through Eurypon’s spine.

Chest heaving, Mydei smiles, cold and cruel. “Did I think what?” he demands. “That we couldn’t beat you?” He laughs. “Old man, your time is done.”

Eurypon looks down at the blade protruding from his chest. He laughs, too, but his laughter is sharp, manic. It grows louder, hysterical, as an energy hums in the air around him, a vibration thrumming in Mydei’s very bones.

His eyes go wide. “Phainon,” he says, urgent. “Leonnius, Perdikkas—” But they’ve already thrown themselves back, stumbling away, except for Phainon, who barrels into Mydei. Mydei’s shoulders scream in protest as the force of Phainon’s impact tears him free of Eurypon’s grip, so agonizing that he thinks he might’ve dislocated both arms. He hits the ground, rolling with Phainon until they come to a stop, and the pain is nothing compared to the terror that grips him when he looks up.

The thing that has replaced his father, all bone-white and shining gold armor, with four arms instead of two, is not man.

When he was a child, Gorgo told him of Nikador, of the Lance of Fury, and his god form. She described a Titan, a god descended to Amphoreus to rule not with might and terror but with justice and honor, a creature of reason.

What stands before him, eyes rolling as it throws back its head and shrieks, is not a creature of reason. It is a god gone mad, drunk on its own power, awful to behold.

“Run,” he says to Phainon, grabbing at his arm and dragging him to his feet.

Phainon huffs out a laugh, wiping a streak of gold blood across his mouth. “Not a chance, Mydei,” he says. He squeezes Mydei’s elbow, hefting his sword. “I let you die before. Not this time.”

“That’s a god,” Mydei reminds him.

Phainon grins at him, and there’s a strange mania in his eyes, too, a wild look that Mydei has never seen before. Not on Phainon. “Good thing we’re demigods, then.” He slaps Mydei on the back. “You and me, Your Highness.”

“Your life—”

“Isn’t more important than yours.” He steps on the hilt of a nearby sword, kicking it into his hand, and he offers it, hilt first, to Mydei. “Together.”

Mydei stares at him. “To—”

Eurypon moves. Like a flash of lightning, the Titan of Strife is between them, lashing out with too many lances. Lances of red crystal descend from the sky, piercing the ground, and Mydei throws himself back, dodging between the falling missiles.

“Run,” he shouts at his somatophylakes. “Flee!”

On the other side of the courtyard, Leonnius drags Perdikkas to his feet, looking not at Mydei but at Phainon. Something passes between them in that strange, frozen moment. Leonnius nods, and maybe Phainon responds, but Mydei doesn’t see it, too busy searching out Hephaestion. Hephaestion leans heavily on Peucesta as Peucesta carries him toward the palace steps, staggering up it, and then all four of them are clear of the courtyard, leaving just Phainon and Mydei to fight a god.

They’ve never fought together, but Phainon moves with Mydei like an extension of Mydei’s own body. Mydei barely has to think and Phainon is acting as if he’s inside Mydei’s head, sharing his thoughts. Together, they trade Eurypon’s lightning-fast blows between them, shoring up each other’s weaknesses. They are, both of them, exhausted, drenched in sweat, the lone bastions standing against a mad Titan.

Eurypon summons barrage after barrage of lances, calling them down from the heavens themselves. They pierce through the palace walls, gouge deep into the earth, sending up sprays of dirt and rock, but when Mydei stumbles, Phainon covers for him, and when Phainon stumbles, Mydei does the same.

Red crystals explode out of the ground, ripping through the earth, forcing them apart, but they work back to each other, guarding each other as they take turns striking at the Lance of Fury. What first appeared to be armor is no more than flesh; they rip at it with their blades, bleeding the Titan, but that’s not enough. Mydei knows it’s not enough. They need to strike a

decisive blow, need to incapacitate Eurypon. They are mortal; Eurypon is not. They tire, but Eurypon’s energy seems boundless.

Once more, he splits them apart, and he turns on Mydei as Mydei sprints away, trying to put distance between them. Lances pierce his sides, and it’s with alarm that he realizes a dreadful truth: Eurypon knows his weakness. How, he isn’t sure, only Gorgo knows the full truth of it, not even his somatophylakes are aware, but Eurypon now targets his back, his spine— only for Phainon to rush in and bat aside the blades at Mydei’s back, giving him time to whirl about and recover.

This isn’t working. Fighting Eurypon fairly isn’t working. He keeps them at bay with crystal and lance, ripping into them, bleeding them, and they can’t keep doing this. They need a decisive blow.

Panting at Phainon’s side, Mydei wipes his brow.

Eurypon stands on the opposite side of the courtyard, laughing hysterically even now. “My own son!” he crows. “My own son seeks to kill me!”

As every son of Castrum Kremnos’s kings has sought to kill his father in turn, but Mydei doesn’t waste his breath on that commentary. “The coreflame,” he manages, breath coming hard. “We need to get his coreflame.”

Eurypon charges forward, separating them. They whirl away from him, coming back together for a brief moment.

They don’t have much time left. The wounds Mydei has accrued have healed, but he’s exhausted, and Phainon’s wounds can’t heal. Blood drips down his arms, across his chest, over his side. There’s a deep cut in the meat of his thigh. Phainon will die if they don’t deal with this quickly, bleeding out in the courtyard.

“Make an opening. Get his lance out of his hands,” Phainon says. “I’ll hold him. You—”

Lances hammer down from the sky, forcing them apart once more, but it’s a good plan.

Mydei rushes Eurypon, baiting him, distracting him, turning him away from Phainon until Phainon can get behind him. Until Phainon can lunge for Eurypon’s back. Strong arms wrap around Eurypon’s chest from behind, and Phainon slings his legs around Eurypon’s waist. He flexes, straining, and uses his own momentum to take Eurypon to the ground.

In an instant, Mydei is on them both, straddling the mad god’s stomach, helping Phainon to hold him down. It’s not that Phainon is stronger than Eurypon. He’s not. He can’t be. Eurypon is a full god, and Phainon merely a Chrysos Heir with the capacity to become one, but Phainon moves as though he knows what Eurypon will do. As though he’s done this before, as though he’s intimately familiar with how Eurypon reacts to being bound.

Mydei brings his blade to Eurypon’s throat.

“You won’t do it,” Eurypon rasps, his voice wrecked from his hysterical laughter. “You won’t—”

Mydei does. He slices the blade through Eurypon’s neck without any hesitation. The thing beneath him isn’t his father, isn’t his god, isn’t any god worthy of worship, and he slays him.

Throwing aside the gladius as Eurypon chokes on his own blood, Mydei reaches for Eurypon’s chest. Something deep inside him vibrates like struck crystal, resonant with something else inside Eurypon—and he wants to reject it. Wants to reject anything he shares with Eurypon. But this must be their blood, not the blood of family but that of divinity. His golden blood and Eurypon’s harmonizing as Mydei grasps some strange power in the aether itself.

It shouldn’t be him. This shouldn’t be him. He wants nothing of his father, not even the power of a coreflame, but there’s no one else except Phainon, and Phainon is many things but he is not the embodiment of Strife. Mydei isn’t, either. Mydei has rejected Eurypon’s vision for Castrum Kremnos, the empire, its war, its deaths. He doesn’t want anything to do with it, sees no

honor in it. But giving up the coreflame means turning it over to Phainon, and Phainon—Phainon possesses yet too many secrets to be given such an overwhelming power that will surely drive him to madness, too.

There is no choice. This, then, must be Gorgo’s ultimate goal. Not just to see her husband killed but her son ascended to godhood, and for a single, aching moment, Mydei feels used. Feels taken advantage of. He never wanted this. Never wanted to kill his father, to slay a god, to pick up the mantle of Strife. Eurypon’s vision of Strife was never one Mydei wanted to emulate. To be a Titan is to be bound by power and ritual and ancient law that Mydei wants nothing of, but he has no other choice.

A crystallized teardrop emerges from Eurypon’s chest.

He gurgles, gasping, flailing weakly in Phainon’s hold.

Mydei pities him. The mad god, reduced to this, alone, not even his guards attempting to defend him.

Leaning over Eurypon’s body, Mydei finds his eyes in the strange form he possesses. “I will be better than you,” he vows. “In every possible way, I will be better.” And he takes the coreflame in his hand and presses it to his own chest.

Lightning fills his veins. Fire burns through him. He gasps, eyes going wide, as power surges beneath skin that is suddenly too tight, too small, to contain everything he is. Beneath him, Eurypon’s armor fades, leaving only a broken, bloodied man with his throat slit wide open, and Mydei burns. He shoves himself to his feet and stumbles away from Eurypon’s dying body and from Phainon, certain he must be blazing.

Pain radiates through him, consumes him. He goes to his knees, bending until his forehead touches the ground, and he screams through it as power remakes him, reforms him, forging him in the crucible of a burning star. He is suddenly so much more than he was, his world expanding the power of Strife and conquest and destruction.

And then Phainon’s hands are on him, cool in comparison to the burning of his own flesh, gentle on his back, his shoulder, his face. “Mydei,” he says, and Mydei climbs on top of the power coursing through him. Mydei takes control of it, forcing it to fit his flesh, demanding it bow to him instead of breaking him.

The pain diminishes. The burning fades.

He is on his knees in the middle of the courtyard, golden blood all over his hands, splattered on his chest, and he looks up to find Phainon before him, a terrified look on his face.

“Mydei?” he asks, his hands like cool water against Mydei’s cheeks.

Mydei wraps his fingers around Phainon’s wrists. “I am—myself,” he manages, hoarse.

Relief washes over Phainon’s face. He bends forward, resting his forehead against Mydei’s. “Thank all the Titans,” Phainon breathes.

The courtyard around them is silent, Eurypon’s death rattles quiet, now. There are no crowds chanting Mydei’s name, no guards cheering his victory, only the quiet susurration of the wind through the strawberry trees.

And then Gorgo’s voice cuts through the silence. “Hail, Mydeimos, Savage God, Master of Legions, and Lance of Fury,” she calls.

He turns toward her voice, turns to find her standing atop the stairs to the inner gates, her veil thrown back from her hair, her expression fierce.

“Hail,” she calls out again. “Hail the King of—”

Mydei rises. “No,” he says, and his voice carries like thunder through the courtyard, silencing her.

Behind her, there is an army of people. His somatophylakes stand flanked by members of the court, those rich citizens who curried Eurypon’s favor. They have seen everything, he is certain. They watched him take the

coreflame of Strife, and they know he is their god and their king, but he doesn’t want it. Doesn’t want any of it.

Gorgo descends the stairs toward Mydei, lifting her arms as though to embrace him, and he is horrified to realize he wants to step back. That same feeling washes over him, the sense that his own mother used him, and it takes everything he is not to pull away from her. “Strife is complete once more in you, my son,” she says, her voice pitched lower so that only he and Phainon can hear. “His honor and reason are restored—in you.”

“What do you mean?” Mydei demands, a cold dread griping him.

“Strife has always been made of his tenacity, his courage, his sacrifice, reason, and honor, but your father cast off reason and honor,” Gorgo says, low and urgent. She lowers her arms, the wind catching her robes. “He thought them useless. Before he could seal them beyond reach, I used sorcery to bind them to you.”

Mydei recoils.

Phainon touches his arm, a steadying presence, but otherwise says nothing. His expression is a strange mix of pensive and disbelief, though Mydei is reeling too much to understand that combination.

“You—did what?” he asks, stunned.

Gorgo leans toward him, pressing one wrist to her chest. “I bound reason and honor to you when you were freshly born, on the same night your father split those aspects away from himself, and when he discovered the truth, he sought to throw you into the Sea of Souls.”

“He drove himself mad,” Phainon says.

“Yes.” Gorgo nods. “He thought honor and reason had no bearing, no meaning. That they were lesser traits for Strife to embody, so he cast them aside, but I knew if we were to have peace, we would need them reunited once more.” She smiles at Mydei, and Mydei can’t help but feel he is about

to devastate her. “Behold the Titan of Strife,” she shouts for the onlookers to hear. “Mydeimos, the Lance of Fury, the king of—”

“I am no king,” Mydei says, turning away from Gorgo. He approaches Eurypon’s corpse, looking down at it, and the blood that pools around the fallen Titan’s ruined throat. Bending down, he takes the laurel crown from Eurypon’s head, and he holds it up for the crowd of onlookers to see.

The guards begin to pour through the gate, murmuring with alarm at the sight of their fallen king and Titan, but no one approaches Mydei.

“I am no king,” he says again. “For decades, the god-king Eurypon has led Castrum Kremnos closer and closer to ruin. No more. The crown of Castrum Kremnos will no longer rest on the head of the Titan of Strife.”

“Mydeimos,” Gorgo whispers, her expression stark and face blanched. “Mydeimos, what are you doing?”

He turns to her, approaching with the laurels held high, and Phainon slips behind her, caging her in, intuiting Mydei’s purpose only a moment before Gorgo does. She has no time to duck away. Mydei lowers the laurel crown onto her shining copper hair.

“Hail, Gorgo!” he shouts, turning first to the guards, who are the most immediate danger, who have been trained not to be loyal to the crown but to Eurypon.

The guard captain looks at Eurypon’s corpse. Looks at Mydei. Looks at Gorgo. His mental arithmetic doesn’t take him long. He clearly understands his position, and he lifts his fist in salute. “Hail, Gorgo!” he calls, and his men fall in line, offering salutes of their own and echoing his cry.

“Hail, Gorgo!” Mydei shouts again, turning this time to the stairs, to the inner gates, to the congregated crowd of onlookers, those noble citizens and members of the military. These represent dangers less immediate but no less crucial, for if Gorgo has no support from them, her rule has no legitimacy.

His somatophylakes respond first. “Hail, Gorgo!” Hephaestion shouts. The others take up the cry, and the pressure of their ready acceptance ripples through the crowd. The citizens echo Hephaestion, but Mydei notices among them the silent generals once allied with his father.

“You mustn’t,” Gorgo whispers, harsh.

Mydei turns to her once again, dropping his hands from her crown. “It is the duty of Strife to hold back the black tide,” he says, loud enough for the guards and the watching crowd to hear. “But not to rule. The rule of Castrum Kremnos passes to Queen Gorgo, and I will turn my attention toward the tide, to hold it back, to protect Amphoreus as Strife did in decades past.”

“Good,” says a new voice, a familiar voice.

The guards react as they were trained, turning their spears on a green-haired man with an eyepatch, barring Anaxagoras from stepping through the main gate and into the courtyard.

He stands with his hands behind his back, his expression placid. “Good,” he says again, speaking directly to Mydei, “because the black tide has overtaken the Grove.”

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 14
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

With only three generals, Themistocles among them; Mydei’s somatophylakes, including Phainon; Gorgo; and Anaxagoras and a young, pink-haired woman who follows behind him, Eurypon’s war room feels empty. Mydei isn’t surprised that the bulk of generals aren’t here, though; they shuffled away in the chaos that followed Anaxagoras’s announcement in the courtyard, slinking into the shadows, presumably to flee the palace itself. Well Mydei knows that plenty of them were only loyal to Eurypon and the crown out of fear, but others were loyal for the rewards he gave them, and now is as good a time as any for generals in either category to escape.

He wonders if he’s a terrible man for mourning the lack of generals more than Eurypon’s death. There is no sorrow within him for the man who was the Strife Titan. No part of him regrets what he did in the courtyard, and he wonders if that doesn’t make him a horrible man, a terrible son. But Eurypon was barely his father, did little more than spend his seed inside of Gorgo to create him; he deserves no grief and less regret.

His eyes drift across the people at the war table, over Themistocles, whose presence surprises him. Themistocles was his father’s most loyal general, and yet here he stands beside Gorgo. Anaxagoras is across from them, his hands braced on the table, that bright-eyed girl at his back, and Mydei’s somatophylakes fill in the spaces between. Phainon lingers behind Hephaestion, beyond the end of the table, his expression a study in neutrality.

Mydei watches him, wary, curious, uncertain. No mere spy, no farmer’s son, could have fought Eurypon the way Phainon did. There is so much more to Phainon than what he’s revealed, and they will need to discuss all of it if there is to be trust between them.

Their eyes meet. Phainon looks away first. His expression is too inscrutable to read.

“—tide is Amphoreus’s most immediate concern,” Anaxagoras is saying, speaking directly to Gorgo.

“You will address the king of Castrum Kremnos,” one of the generals snaps, and Mydei resists the urge to turn his eyes to the heavens in supplication— if only because he is now one of the Titans to which men pray, but also in an effort not to reveal his own exasperation.

He turns to the general. “Did I not give the crown to my mother?” he asks.

“Indeed,” Gorgo says dryly, “Mydeimos abdicated in front of the court and other numerous witnesses.”

“By laws both ancient and modern, Her Majesty now the queen of Castrum Kremnos,” Themistocles says to the general, his expression frigid, and Mydei wonders at that. Wonders if there isn’t something between Themistocles and his mother that he’s missed in these recent months. “Anaxagoras is right in addressing her.”

The general’s face mottles red, but he gives a stiff nod of his head to Gorgo while Anaxagoras rolls his eyes and drawls, “Now that you have the order of succession ironed out, can we focus on what matters? The black tide will be on Castrum Kremnos inside of a week.”

That stuns everyone at the table into momentary silence, until Themistocles leans over the war table and assembles pieces representative of legions around the Grove. “Show us,” he says.

“I can do better,” Anaxagoras says, extending his hand. “Hyacinthia.” The girl, Hyacinthia, reaches into a bag at her side and removes from it a rolled parchment. Anaxagoras takes it and snaps it open, laying it across a clear space on the table.

As one, all the men surrounding the table except for Hephaestion lean over the map, and they take in a collective breath. Mydei rubs a hand over his

face, staring at the detail of the black tide’s advancement, at the notations Anaxagoras has made of its inevitable progress toward Castrum Kremnos.

“This is accurate?” Themistocles demands. “What proof have we that you aren’t lying to us?”

Anaxagoras makes a derisive noise. “Why would I waste my time—?”

But Hephaestion, who had turned away to accept another rolled parchment from a servant, unrolls a second map. “I can confirm it,” he says, laying his map across the table, too.

“What is this?” Gorgo asks.

“A map,” Anaxagoras volunteers.

The rest ignore him.

“I’ve had my own men keeping an on the black tide’s progress,” Mydei admits, “but this…” There are miles of difference between the edge of the black tide on Anaxagoras’s map and Hephaestion’s. “This is too quick a change.”

Anaxagoras shakes his head. “The tide’s forward momentum has increased exponentially these past few weeks,” he says, indicating its progress on both Hephaestion’s map and his own, showing where the progress is mirrored. “See here, it was here two weeks ago, and it covered twice the distance between these two city states in half the time it took to reach between these. If the progress is dated correctly on your man’s map—”

“It is,” Hephaestion says.

“—then we can confirm the two maps show the same rates of change.” Anaxagoras taps on the black tide’s closest frontier line on his own map. “A week,” he says again, and Mydei inhales deeply. That’s barely enough time for an evacuation, and they will certainly need to evacuate. “And you will notice something particularly strange about both maps,” Anaxagoras adds.

Mydei leans closer, peering at the lines describing the black tide’s most recent front on both maps. His eyes go wide, and he parts his lips to speak.

“The black tide points toward Okhema,” Phainon says before Mydei can.

Mydei lifts his eyes to Phainon, who remains behind Hephaestion. Perhaps if he craned his head, he might be able to see the table, but surely not clearly enough to make such an observation.

Again, Phainon meets his eyes. Again, Phainon looks away.

Themistocles utters a mild oath to ward off evil. “Its path will take it directly though Castrum Kremnos,” he observes.

“As I have intimated,” Anaxagoras snaps, clearly irritated. He jabs a finger at the map. “If the tide continues, it will destroy the entirety of the known world.”

“Then we will send Mydeimos,” Gorgo says. “Strife is the tide’s ancient enemy. He will push it back.”

“Will we trust a man who abandoned his birthright to uphold his oaths?” another of the generals demands.

Themistocles frowns. “And what of the Goldweaver’s armies?” he asks. “Do any of us think she will withdraw in the face of the black tide?”

“Let her conquer an empty city,” Hephaestion volunteers. “Evacuate Castrum Kremnos.”

“And then we will leave our women, children, and elders vulnerable to her forces,” Themistocles says.

Anaxagoras scoffs. “They’ll die regardless if you stay here,” he says.

“Who’s to say the people will accept their new queen while Mydeimos yet lives,” that first general says, pounding his fist on the table.

The gathering turns to shouting—Themistocles maintains his concerns over Aglaea’s forces, which one of the generals insists will have to turn back or come face to face with the tide as well. Anaxagoras is relentless about the tide’s approach not just on Castrum Kremnos but on Okhema as well, and Gorgo takes up the position that Aglaea isn’t unreasonable, that she, in the face of certain destruction, would welcome Castrum Kremnos’s vulnerable population. Anaxagoras is quick to point out that falling back to Okhema won’t save anyone.

Quickly, the back and forth devolves into insults, though Mydei is amused by how Anaxagoras manages to position himself as the mental superior to them all while slinging as much verbal mud as the rest of them. His head begins to throb, but he’s quick to note that though even his somatophylakes join in, Phainon is uncharacteristically silent. He regards the maps over Hephaestion’s shoulder, his jaw flexing.

He knows something about this. Somehow, Phainon knows something about Anaxagoras’s map, or perhaps the black tide itself. Mydei leans over the table, parting his lips to call Phainon’s name.

“Enough!” Gorgo shouts, throwing both arms in the air with enough force that her long sleeves fall away from her wrists. All of the generals but Themistocles look away; Anaxagoras, always the contrarian, looks too closely, as if he can discern some fundamental truth about Gorgo through the loss of her hands. “Enough,” Gorgo says again in the quiet that follows. “My son has returned from the dead, Eurypon’s body is still warm, the vast majority of our generals have deserted us, and the transfer of power from Mydeimos to me isn’t yet complete.” She closes her eyes for the briefest of moments. “It has been… a long day.”

A murmur of assent ripples around the table.

“The black tide will be here in a week, but we can take this afternoon and evening to rest,” she says. “These few hours won’t hurt us.”

“Won’t they?” Anaxagoras asks sharply.

Gorgo fixes him with a cold look, one that quailed even Mydeimos as a boy, but Anaxagoras doesn’t back down. “They will not,” Gorgo insists. “None of us are ready to make decisions in this moment. I will find a room for you and your student, Anaxagoras. The rest of you are dismissed.”

The generals push away from the table, but Themistocles lingers. Mydei’s somatophylakes drift into a clump around Phainon—and how strange that is to see—as Hyacinthia approaches them with an offer of healing. Mydei steps forward; she is a stranger, he doesn’t trust her, not with Phainon, but Gorgo touches his arm in supplication.

“A moment, my son,” she says.

Mydei flicks one last look at his somatophylakes and peels away from the table. He and Gorgo move across the room toward the interior courtyard, and they stand between two pillars, silhouetted by the late afternoon sun, silent. Mydei doesn’t know what to say to her. She used him. He killed her husband, her king, and took Strife’s power into himself, exactly as she must have wanted.

“I…” He can’t bring himself to apologize, and he wonders if he should hate himself for that, but nor can he rail against her.

Gorgo shakes her head. “No,” she says softly. “You needn’t apologize to me. My husband died long ago when he separated himself from his honor and his reason in pursuit of building an empire. The Titan you felled today was not Eurypon, but rather a pale shadow of him. An imitation.” She smiles, but it’s a sad thing, and her eyes are wet with tears.

This guts him more than slaying his own father did, and he reaches for her, wiping a tear from the corner of one of her eyes. “Did you want this?” he asks. “Have you plotted this end over the long years?”

She leans into his touch and closes her eyes. “I had hoped,” she says. “If anyone was to end his reign, it was always going to be you.”

This time, there is no feeling used, only a hollowness that spreads through his abdomen. “Then why send Phainon to me?”

Gorgo opens her eyes and takes her face from Mydei’s hand. “Because I needed someone to catalyze you. I had hoped his presence would be radicalizing one. Aglaea’s letters to me made it very clear how much he loathed Eurypon.”

Did he? When he spoke of Aedes Elysiae, certainly there was hatred for the man who destroyed it, but Mydei struggles to think of other conversations where Phainon outwardly loathed Eurypon. Perhaps he took Mydei’s own warning to heart, burying his sentiments, but Phainon has never been one to be cowed. “I see,” he says.

She laughs quietly. “You don’t believe me.”

No, it’s not that he doesn’t believe her, it’s that the world doesn’t align with her premise, and it’s a strange thing to see someone fool Gorgo. He shakes his head. “I suppose I don’t,” he says, surprising himself. But there is more going on with Phainon than he knows, and it needs addressing before he is truly honest with his mother. “You took him after my death?”

“I did.” She regards him. “He is a useful tool.” Mydei tries not to react to that, but something must show in his eyes, in his face, because Gorgo says, “But not, I think, as much now that Eurypon is dead.”

That startles him, and he can’t hide his surprise at all. Gorgo never gives up someone she can user—he is proof of that.

“He’s yours again, child,” Gorgo says. “I’ll have Iason transfer the contract officially, and—”

“Don’t transfer it,” he says. “Free him.”

Gorgo lifts a single brow. “That’s your desire?”

Mydei gives her a clipped nod. There will be no unraveling of Phainon’s secrets if there isn’t parity between them, and he was never meant to be more than a spy posing as a slave. This farce needs to end.

“Then it will be done,” Gorgo promises him. “You have my word.”

They are, all of them, in various states of disarray, covered in blood and wounded, and Phainon, who tied off the gouge in his leg with a strip of his own chiton, wants to sink into the ground and perish. He is exhausted, and he shouldn’t be in this war room, but no one turned him aside, and now Mydei’s somatophylakes—his somatophylakes—have closed ranks around him as though to protect him from everyone else. Themistocles watches him with clear distrust, and he supposes that’s a reasonable reaction to his presence. A slave, a spy, his presence in the war room is a problem for everyone. He’s surprised Themistocles didn’t throw him out immediately, but maybe Gorgo’s silence motivated Themistocles’s own. Gorgo surely has her reasons for wanting him here.

He watches as she and Mydei pull to the side of the room, heads bowed, intimate space between them, a nervous frisson running through him. Gorgo controls his contract, Gorgo commands his obedience, but surely he has no use to her now that Eurypon is dead. Unless she means to use him against Aglaea, which—

“I’d like to help,” Anaxagoras’s young charge says. Phainon watches her through the barrier of his somatophylakes. There’s no guile on Hyacinthia’s face, no indication of deception, and she holds up both hands to reveal a healthy, verdant glow. “I’m a healer.” She was never one to lie.

“And a Chrysos Heir,” Leonnius says. “Where were you when we visited the Grove last?”

She smiles pleasantly. “Away. Please. Your companion is very injured.”

The weight of those injuries grows, and Phainon touches Hephaestion’s shoulder. “Let her,” he says, weary, light-headed. To his surprise, Hephaestion gives way, allowing Hyacinthia to approach.

Phainon holds out his hand to her, and she, though startled for a brief second, takes it. A cool, soothing energy rushes through him, and his skin tingles in the wake of its passing.

“This will do most of the work,” Hyacinthia explains, her gaze pointedly fixed on him and not at all on the somatophylakes who watch her like a hawk. “But you should still mind the deeper wounds.”

“Thank you,” Phainon says.

“It’d be better if I could—”

“This is enough,” he assures her, not wanting her to touch him more than necessary.

She frowns but doesn’t fight him, releasing him a moment later. Her healing hasn’t restored his energy—he’s still exhausted—but the wounds all over his body have closed, even the viciously deep one on his thigh.

“Would you tend to them, too?” he asks, releasing her hand and gesturing toward the others.

Her eyes linger on him for another second before she beams. “Of course,” she says, and she turns to Hephaestion first, laying her hands on his side as she explains her healing powers to him. When she moves on to Leonnius, Hephaestion drifts toward Phainon’s side, joining him in studying Mydei and Gorgo.

“It’s divine justice,” Hephaestion says. He speaks quietly, a murmur barely audible beneath Hyacinthia’s chipper explanations. “Three days dead and he comes back to slay a Titan with your help.” Awe flavors Hephaestion’s tone, and Phainon doesn’t quite know what to do with it.

“You’re not…” Phainon frowns. “Angry?”

“My loyalties have always been to Mydei before anyone else,” Hephaestion says. “And, now, to you after him. Castrum Kremnos will change.” His voice shakes with faint tremors. He’s afraid, and Phainon supposes he should be. “But we will weather those changes at his side.”

He wants to speak of Mydei’s survival, the reality of it only now starting to dawn on him, but he doesn’t have the words. His throat swells with

unnamable feelings, forcing him to swallow them back lest they choke him. Mydei is alive, and together they slew a Titan. Mydei is alive, and Phainon will have to answer for so many things.

He hazards a glance at Leonnius, who leans against the table as Hyacinthia sweeps her hands over him, speaking in low tones to Peucesta. As though sensing the weight of his gaze, Leonnius glances Phainon’s way and inclines his head ever so slightly before returning to his conversation. Strange how that isn’t relieving. Maybe ending Eurypon’s reign was enough to balance the scales in Leonnius’s mind, but Phainon doesn’t think that’s the case. Can’t.

“Hey,” Hephaestion says, and he lifts his chin in the direction of Mydei and Gorgo.

Phainon turns as Mydei approaches, an inscrutable expression on his face, and Phainon finds he doesn’t know what to do with himself. There’s so much between them, all of it confusing, that he remains rooted in place.

“Good news,” Mydei says.

“You’re alive?” Phainon proposes, a vain attempt to lighten the heaviness in the air around him.

A grin cracks Mydei’s face. “There is that. But better news.” Nothing can be better than Mydei alive, but Phainon remains silent. “My mother has agreed to free you.” No, not even that is better than Mydei being alive, because Phainon, despite the torc around his throat, has never truly been a slave, nor can he be kept as one.

But Phainon allows himself a surprised expression, a hopeful one. “Will she really?”

“Her word is good,” Mydei assures him, and he reaches forward, reaches toward Phainon, only to catch himself and pull back. Everything is strange, and Phainon doesn’t know if he should step forward and bridge the gap between them. They aren’t truly lovers, and Phainon’s actions killed Mydei.

He’s responsible.

“Thank you,” he says, and he means it, but this isn’t the place.

An awkward silence hangs between them, and he wonders if Mydei wasn’t expecting more.

Leonnius saves the moment, slinging his arms around both their shoulders and hanging between them with such aggressive cheerfulness and force that he drags them both forward. “No somber moments,” he declares. “One of you is back from the fucking dead! Both of you survived felling a Titan. One of you is a Titan!” He laughs, and Phainon is certain it’s a forced laugh, but it helps to break the strange tension even more. “We should celebrate!” Leonnius charges forward, all but dragging them with him, and Mydei begins to laugh, too.

“You fought a Titan,” Ptolemy says, clearly meaning it as a point of celebration. But instead of cheering, the group falls silent, no one willing to speak, to name the truth: Mydei fought and killed a Titan, but that Titan was his father.

Hyacinthia lifts her hands from Perdikkas, gives a brief bow in Mydei’s general direction, and ducks away, leaving them to their silences.

“Enough of this,” Mydei says, shattering the moment. “There was nothing of Eurypon left to mourn. There’s no need to dance around his death. Let us be glad.”

The strangeness persists even as Leonnius lets out a raucous whoop and begins to drag Phainon and Mydei from the war room. “We feast! We celebrate our prince’s return from death!”

“We must have the story,” Peucesta says.

Phainon allows himself to be pulled along, wishing everyone would forget about him, wishing Leonnius would release him so he could fade away into the aether. But Leonnius’s grip remains firm, and he hauls him and Mydei

—though Phainon thinks it’s mostly him—through the palace to Mydei’s rooms.

“A feast!” Leonnius says again, all but kicking Mydei’s door open.

Hephaestion clears his throat. “Perhaps,” he says, “Mydei and Phainon might like time to recover from their ordeal before you force feed them lamb and wine until they burst.”

Leonnius stares at him for a long moment. And then he breaks away from Mydei and Phainon, clapping his hands together. “Of course, of course,” he says. “For tonight, we’ll leave you in peace so you can rest.” He grins, broad and cheerful, as though he can’t read the room at all. “But tomorrow, there will be feasting, celebrating, and the telling of tales.”

“Tomorrow,” Mydei agrees.

And then they are alone, Phainon and Mydei, neither of them willing to regard each other, both looking everywhere else—the hallway, first, and then the half-packed room beyond Mydei’s door. His suite is quiet, devoid of servants, and Phainon finds the silence stifling.

He doesn’t know how to break it.

In the end, by unspoken mutual agreement, they make their way to Mydei’s bathroom, where the pool-like bath has yet to be emptied. Mydei sinks into it with a groan, but Phainon lingers at the edge, unsure of himself, of his welcome. He’s fucked up so many things over the years, and this… He could have done all of this better. Could’ve saved Mydei so many deaths. He sinks into the silence, rubbing his face, embracing the cruel weight of it broken only by the quiet sound of rippling water.

“Phainon,” Mydei says.

Not yet. Just a little more silence, even if it’s uncomfortable. He’s not ready to explain everything yet.

“Phainon, you’re still covered in blood and dirt. Come here.”

Phainon opens his eyes. Mydei stands in his bath, one hand outstretched, and Phainon shouldn’t go, but he does. He rises carefully, mindful of his leg, and crosses the bathroom. He steps into the pool but sits on the edge of it, watching Mydei warily, uncertain of his own welcome despite the overture he’s been given. “I owe you an apology,” he says. “Many apologies.”

Mydei approaches through the water, a cloth in one hand and soap in the other. “You do,” Mydei agrees, and those two words land like a blow even though they’re fully justified.

“Everything I’ve done here… you died because of everything I’ve done.” Phainon stares at the water between his knees, and he closes his eyes when Mydei shifts between them, when Mydei runs the wet, soapy cloth over his chest, his shoulder. He doesn’t deserve such care, but he can’t bring himself to knock Mydei’s hand away. “We thought you were gone.”

“I did,” Mydei agrees. “And I was. I spoke to Thanatos themself in the underworld.”

Phainon swallows. “Did they force you to bargain with them to return?”

“No.” Mydei’s cloth pulls down Phainon’s arm and then back up, a gentler caress than he deserves. It ghosts over his chest once more, his abdomen. “They haven’t had a hold on me since my mother plucked me out of the Sea of Souls.”

“But your body…”

“It came back to me as I trudged from the underworld as nothing more than a spirit.”

Phainon shudders, as much from the gentleness of Mydei’s touch as from the horror of his words. “Did it hurt?” he asks.

“Tremendously.” Mydei runs the cloth over the outside of Phainon’s leg, and he finally opens his eyes, watching Mydei wipe away the dust and blood that coats his skin.

Hoarse, Phainon says, “I’m sorry. For being the reason for that pain. You went because of me, because of what I told Cipher, and—”

“You’re not as important as you seem to think you are,” Mydei says gently, moving to Phainon’s other leg. “But you’re not wrong. If I hadn’t gone to the field to fight Castorice, you would have died.”

“You should have let me.”

Mydei’s lips quirk. “We’ve had this conversation. My deaths are cheap. Yours aren’t.”

His deaths are cheaper than Mydei realizes, but he can’t say that, can’t tell him that, not yet. Not ever, no matter how much some traitorous part of him wants to. Maybe this time… “Mydei,” he begins.

Mydei curves his hand around Phainon’s jaw, his thumb pressing against Phainon’s mouth. “Don’t,” he says, letting the cloth go. It sinks beneath the surface of the bath, and Mydei leans closer to him. “You aren’t as important as you think you are, except to me.”

Titans, it wasn’t supposed to be like this. Phainon’s heart aches as he presses a soft kiss to the pad of Mydei’s thumb.

“I would die a thousand times over for you,” Mydei continues.

Now it’s Phainon’s turn to say, “Don’t,” ever so softly. It truly wasn’t supposed to be like this, but here he is, so-called enemy between his knees, vulnerable in a way he’s never allowed himself to be.

Mydei leans into him, moving his thumb aside and pressing a kiss to Phainon’s lips. Phainon answers with a quiet groan, his hands sinking into Mydei’s hair, and he kisses Mydei back with a banked but desperate hunger. He died. Mydei died, and it shouldn’t have mattered to him, but it did, and for so many terrifying reasons.

Their mouths part, a scant breath of space between them. “I don’t deserve your forgiveness,” Phainon murmurs.

“That’s for me to decide.”

His heart aches. “Mydei,” he breathes, bringing their mouths back together for another kiss, just as slow and tender as the first. They linger over each other, lips never separating for more than the space of a moment, and the world becomes something soft and hazy. Phainon lets himself forget that Aglaea’s army still marches on Castrum Kremnos, lets himself forget that he just helped Mydei kill his own father, that the black tide encroaches rapidly on the city. He sinks into the heady burn of Mydei’s mouth against his, of their tongues sliding into each other’s mouths, of their rough and callused hands on each other’s faces.

The lingering throb in his leg becomes a distant afterthought, barely noticeable as desire hums through him. He wants to push off the side of the bath and sink into it, but this is good enough. Just having Mydei’s mouth on his is good enough.

Time crawls by, and Phainon measures its passing in the way Mydei gasps quietly against his lips, in the way Mydei’s free hand flexes on his good thigh. Mydei presses closer to him, and Phainon groans, trying to grind his half hard cock against Mydei’s stomach. The flex of his hips pulls at his still-tender wound, and he flinches back, hissing.

Mydei lets him go, though not too far. “This isn’t the right place, is it?” he asks, his eyes closed but his lips quirked in a wry smile.

Laughing, Phainon shakes his head. “No where’s going to be the right place with this wound.” He exhales. “But, Titans, I—” He catches himself with another laugh. “Is it weird if I swear oaths by you?”

“No,” Mydei says, biting down on Phainon’s lower lip until he gasps, until he rakes his nails over Mydei’s scalp. The pain is good, a sharp contrast to the ache in his leg and the smoldering pleasure low in his stomach. “Swear by me and me alone, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Among the many Titans, Mydei alone deserves Phainon’s oaths.

“I want you, Mydei,” he murmurs, thumbing the corner of Mydei’s lips. “I want to be inside you. But I am so damn tired.” He breathes out a laugh. “And I don’t deserve you.”

“That’s for me to decide,” Mydei says again. His hand pulls down Phainon’s jaw, resting on his neck and over the torc enclosing it. “We should remove this.”

Phainon tips his head back, giving Mydei more of his neck, and Mydei’s mouth brushes along his skin, punctuated by suckling kisses. “Aren’t there a bunch of legal processes that come first?”

“Fuck them,” Mydei says. He pulls back, pinching his fingers together, and in his hand he has conjured a small, red crystal in the shape of a blade. “Do you trust me?”

Phainon eyes the edge of that crystal, keenly aware of how dangerous it might be but equally intrigued. This crystal, wielded as an instrument of death by Eurypon, becomes an instrument of freedom in Mydei’s hand. “More than Periander,” he says.

Snorting, Mydei presses the crystal’s sharp edge against the torc. “Anyone is more trustworthy than Periander. Hold still.”

Beneath Mydei’s blade, Phainon doesn’t move. Barely breathes. Its sharp edge brushes over his skin as Mydei presses it through the metal of the torc, cutting it like so much fat. The two pieces of the torc fall away, and Phainon catches one half, Mydei the other.

“This is a despicable practice,” Mydei says, staring at the piece of metal in his hand before looking at Phainon, before letting the metal fall from his fingers to take Phainon’s face gently once more. “You have always been my equal.”

Phainon lifts a brow. “Was, maybe. Hard to be the equal of a Titan.”

Mydei slides his hand around the back of Phainon’s neck, drawing him close until their foreheads touch. “As men, we are equals, Phainon of Aedes

Elysiae.”

“As men,” Phainon agrees, and he thinks it might be true.

Mydei helps Phainon to the bedroom, where, thankfully, the bed still stands with a sheet still draped across it. Phainon sinks heavily onto it, grimacing. Pain throbs in his thigh, persistent enough to be distracting, and he sprawls across the bed with an arm thrown over his face.

“We should call your friends,” Phainon says.

Settling beside him, Mydei makes a quiet sound of denial. “Tomorrow can be for them and for the rest of the people. Tonight can be for us.” He lays on his side, his head propped in his hand, and he rests his hand on Phainon’s chest. His thumb rubs idle circles across Phainon’s skin, and Phainon melts beneath the touch. “This is the first time we’ve ever been truly alone.”

Phainon smothers a grimace, keeping his face relaxed and serene. “If only I had the energy to fuck you.”

“Is that all you think about?”

There’s a glib answer on the tip of his tongue that Phainon swallows back. Instead, he says, “I want to be close to you.” It feels like a profound confession, and he wonders if Mydei understands the layers of meaning behind his words.

Mydei shifts closer, pillowing his head on Phainon’s shoulder, and Phainon loops a hand over Mydei’s waist. “Then talk to me,” Mydei says. “Tell me of Aedes Elysiae before Eurypon ruined it.”

Haltingly, Phainon speaks. He describes endless fields of golden wheat, a vast blue lake rippling with possibility, a family that loved and cherished him—a mother and a father, no siblings. His voice catches as he describes his teachers, his friends, his extended families of aunts and uncles who oversaw his safety during the day. He skips over the children who teased

him for his dreams of being a swordsman, mentioning them only to say, “Cyrene was the only one who believed I could become a warrior.”

“She sounds like a true friend,” Mydei says.

“My best.” Phainon laughs. “Maybe my only.”

“That cannot be true.”

Warmed by Mydei’s words, Phainon urges him closer. He presses into Phainon’s side, and Phainon bends his face to touch a kiss to his forehead. “I was a strange child. Farmers’ sons don’t dream of changing the world.”

“But you did.”

Phainon is quiet for a moment, turning his gaze back to the ceiling. “I did. I… just wanted everyone’s dreams to come true.” His lips tug in a lopsided, sad smile. “My dream was to make everyone else’s dreams real.”

“You were a selfless child,” Mydei says, drawing idle designs on Phainon’s chest. “And now?” He lifts his head, leaning over Phainon.

“Still working on it,” Phainon admits. “The world’s a lot more complicated, and some dreams clash.”

Mydei studies him, and Phainon wonders if he’ll see through to the truth. “A hard truth for a child to learn.” He leans down, returning Phainon’s kiss with one of his own, one that lingers, one that offers succor. Phainon drinks down Mydei’s kindness, letting it fill him, renew him. Mydei draws back, expression intense. “Will you help me fulfill my dreams, too?”

Another glib reply dances on Phainon’s tongue—but he doesn’t want to hide behind sarcasm. Not with Mydei. Not anymore. As much as possible, he wants to reveal himself to the man beside him. “And what’s your dream?” he asks.

“To push back the black tide,” Mydei says.

Phainon tips his head to the side. “Is that really Strife’s concern?”

“It should be every Chrysos Heir’s concern,” Mydei says. “Strife used to sweep across the borderlands with an army of Chrysos Heirs, holding the tide at bay. Eurypon destroyed that tradition. It’s time to renew it.”

“That was decades ago,” Phainon says, the protest weak.

Mydei snorts. “Are you worried for me?”

Yes, but that’s not all. “Of course. You were dead for three days. You—”

“Came back. Castorice herself couldn’t keep me down. Do you think the black tide will?” Mydei scoffs, and he is right and righteous in his indignation.

“I’d prefer you to not spend three days dead again,” Phainon replies dryly.

Mydei settles against Phainon’s side once more, his head returning to Phainon’s shoulder. “Then I will not die.”

“You say that with such surety. Maybe your immortality is gone now that you’re Strife. All the Titans can be killed. Maybe—”

“You worry for nothing,” Mydei insists. “The black tide has always been Strife’s concern, and it will be mine, too.”

Phainon relents. “As you say, oh great Titan.”

Huffing, Mydei slaps his hand across Phainon’s ribs, pulling a laugh from him. Phainon wrestles Mydei onto his back, settling over him to drink more lingering kisses from his lips, and he holds his peace.

The black tide has, historically, been Strife’s problem. But it is also Phainon’s.
