chapters.title: Chapter 15
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

“We will begin with a message to Aglaea,” Gorgo says.

The morning is cool, the war table filled with juice and a smattering of fruits and cheeses, and the air tense. Gorgo has reconvened her council, though this time it’s even smaller: one of the other generals fled in the night, leaving just Themistocles and the second, Anaxagora, Mydei and his somatophylakes, Phainon, and Gorgo herself. It’s not a phenomenal start, and Mydei’s concern is deep. His mother lacks military support, and that frightens him with Aglaea’s army marching toward them.

“I remain concerned that any messenger we send will meet with swift death at Castorice’s hand,” Themistocles says, studying the war map before him. He doesn’t countermand Gorgo, but he is more honest with her than he ever was with Eurypon. But Gorgo hasn’t gone around burning Chrysos Heirs at the stake and exploding men with virulent, red crystals.

Mydei looks at his own hand, flexing it, watching his skin ripple with a strange light. His stomach turns.

“The general is right to be worried.” Every head in the room turns toward Phainon, who has been silent up until now, who has hung back behind Hephaestion and Leonnius as though the men could be some kind of shield for him. Now, though, he’s at the center of everyone’s attention, and his expression is grim. “If Aglaea is marching on Castrum Kremnos, I’m not sure she’ll stop just because Eurypon is dead and Her Majesty is queen.”

Themistocles throws an open palm in Phainon’s direction. “And who is this?” he demands. “Why have we included the prince’s bed slave in our war council?”

Leonnius shifts forward, a sneer on his face. “As the only Okheman in the room—”

“An Okheman!” Themistocles exclaims.

“An Okheman who helped eliminate Eurypon,” Ptolemy says.

Themistocles’s face reddens with anger, and he leans forward. “And we should trust a king-slayer at our war table?”

“You trust me,” Mydei says, earning a vicious glare from the general.

Gorgo brushes her arm against Themistocles’s own. “Enough.” She inclines her head toward Phainon. “Phainon was part of a plan I hatched in secret with the Goldweaver.” Themistocles stares at Gorgo not with shock but rather a curious sort of appreciation. “I had intended for him to kill Eurypon directly and, perhaps, take his coreflame from him.” Gorgo makes a soft sound and then says, “He is a Chrysos Heir after all.”

Mydei suddenly finds himself the recipient of sidelong glances traded between him and Phainon, but he is unsurprised to note that his somatophylakes are unbothered. They knew. Well, Hephaestion certainly always knew, but Phainon must have told the others when Mydei was dead.

“And so now you ask us to trust a double agent,” Themistocles says to Gorgo, clearly unwilling to bend on this. “That man is almost certainly Aglaea’s creature.”

“He is trustworthy,” Mydei says, ignoring the way Anaxagoras watches them as if they are all insects he’s studying, how he takes them in with a curious, almost gleeful expression.

Choking on a disbelieving laugh, Themistocles gestures toward Phainon again. “Trustworthy? This man who came to you under not one but two false pretenses? Who saw the skin flayed from your back and your death at the hands of the Maiden of War? No.” He holds up a hand to keep Mydei silent. “Everyone who stood in the war room at the time knew you went to that battlefield to keep your father from killing your bed slave.”

“Phainon was never a slave,” Mydei hisses. “That was a pretense—”

“So the torc on his neck was—”

“General,” Gorgo snaps. “Mydeimos.” Her cutting gaze silences them both, and Mydei is perversely pleased to see her so easily cow Themistocles despite his annoyance at being cowed alongside him. “Phainon’s history with us is no longer a point of contention. He knows Aglaea well and thus is valuable for our current pursuits.” She turns her attention to Phainon. “The Goldweaver is no conqueror. The Titan of Romance is rarely vindictive.”

Phainon regards the map on the table, studying the position of the armies, Aglaea’s advancement, and he rubs a hand over his mouth. “Aglaea is…” He inhales deeply. “She’s not a conqueror, but I don’t think this is about conquering. She’ll see this as retributive justice, crushing Castrum Kremnos so it can’t crush anyone else. You can try sending a messenger, but I wouldn’t hold out hope she’ll stop her advance.”

“Do you think she’ll kill a messenger?” Gorgo asks.

Shaking his head, Phainon says, “No. I don’t think she’d kill someone who came under a banner of peace.” His jaw flexes, and Mydei wonders if anyone else notices.

“Now is not the time for secrets,” Gorgo says softly. Of course, she would notice the subtle tell.

Phainon sighs. “Aglaea has been the Titan of Romance for a long time, and it’s changed her. She… she cares about humanity, but she is ruthless in her pursuit of protection for those she considers her own. Compassion isn’t easy for her. Not anymore.”

“You know her very well,” Anaxagoras observes.

Waving this off with a shrug, Phainon says, “Anyone who spends a reasonable amount of time with her would be able to tell these things.”

Mydei—and clearly everyone else at the table—doesn’t think that’s so true. Phainon talks about Aglaea with a casual familiarity that suggests he spends more than a reasonable amount of time with her. Perhaps this isn’t such a strange thing: Phainon is a Chrysos Heir, and all Titans have kept Chrysos Heirs close to them for one reason or another over the centuries. To some, as with Nikador, Chrysos Heirs were squires to help fend off the black tide. To others, like Eurypon, they were a nuisance, kept close to be controlled or, more often, killed.

“Send a messenger,” Phainon says to Gorgo. “Tell Aglaea that Eurypon is dead, that you’ve assumed control of the city, and you would like there to be peace between Okhema and Castrum Kremnos so that no one else has to die. If you emphasize wanting peace… that should be enough.”

“Should be,” Themistocles says, low and gruff.

“No guarantees, of course,” Phainon replies.

“Then I will draft a message to Aglaea in the hopes that our old alliance moves her heart,” Gorgo says, “and telling her that we have accomplished our mutual goal even if the outcome is not as we anticipated.”

Mydei stares at the map, ignoring the way gazes fall on him.

“Aglaea is all well and good,” Anaxagoras says, “but the black tide remains a more pressing concern.”

“More pressing than an army bearing down on us?” Themistocles asks.

Hephaestion hits his fist on the table. “We are caught between two monsters, but an army of men is more easily turned aside than an eldritch force.”

“But we have Strife,” Mydei reminds them. “And we can gather up any other Chrysos Heirs to fight back the tide as Nikador once did.” He leans over the table, indicating on the map where the black tide has speared forward in the direction of Okhema. “I will take my somatophylakes and Phainon—”

“As the only one of us who knows Aglaea,” Gorgo says, “I would prefer to keep him here.”

Mydei presses his lips together. “The blood of Chrysos Heirs can help push back the tide,” he reminds her.

“Only Strife’s blood,” Phainon says with a studied casualness that raises Mydei’s hackles. There’s much Phainon isn’t saying, that he’s trying to avoid saying.

“Any Chrysos Heir,” Mydei begins.

“No,” Anaxagoras says, cutting him off. He lifts his left hand, removes a dagger from his belt, and cuts his own palm. Golden blood wells there.

Frustration replaces shock, a quiet irritation that Anaxagoras was right under his nose the whole time he was in the Grove at his father’s request. Not that he would have turned the man in, not that he would have seen the man executed, but—

Mydei gives him a tight smile. “And you’ve tested this?” he asks.

“Yes,” Anaxagoras says, wiping his dagger on his chiton before cutting a piece of it to heal his hand. His protégé, who should have been a tell, too, Mydei supposes, is not present. “Both Hyacinthia and I tried to use our blood to ward off the tide, but it fears only Strife. While we can safely traverse the tide and confront its monsters as humans cannot, we can’t turn it aside the way you can.”

Phainon knew this. Phainon knew this when they were at the Grove. Now, he stands at the end of the table, sandwiched between Hephaestion and Leonnius as though to protect himself, not looking at Mydei, and Mydei knows he’s hiding more.

“Then Phainon remains,” Gorgo says.

“I would advise against that, Your Majesty.” Anaxagoras wraps his hand. “Phainon’s blood won’t deter the black tide, but to send your son and his

somatophylakes will see the latter all dead and the former ineffective. Phainon may know Romance—”

Phainon continues staring at the map without looking at anyone else, and Mydei is even more certain that he’s still hiding so many things.

“—but he will be of greater service delaying the black tide’s inevitable progress.”

“If it’s inevitable,” the other general says, “then we must evacuate Castrum Kremnos immediately. Let it take us and Okhema—”

Themistocles lets out a loud, wordless protest, echoed by most of Mydei’s somatophylakes, though Mydei himself remains silent. There’s wisdom in giving up the city, but his gut churns at the thought.

What surprises him, though, is Anaxagoras’s mocking laughter. “Ah, yes,” he says. “Let’s destroy the known world out of spite, nationalism, and xenophobia.”

“We can’t let the black tide reach Okhema,” Phainon agrees, his expression fierce as he rounds on the general.

“Indeed.” Gorgo leans over the table. “Castrum Kremnos and Okhema are the greatest of Amphoreus’s cities. We can let neither fall if we mean to preserve society.”

Anaxagoras claps, and Mydei can’t help but think there’s mockery in it, and it takes everything in him not to lash out at the so-called feeble scholar. There’s an energy about him, a strange resonance that hangs in the air, that rattles Mydei’s bones and leaves him uncomfortably on edge, and he wants to eliminate it. Escape it.

“I will not be responsible for the downfall of civilization in my first act as queen,” Gorgo continues. “And so this is what we shall do: I will recall the Senate.” Mydei startles, but he shouldn’t be surprised. Eurypon feared the citizens’ power. Gorgo would not. “The Senate will decide how we will answer the black tide’s progress.”

“Too slow,” Anaxagoras mutters.

Gorgo speaks over him. “The citizens must have a say. While the Senate comes together to vote on whether or not we evacuate, we will send a messenger to Aglaea’s army in the hopes that she will spare not just Castrum Kremnos but the other city states in the way. The black tide is the most pressing concern, so we will inform her of our discovery that its goal seems to be Okhema. Meanwhile, Mydeimos will take his somatophylakes and Phainon to buy us what time they can.”

“You send away our most valuable wartime assets,” Themistocles says.

“My century is the queen’s,” Mydei says.

Themistocles gives him a pointed look. “It is not your century that matters. If Castorice attacks us…”

Mydei throws wide his arms. “I should die again to slow her down? It took me three days to recover, you might remember. Throwing myself at Castorice will do little good.”

“This from the man who—”

“Be silent,” Gorgo says, her voice a roll of thunder through the war room. “Hyacinthia,” she continues, and Mydei smarts at how she ignores him and Themistocles. “Anaxagoras, you will send Hyacinthia as a messenger. Aglaea is unlikely to outright kill a healer and a Chrysos Heir.”

Anaxagoras looks supremely displeased. “No, she’ll just keep her as a hostage.”

“Would you prefer to go in her stead?”

His expression transforms into an almost feral smile. “You would trust me with your message?”

“No,” Gorgo says flatly. “Nor do I trust your Hyacinthia, which is why I will be sending a sealed scroll and two guards alongside her.”

“How boring,” he drawls, crossing his arms and turning away.

Gorgo eases away from the war table, settling on a kline placed behind her. “Then let us go. I will draft my message. Themistocles, call in the senators. Mydeimos, I trust you will be able to rally your friends and depart as soon as possible.” She is quiet for a moment. “You will take Phainon as well,” she says, with obvious reluctance. “The scholar is right about this.”

Mydei nods. “Of course,” he says, offering her a respectful dip of his head.

“Then let us be about our business,” the Queen of Castrum Kremnos declares.

After sending his somatophylakes to their rooms to collect what they’ll need, Mydei corners Phainon in his own.

“You’re hiding something still,” Mydei says, standing in the entrance to his bedroom. The servants worked fast this during their time in the war room, unboxing everything they’d boxed during his death, returning his room to its proper state.

Phainon, just inside the doorway to the little closet that should be his own room, freezes—and that’s all Mydei needs to know he’s right, even as Phainon says, “I’ve told you everything you need to know.”

“Everything I need to know,” Mydei echoes, prowling toward him. “That implies there’s more that you think I don’t need to know.”

Panic flashes in Phainon’s eyes, there and gone in an instant, and Mydei knows he’s right. He catches the sides of the door, leaning into the closet, forcing Phainon deeper. Phainon has precious few belongings, little that needs packing for a journey such as this, but the armguards Mydei bought him lay on his pallet.

“Phainon,” Mydei says. “Do I not deserve the whole truth?”

And to his surprise, Phainon crumples to the ground, sitting on his pallet as he pulls his hands down his face and draws his knees to his chest.

Mydei glances back, but his servants are busy in the main room of his suite, affording them at least the facsimile of privacy. He slips into the tiny room and sits beside Phainon, studying him.

“It’s too much,” Phainon says into his hands.

“We’re going to risk our lives pushing back the black tide, and you know something.”

“I know,” Phainon groans. “I know so much.” He drags his hands away from his face.

A lone window high on the wall offers a pittance of light, a slash of it across their sandaled feet. Shadow enshrouds the rest of them, hiding the bulk of Phainon’s expression but not the agony of his words.

“Then why is the black tide traveling as the crow flies toward Okhema?” Mydei asks.

Phainon shudders and leans back, resting against the wall. “Because that’s where THEY are,” he says with tremendous resignation. “That’s where THEY’ve always been, trapped in a prison beneath the city, biding THEIR time.”

A strange feeling of dread curls around the base of Mydei’s spine. “THEY?” he asks, perturbed by the weight Phainon gives the word.

“The primordial ones, the precursors, the Titans’ own gods who created the universe,” Phainon says, closing his eyes.  “But you don’t believe me. That’s fine. I’ve done this… thousands of times, and Aglaea’s only ever believed me once.”

Silent, Mydei sits beside him, waiting for Phainon to laugh, to make some joke of the nonsense he’s just said. In isolation, Mydei understands all those

words, but the way Phainon has strung them all together has him baffled. Bewildered. And angry.

“What lies are you spinning?” he asks, his voice a low hiss. “I ask for the truth, and you—you give me… mythology?” He pulls away.

Phainon takes him by the wrist. “When Eurypon drowned you,” he says quickly. “You were five, and you’d secreted a palace cat with a broken leg into your room, intending to help it heal.”

Now, Mydei goes still, staring in disbelief at Phainon. He’d told Phainon about his drowning, yes, but not what precipitated it.

“One of your servants betrayed you to Eurypon, and he drowned you and the cat to teach you a lesson. That you shouldn’t care for anything outside of yourself,” Phainon continues. “That care is weakness.”

Mydei tries to shake off Phainon’s hand. “Did Hephaestion tell you that while I was dead?” he demands.

“No,” Phainon says, holding tighter to his arm. “Eurypon did maybe… fifty cycles ago? One hundred?” He shakes his head. “I’ve seen so many, they blur together. It was the last time I tried to work with him to stop the black tide from reaching Okhema.” His expression is shadowed but still clearly earnest as he looks up at Mydei. “You don’t believe me.”

“Because you’re speaking nonsense,” Mydei snaps, frustration boiling within him. “At every opportunity, I have helped you, protected you. Just last night, you apologized to me, you—” He bares his teeth, a terrible smile as he breaks into ragged laughter. “More lies, Phainon?”

Phainon lets go, his head drooping between his shoulders, his arm falling limply to the ground. “Every time,” he says, his own laughter weary. Broken. Pained. “Every time I try to tell someone.” He draws back, curling around himself, and the sight is so disconcerting that it roots Mydei to the spot.

He’s never seen Phainon look so small, and he tries to tell himself it doesn’t matter, that he doesn’t care, that Phainon has cut him with lies one time too many. But it does matter, he does care, and he finds himself on his knees, his anger fizzling out. Eurypon always acted out of anger and fear, and he will do neither.

Taking a deep breath, he sets a hand on Phainon’s leg, just above his knee, inviting. “Try again,” he says, with more patience than he thinks Phainon deserves.

Phainon doesn’t move for a long moment, so long he wonders if Phainon somehow didn’t hear him. But then, Phainon says, “The first time, Cyrene and I had traveled to Okhema. Eurypon’s armies razed Aedes Elysiae, and we were the only survivors.”

Mydei frowns. When Phainon has spoken of Aedes Elysiae and Cyrene, he has always made it sound like Cyrene died in the attack.

“We took refuge there, scared and alone, until Aglaea heard of us. Two Chrysos Heirs, one a priestess in service of Oronyx.”

“Oronyx is dead,” Mydei says. “Nikador killed them.”

Phainon shakes his head. “No. No, Cyrene… she…” He sits back and rakes a hand through his hair, lifting his face to Mydei. Unshed tears brighten the brilliant blue of his eyes, and he looks so vulnerable, so pained. So very distressed and alone.

How many times has Mydei felt that way? How many times has he crawled into his own bed, afraid to let anyone see his vulnerability after Eurypon visited some horror on him?

“What did Cyrene do?” Mydei asks, willing to hear Phainon out.

“When the black tide came to Okhema that first time,” Phainon says, “it revealed a mausoleum beneath the city. THEY are entombed there, the ancient gods who wove together the universe, and the black tide seeks THEM. Seeks to wake THEM. We didn’t understand, not at first. THEY

woke and begin to rip apart the universe.” He looks aside, ashamed. “I couldn’t react fast enough, but Cyrene did. She bargained with Oronyx, sending me back to my childhood so that I could prevent THEIR awakening. But doing that shattered Oronyx’s coreflame and killed Cyrene.” He touches his chest. “They’re…” He swallows hard, lifting his eyes back to Mydei’s. “They died for me, too. So that I could do this again and again. So that I could stop the black tide.”

Mydei leans back. “I don’t understand.” The words are hard to say; ignorance so often leads to death for him.

Grimacing, shuddering, Phainon exhales. “It’s hard to explain. It’s all… jumbled in my head. I’ve done it so many times.” He runs both hands through his hair, pushing it out of his face, clearly distressed. “Cyrene created a loop in time. Every time I die, I go back to the day Eurypon razed Aedes Elysiae to the ground. She created the loop so that I can find a way to stop the black tide from freeing the primordial gods entombed beneath Okhema, the gods who created the universe and the Titans.”

“The Titans created the universe,” Mydei insists, reeling. “Janus—” He catches himself. Janus was born from the primal coreflame, created by the confluence of fate and chaos, and then split that primal coreflame into the other Titans’ own coreflames. “Where did fate and chaos come from?” he asks.

Hope lights Phainon’s eyes. “The primordial ones. THEY created whatever was there at the beginning, and THEY crafted the environment for life, for Janus to emerge from the aether,” he explains, low and urgent. “But THEY fought with the Titans, a brutal war before even Era Luminosa, and the Titans sealed THEM away.”

“Why would THEY want to destroy THEIR creation?” Mydei asks.

Phainon shrugs. “I don’t know why, only that when THEY were freed in that first cycle, THEY went first for the Titans, retaliating against them, and then began to pull apart the very firmament, ripping it asunder.” There’s a stark look on his face. “Even now, I remember… I remember blue hands and a doll’s jointed fingers tearing through the sky as something with a

great, red eye rent the very earth until magma spewed forth from the rocks.” He shakes his head. “It sounds unbelievable.”

“It does,” Mydei agrees. “Like something out of an epic.” But it’s so absurd that it rings of truth. No one would lie about this. Phainon, certainly, would pick something else. Something more believable. “You have… attempted to stop the black tide multiple times?”

A hysterical sound catches in Phainon’s throat. “Thousands,” he whispers, hoarse. “I’ve lost count. I don’t know—I don’t know any more how many times.” Raw, visceral pain fills his every word, and there’s a terrible hollowness in his eyes, an ancient haunting of time passed, and Mydei realizes he believes Phainon. He believes him entirely, no matter how ludicrous the story sounds.

His hand squeezes Phainon’s leg, and Phainon jumps. “I believe you,” Mydei says.

Phainon lets out a sob, bending his head to cover his eyes, and Mydei is silent, allowing him the time he needs to collect himself. He doesn’t cry, but he shakes, his hands pressed to his face as though to hide himself. Not knowing what else to do, wanting to give him the privacy his grief demands, Mydei sits silently, leaving his hand on Phainon’s leg until Phainon takes it in his own.

“You’re the second,” Phainon says, red-eyed when he looks up. “In all this time, you’re the second.”

He doesn’t quite like being second to Aglaea in this, but he supposes he’s second to her in many things. It’s hard not to be when the Romance Titan has been alive for so long. But instead of saying that, he squeezes Phainon’s hand. “This whole time, your whole goal has been to fight back the black tide? Why come here?”

“Because I hadn’t tried it yet,” Phainon says. “I’ve recruited Eurypon to my side a handful of times, but—” He catches himself. “There’s something you need to know about the black tide and the Strife Titan.” His voice shakes.

Mydei strokes his thumb over Phainon’s hand. “Tell me.”

“Every time I’ve brought Eurypon to face the black tide and fight it back, it has possessed him,” Phainon says softly. “It has overtaken him, ravaged the battlefield and our other allies, if we’ve had any, and then freed THEM from THEIR prison.”

That can’t be right. “But Strife is the tide’s old enemy. It fears my blood. Strife’s blood.”

Phainon turns away, brows drawn. “You… you always contained Strife’s honor and reason,” he says slowly. “Perhaps that’s why it feared you, and why it could possess Eurypon so easily.” He laughs, the sound unpleasant, and Mydei squeezes his hand again. How Phainon hasn’t gone truly and completely mad, he doesn’t know and can’t begin to imagine, but there is a hint of madness in Phainon now. “I never would have known if I hadn’t come here, in this way. Thousands of these cycles and I’m still learning new secrets.” He tips his head back and makes a sad, mournful noise.

“You’re one secret closer,” Mydei tells him, surprising himself with his own insistence. But Phainon has let so many of his walls down, and now Mydei sees how close he truly is to broken, and it terrifies him. Phainon, who would never have broken as a slave, worn down by endless repetitions of time. “We will be careful when we pursue the tide. We won’t take risks, but we have to try to push it back.” He pauses, thoughtful. “What do you know about it? What have you learned?”

Phainon shakes his head. “Surprisingly little. Every time I’ve met the tide myself or with allies, we’ve been killed and time has restarted in Aedes Elysiae. A few times…” His lips twist. “Many times, I’ve killed myself when I’ve thought a cycle lost.”

Mydei’s throat works. All this time, Phainon has known death as intimately as Mydei himself. They could have shared this, though he recognizes that he wouldn’t have believed Phainon previously. Can barely believe him now.

“Surely, you’ve spoken with Anaxagoras,” Mydei says. “You’ve sought his understanding.”

Another shake of Phainon’s head. “He knows less than I do. The tide hasn’t been his mission. I know that it originates somewhere to the west, but I’ve never been able to cross to its origin by myself, and when I’ve tried with help, they’ve all been overwhelmed and then killed by monsters.”

Mydei squeezes Phainon’s hand again. “Then we will go together, and it will be different.”

“The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over expecting different results.”

Mydei hesitates. “You’ve never gone with me, have you?” he asks, suddenly unsure of himself, his heart thundering. What if they’ve done this before? What if they haven’t? But if they had, surely Phainon would have known Gorgo’s secrets from a previous cycle.

A smile pulls at Phainon’s lips. “I’ve never gone with you,” he admits. “I’ve never tried this route before, killing your father and recruiting you in his stead. It’s… hard to remember what I have and haven’t tried, truthfully, but I’ve attempted to be methodical. I’ve burned so many cycles with Aglaea, with Cipher, with Castorice. Your father. This is the first time in any cycle you’ve become Strife.” His smile widens. “Maybe this time will be different.”

“It will be,” Mydei assures him, not quite liking the assurance. If they fail… If he’s wrong… But he won’t let himself think like that. Not yet. “I have a question for you, though.”

“Ask. I’ll answer.”

“Why didn’t you kill yourself when I died?” Mydei asks.

Phainon’s laughter this time is something genuine, and genuinely amused. “I tried to. I wanted to. I thought the cycle lost without you, and I… I couldn’t bear it. Then, Hephaestion swore himself to me. Then the rest of them did, too, and they must have thought I wanted to end my own life, because they wouldn’t leave me alone for a minute.” His smile is genuine,

too. “They looked after me, and because they did, I…” He touches Mydei’s face, thumbing the corner of his lips, and Mydei leans into the touch.

“This is the first time you’ve recruited me,” he says. “Then this is the first time we’ve…?”

“It’s the first time I’ve loved,” Phainon admits, a whisper, and Mydei sucks in a sharp breath. “And Mydei, Mydeimos, my prince—” He shifts onto his knees, taking Mydei’s face in both his hands, tipping it up and back until their eyes meet, and his gaze is fierce. “If I lose you, if we fail this time, I…” He swallows hard, and Mydei sees how close to the edge of broken Phainon truly stands. There is a yawning precipice at Phainon’s feet, the edge crumbling beneath his sandals, and no one to pull him back.

Mydei could pull him back. Mydei wonders if he should, if he ought to, if he should sacrifice this much more for Phainon’s sake. But of course he will. He can’t not, if only because he’s so profoundly selfish.

It’s the first time I’ve loved.

In all these cycles, Phainon has never given his heart away, and now he’s given it to Mydei. This is precious, and Mydei can’t bear to lose it. Can’t bear the idea of forgetting this, of forgetting Phainon, of forgetting the indelible mark Phainon has left on his very soul.

“Then we won’t fail,” Mydei says, lifting his mouth to Phainon’s for the barest whisper of a kiss. “You must know I love you, too.”

An aching sound pours from Phainon’s mouth, and Mydei wraps himself around Phainon’s body as though he can be some kind of shield. He doesn’t have the power to stop the cycles. Titan he may be, but he is no Oronyx. Strife can’t unwind what Time set in place. But the future isn’t some foregone conclusion, the world is a twisting, confusing thing, and forces swerve from causal paths constantly. He will be one of these forces rewriting Phainon’s own fate. He will use every ounce of his newly acquired divinity to help Phainon to succeed, if only so that this doesn’t become one more cycle. For his sake. For Phainon’s.

His mouth finds Phainon’s again. His hands wrap around Phainon’s shoulders and draw Phainon down, down, as he lays himself out on what should have been a slave’s pallet but never was. He draws Phainon over him, and Phainon brings their bodies together as their lips part only to meet again.

“You weren’t supposed to,” Phainon whispers against his mouth. Rough fingers stroke over Mydei’s cheeks and sink into his hair. Phainon’s thumbs brush against the corners of Mydei’s mouth, and Mydei arches into Phainon’s body with a hungry groan. Heavy atop him, Phainon’s weight is grounding, his warmth sizzling like lightning across Mydei’s skin. “None of this was supposed to happen like this. You weren’t supposed to care. I wasn’t supposed to care.”

“But you do,” Mydei says, turning his face to rake his teeth along the pad of Phainon’s thumbs. “I do.” And failing this time might destroy whatever is left of Phainon’s sanity. Phainon clings to his sanity by the fragile thread joining their hearts, and Mydei will do anything to strengthen that thread, to protect it. To protect Phainon, who should be his enemy. “We will succeed, Phainon.” It’s a promise, an oath, a binding, and he wraps his hand around the back of Phainon’s head to draw him into another kiss.

Phainon’s mouth is desperate against his own, suckling and hungry, their lips clinging, their kisses slow but hardly drugging. There’s a deep longing in how Phainon takes Mydei’s mouth with his own—a profound loneliness. Phainon has been so utterly set apart for uncountably many years. Thousands of cycles, a decade of his life repeated over and over, and no one to comfort him, to help him, to believe him when he told them the truth.

No more.

Mydei’s tongue slides into Phainon’s mouth, licking, tasting. He slings one leg high on Phainon’s hip, inviting him closer still, and Phainon sinks into him like a man starved.

Thousands of cycles, tens of thousands of years, and no one has seen Phainon. No matter the relationships he built, no one knew the truth, the weight across his shoulders. Not just the conflict between Castrum

Kremnos and Okhema but the fate of an entire world, borne alone by a single man no one believed—a single man the world continuously forgot. How unimaginably painful.

Hot tears splash against Mydei’s cheeks as Phainon kisses him, as Phainon pulls at his chiton, working it free. Mydei strips Phainon in turn, their hands hungry across each other’s bodies, grasping and clutching as though they can devour each other with their fingertips and palms.

Naked, they move against each other, their cocks rocking together, smearing precum across their bellies. It’s messy and fumbling, all clumsy hands and arrhythmic rolls of their hips, but it’s real and its theirs, something all theirs, something that no one should be able to take from them. Death or time will surely make an attempt, and that spurs Mydei on, makes him desperate, too, as he tugs Phainon closer still, as if they could melt into each other.

When they are spent, slick with sweat and cum and still tangled around each other, Phainon’s lips still press urgent kisses to Mydei’s—fearful, fretful. Mydei strokes his hands down the length of Phainon’s back. He wants to offer reassurances, but anything he says will be empty. There’s too much they don’t know, too much Phainon still doesn’t know. But they will find out together.

His heart clenches. Phainon has sought such answers with others and failed to find them. If this time is to be different—no. No, it will be different, and he will allow himself to think nothing less.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

They depart with the sun, mounting their horses and speeding off in the direction of the Grove. Without a century at their backs, they cover ground quickly as the sun slides lower and lower on the horizon.

Phainon has put himself back together as best he can, sealing up the cracks in his mind and his soul with Mydei’s affections. It’s not fair, it’s not right, he shouldn’t depend on another person so much, but he does. If Mydei hadn’t believed him in that little closet, he would’ve fallen apart. Even now, every hoofbeat beneath him rattles, and he grips his reins until his nails press crescents into his palms.

“You’re going to ruin yourself if you keep sitting like that,” Leonnius calls out to him, pulling his horse alongside Phainon’s own.

Scoffing, even though Leonnius is right, Phainon adjusts his posture and lets the tension flow out of him. “I know how to ride, thanks,” he fires back.

“Has our good prince been teaching you?” Hephaestion asks from ahead of Phainon, where he rides beside Mydei.

Phainon, flushing, has no idea what to say to that.

Mydei saves him. Sort of. “HKS,” he says without much feeling, reaching out to smack Hephaestion upside the head.

Laughing, Hephaestion bats Mydei’s hand away. “Right, right, our prince knows plenty about riding, doesn’t he?”

Phainon sputters.

“And you!” Perdikkas calls from behind Hephaestion. “When was the last time you took someone to bed? What experience do you have that allows you to malign our prince and his lover so?”

“I should think I’m the best positioned to do just that,” Hephaestion shoots back, voice warm with yet more laughter.

Phainon can’t decide if he should be horrified at the reminder that he’s the final bough in the funeral pyre of Mydei and Hephaestion’s relationship or if he should sink into the ground and simply cease to exist.

“You deserve this,” Leonnius says casually, reaching out to slap Phainon’s shoulder.

Groaning, Phainon drags a hand down his face. “Do I?”

“Scales,” Leonnius replies.

Phainon throws both hands in the air. “Did helping Mydei kill Eurypon do nothing for me?” he asks, bewildered.

“Oh, it did quite a bit. But that doesn’t preclude this sort of thing, which will only get worse until the two of you end up married.”

Phainon chokes.

“Leonnius,” Mydei says, his voice a low warning.

Leonnius throws a grin over his shoulder at Mydei. “Am I wrong? You overthrew an empire together. As far as Kremnoans are concerned, that’s the purest form of love.”

“I will kill you,” Mydei growls, but he shoots what can only be described as a nervous look at Phainon, and Phainon offers him a reassuring sort of smile.

It’s a strange thing for Mydei’s friends to see their relationship so clearly. He’s been alone for so long, he’s forgotten what it’s like to have people see right through him, and though it’s unnerving, there’s something pleasant

about it, too. A reassurance that even if he lies to himself, he can’t lie to everyone else. But the somatophylakes relent, turning from their jokes about his and Mydei’s relationship to Kremnoan epics, to stories of heroes the ranks of which they’re sure to join if they can only turn back the black tide. They play about their epithets and titles, making up increasingly gregarious and utterly insane appellations until even Phainon is hunched over his saddle, laughing so hard his sides hurt.

When they make camp that night, the seven of them in a ring around a small fire, they grow more somber. They’ll reach the Grove by noon the following day, and Phainon knows he can’t hide truths from them any longer. Quietly, haltingly, and with Mydei’s hand on the small of his back, he reveals to them what he knows of the world with more cohesion than what he gave to Mydei. He tells the story of his own cycles of existence, the horrors buried beneath Okhema, and the mystery and danger of the black tide.

“Gods more powerful than the Titans?” Leonnius asks, scoffing. “That sounds like a child’s story. Something to make scared little Okhemans sleep better at night when they’re scared of Strife.”

“I was suspect, too,” Mydei says. “But then I remembered the story of Janus’s genesis, her coreflame emerging from fate and chaos. Surely, fate and chaos came from somewhere.”

Peucesta idly plucks the strings of his lyre, cradled in his lap. “Hesiod speaks of this,” he says thoughtfully.

Leonnius snorts. “You’re joking.” He turns to each man in turn, spreading his arms wide, and Phainon cannot help but grimace. Of course Leonnius would doubt him. “You buy into this insane story?”

Fingers moving over the strings of his lyre, Peucesta closes his eyes and begins his recitation. “At the first, Chaos came to be, and in opposition to Chaos came forth all-consuming order, who separated night from day and cleaved the wide-pathed abundance of earth from the firmament, who carved out the memory of past and present and future, and the end of all things, and the ability to understand it. From Chaos sprang endless creation

and destruction and the pursuit of death. Wild these forces warred until THEY beget the journey of fate itself, from which grew the coreflame of Janus.” His fingers still and his eyes open. “Hesiod’s Theogony.” His lips quirk. “Few pay much attention to this brief creation myth, preferring the exhortation of the muses at the start and the creation myth of the Titans that follows.”

A stick snaps in their fire, sending up a shower of sparks, spiraling toward the heavens above. Leonnius is silent, rubbing his face with his hand. Hephaestion sits quietly, elbows brace on his knees, expression intense.

“It is said,” Ptolemy begins, “that Okhema was built on the ruins of ruins. That it was the Holy City before Janus manifested herself and carved out Janusopolis for her seat.”

Leonnius swears.

“I know how it sounds,” Phainon says quietly, taking no small comfort in the weight of Mydei’s hand against his back. “And I have less proof than what Peucesta and Ptolemy have said. My word…” He exhales heavily. “I understand if it’s not good enough for you.”

“Does the Goldweaver know?” Perdikkas asks.

Phainon shakes his head. “No. The only time I managed to convince her, I brought her to the tomb beneath Okhema.” He laughs, the sound bitter. “We still failed, that time.” Raking his hands through his hair, he stares at the ground between his feet, at the flickering shadows washing over the earth, painting it in midnight stains. “The next time, I brought her to the tomb earlier than the previous, and she took me for a herald of the primordial ones instead. She stabbed me in the back, and I bled out while she watched.”

“Surely, the Titans would know of this history,” Leonnius says. He gestures to Mydei. “Did your accession come with some kind of… enlightenment?”

“No.” Mydei says. “No, and perhaps that’s the trouble. There are hundreds of Chrysos Heirs who have become Titans over the centuries, and we’ve…

lost the Titans’ origins.”

The men are quiet, but their silence isn’t disbelief. It’s shocked resignation, the slow acceptance of the truth. Phainon finds himself shaking. Mydei’s hand draws along the length of his spine, and some of the tension eases out of him. He sinks into that touch.

“Then we must stop the black tide before it reaches Okhema,” Hephaestion says, lifting his gaze first to Mydei and then to Phainon. “If these primordial ones are the Titans’ creators, are greater than even them—” He breaks off, thoughtful. “Have you never recruited all the Titans at once?” And then he laughs. “No, that was foolish. Getting even two of them to agree the sky is blue would be a small miracle.”

“Perhaps because the sky isn’t blue,” Ptolemy drawls.

Hephaestion rolls his eyes. “Be silent. No one needs your unique brand of pedantry right now.”

“Oh, is that what it is?” Ptolemy asks, but his tone is good-natured. He shoves at Hephaestion’s shoulder, and Hephaestion casually shoves him back—hard enough that he totters into Perdikkas instead.

Hephaestion turns his attention back to Phainon, to Mydei. “If it is our prince’s command, we will ride with you in the defense of the world, Phainon,” he says. And then he chuckles. “Perhaps even if it wasn’t.”

Phainon’s throat threatens to close, his chest swelling with emotion. He can barely breathe around the fullness of his heart.

“Let us make this the last cycle Phainon lives through,” Mydei says, his hand warm on the back of Phainon’s neck, comforting. His thumb presses against the base of Phainon’s skull, and Phainon could melt into that touch.

“Thank you,” Phainon says softly. “I… I have done this so many times and have made so many different allies, but over the millennia, men have become as tools.” He places his hand on Mydei’s knee, squeezing gently. “I lost sight of the power of good friends at my side.” And he is, he realizes,

terrified of losing them. “I hope I can say that of you. There’s… still a lot I need to make up for.” Leonnius grunts. “But to have all of you beside me in this is a relief. It’s been a long time since I’ve allowed myself to think a cycle might end well.”

“It will end well,” Mydei insists.

“We will see to it.” Hephaestion agrees.

The others put up a cheer of agreement, even Leonnius.

Blinking back threatening tears, Phainon grins. “You are, all of you, good people.”

“Oh, shut up,” Leonnius groans. “For the love of the Titans, enough of this sentimentality.” He leans forward, extending the waterskin in his hand. “I at least need to be drunk to deal with all these feelings. Let us drink to our future successes!” He roars the last word, earning more cheers from the other somatophylakes, and even one from Mydei, who also lifts his skin in toast.

Water is a poor substitute for wine, but the company is good and it’s warm, and for the first time in many, many centuries, Phainon allows himself hope for the future.

The sun is bright above them when they reach the boundary of the black tide, the Grove on the nearby horizon, and Phainon’s internal resolve surprises him. With Mydei at his side and the somatophylakes at his back, he’s supported in a way he hasn’t been in so many cycles—perhaps in any of them. Perhaps, with these men at his side, with this support, he can finally put an end to these miserable cycles.

“We can go no further than this,” Hephaestion says, reining in his horse at the edge of the tide.

Mydei nods, surveying the scorched forest beyond them, the desiccated husk of the land. “I’ll leave you with defending this border for us,” he says.

“Push back the monsters where you can but take no risks. Don’t sacrifice yourselves.” He turns toward Phainon with a deferential nod of his head.

It’s a strange thing to have a prince and a Titan defer to him, to have Mydeimos specifically defer to him, but it’s not the first time a god has bent to him. It’s not like it goes to his head—everyone who’s subordinated themselves to him has ended up dead thousands of times over.

Sitting straighter in his saddle, Phainon considers his next words carefully. He’s made allies of so many Titans and Chrysos Heirs, but they’ve never been his friends, not in the way these men are. “We’ve guessed from Hephaestion’s map and Anaxagoras’s that it will take us two days on foot to reach the epicenter of the tide,” he says. “If we aren’t back on the fifth day…” He trails off. If they run into trouble, he’ll have to kill himself and reset the cycle, but the very idea terrifies him. With resolve, he continues, “If we aren’t back on the fifth day, return to Castrum Kremnos and advise the queen to evacuate the city, if she hasn’t begun to do so already.” He spreads his arms in something almost like defeat. “If Mydei and I fail here, the cycle will reset.” His voice remains steady despite himself. “But save as many lives as you can in advance of that.”

Hephaestion leans forward, grasping Phainon’s forearm. “This time will be different,” he says with a conviction Phainon hasn’t felt in so very long. His expression is fierce, eyes blazing. “It will be. Believe in that.” He releases Phainon and wheels his horse to the side.

Each of the somatophylakes say their goodbyes, both to Phainon and to Mydei, as he and Mydei dismount and pass their reins to Hephaestion and Perdikkas.

In the end, it’s just Phainon and Leonnius, and Leonnius takes him by the forearm as Hephaestion did, that ancient Kremnoan salute. “Don’t fuck this up,” he says.

Phainon can’t help his quiet laugh. “Save the world and balance the scales?”

Leonnius grins. “Save the world and balance the scales,” he agrees, shaking his head. “I don’t claim to understand it, but you make him happy, and that’s more than he’s had in years.”

Another reason this cycle has to be the last one. Phainon squeezes Leonnius’s arm before releasing him. “I would do my best to make him happy for years to come,” he says quietly.

“Then you’ve got the motivation you need to figure it out this time.”

“But no pressure,” Phainon drawls.

Leonnius lets out a booming laugh. “None at all.” He steps back, nodding toward the tide and its meandering monstrosities. “Cut your way through, sons of Amphoreus.” He makes a sharp salute, and the others follow suit as Phainon and Mydei step onto the oily surface of the tide.

Short, fat fingers of the substance lift from the ground, clawing at their sandals only to shrink away from Mydei. A patch of bone-dry earth appears beneath his feet, and both he and Phainon grimace. If that’s what remains beneath the tide, recovering Amphoreus from it will be a long, arduous task.

They give their somatophylakes a final wave each and then set off across the tide at a loping gait. Without their horses, the going is slower, but the tide consumes all flesh that doesn’t belong to a Chrysos Heir, human and animal alike. Where they pass, the tide pulls away from Mydei only to close ranks behind them, somehow even more ominous in their wake. As they progress deeper, their somatophylakes becoming distant smudges on the horizon, the air grows oppressively heavy. Stagnant, it hangs heavy on Phainon’s shoulders. The sun above them reflects off the oily surface of the tide, the heat wafting around them with such strength that it distorts the landscape ahead.

“You said the black tide possessed Eurypon in previous cycles,” Mydei says abruptly.

Phainon, suddenly wary, nods. “It did. Why?”

Mydei looks at his feet, where the tide has peeled away from the ground like so much decayed flesh. “I don’t think that’s going to be a problem this time.”

“At least one thing is going well for us,” Phainon says, gesturing toward the monstrous creatures staggering toward them.

There remains considerable distance between them, but Mydei’s eyes narrow. “We will need to measure our progress carefully.” Speed against the possibility of combat. “Pace ourselves.”

“It would be a problem if we exhausted ourselves only to be set upon,” Phainon agrees.

They slow their pace, their hands on their weapons, but the beasts keep their distance. Perhaps it’s Mydei’s presence that wards them off, Phainon isn’t sure, but he is grateful that they aren’t attacked as they cross the tide, piercing deeper into its territory until there’s nothing green left on the horizon and the sky itself takes on an eerie, reddish hue.

Above them, the sun dips lower, sinking in the cradle of the earth, and they’re forced to stop for the night on a barren stretch of earth, no shelter in sight. With no trees, they cannot light a fire, so they tuck into each other against the easy slope of a hill, draping a linen blanket from Phainon’s gear over their shoulders.

“Phainon,” Mydei says.

“Mm?” Phainon’s head rests on Mydei’s shoulder, and he sits in the crook of Mydei’s arm, wrapped in warmth despite the lack of fire.

Mydei is silent for a moment before he tips his head to the side, looking down at Phainon, who looks up at him from his shoulder. “Are you afraid?” he asks.

A papery roar issues from the darkness, but it’s distant. The black tide’s monsters have kept well away from the incarnation of Strife.

“Yes,” Phainon says anyway, because it’s not the monsters that scare him. “For all these cycles, I’ve had so little to lose.” He reaches for one of Mydei’s hands, lacing their fingers together, trying not to cling and failing. “It didn’t matter if an ally fell. I could fail or kill myself, and they’d be fine in the next cycle. But the cycle after this one…”

Mydei makes a quiet, encouraging sound, his nose in Phainon’s hair.

“You would be alive. All of our—our friends would be alive. But you wouldn’t know me. Wouldn’t love me.” Phainon swallows, looking down at Mydei’s hand in his. He turns Mydei’s hand palm up, and with his free hand traces the lines and calluses that define it. “If we were to love each other again in the next cycle, it would be a different you. And I don’t want a different you, Mydeimos.” He tips his head back, meeting Mydei’s golden eyes. “I want this you, and I’m scared I’ll lose you. That I—that we—will fail again.”

Instead of offering him empty platitudes, Mydei kisses him. A slow kiss, a tender one. Sweet and reassuring in its own way, but innocent of lies of certainty.

When he lifts his face, Phainon manages a small smile. “I don’t deserve you.”

“Perhaps not,” Mydei agrees, earning a small laugh from Phainon. “But you have me. I’m with you, Phainon. Until the end, until we have no options left, and beyond even that.” He turns his face toward the starry skies. “You’ve already learned valuable information about Strife, and now you’re trying something new and wholly different than previous attempts. Even if we fail—” Phainon’s heart squeezes with fear. “—you will have gained valuable information for next time.”

“I don’t want there to be a next time,” Phainon says, hoarse. “I don’t know if there can be a next time.”

“Maudlin,” Mydei accuses.

Maybe he is. “Realistic,” Phainon counters. “You saw me. When I told you the truth, you saw…” He makes a vague gesture, encompassing the whole of himself. “There’s so little left of me.”

“There is enough,” Mydei replies.

What’s left of him is surely built on the foundation of Mydei’s own regard, and Phainon can’t stand the thought of losing it, of waking in world where there’s no familiarity in Mydei’s eyes.

“There is enough,” Mydei says again, and Phainon tucks himself closer into the comfort of Mydei’s embrace.

Maybe there is. Maybe he isn’t the shattered shell of a man who has seen too many horrors. Maybe, with Mydei, he can prevent the primordial ones from destroying the entirety of the world. Maybe hope isn’t a blade with two edges.

On the morning of the second day, Phainon spots smoke on the horizon.

“There’s nothing to burn,” he says, baffled.

Mydei frowns. “That’s the direction in which we must travel.”

They trade wary looks.

“Only a Chrysos Heir could survive here,” Phainon says. “But even one of us needs food, water.” There have been precious little of both. Black tide monsters fade into nothing when they’re killed, their corpses disintegrating. There are no animals, there is no water, just an endless expanse of slick, oily blackness. “I don’t feel good about this.”

“Nor I.”

They make their way toward the smoke regardless, trekking over ground that continues to reflect the brutal heat of an unrelenting sun until they are soaked with sweat. Their water runs low, though they’ve been careful to

ration it. Neither expected to bake on the black tide’s expanse, and they’ve consumed more of it than anticipated as a result.

Phainon holds out some small hope that the smoke indicates a break in the tide, a bastion of civilization where they might find more water, but the very idea of that leaves him disconcerted. The tide devours without discretion. For it to have spared any part of Amphoreus is a variable he doesn’t know how to account for.

“Stop overthinking,” Mydei says as they climb a sloping hill, its slippery surface like so much glass.

“What makes you think I’m overthinking?”

“You’ve got that funny, constipated expression.”

Phainon rears back. “Constipated?” he demands.

And Mydei laughs, offering him a hand to help him up the hill. “Your brows come together like you’re straining very hard.”

Phainon sputters.

“Try not to hurt your small brain.”

“I don’t know why I like you,” Phainon mutters as they gain the crest of the hill and find themselves looking down into a shallow valley.

A valley untouched by the black tide.

Grass spreads for an easy mile in either direction. Tall carobs spread wide their boughs to offer shade over a pond of clear, sparkling blue, fed by a bubbling spring. Bushes of oleander bloom throughout the valley, a mad tangle of uncultivated beauty. And in the center of it all is a squat, one-story oikos, smoke puffing from a fire in a cozy, well-maintained courtyard. Lilting birdsong fills the air, twittering and sweet.

There are no monsters nearby. Nothing prowls the borders of the valley. In fact, it occurs to Phainon that they haven’t seen any of the black tide’s

creatures for the better part of an hour.

“Is this better or worse than finding a city?” Mydei asks.

Phainon shakes his head, bewildered. “I can’t decide. But I don’t have a good feeling about it.”

“We’re in accord, then.” Mydei puts his hand on the hilt of his sword. “Stay on guard.”

“Trust only each other.” Phainon slides carefully down the hill, stumbling onto the soft grass of the valley’s floor with Mydei close behind.

As they approach the oikos, a humanoid figure—a human man, stooped with age—emerges from a door painted vibrant blue. He lifts a hand high, waving it once, twice, above his head. “Ho, travelers!” he calls.

It’s an awkward thing to trot up to him, neither Phainon nor Mydei increasing their pace. They are of silent agreement: as before, neither wants to waste energy now when it might be needed later.

“Travelers,” the man says again as they approach the oikos’s courtyard. Heavy lines weather a bearded face, and thick, bushy brows overhang eyes of piercing gray. “How good it is to have company after so many years! Welcome, welcome!”

Phainon trades a wary look with Mydei as they cross into the courtyard. He half expects the air to change, to feel somehow different, but it doesn’t. “Grandfather,” he says, taking in the worn fabric, tattered around the hems, that wraps the man’s lean form. Lean, but not gaunt. “Grandfather, how have you come to live here, at the center of the black tide?”

The old man laughs, warm. “Ah, now that is a story. But first, let us trade names.” He offers a Kremnoan salute, and at Phainon’s side, Mydei stiffens. “Once a senator of Castrum Kremnos, I am Lygus.”

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 17
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Eurypon disbanded the Senate before even Mydei’s birth, one of his first acts as Castrum Kremnos’s tyrannical king, and so Mydei has never met a senator before, but normal men don’t live so long as this Lygus must have. Mydei trades a look with Phainon, whose gaze is sharp with the same suspicion.

“Then you’ve been here for many years,” Mydei says slowly.

“Oh, yes,” Lygus agrees with a congenial smile, as though he doesn’t understand the implications of this. Even Mydei knows young men weren’t elected senators. “A decade or two, certainly.”

Phainon sets his hand on the hilt of his sword. “Respectfully, grandfather, how has the tide not killed you?”

“The tide has no reason to bother an old man,” Lygus says.

“Nor is it particularly discriminating,” Mydei replies, equally on edge.

Lygus laughs, not unkindly but with joviality of a man amused by the impetuous youths surrounding him. “Warriors true, and you with the look of your mother,” he says to Mydei, but that isn’t enough to startle Mydei. It’s no surprise that senator would recognize Gorgo in his features. “Come, come, let us have this discussion over fruit and bread.” He turns away, giving them his back, and Mydei briefly considers plunging his blade into it. There is danger here, and he’d rather address it swiftly.

Phainon’s fingers brush his wrist. “This is strange,” he murmurs, “and we shouldn’t act rashly.”

“This from you,” Mydei replies with amusement. “But you’re right. Perhaps he knows a way to hold the tide at bay.”

Phainon nods. “He may. He’s worth talking to.”

“For now,” Mydei agrees. He releases his grasp on the hilt of his sword, and he and Phainon follow Lygus through the oikos’s courtyard and into an open-air room.

There, Lygus has laid out a tray of fruits—dates, pomegranates, persimmons—and flat breads alongside an amphora, presumably of wine.

“Sit, sit,” he says, gesturing to the seats around his table. “We have much to discuss, if you have sought me out at last.”

Mydei trades a look with Phainon, and they both take seats flanking each other, opposite Lygus, with the table between them and their backs to an interior wall. From here, Mydei can watch the oikos’s few doors, and nothing can sneak up on them from the valley beyond. A prickling unease washes over him, and he regards the food before him with no small amount of distrust. Surely, there’s no way this Lygus could have anticipated them. Surely, he harbors them no ill will.

“How did you come to be here?” Phainon asks. He, too, sweeps his gaze over the food before them without touching it.

Lygus has no compunctions about his offerings, pouring himself a cup of wine and biting into a fig. “I was run out of Castrum Kremnos ages ago,” Lygus says, “and found this place after many days of wandering.”

“Why?” Mydei asks, leaning forward. Though Lygus peruses the spread of food with impunity, he still doesn’t trust it. “Not just because of my father. Other senators remained behind.”

Lygus’s mouth pulls at the corner, and Mydei can’t tell if it’s disdain or amusement on his face. “Your father didn’t approve of my unique perspective on lawmaking,” Lygus replies, sipping his wine. When Mydei and Phainon remain silent, he continues, “I have always sought the

enumeration of order, and your father has long been an instrument of chaos.”

He doesn’t know, then, that Eurypon is dead. But how could he? He is isolated in the midst of the black tide, and its creatures know no language. Beneath the table, Phainon touches Mydei’s knee, and Mydei intuits his meaning well enough. Say nothing on Eurypon’s death. Don’t let this man know someone else has taken up Strife’s mantle, least of all Mydei.

“Eurypon would disagree with you,” Mydei says instead. “He seeks to bring order to Amphoreus under his rule.”

Lygus laughs. “And what will he do when he has succeeded? He cherishes conflict and violence, and when he has achieved his goals with both, will he not grind society into the very earth? Such behaviors are a cancer.”

“You disagreed with him publicly, then,” Mydei surmises.

Spreading his arms wide, Lygus inclines his head. “I had hoped he and I might be allies in restoring order to the world, but our methodologies were… at odds. He sought conquest. I sought the rule of law, but tyrants are quick to discard the laws that do not favor their views.”

“And so you fled,” Mydei says.

“How have you survived here?” Phainon asks.

Lygus sets his cup down and picks up a knife from near the tray. While Phainon and Mydei draw back, increasingly guarded, he merely presses the tip of the blade against the pad of one finger. “Is it not obvious?” he asks, displaying the finger for them to see.

Golden blood beads on his skin.

Mydei’s eyes narrow. A Chrysos Heir who opposed Eurypon from the start? “You’re the reason Eurypon fears and hates the Chrysos Heirs,” he says.

Lygus’s bushy brows lift. “What measures has he implemented in my absence?”

“He purges Amphoreus of Chrysos Heirs at every opportunity,” Mydei says. “Often, he burns them at the stake, publicly, but he has crucified some and simply slit the throats of others.” His expression is grim. “It depends on wholly on his mood.”

“And yet you both live.” Lygus’s tone is musing, curious. “You, he must be unaware of,” he says, nodding to Phainon. His gaze shifts to Mydei. “And you, he must suffer.” Lygus makes a thoughtful sound. “Ah.” He chuckles. “Eurypon is dead, isn’t he? He wouldn’t allow his son an excursion into the black tide were he alive.”

A chill washes through Mydei.

“A fortunate thing,” Lygus says, smiling, “though I’m sure you mustn’t agree.” He gives a deferential nod toward Mydei. “He was your father, after all.” Mydei says nothing. “Who, then, bears Strife’s mantle in his absence?”

Another touch of Phainon’s fingers against his knee, though Mydei needs no warning to keep his silence on this topic. He doubts it will matter.

“It can’t be that Anaxagoras,” Lygus continues. “For he has been Reason’s creature for years.”

Mydei startles at that. “Anaxagoras is Reason?”

“No, no,” Lygus says, waving him off. “Although, by now, who can say. Only that when I was still in Castrum Kremnos, Anaxagoras was, even as a child, much beloved by the previous Reason. I wouldn’t be surprised to learn he killed Cerces, took her coreflame, and ascended himself in these past few years.” He regards Phainon and Mydei each. “If not Anaxagoras, then… Is it you, my boy?” he asks Mydei. “My condolences. Patricide may be the way of Castrum Kremnos, but I cannot imagine it an easy thing.”

Unease wells within Mydei. Though the sun is bright above them, the world takes on an ominous cast, and he can’t help but think they have somehow walked into something very dangerous. Lygus is too keen.

“Your silence betrays you,” Lygus says. He reaches for another date.

They need to wrest control of this conversation from Lygus. “And you,” Mydei says. “You live in the midst of the black tide, able to push it back as only Strife can. What power is this?”

“Oh, that.” Lygus laughs. “Why would the tide bother its father?”

They are both out of their seats, weapons drawn, a moment later. Mydei’s heart hammers in his chest, a cold sweat beading on his brow despite the warmth of the day.

Lygus is unperturbed. “There’s no need for violence,” he says mildly. “Have I done you harm?”

“Yes,” Mydei says.

“Great harm,” Phainon replies. “You’re destroying the world. You claim your methods are different from Eurypon’s, but you seek the same destruction.”

“Eurypon’s ambitions were small, his methods petty. He wanted to rule the world. I desire nothing more than to see it remade into something more… orderly. Something neat.”

Beside Mydei, Phainon trembles. He wants to reach out, to touch Phainon, to offer him some comfort, but he doesn’t dare take his eyes away from the man still seated so casually in front of them, possessed of the same affectation someone might use to discuss the weather.

“To remake it,” Phainon says, his voice shaking, too.

Lygus gestures to the valley beyond his oikos, as if to the whole of the world. “Eurypon is a prime example of why. The world is fundamentally corrupt, evil. Born from chaos, it possesses no inherent order. Men like Eurypon crawl across Amphoreus at the head of a swarm of locusts and visit suffering upon us all.” He gives Mydei a pitying look. “Surely, you understand.”

“I understand you’re mad,” Mydei replies, not lowering his blade.

This. This is why Phainon is trapped in endless cycles: because this man seeks to cleanse the world of evil.

“Great men are usually considered mad. Eurypon was a great man, uniting Amphoreus beneath one banner, was he not? How far did he get before you killed him?” Lygus asks.

Mydei says nothing.

“Okhema still stands,” Phainon says. “Okhema resists.”

“And with his death, Okhema will become the aggressor Eurypon was,” Lygus says. “The Goldweaver may temper her people, if she has the humanity left to do so, but they will call for Kremnoan blood. The people who Eurypon wronged over the many years will rise up in his absence to tear down whatever legacy of his remains. You.” He indicates Mydei with a fig. “Your mother, if she still lives. Ah, she does. Marvelous. Gorgo would have made an excellent ally.”

“Gorgo would never have allied with you,” Mydei snarls. “She doesn’t want the world to burn.”

“Nor do I,” Lygus says mildly. “The rot of humanity goes too deep for us to cleanse the world with mere fire. No, it must be completely destroyed. Remade.”

Phainon makes a strangled noise. “So you plan to release the primordial ones from THEIR prison. To annihilate not just Amphoreus but the divine heavens above us?”

Here at last, Lygus is taken aback. “How do you know of the primordial ones?” he asks.

“Even my bard knows of the primordial ones,” Mydei says sharply, grateful for Peucesta’s recitation.

Lygus makes a thoughtful noise. “Some pay attention to Hesiod, but everyone knows he was a dreamer and prone to embellishment. That’s why no one has ever taken his Theogony seriously.” He takes another sip of his wine. “Do sit back down.”

They don’t sit, but they do lower their blades. Somewhat.

“You talk like you knew him,” Phainon says. “Hesiod.”

Lygus gives him a wan smile. “We all have our curses. Mine is endless life.”

“Immortality?” Mydei asks, startled.

Lygus shrugs. “Perhaps. I have never died. In light of everything, I simply… continue. I reached this age one… two thousand years ago and never changed—and neither did the world around me. Do you think I came to this conclusion that the world must end lightly?” He scoffs. “No. I have watched men become increasingly degenerate over these two thousand years, their depravity unmatched, and so I created the black tide some centuries ago.” He bares his teeth in a facsimile of a smile. “But you,” he says to Mydei. “Your legacy of Strife has always stood between the tide and its ultimate goal. It is why you have been such an inconvenience in my search for an adequate vessel.”

Phainon’s face blanches of color. “All those times,” he whispers. “All those times the Titans were possessed.”

“The Titans?” Lygus asks. “No, they would never do. They are too fixed in what they are, too ordered for something like the black tide to control.” His smile becomes something terrible, something almost feral, as his attention shifts to Phainon. “But you…” He rises, and their blades rise with him. “Time bends around you. You are… familiar. As though the tide has seen your reflection as you bear up under the strange weight of time.” He spreads wide his hands. “You would do quite nicely.”

Phainon lurches back a step, hitting the oikos’s wall behind him, as Lygus’s form shudders, as it distorts, as it begins to grow. His skin tears like so

much fabric, coming apart at the joints, bloodless but no less disturbing. Flesh peels away to reveal a twisted form of black metal surrounding a magma core of molten gold. Heat spills from it as Lygus—or the creature who once was Lygus—shakes himself free of his skin. Gone are his human proportions, replaced by gargantuan hands tipped with magma-like claws      and legs that spiral into a sharp, pointed spindles. Fiery wings emanate from his back, as golden as the core of him. He towers above them, hunched against the oikos’s ceiling, which cracks as he grows larger still.

“Run,” Mydei says, grabbing Phainon by the wrist and yanking him out of the way as stone crumbles and begins to fall.

No sooner has Mydei dragged Phainon to the side than Lygus attacks, crashing his massive fist into the wall. It, too, shatters, exploding outward into a cloud of rock shards that slice along skin.

Phainon tugs his wrist free of Mydei’s hold as they reach the courtyard. Together, they turn, brandishing their weapons as Lygus recovers from his missed strike.

“Do you think he’s still…” Phainon trails off.

“Child of Time,” Lygus growls, his voice grating like the clash of two blades. “Your flesh will be mine.”

“Still in there,” Mydei confirms.

Lygus slams both fists down. Terrible spikes of virulent gold burst from the ground. Mydei dodges in one direction and Phainon in the other, the both of them throwing themselves out of the way of the attack.

Recovering quickly, Mydei rushes Lygus from one side. Phainon moves in a mirror of him, coming at Lygus from the opposite, and Lygus makes his intentions clear. He lifts one hand and fires a volley of magmatic lances at Mydei as he rounds on Phainon.

Mydei twists through the volley, knocking the lances aside with his blade and ignoring the ones that graze his shoulders, his hip. By the time he’s

cleared the lances, Lygus is hammering Phainon’s own sword with mighty fists, pounding Phainon back, back, back toward the entrance to the courtyard, where a small army’s worth of black tide monsters are rushing toward them.

“Fuck,” he mutters, crossing the courtyard in a rush, engaging the oncoming monsters to protect Phainon’s back while Phainon deals with Lygus.

Twin behemoths roar from backline as more humanoid terrors bear down on him. Mydei’s blade is quick; he carves through him efficiently, twisting to dodge their scythe-like arms and the hammers of their fists. With a dancer’s grace, he cuts them down, and when they come too close, he touches the coreflame’s power within him and summons a burst of vibrant red crystal. Shards of crystal pierce the ground in concentric circles, spearing through the monsters. They fade into a black and gold mist, but he pays the defeated ones little mind as he turns to the approaching behemoths.

Though he hates to admit it, he recalls the conflict with Eurypon and how Eurypon fought them not just with blade but with his Titan’s power. He, too, is the Lance of Fury, and much like Lygus just now, he calls forth great lances from the sky, spearing the behemoths to the ground.

The wave of monsters seems endless. The more that fall, the more arrive, and Mydei finds himself panting as he cuts them down, as he glances behind him to find Lygus chasing Phainon across the courtyard.

This isn’t enough. Separated, they aren’t as powerful. Together, they took down a god, and Lygus, for all his talk of cleansing the world’s corruption, is no god.

Mydei grasps the power of Strife within him and summons a mighty wall of crystal, sealing off the courtyard. The monsters on the other side of it pound against it, their inhuman wails filling the air as they throw themselves repeatedly onto the barrier. It holds strong.

Dispatching the last few monsters, Mydei whirls on Phainon and Lygus.

Lygus leaps backwards, taking to the air with those glowing wings of flame. He hovers, spreading his arms wide and then bringing them together, clapping his massive fists. A boom precedes a burst of flame, one that Phainon barely dodges.

But with Lygus’s attention focused squarely on Phainon, Mydei has an opening.

Adjusting his grip on his sword, he lunges forward, rushing the creature from behind. He kicks off a shattered column that once supported the oikos’s roof and drives his sword into Lygus’s back.

Howling with rage, Lygus whips around. The force of the spin hurls Mydei off him, but he manages to take his sword with him as he rolls across the grass, tumbling to his feet in a crouch.

Phainon is at his side a moment later. “Glad you could join me.”

“Don’t expect me to apologize for dealing with the other monsters.”

Phainon laughs, panting. “Oh, I wouldn’t dream of it. Ready?”

“Ready.”

As one, they rush Lygus. They are twin whirlwinds, ducking under the pounding attacks of his fists as they parry with quick strikes of their blades, ripping into the dripping core of him. Phainon fights with thousands of years of experience, anticipating not just Mydei’s support but Lygus’s attacks, forcing Lygus onto the defensive.

With Lygus on the backfoot, Mydei calls lances from the sky, hammering them down in the courtyard, forcing Lygus to dance between them. He moves with a monstrous grace, deeply unsettling to behold, dodging each lance until one clips one of those fiery wings.

Crashing to the earth with a howl, he slaps the ground.

Mydei and Phainon leap backward as more yellow-gold crystal explodes from the earth, giving Lygus the space he needs to recover.

“I am far older than either of you,” Lygus says, voice booming across the courtyard.

The howling of the monsters on the other side of the crystal barrier grows louder, and Mydei chances a look back. It holds, but through the transparent crystal, cracks have formed on the far side.

“With more experience than you can hope to muster!” Lygus clenches a first, and searing light bursts forth from his wings. Only just turning back, Mydei isn’t blinded, but Phainon, who was looking directly at Lygus, staggers. “What are you ants to the millennia I have lived?”

Mydei lunges forward, ready to defend Phainon, but Phainon, eyes closed, deflects Lygus’s crystalline spears.

“Time bends around me,” Phainon says with a laugh. “Because Oronyx broke it for me. Your two thousand years are nothing to me, Lygus!”

Mydei catches himself, hanging back as Phainon, eyes still closed, engaged Lygus with a perfectly executed flurry of blows, his blade flashing in the sunlight. He slices through one of Lygus’s arms, ducks beneath his guard, and cuts clear through the center of that molten core, cleaving it in half. It is a perfectly executed attack, built on the experience of a man who has suffered for thousands upon thousands of cycles, an incalculable number of years, and while Lygus shrieks in horror, there is nothing he can do to prevent the deathblow.

In pieces, Lygus crumples to the ground. The disparate parts of his tide-tainted body linger there as Phainon stands over him with his bloodless sword, and then even he dissipates into nothing, dissolving like so much chaff.

The howling of the monsters beyond the barrier ceases. Mydei looks over his shoulder, spying the dark smudges of the creatures through the crystals. They remain, but with the loss of their commander, they are, perhaps, confused. Uncertain of what to do. He grimaces, not sure if that’s better or worse. But for now, he turns back to Phainon.

Phainon who stands over the spot where Lygus fell, his face an expressionless mask.

“Phainon,” Mydei says.

“He created the tide,” Phainon says, voice hollow. “He could have told us so much. But he forced us to kill him.” He lifts his face to Mydei’s own. “If he controlled the tide, too—”

A strange groaning fills the air, and they both turn toward the tree beyond the courtyard, watching as the tide consumes it, watching as the tide covers the oikos, as it eats away the grass beneath their feet until Phainon stands on that slick, black surface, and Mydei occupies the only green space that remains.

“Fuck,” Mydei says, raking a hand through his hair. “It’s never moved that fast before.”

Phainon shakes his head. “No, never. It—” He goes utterly, terribly still. “Castrum Kremnos. If it’s moving this quickly, can Leonnius outrun it back to Castrum Kremnos?”

Horror washes over Mydei. “I… don’t know.”

“And then onto Okhema.” Phainon rushes up to Mydei, grabbing him by the shoulder. “How long until it reaches Okhema, if it moves so quickly?”

Mydei isn’t Ptolemy. He doesn’t know how to do this math. “I don’t know.”

“We need to get to Okhema,” Phainon says.

Mydei’s heart aches. “Castrum Kremnos—”

“The tide may take Castrum Kremnos,” Phainon says, his voice cracking, his face breaking with grief. “It may, Mydei, but we can’t let it take Okhema.”

Throat closing, Mydei wraps his hand around Phainon’s wrist. “My friends. My mother.”

Phainon’s eyes are bright, his expression as pained as Mydei’s own. “We can’t be in both places. We can’t save both cities.”

And Mydei, for all he hurts, knows Phainon is right. “Castrum Kremnos for Okhema,” he says softly. “Castrum Kremnos for the world.”

“We will save what we can,” Phainon promises him, gripping his shoulder now for comfort. He pulls Mydei close, embracing him. “We will fix this. Somehow, we will stop the primordial ones, and we will fix this.”

Mydei presses his face into Phainon’s neck, taking a shuddering breath. He allows himself the pain of loss, the ache for his mother, for his friends, for the whole of Castrum Kremnos, knowing there’s no way for them to evacuate the entire city before the black tide arrives. Maybe—maybe— Themistocles will evacuate his mother ahead of the people. Maybe—maybe —his friends will outrun the tide. Maybe, maybe, so many maybes but nothing certain.

Now isn’t the time for grief. The world hangs in the balance.

Withdrawing from Phainon, he chokes down his sorrows and his fears. “We can’t outrun the tide on foot, but Strife can cut through the air.”

Phainon’s eyes widen. “You mean to take Strife’s form?”

“For this, yes.” Mydei’s lips twist in a rueful smile. “Though I have no idea how to do as Eurypon did, I will try. Step back?”

Phainon does so. “I believe in you,” he says, and Mydei’s heart swells. “You’re the only hope for Amphoreus.”

“But no pressure,” Mydei drawls, an almost ironic echo of Phainon’s words to Leonnius.

Closing his eyes, he takes a deep, centering breath. Drawing on Strife’s power isn’t difficult. It craves conflict and wants to be used, springing easily to his hands. His blood pounds in his veins, burning with the desire to turn to the creatures beyond his crystal wall to cut them down. Wrestling

past the desire to fight, he cuts deeper into himself, plunging into the depths of the coreflame inside him.

Power throbs through him, and he discovers the transformation is an easy thing. His desire to crush the primordial ones fuels it, twisting his limbs into white and gold, until he is a massive creature, towering over Phainon, something beyond human ken. A Titan.

Phainon stares up at him, so small and fragile, and Mydei is seized with the desire to protect him, to hide him away from this. But Phainon is at the heart of all this turmoil and protecting him will do nothing to solve it.

Growling low, he bends down, offering Phainon his three-fingered hand. “Climb on,” he grates out. Phainon steps into his palm, holding to his thumb. Mydei bears Phainon to his back, and Phainon climbs onto him. “Do not let go,” Mydei warns.

“You’re all smooth armor. Holding on isn’t going to be easy,” Phainon shouts back. But he finds a seat and settles himself, his small hands grasping onto a piece of Mydei’s armor. Phainon is like an ant, an itch on his back that he wants to scratch. “Right. Ready.”

Strife launches himself into the sky. He hangs there for a second, orienting himself in the direction not of Castrum Kremnos but the Holy City of Okhema. With a howl, he launches himself forward, racing the tide.

Chapter End Notes
