chapters.title: Chapter 18
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

It takes them far too long to outstrip the tide, and Phainon’s stomach churns with anxiety. Somewhere down there, their somatophylakes are hopefully astride their horses, fleeing. Somewhere down there, the city of Castrum Kremnos is likely under siege by the black tide. And somewhere down there, Aglaea’s army will need to turn and flee lest they, too, are devoured by a force of nature that renders the machinations of men meaningless. All the politicking, all the subterfuge and war, and none of it matters in the face of the black tide racing them to Okhema.

Mydei—Strife—does manage to outpace the tide. They catch up to it and then push ahead of its frontier, but it moves at a visible pace, consuming the land in a rolling wave of darkness. Clutching at Strife’s armor, Phainon shudders, but he has a sliver of hope—the black tide was created. A man, a Chrysos Heir, crafted it. If it was created, surely it can be destroyed. Nothing made by men, or even by Titans, can’t be undone somehow. Their confrontation with Lygus gave him this small hope, and he clings to it as Strife races above the ground, touching down but briefly to launch himself into the air once more, cutting through the skies.

Okhema grows large before them, and Phainon briefly entertains the idea of landing and approaching as men—but if they do that, they will be arrested, certainly, and have to go through bureaucracy they don’t have time for to meet with Aglaea. No, they’ll make an entrance. Perhaps Strife is of the same mind because he doesn’t balk as they approach.

The great statue of Kephale rises above the city, the Worldbearer bearing a golden sculpture of the world, and it’s there that Phainon directs Mydei, to the amphitheater beneath Kephale’s watch where Aglaea and her own senate meet. As they approach, golden threads spear through the air around them in shimmering beams, and Strife snarls.

“Don’t fight her,” Phainon calls out. “We’re here as friends. Let her restrain us—a show of good faith.”

Strife snarls again, clearly displeased with this, but allows Aglaea’s threads to weave around his wrists, his ankles. More threads, delicate and gentle, wrap around Phainon, and though they don’t fully pin him down, he knows that the wrong move will see them painfully tight and restrictive.

With the threads wrapped around them, they’re borne down to the center of the curia, a large, circular area set apart from the rest of the city and surrounded by standards of each of the Titans. And as they approach, to Phainon’s shock, the Titans stand before the glowing sigils representing their coreflames. There is Law and Death, Passage and Ocean. Earth. Aglaea stands apart, closer to the center of the curia, her face uplifted toward them as she takes them to the ground, her expression one of fierce concentration.

All of them are present—except for Sky and Reason—and Phainon is as relieved as he is frightened. In no previous cycle have the Titans all gathered together like this. He tried a handful of times to convince them to work together, but they defied him in each attempt, keeping their own counsel. Thanatos was always the most difficult, one of the Titans who survived from the genesis of the world, content to keep themself in their underworld where they thought they would remain untouched by the black tide.

“You’ve done the impossible,” he says to Aglaea as she binds Strife to the ground. “How did you manage to bring them all together?”

She looks up at him with narrowed eyes. “You used me, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” she says in lieu of answering him.

He inclines his head and, mindful of the threads still loose around his body, slides from Strife’s back. “And you, me. So maybe we agree to let bygones be bygones and focus on the larger issue of the black tide.” He extends a hand to Aglaea.

She doesn’t take it.

Law steps forward. She is a slight thing, all long and willowy limbs, with a chiton of vibrant violet edged in gold and a waterfall of black hair spilling down her back. No one knows how she slew Cerydra so many centuries ago, only that she did, and that no one has been able to dethrone her since then. But where Cerydra was, like Eurypon, obsessed with conquering all of Amphoreus, Eunomia believes only in the letter of the law and executing it. She serves as judge and jury for the Titans, a calmer hand than Cerydra was. “Indeed,” she says, “we are convened to discuss the black tide.”

Aglaea’s threads abruptly tighten, and Phainon wheezes, gasping. Strife makes a pained sound as they are both forced to their knees under the oppressive force.

“And we must thank you,” Eunomia continues, “for bringing its source to us.”

Phainon freezes. “I—what?” The statement is so preposterous he can’t even begin to make sense of it.

“For nearly one hundred years,” Aglaea says, “we have struggled against not just the encroachment of the black tide, but its master, as Eurypon’s advance cleared the way for the tide’s destruction. And now you come to Okhema, heralds of the end, with the black tide rushing after you.” She crosses her arms. “You must be proud, for at last Okhema’s armies are defeated.”

Cold horror grips Phainon. If the army is dead, then Hephaestion and the others—he has killed—he can’t think about this. Not now.

Beside him, Strife howls with fury. “Eurypon is dead,” he snarls. “Do you think I would uphold Eurypon’s legacy? Did you not receive my mother’s messenger? Do you not know I struck the final blow against Eurypon, felling him and taking his power?”

“We know,” says Amphitrite, Titan of Ocean, who wears a gown made of water. Small fish swim through it, swirling around her knees, her thighs, her hips. “We felt your accession. But this changes nothing. Your father—”

Strife growls. “—sought to conquer the world with his sword in one hand and the tide in the other. You, apparently, seek only to use the tide.”

Phainon swings his gaze over the Titans. Tribbie and her many siblings cluster together, holding onto each other, their eyes downcast. They are sweet and well-meaning, and perhaps if this was just Aglaea, they would speak in Phainon’s defense, but its unlikely they’ll speak against Law and Ocean—and the other Titans, many of them murmuring in agreement with Amphitrite’s words.

“The black tide is Strife’s ancient enemy,” Phainon protests, bewildered. But he’s seen men—and Titans—believe in stranger things than this. “It flees before Strife’s might and—”

“A ruse,” Eunomia declares.

“It was shortly after Mydeimos’s accession that the tide began its rapid advance,” mighty Kephale says, crossing his arms over his chest. He wears a shining breastplate and a wickedly curved sword on his hip. A helm rests near his feet; he is dressed for war.

Phainon makes a frustrated noise. “It was days,” he corrects. The threads around him grow tighter. They cut into his wrist, his ankles, and wind around his abdomen and his throat as he struggles against them, wanting to rise to his feet.

But even Titans are blind to the truth when they’ve made up their minds, and Kephale waves him off.

Phainon whips his head around, searching out Cipher. She hangs back, her expression clouded. “You know,” he says to her. “The information I gave you about the Acheron—that came from Mydei. He betrayed Eurypon to help us. You know—”

“I know what?” she asks, glib and dismissive as always, though her eyes remain shadowed. “I know that you told me the crown prince would be at the Acheron, which allowed us three days to advance on Castrum Kremnos. Now you claim that information came from him? Why should we believe

that?” She, at least, doesn’t sound convinced of her disbelief. And if he can bring Cipher to his side, then he can sway Aglaea.

“Think, Cipher,” he says. “How would I have had insider information about troop movement if Mydei hadn’t given them to me?”

Her frown deepens, but she says nothing as she leans deeper into the shadow of her own standard.

“Enough of this,” Kephale says. He doesn’t draw the blade at his side but rather manifests one of brilliant black light in his hand. It writhes with shadow at its center, and glows horribly at its edges, rippling with the heat of lightning. “We have Strife before us. We will end him.”

Phainon’s eyes grow wide. “Mydei is immortal. He—”

“A Titan can be slain,” Kephale says, cold and cruel. “We will take his coreflame and give it to an ally.”

Phainon jerks in his bonds as Eunomia and Amphitrite summon their own weapons. Earth follows suit. Even Tribbie and her sisters call their own weapons, though their eyes remain downcast. Aglaea’s threads tighten even more as Strife bellows with fury.

“You can’t!” Phainon shouts. “Strife, whole and complete, can fight back the tide! You have to listen to—”

But they’re not listening. Kephale lifts his blade. Amphitrite hefts her hooked spear. Eunomia brandishes a bow. The eight of them ready their weapons, excepting only Cipher, whose laughter has a nervous edge.

“For Amphoreus,” Kephale says with complete conviction. He brings his sword down in as sweeping arc, and curved, black-white light leaps from it. Strife roars once more, rearing back, and Phainon realizes they have completely and utterly failed. Once more, his actions will see Mydei dead. Once more, he has ruined a cycle. He’ll die, too. There’s no way Kephale won’t kill him, and he’ll lose the only person he’s ever loved in all these cycles, and he doesn’t think he can bear that. He doesn’t want to find Mydei

again, doesn’t want to fall in love again. He wants this Mydei and this world, and he just can’t fucking win.

He screams, too, in furious defiance of the destiny he’s wrought, straining against the threads until one snaps, another, but it’s not enough, not fast enough, as that terrible light slices through the air toward Mydei.

Only for thick roots to burst forth from the earth, taking the hit on Strife’s behalf. Kephale’s attack shears through a layer of the roots, but can only make it halfway through the thicket of them.

“That,” Anaxagoras says, striding into the curia, “is quite enough of that.” His apprentice, Hyacinthia, is at his side, clutching a staff glowing with green light.

The other Titans turn their blades on him, Kephale frowning deeply. “Reason,” he says, and Phainon is less surprised than he thinks he should be to hear that. No, he’s relieved to hear that.

“The only voice of it,” Anaxagoras agrees. “You old fools are so set in your hatred for Eurypon that you can’t see the truth of this situation.” He waves at Phainon and Strife. “They come to you at an inflection point, and you choose to destroy the only people who could potentially save you?” He pinches the bridge of his nose. “Truly, I am surrounded by idiots. Destroy Strife, and you destroy the one Titan capable of holding back the black tide.”

“What proof do you have?” Kephale demands.

Anaxagoras scoffs. “Did you not stand shoulder to shoulder with Gnaeus at the first incursion of the tide, watching him bleed to push it back? Did Nikador not bleed himself almost dry not three hundred years ago? The centuries are long, but your memory is longer, and we all know it. You’re blinded by hatred.” He laughs. “Aren’t you better than that?”

Kephale’s face mottles with rage. “You dare—”

“And do you really think Strife would come here himself and lay himself before your blades if the situation wasn’t dire?”

Strife growls, somehow sounding like agreement, and Phainon looks from Anaxagoras to Kephale and then onto Aglaea. Kephale may lead the Titans, but if enough of them question him, if Aglaea dares to, the others will turn, too, and he’ll be forced to acknowledge the truth of Anaxgoras’s words.

“The black tide is no more Strife’s creation than you are, Kephale,” Anaxagoras continues. “While you can be exceptionally dense—”

Kephale points his blade at Anaxagoras. “Watch yourself, Reason.”

“—you aren’t that much of a fool. Set aside your pride.” He rounds on Aglaea. “And you. You have been in the right, defending your people against Eurypon, but now you lash out at his son—why? For the circumstances of his birth?” Anaxagoras sneers. “Are we not supposed to be better than this? Are we not supposed to care more about the whole of Amphoreus than our petty city states, vying for power between each other? The black tide has swept over Castrum Kremnos—” Phainon’s heart sinks, and he drops his head. “—and encroaches on Okhema, but you focus on assassinating Strife to feed your own egos?” He points a dramatic hand at Phainon. “Listen to him. Hear him.” When Phainon doesn’t immediately start talking, Anaxagoras snaps his fingers. “Speak, boy.”

Lifting his head, Phainon does. “The black tide was created hundreds of years ago,” he says. “By a madman who wants to destroy the world so it can be remade. It will do that by freeing the primordial ones, ancient gods entombed in a mausoleum beneath Okhema.”

Many of the Titans scoff at this, laughing as they glance between each other, but Aglaea is silent, her brows drawn tight, and Thanatos leans forward, extending darkness from their form like a reaching hand.

Phainon turns to Thanatos, who stands silent before their standard, cloaked in wine-dark hues, a veil over their face. “You must remember THEM. The others, they’re all newer, but you and Kephale were there.” He glances at Kephale, whose face has begun to fall into one of dawning horror.

Phainon’s attention return to silent Thanatos. “The black tide seeks THEIR prison. Seeks to free THEM. All of this is in service of using THEM to destroy and remake the world.”

“This must be a joke,” Eunomia says, laughing.

“No,” Thanatos rasps, their voice like so many whispers, like sheafs of parchment rustling. “No, the boy speaks true. Before the Titans, the primordial ones were.” Thanatos inclines their head toward Kephale. “You remember, brother.”

Waxen-faced, hand covering his mouth, Kephale nods. “I remember. THEIR wars were the things of nightmares. THEY created and destroyed with indifference, neither act different from the other. We entombed THEM.” He touches his chest. “With the coreflames, we locked THEM away where THEY could do no harm.” He leans forward. “Who is it who created the tide and seeks to free THEM?”

“An old man calling himself Lycurgus,” Phainon says.

Aglaea chokes. “The senator from Castrum Kremnos.”

Eunomia looks sick. “I taught him.”

“He’s dead,” Phainon says. “For what it’s worth.”

Aglaea twists her wrist, and the threads restraining him and Strife finally fall away. In an instant, Mydei stands beside him once more, rubbing his wrists, disdainful. He steps closer to Phainon, and Phainon rises from his knees, desperately wanting to take Mydei’s hand and fearing any indication of affection will be seen as weakness.

“We killed him,” Mydei says. “And his death expedited the tide.” He looks to Anaxagoras, expression tight. “Castrum Kremnos fell?”

Anaxagoras nods. “But I convinced your mother to flee before the tide arrived. How many survived, I do not know, but she races ahead of it to Okhema.” He gestures to Hyacinthia. “We were simply faster on our own.”

Relieved, Mydei exhales, closing his eyes. “Thank you, scholar,” he says.

The other Titans have turned on Kephale and Thanatos, Aglaea first among their number, fierce with her anger. “You have known?” she demands of them. “All this time, you have known the black tide sought to free monsters entombed beneath my city?”

“No,” Kephale says, warding her off with upraised hands. “We knew the primordial ones were buried there, but THEY were meant to be forgotten. That this Lycurgus discovered THEIR existence, that he meant to free THEM…” His fingers brush over his own chest.

Phainon notices. “You said the coreflames were used to entomb them,” he says. “If they were strong enough to overwhelm and lock away the primordial ones, could they not be used again to turn back the black tide? Wouldn’t they be powerful enough?”

Unease passes over Kephale’s face. “It’s not so easy a thing to master all the coreflames, and with Oronyx’s missing… I worry the balance would be unstable.”

“Then we stand aside?” Aglaea asks softly. “We stand aside and let the black tide destroy us?”

“We can’t,” Phainon says, clenching his fists.

They all fix him with heavy gazes, weighty and terrifying; he is the lone human man among the Titans. An ant. They could crush him.

“Tell them,” Mydei murmurs, reaching out and touching his fingers to Phainon’s shoulder, an incredible comfort. Aglaea’s lips part with realization, but she says nothing. “Tell them what you’ve done,” Mydei says.

“This has happened before,” Phainon says, lifting his eyes to meet Kephale’s. “Not exactly like this, but the black tide has reached Okhema before, destroying it, freeing the primordial ones to let THEM destroy the universe. But when it did, my childhood friend, Cyrene, she was there—we

were both there—and she and Oronyx shattered Oronyx’s coreflame to create a time loop. They destroyed themselves for us. For me. So that I could do this again and again, so that I could stop the primordial ones.” He swallows hard. “I have done this… so many times.”

Aglaea presses a hand to her chest.

“This is a lie,” Amphitrite says. “Oronyx has been dead for thousands of years.”

“Because in this cycle, Oronyx never existed,” Phainon insists.

“Liar,” Amphitrite hisses.

Cipher finally steps out of the shadows. “The truth,” she says. All attention turns to her, and though she quails, as if she hates to be so noticed, she doesn’t step back. She fixes her gaze on Aglaea. “We know I can tell truth from lie.”

“Because you yourself are a liar,” Eunomia drawls.

“She did not lie when she brought news of the Acheron to me,” Aglaea says, quick to Cipher’s defense.

Eunomia scoffs. “One instance of honesty doesn’t mean—”

“Believe me or not,” Cipher says. “We waste precious time arguing when Phainon is telling us the truth: Oronyx shattered themself, as he says, to create a loop for him.” She studies him. “How many times?”

He allows his weariness to show, allows himself to slouch. “Thousands? Tens of thousands? I’ve lost count. But this time, you’re all here, and I’ve learned more from you. The combined power of the coreflames locked away these primordial ones. Surely, even without Oronyx, if Kephale is careful—” For who else but Kephale could do this? “—then we can use that same power to drive back the black tide. To destroy it.”

Anaxagoras claps, slowly and with great irony. “Now that we have reached our inevitable conclusion, perhaps we can act.” He gestures to the red-

stained horizon, where slick black coats the ground and rolls increasingly closer. “We don’t have much time.”

Still clearly uncertain, Kephale shakes his head. “Without Oronyx’s coreflame…”

“If we give over our coreflames, we will make ourselves defenseless,” Eunomia says. “This could all serve the tide’s ends.”

“And what other choice do we have?” Mydei suddenly demands, rounding on her and Kephale both. “Janus—Passage—may have been the first among you—us—” He throws a hand in the air, frustrated. “—but the Worldbearer has always led the way for the others. Will you gods condemn a human man to repeat more of these cycles out of fear and arrogance? Out of worry that you will lose power?” He slaps his hand against his chest. Golden sparks crackles around his palm as he draws it back, removing with it the coreflame housed inside him. “If we fail, we are destroyed, and Phainon lives again, knowing he can’t trust any of us to do what we should: protect humanity before ourselves and our own interests.” Mydei extends his hand and his coreflame to Kephale, thunder in his voice and lightning in his eyes. “Do as you were created to do,” he says to Kephale, “and bear the weight of responsibility for this world.”

Silent, Kephale reaches for Mydei’s coreflame. He takes it in cupped hands, reverent in his quiet. “You are right, Strife,” he says. “What are we if not the guardians of what we created? Let us protect it once more, as we did in the days of old.”

“Let epics be sung in our honor,” Aglaea says as she, too, coaxes her coreflame from her chest. When Kephale has absorbed Strife’s coreflame, he takes Romance’s into himself as well.

Anaxagoras spares a scathing look for the other Titans before offering Reason’s coreflame, and Hyacinthia follows with Sky’s. Cipher is hesitant, ducking forward and giving over Trickery before skuttling back.

Hope burns in Phainon’s chest. His skin tingles as power wafts through the air, as the other Titans, slowly and haltingly, come forward with their own

coreflames. Next Thanatos. Reluctantly, Amphitrite. Reservedly, Eunomia. Tribbie and her sisters with more enthusiasm, offering their coreflame with a smile.

Anaxagoras leans over Phainon’s shoulder. “You’re sure Oronyx’s coreflame was destroyed when your Cyrene bent time?” he asks, sotto voce.

Phainon hesitates. He remembers only Cyrene’s impassioned prayers and the moment she grasped pure power between her hands, Oronyx’s coreflame in her palms. And then the world was sundered, and he in that cellar beneath his home in Aedes Elysiae, listening to slaughter. “I’m sure,” he says.

“Hm.” Anaxagoras withdraws.

Letting a frown fade, Phainon turns to Mydei. “Thank you,” he says.

Mydei answers with a small smile. “This will be the last,” he replies, gripping Phainon’s hand.

Finally goes Earth, a boy child locked in eternal youth, who has kept his peace this entire time. “For the future of humanity,” he says to Phainon, not Kephale, before giving over his coreflame, too.

Kephale, panting, takes this last coreflame into his hands. Strain marks his face as he absorbs this final coreflame.

“It is done,” Aglaea says. She reaches for Kephale. “Go forth and turn back the black tide.”

Kephale takes her wrist in his hand—and Mydei and Phainon see it in the same moment: the blue-black of Kephale’s eyes. Fear carves through Phainon, but it doesn’t paralyze him. He lunges forward with Mydei, both of them striving for Aglaea. They cannot reach her before Kephale snaps her wrist, summons his blade of black-white light, and drives it through her stomach.

chapters.title: Chapter 19
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Tribbie screams. Cipher, too.

Phainon grasps Aglaea by the shoulders and pulls her back, off of Kephale’s sword, as Mydei catches the next blow of the Worldbearer’s blade on his gauntleted fist. Blood pours from her wound, staining her belly, and Phainon drags her backwards as Hyacinthia rushes forward, her hands glowing with healing energy.

“Let me!” she exclaims, pressing her hands to Aglaea’s wound as Aglaea, white as her dress, groans.

Mydei isn’t alone engaging the Worldbearer. The Titan swings his blade wildly, and Anaxagoras and Thanatos both lunge forward to deflect his strikes from landing on Mydei. The three of them barricade Kephale as Kephale lets his sword vanish, drives his hands into his hair, throws back his head, and roars.

Black-white light pours from his mouth, piercing the skies.

A mistake. Giving Kephale the coreflames was a mistake—another mistake —Phainon can’t stop making mistakes—there has to be a right answer in here somewhere, but as he clutches Aglaea’s shoulders, as Hyacinthia heals her and Tribbie sobs and Cipher pleads, he can’t find it.

Kephale screams, turning his face toward the former Titans, and Mydei tackles him to the ground, catching him by the jaw and angling his face up so he can’t hit anyone with that beam of terrible light, but Kephale quickly throws him off and flings him halfway across the curia, into a pillar. Mydei’s impact cracks it in half.

“Go,” Hyacinthia says. Phainon whips around to look at her, her expression drawn with concentration as she heals Aglaea’s wound. Tribbie wails, and Cipher clutches Aglaea’s hand. “Go help them,” Hyacinthia says again. “You’re a warrior. You’re wasted here.”

She’s right. He can’t help Aglaea, but he has fought alongside Kephale before; he recruited the Worldbearer for one cycle, and fury floods him. Kephale hadn’t believed him about the black tide, and they’d failed. Kephale lied to him. Kephale damned the world. And now, ripe with the power of all the coreflames, Kephale is insane with power, damning the world again.

Phainon passes Aglaea to Cipher, climbing to his feet. Mydei, too, staggers upright.

This time, somehow, Phainon won’t let the world be damned, to hell with Kephale’s weakness.

They need to trap him.

“Pelius,” he says to the former Earth Titan. “Can you still manipulate rocks?” Pelius inclines his head. “Create a domed barrier and do everything in your power to hold it. Amphitrite, share your energy with Pelius. Keep him shielded at the same time.”

She sputters. “That is—”

“Your only fucking option,” Phainon snaps, drawing his sword. “Keep Kephale trapped here unless you want him to do the tide’s work for us.”

“He warned you,” Eunomia hisses, grabbing at Phainon’s sword arm.

He throws her off him, turning his blade on her as Anaxagoras and Thanatos batter Kephale back. “You,” he says to her. She has limited power over the rules that govern the world, and he’s not sure he trusts her to actually help. “You can increase our strength, our speed.”

She sputters.

“Do it,” he says. “Bless us with superior, Titan-like capabilities, or we will all die here.”

“We’re going to die anyway,” she says.

“Then die fighting.” He whirls away from her and throws himself into the fray alongside Anaxagoras and Thanatos.

Mydei is by his side a second later, sword in hand.

Kephale wastes no time pretending to be mortal. He blasts them all back with tremendous force, giving himself meager seconds—seconds he takes to transform into something grotesque and monstrously glorious. A goat’s head emerges alongside a lion’s from a lion’s torso. A long tail slithers across the floor, ending in a snake’s head that hisses at them. Kephale stands on his hind legs, two humanoid, golden arms sprouting from either side of his abdomen. Wings of white ivory burst from his back, and he hovers off the ground, not unlike Lygus. Flowers sprout along his limbs, glowing with verdant life.

Mydei swears. Thanatos says nothing but growls low in the back of their throat. Phainon, who has seen all these parts in different configurations, feels his heart drop.

“A chimera,” Anaxagoras says, adjusting his hold on his blade. “Don’t let the snake head bite you.”

“He’ll have all the powers of the Titans at his disposal,” Phainon warns.

A hand touches his back. “Good thing you have me to reinforce you,” Eunomia says. She slaps her hand between his shoulder blades, and he launches himself forward at a superhuman speed.

Kephale matches him.

They clash in the center of the curia, their impact rattling the earthen dome closing above them. Phainon grits his teeth, pushing against one of Kephale’s black-white blades. The ground beneath his feet cracks. Shatters.

Mydei feints at the Worldbearer’s side, and is joined by Anaxagoras, forcing Kephale to turn from Phainon to defend himself. He sweeps a fist at them, trailing deadly arcs of black-white lightning. The scent of ozone fills the air, and Thanatos descends from above, driving a spear downward and forcing Kephale to leap backwards. Eunomia weaves between them, touching them on their shoulders to give them bursts of speed and strength as they take lancing stabs and sweeping strikes at Kephale.

Sweat drips down Phainon’s face as he calls out to the others, directing them to leap back when Kephale summons bolts of lighting, warning them before more of those sweeping attacks hit home. At his urging, Anaxagoras swings around Kephale’s back, dancing with the snake-headed tail, keeping it occupied.

While Mydei and Phainon stab at Kephale’s heart, Thanatos manages to shear off one of those golden arms—only for two to grow back in its place, each wielding spears of virulent red crystal.

“Fuck,” Mydei gasps.

A wave of earthen spikes burst from the ground, followed by those crystals. One catches Eunomia’s ankle, closing around it. She screams, hammering at the crystal with her fist as crystalline lances coalesce in the air above her.

“Mydei,” Phainon shouts.

Mydei swings around Phainon, sheathing his sword in one motion and driving his gauntlets into the crystal encasing Eunomia’s ankle in a one-two strike. The crystal shatters. She scrambles backwards as Mydei fluidly turns back to Kephale and the lances strike where she was trapped not seconds before.

Throwing herself to her feet, she weaves once more through the fray, undeterred, reaching for Mydei to bolster him, too. “A life for a life, Strife,” she calls to him.

Mydei grins back at her, all teeth.

Energy sizzles through the air as Kephale reaches into the very fabric of reality, twisting it, tearing it, summoning orbs of that same black-white light to smash down on Phainon and the other former Titans. They dodge the strikes, but the damage they do is minimal. Kephale can see every attack, has eyes in all directions, and when they pin him down, he launches himself upward. No, he can’t go far, but he hovers out of reach as Eunomia switches to her bow and—

“Snowy! Ahead!” Phainon doesn’t glance back at Tribbie. He’s done this with her before, he remembers this from previous cycles. He runs forward at her command, and a gate opens before him. The portal drops him in the air above Kephale, and he plunges downward, landing on his back.

Golden threads snap around Kephale’s limbs, and now he does glance up to see Aglaea on her knees, her hand extended, her face a mask of concentration. Hyacinthia still has her hands pressed to Aglaea’s stomach, working a healing power diminished by the lack of her coreflame, but clearly determined to do what she can.

Beneath him, Kephale explodes with black-white light. It bursts out of him like so many shooting stars, peppering the curia. One line of void-color rips through Thanatos’s shoulder, and they cry out in agony, clutching at the wound. A series of lines streak after Mydei, who dances away from them with a warrior’s fluid grace, quite literally punching them from the air and creating small explosions. He is beautiful, deadly, and he doesn’t see the void-color line approaching him from behind.

“Mydei!” Phainon calls out.

Kephale roars, shaking violently beneath him, forcing him to pay attention to his unstable footing on the Titan’s back. He can’t spare attention to make sure Mydei is alright, can only fist his hand in the lion’s mane. Clinging, he drives the point of his blade into the side of Kephale’s throat. Golden blood bursts from the wound as he forces his sword through flesh, leaving a ragged slash in his wake.

One of Kephale’s hands reaches back, and he grabs Phainon around the middle before Phainon can skid away. He hurls Phainon away, and Phainon

tumbles through the air only for Anaxagoras to snatch his wrist, and drag him down. They slide across the ruined rock of the Curia’s floor.

“Quickly,” Anaxagoras pants. “We can’t keep this up.”

Kephale lets out another bellow, so loud it knocks Phainon back a step. Aglaea’s threads sag, and in that moment Kephale leaps forward, pouncing on Eunomia. He pins her down as she screams, opening the maw of his lion’s mouth. Fire coalesces between his teeth.

No. No, they can’t afford to lose a coreflame’s vessel.

“Mydei!” he shouts, and Mydei rushes Kephale in time with Phainon.

Tribbie opens twin gates, one in front of Mydei and another before Phainon, and neither hesitates. They plunge inside, appearing in the air above Kephale once more. Time stretches before them, the world slowing down. Mydei lets out a wild war cry, summoning a giant spire of red crystal up from the earth to spear Kephale through the middle as they descend on the lion’s neck. As one, they bring their blades down with tremendous force, their momentum aiding them as they sever the head from the body.

Golden blood gushes forth, and the fire sputters out as the head tips forward. Anaxagoras is faster, snatching Eunomia out from beneath Kephale’s paw before the dead Titan’s head crashes down.

Phainon hits the floor hard, his knees rattling, sweat dripping down his back. He’s panting as he turns to the Worldbearer’s dead body, relieved and horrified in equal measure. The Worldbearer is dead.

“We must take our coreflames back,” Eunomia says around her own labored breathing. “This was a fool’s errand. If Kephale could not bear their combined might—”

But Kephale was out of balance. Kephale didn’t have Oronyx’s coreflame.

You’re sure Oronyx’s coreflame was destroyed when your Cyrene bent time?

Anaxagoras’s question rings in his mind as Eunomia shrugs him off, as she staggers toward Kephale’s body with an outstretched arm.

She’s not as close to Kephale as Phainon, who plunges his hand into Kephale’s back, driving it in up to his shoulder, reaching as deep as he can. Fingers spread wide, instinct guiding him, he strains toward the burning power of all those coreflames and feels an answering resonance from within his own chest, a strange stirring.

“No!” Eunomia shrieks.

“Phainon—!” Mydei lurches forward.

Anaxagoras yanks them both back as Phainon finds the power in the center of Kephale’s being and, instead of taking it from Kephale as the others did from themselves, simply absorbs it directly into his body.

Agonizing pain drives him to his knees. Power hammers through him, cracking inside his skull, and he grips his own hair, gasping, staring blankly at the ground in front of him as he screams, as fire consumes him, as he drowns, as thorns pierce his flesh, as rock crushes him, as he loses Mydei over and over and over again. He is tormented by the law, driven mad by the need to reach the heights of the sky itself only to fall from grace. He is trapped in a maze from which there is no escape, chased by the shadow of Death itself, possessed of the desire to tear the very world apart and reduce it to its foundations.

No.

Over thousands of cycles, over countless years, he’s seen the world reduced to so much ash. No, he doesn’t want that at all.

And he remembers. He remembers every time he failed with sudden, perfect clarity. Remembers every attempt he’s made to stop the primordial ones, remembers each failure, every death, both the ones caused by his own hand and the ones caused by THEIR destruction. He’s never won. All this time, and he’s faced nothing but defeat—and he thinks this time will be

different? He thinks he can create a new memory? Carve a new path for the world?

Who is he, a farm boy from Aedes Elysiae, to want a better world? Should he not be content with the one he has, with the time he has? Is he not exhausted, sick of trying?

Tears cut down his face. He sinks lower, closer to the ground, scratching at his clothes, his chest. He burns, he aches, he is nothing but pain, but regret. Remorse cuts him into ribbons, savaging him as he bows his head and howls with misery.

His name cuts through the agony. “Phainon!” Hands grip his shoulders, warm and callused, wet with golden blood.

He lifts his head. Phainon lifts his head, and he stares into golden eyes, blazing with resolve.

Phainon is a farm boy from Aedes Elysiae who wants to change the world. At first, for everyone else—for so long, for everyone else. For Cyrene, for the friends he’s made and lost, for the people of Amphoreus. But, now, for none of them except Mydei. For Mydei, who deserves to live. For Mydei, who he loves, who is more important than any of it, who he wouldn’t die for because to die for Mydei would be to lose Mydei and he will—not— lose—Mydei.

Clutching Mydei’s wrists, staring into Mydei’s eyes, Phainon wrestles back the power that burns through him, hotter than the sun, than a thousand suns. He is in one of Eurypon’s fires, but he has the Ocean at his fingertips, and he draws on that power now, letting it wash through him, braiding it with Sky’s healing. Soothing power surges forth, washing away the agony of the flames.

“Mydei,” he grits out, squeezing harder.

“Phainon.” Mydei’s fingers dig into Phainon’s shoulders. “Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, Deliverer of Okhema. Of Amphoreus. Will you yield to this?”

He binds the pain with Romance’s threads, buries it with Earth’s rock, restrains it with Reasons’s vines. He climbs on top of it, of the memories. His failures have worn him down, exhausted him, but this time—this time —he has so much more to fight for. So much more to win for.

“Will you yield?” Mydei demands.

Phainon grasps the power within him in a mighty fist—and then lets it go. Like Sky’s power sweeping through him, he embraces it. Wraps himself around it. Victory is not about control.

Releasing Mydei’s wrists, he extends his hands, glowing with golden light, and takes Mydei’s face. “Never,” he rasps. “For you. For you, I will never yield.” The power settles inside him, finding a home in his chest, twelve coreflames burning relentlessly. They hurt, but they can’t destroy him. Not when he has this thing worth fighting for. Not when he has Mydei.

Mydei has done so much for him. Now, he will make the world a place where Mydei can live.

He pulls Mydei close and kisses him. Mydei’s hands find his jaw, his neck. They cling to each other as the last of the pain fades to a dull burn in Phainon’s chest, not defeated but manageable.

For Mydei. He will do this for everyone, but for Mydei most of all.

They break apart, panting, resting their foreheads together.

“Well,” Anaxagoras says. “That was quite something.”

And then they’re laughing, Phainon ducking his head with embarrassment as Mydei lifts his own with that princely arrogance he wears so well.

“Can we assume Phainon won’t be attacking us the way Kephale did?” Anaxagoras asks, sheathing his sword.

Hyacinthia has moved from Aglaea, who stands nearby, holding both Tribbie and Cipher’s hands, to Thanatos, who is no longer bleeding gold but whose arm hangs limp and useless at their side.

“No,” Phainon says, trying and failing to suppress a smile as he glances at Mydei. “No, Phainon won’t be attacking anyone.”

Amphitrite and Pelius drift toward them, but Eunomia keeps her distance, fury on her face. “Was this your plan?” she demands. “To poison Kephale with power and then—”

“Oh, shut up, Eunomia,” Anaxagoras says. “Kephale didn’t have Oronyx’s coreflame within him.” He gestures to Phainon. “But Phainon did.”

“I didn’t…” Phainon presses his hand to his chest, rising with Mydei’s assistance. “I didn’t know. I just… hoped. When I reached into Kephale’s body, I simply hoped. You knew?”

Anaxagoras shakes his head. “Surmised. Presumed.” His expression is smug. “It’s pleasant to be correct.”

“Then what now?” Aglaea asks. “Attempt to turn back the black tide as planned?”

They turn toward the horizon, the former Titans and Phainon, and Phainon’s heart sinks. The green lands beyond Okhema are a sea of black, the sky tinted red. The far walls of the city are slick and dark.

“The black tide is here,” he breathes. Fear shivers down his spine, but he ruthlessly suppresses it.

Aglaea makes a pained sound. “Then we’re too late.”

“Not yet,” Mydei says, his hand still in Phainon’s. “Kephale said the primordial ones’ original prison was made with the coreflames. Phainon, go to the prison, you know the way, and maybe you can reinforce it. We can hold the monsters at bay and evacuate as many citizens as we can.” He looks toward Aglaea. “You have collected plenty of Chrysos Heirs.”

“They man the walls,” she says softly.

“Then they’re already doing what we need them to do,” Mydei says. “We hold the line for Phainon.”

Anaxagoras smiles. “That’s the smartest thing any one of you have said since I arrived.”

Rolling his eyes, Mydei turns to Phainon, taking his face in his hands once again. “For our friends,” he says softly. “For Castrum Kremnos and Okhema. For the world.”

Phainon gives him a hard kiss, a desperate one. The kind of kiss lovers exchange when the world is on the line and one—or both—might die. No. No, neither of them will die. Not this time. “For you,” he says, hitting his fist against Mydei’s chest. “For you.”

Aglaea’s threads bear her command to the Chrysos Heirs at the wall: defend. They bear her command to the former Titans: organize the people. They bear her command to the people throughout the city: flee. But the people are panicking, and Mydei can’t get them to organize neatly ahead of the oncoming tide. Their panic causes them to flood the streets, clutching their children and precious possessions—and some that seem less precious, but he doesn’t have the time or energy to judge them too harshly. Despite his attempts to keep them orderly, they push and shove, and he spends more time fishing people off the ground to prevent them from being trampled than he does actually getting anyone out.

He is wasted here, and he knows it, but he can’t do much at the walls, either. The other Chrysos Heirs will have to hold back the tide’s monsters and, hopefully, the tide as an extension. If he goes to them, they will want him to bleed across the battlements, and there’s only so much of that he can do before killing himself.

Groaning, he yanks a little girl off the ground, sets her on her feet, and pushes her toward her father. “Go,” he says to her, as gently as she can, and she takes off at a run, her short legs working.

People are going to die today in uncountable swaths, and he hates how pointless this feels. If Phainon isn’t successful, if the tide continues, then everyone in Amphoreus will die, the tide will consume the world, and these primordial ones will tear down the very heavens. He wants Phainon to

succeed. He hopes Phainon will with everything he is. But as he urges the people toward the northern gate and out of the city, away from the oncoming tide, he can’t help but fear the odds are against them. The weight of Phainon’s previous failures are heavy on Mydei’s heart, and he hates himself for that. He should believe with everything he is, but he is afraid. He is so very afraid.

Screams pierce the air, and Mydei whips around. Black tide monsters fill the sky, and though the Chrysos Heirs at the walls are doing the best they can, many have broken through. They careen downward, striking at the crowd and infecting those they touch.

Swearing, Mydei pushes through the crowd as the people flee, shoving against their flow. He breaks through them to find spindly creatures lashing out at those who are unfortunate enough to be too slow at the back of the crowd.

He leaps forward, insinuating himself between the people and the monsters, grasping one creature by the face and throwing it through a nearby wall. Though he’s given up his coreflame, he’s still a Chrysos Heir, still stronger and faster than a normal human, and he uses these strengths to his advantage, the vanguard of an entire city. He beats the monsters back, holding them at bay until the street behind him is empty, and then takes off at a run to find the next street that needs his protection.

There comes a distant explosion, loud enough to ring in his ears, forceful enough to knock him back a step, and he mutters another oath. He clambers up a nearby ladder, taking it to the roof of an abandoned home, and turns in the direction of a plume of smoke, squinting against the distance.

Aglaea’s threads light up, carrying the whisper of her voice to his ear. “The southern wall has fallen to the tide.” Mydei’s heart seizes. “Fall back to the agora. All Heirs, fall back to the agora.”

They’re going to lose the city. Of course they’re going to lose the city. They can’t fight the tide itself, only its monsters, but they don’t need this hit to their morale.

“Do not give up,” Aglaea’s voice says, vibrating through the threads. “Remain strong. We are the bastion standing between the tide’s monsters and the annihilation of all of Amphoreus. What we save today we will use to rebuild our world from the ashes. Stand firm, children of golden blood, and fight to weave a new fate, a new future.”

Pretty words. Mydei can only hope they’re enough.

Steeling himself, he turns in the direction of the agora.

Energy slams into him from behind, and he staggers forward, gasping. This isn’t the force of an explosion, it’s pure power, and with it comes a terror that eclipses reason. He drowns. He’s back in the lake, weighted to the bed, clawing at the water, desperate for air as he dies and dies and dies. He’s choking on vomit as poison courses through his system. He’s kneeling at Eurypon’s feet, shaking and cold, with Eurypon’s sword resting against his shoulder. Every horrible moment he’s survived, every terror, every fear, screams through him. He relives them all at once, the agony of them hammering down on him.

Mydei finds himself on his knees, vomiting bile, trembling. His vision tunnels; he can see only the limestone roof beneath him, and his every instinct screams that he run, that he flee, that he get as far away from Okhema as he possibly can.

And he knows.

Whatever has sealed THEIR prison has broken.

chapters.title: Chapter 20
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

The entrance to the primordial ones’ prison is deep in the heart of the Marmoreal Palace, hidden behind a maze of storerooms and locked doors for which the keys have long been lost. Phainon breaks down these ancient doors, shoving bodily through rotting wood until he reaches a staircase long, narrow, and curving.

Cold sweat beads on his forehead. His palms go damp and clammy, and he swallows convulsively as his mouth floods with saliva. Every muscle screams in protest as he forces himself to take the first step onto that staircase, hundreds and thousands of failures in this very same place rushing over him. Aglaea’s betrayal. Kephale’s. He’s died here so many times that his body is convinced he’ll die here yet again.

“Not this time,” he says to himself, forcing his foot onto the first step. “Not this fucking time.” He takes another step down. “For Amphoreus.” Another. “For Cyrene.” He picks up his pace. “For my parents. For Queen Gorgo.” He rests his fingers against the curving wall for stability as he descends faster. “For each of those stupid bastards.” He laughs, thinking of the somatophylakes, of their wit and their wisdom, of their slow-won friendship. Of Leonnius’s scales and Hephaestion’s warming heart. “For Mydei.” His hand clenches in a tight fist, knuckles dragging over ancient stone. “For Mydei.”

This time will be different. It has to be. Not just for himself—he can’t start over again, he can’t—but for Mydei, this Mydei, who he loves.

The stairwell grows darker, darker, but he’s been down this way so many times that he doesn’t need light. And then, ahead of him, long minutes later, the faint glow of luminous moss. Phainon emerges into a massive underground cavern, carved and polished by Amphoreans long dead, a place that reeks of stale air.

Once, this ancient mausoleum instilled in him a sense of wonder. The cavern is vast, its curving walls extending high above his head, as though there’s only a thin layer between the roof of it and the city above. Thick stalagmites have been carved into towering columns, adorned with depictions of the primordial ones instead of the Titans. He walks between these monoliths on a fragile bridge of dark rock. Far below, an underground lake glows with more of that iridescent moss.

Ahead of him, the bridge opens into a circular space not unlike the curia except that it’s several times smaller. More intimate. Statues of eighteen impossible creatures ring the space, each more bizarre than the last. Looking at them makes Phainon’s head hurt and his stomach heave with nausea, and so he turns his attention to the center of the space. There stands a small altar, and on the altar, an empty basin carved with the symbols of each Titan.

He doesn’t know what to do. He carries the twelve coreflames inside of him, but he doesn’t know what to do with them. Doesn’t even have an inkling of—

Stone cracks. Shatters.

Phainon, standing at the end of the rock bridge, reels back. He forces his gaze onto the statues, fighting visceral nausea and a sudden, pounding headache. There. Golden light shines between hairline cracks that grow and grow as the statue closest to him begins to crumble.

Pain slices through his head, and Phainon collapses to his knees with a cry, pressing his hands to both eyes. His head pounds, he feels his pulse in his ears. He can’t breathe, and bile climbs his throat, and when he drops his palms to the rock beneath him to heave, they come away bloody. And they land not on rock but on slick, red-tinged blackness.

“No,” he whispers as the tide consumes the rock bridge, reaching for the statues before him. “No, not this.”

The tide creeps closer to the statue, and the statue breaks more, great pieces of stone falling away to reveal a man’s broad and naked back. White hair

spills around THEIR shoulders as THEY stretch and twist, freeing arms that —that aren’t attached to THEIR body. Arms that look like ribbons of curled papyrus.

This is the end. The black tide reaches for the statue, for the primordial thing crawling free of its stone prison, and Phainon knows this is the end. The tide will destroy this prison once more, Phainon will fail, and the world will be torn apart only for him to try again. He curls his fingers into fists as blood drips from his nose.

It splatters on the tide, and the tide recoils.

Phainon’s breath catches.

Reeling upright, he casts his gaze around himself and discovers the tide has given him a wide berth—just as it does Mydei. He contains Strife’s coreflame, and the tide has always fled from Strife. But not just Strife. He contains all the coreflames, and those pieces of crystalized power, born from the chaos of the world, created this entire prison.

A power to imprison gods, and a power to free them.

More of the statue crumbles, the man-shaped thing contained within shaking rock off THEIR hips, THEIR legs.

Phainon reaches out. He digs his fingers beneath the edge of the tide as it tries to race away from his touch, and he closes his fist around the strange, slippery surface of it, grasping it.

“You with the power to destroy a prison meant for things older than gods,” he says, mesmerized by the oil-slick surface. He pulls against its retreat, pressing his fist against his chest. “What is destruction if not a vehicle for the creation of something new?”

The tide fights his hold, but he has had thousands of years to hone the strength of his will.

“If twelve coreflames can contain the gods that created the universe,” he says, driving the edge of the tide into his chest, “then they can contain whatever you are, too.”

With the force of his will, he grasps the raw power of twelve Titans. With the force of his will and that power in his hand, he grasps the black tide. And he feels the tide’s destructive intent, its need to tear down to make room for something new.

The first of the primordial ones shakes off the last of THEIR prison. THEY turn toward Phainon, expressionless. Bored.

“Yes,” Phainon breathes, watching THEM in turn as he whispers to the tide. “Let’s do that. Together, we can do just that.”

The tide stops fighting him.

Instead, it consumes him.

The agora is full of monsters, of creatures that were once men twisted beyond recognition. Every time Mydei cuts one down, his heart grieves. Was that a mother? A father? A child? Was that monster from beyond Okhema’s walls? Has he just struck down one of his somatophylakes? His own mother?

He can’t think like that. None of them can. With black tide monsters surging around them, the Chrysos Heirs scattered throughout the city, they hold the line for Phainon, for whatever Phainon can do in the depths of the earth against the primordial ones. Mydei strikes down monsters who were innocents so that Phainon can have more time. He kills to stave off what feels more and more like the inevitable end, the certainty that they will do this again and that he won’t remember and that Phainon will well and truly break.

“Do not despair.”

She is at his back. Castorice, the Hand of Shadow, Thanatos’s heir. They have been protecting each other for agonizing minutes now, for what feels like hours. Her miasma is thin, and his arms are weary, but neither of them gives up. If there are people left in Okhema, the two of them provide protection to their fleeing backs. And if there aren’t, if all are gone or turned to monsters, they do what they can for Phainon.

For Phainon.

“I don’t,” Mydei grits out, cutting down another monster. Where it falls at his feet, the black tide glimmers strangely, more like rushing water than a stable coating over the earth beneath. “I won’t.”

Castorice whips out a tendril of her miasma, disintegrating an approaching monster as she dances around him. “Stay focused,” she admonishes.

But his attention is wholly arrested by the way the black tide seems to move beneath him, the way it ripples and shimmers. Where it has covered the earth in the past, it is still. But this tide isn’t still. This tide shivers with movement.

A sudden compulsion seizes him.

“To the roofs,” he says to Castorice, swinging to the side as he pulverizes the abdomen of yet another monster and offers a prayer for forgiveness to whatever benevolent gods may exist—if any. The Titans don’t answer prayers like this, and the primordial ones likely don’t care to; Mydei can’t imagine there’s anything left beyond these powers. “We need to get to the roofs.”

Castorice throws a bewildered glance his way as she circles behind him. “Why?”

“Trust me,” he says, though she has no reason to. But he has no reason to trust her, either. Not truly. She killed him, once. The end of the world makes strange bedfellows, and he supposes it’s better to have Death’s heir on his side than against him.

Together, they cut through the surging tide of monsters, making their way to a tall building on the edge of the agora. The door has already been battered down, and Mydei hurries through it, ducking between the broken boards of wood.

Castorice follows. “There’s nothing to barricade the doors,” she warns him as he slams open another door, revealing a staircase up.

“So we keep fighting. This way.” He hurries up the steps, taking them two at a time, his heart pounding in his chest not from the exhilaration of the fight but rather something else entirely. Something is different. Something has changed. The tide doesn’t shimmer and ripple like that, and he has his suspicions. He just has to confirm them.

A ladder greets him on the second floor, and he takes that, too, throwing open the hatch to the roof when he reaches it. He hops onto the roof, reaching through the hatch for Castorice. She takes his gauntleted wrist in her hand.

“Hurry,” she says, and he yanks her up through the hatch, depositing her on the roof beside him.

They both move quickly, slamming the hatch down. Mydei keeps his weight on it, holding firm against the black tide monsters that batter it from below, until Castorice manages to drag several heavy crates over it. Only then does he pull away, closing his eyes for a second just to breathe. But they don’t have seconds, and he can’t afford to take this time. He turns to the horizon, where the world should be dark and glassy from the black tide’s consumption and finds only naked, barren earth.

Castorice approaches from the side. “Where is the tide?” she asks softly, her voice trembling. “What’s happened to it?”

Mydei throws himself to the side of the roof, leaning over, and he is just in time to watch the backline of the tide crawl across the ground of the agora, glimpsing it between the clashing of monsters and men, as it rushes through Okhema as though being pulled somewhere.

Where it passes, the monsters go still. Some of the Chrysos Heirs take the easy shots, but others step back, horrified, as monstrous flesh melts away. Humans stand where once were monsters, naked, reeling.

Dread cleaves through him.

“What’s happening?” Castorice whispers as she joins him.

“Phainon,” Mydei breathes. “Phainon, what are you doing?”

Freedom tastes of stale air and the desperation of dying men.

Disgusting.

Even if destruction wasn’t THEIR nature, THEY would be motivated to tear this place, this world, this cosmos, to pieces.

THEY shake off the confines of THEIR statue prison, tearing THEIR way free of THEIR stone sarcophagus. Behind THEM, an ant falls to its knees, and THEY glance back to observe the insignificant creature. It burns with light, with golden blood, but it’s less important than the red-black tide of death approaching THEM. This is a foreign destruction, a dismantling power that isn’t THEIR own, but it’s old and somehow familiar—and friendly, too. It whispers promises of freedom not just for THEM but for THEIR siblings. The very corners of THEIR lips turn upward.

Good. Let THEIR siblings break free of the shells that cage THEM, too, and let THEM all tear down this putrid, rotting universe and its upstart gods.

THEY step out of THEIR stone prison, shaking off the last of THEIR shackles, and crouch to reach for the destructive energy. THEY will nurture it, guide it, make it so much more than what it currently is. THEY will help it evolve and—

And it swerves away from THEM, a tide pulling out to sea before the terrible wave of a tsunami crashes down on the shore.

THEY lift their face toward the ant on its knees before THEM, watching it absorb the blackness. This is intriguing, this is fascinating. This is a creature that has the potential to be so much more, and THEY want to peel back its skin to find out how it can grow to eclipse itself. THEY are not prone to nurture, that’s the domain of one of THEIR myriad siblings, but this little ant could be cultivated into something of use. Something that could help THEM tear down the universe to make room for a new one, and perhaps there might be a place for it in that new universe, a tool for continued destruction.

More, more, the ant takes in yet more of the blackness, absorbing the tide into itself, and the air vibrates with expectant power. Static fills THEIR mouth. A strange sensation twinges in their belly.

No simple human ant could absorb this power. Now, THEY see beyond its skin to the golden light beneath, the twelve hated coreflames it carries inside itself, and that uncomfortable sensation grows. THEY rise. THEY take a step back only to catch THEMSELF. THEY are destruction incarnate and THEY flee from nothing, especially not an ant like this.

“You,” the ant says as darkness disappears into its body, as it absorbs the strange tide that should be THEIRS by right. It rises, the ant, and hatred burns in its eyes. It draws a puny, human blade, and the darkness inside it envelops the sword, changes it until it glows with a white-black light, a void of death. The ant laughs, low and strained and unhinged. “You don’t get to win this time.” It lunges for THEM.

That strange sensation in THEIR gut churns.

Casually, THEY sway the ant aside, throwing it into a nearby wall. There is work to be done, and THEY cannot be bothered by such trivial things, even if the ant has claimed what should be THEIRS. Later, THEY will take that black tide back. Now, THEY must ready the way for THEIR siblings.

THEY leap from the ground, pulverizing rock above THEM with a mere thought, annihilating that which is between THEM and THEIR goals.

THEY burst free of the earth, emerging into a sun-drenched agora filled with more golden ants. Ants that stare up at THEM, agog, baffled, and THEY allow THEMSELF a moment of contented satisfaction. This is how it should be, these tiny, insignificant creatures paralyzed by THEIR presence. A shame none of them will survive the remaking of the world.

Extending THEIR hand, THEY work their fingers into the spaces between atoms where the world is thin and the laws of the universe mean nothing. The air around THEM cracks so much like THEIR stone prison, and THEY work THEIR fingers deeper as the ants begin to scream, as they begin to pepper THEM with pathetic attacks that barely register as sensation. What can they do to THEM? How could these ants possibly interfere with THEIR driving motivation? This universe will end, and THEY will be one cause of that ending. THEY will—

Something that is not an ant slams into THEM, tumbling THEM from the sky. THEY crash through a building, battering down walls as THEY slide across the ground. When THEY catch THEMSELF, when THEY gain THEIR feet, THEY look up to find a creature alight with golden energy, bathed in it as though in flames.

THEY realize at once what that strange feeling is in their stomach, that twisting, knotting sensation that so persists.

Fear.

THEY are afraid.

Burning, burning, burning, inside and out, he is on fire.

Golden blood stains his skin, there is a ringing in his head from his collision with the rocks, but he is burning and he is fury and he will take his fury out on the creatures that have driven him past the point of all reason. He is hatred, and he hates THEM. Oh, he hates THEM the way the night hates the day, the way the moon hates the sun. THEY have taken everything from him—everything—over and over until there’s nothing left, until he’s an empty shell, and still THEY take yet more, ripping him open, hollowing

him out, but now he has something and he won’t let THEM take from him again.

No, he will burn THEM as he burns, he will light THEM up until THEY, too, are consumed as he is consumed, he will reduce himself to ash and take THEM with him.

Roaring, screaming, throat raw, blade of void and light in hand, agony within and without, his form twisting, changing, becoming more more more. Golden light, red-black slick, he is everything in the universe and the desire to consume it, to free the wild chaos of creation dressed in the mourning veil of destruction.

He plunges from the sky, shattering limestone homes into splintered spiderwebs, atomizing the rock. The world screams in protest, the air exploding in his wake like so much thunder, a mighty boom that cracks his eardrums—he doesn’t need them, doesn’t need to hear, doesn’t need to see, either, because THEIR power is a lodestone pulling at his own.

THEY aren’t there. THEY aren’t there when his sword meets stone, THEY are gone, THEY are above him, wrenching open reality to summon forth monsters from beyond Amphoreus to assault him. They are but ants, these creatures, and he towers above them, engulfing them in the fire that pours from his flesh, so hot it is as liquid. He rips them asunder and burns them alive, and they scream as THEY back up, up, up, putting so much space between them, and THEY can command space, THEY can twist it bend it break it change it rend it but he won’t let it twist bend break change rend.

He remembers.

The air splits and magma pours from it, but he remembers there are no volcanoes, not here, not in this place, never in this place. Resolute, he remembers the world as it was and is and has been because he has seen it so many times, thousands of times—it is etched into his memory as he carries the past into the future.

The future, the future, he will make the future anew, he will destroy what threatens the future he cherishes so deeply. How strange. He remembers

hating the future, fearing the future, but now the future is red-painted flesh and golden hair and leonine eyes and it is laughter and warm hands slapping his back and friendly mockery and empty wineskins. It is scales that will never balance but the desire to strive to make them so, and THEY will try to take all this away from him, and he—

HE will not allow it.

HE screams, embracing the fire inside HIM, and it burns burns burns into wings of shining red-black and glittering gold.

“Flee!” Aglaea cries along her threads, but Mydei doesn’t move. He stands rooted to the roof as a flaming Phainon clears the agora of black tide monsters, burning them away. The heat of him blazes across the agora, reaching up the sides of the buildings, scorching Mydei’s every breath, but still he doesn’t move. He is transfixed by the sight of Phainon leaping into the air, of white-black light trailing Phainon’s sword, as he closes rifts in the world with one hand and swings on THEM with the other.

The primordial one swerves away from Phainon’s strike, barely escaping the smoking line of destruction the attack leaves both in its wake and before him. Though Mydei is too far from THEM to make out THEIR expressions, there is clear terror in the way THEY hold THEMSELF, an almost disbelief that some mere mortal might challenge THEM.

But Phainon isn’t a mere mortal. Blazing light erupts from him as he chases down the primordial one, framing twin wings of red-black and gold. A halo like the sigil of Worldbearing gleams at the back of his head, and he is—he is—HE is.

HE is so much more than anything Mydei has ever seen before, something beyond human, akin to a Titan but still more, bearing the tide in one hand and all the coreflames of the Titans in the other.

When the primordial one tears reality, HE stitches it back together, dancing across the open skies with HIS midnight bright sword. The primordial one screams with fury, and Mydei falls to his knees, suddenly somehow less

than he was before, and the remaining trees untouched by the tide turn to dust and the light from the sun dims, and, oh, THEY are consuming the very essence of the world as THEY surge forward to meet Phainon’s blade with THEIR own.

HIS weapon is a midnight sun, blackness haloed by light, but THEIRS is pure absence, the space between all things crafted into a sharp-edged blade, and when THEY cut against Phainon, THEY cut through the world itself.

There are worlds beyond imagining visible through the holes in the sky, echoes of impossible things that crumble into nothingness. Pink skies and orange oceans, creatures with shapes that bend the mind. THEY absorb the destruction of these worlds, taking some essence into THEMSELF, and Phainon isn’t quick enough to close all of the holes in reality as HE parries relentless attacks.

The two of THEM dance across the darkening sky, light visibly streaming from the far-distant sun into the primordial one as THEY destroy it, as THEY beat Phainon back, as they dip beneath HIS guard to slice through arm and wing, and Mydei struggles to his feet with a cry, watching Phainon crash to the ground.

“No, Mydei, don’t—!” Castorice reaches for him, but he fights the strange gravity of their dying world, throwing himself over the edge of the roof.

He hits the ground hard, glancing toward the sky, but THEY have no interest in him. THEY have put away their blade as THEY once more rip into the fabric of the world, tearing it open, exposing the soul of the world for THEM to consume. This is destruction in its purest form, the end of all things. They are going to die.

Weaving through the corpses of Chrysos Heirs, through the debris fallen from two gods clashing, Mydei makes his way to HIM, to Phainon, to what remains of HIM in a pool of golden blood. The heat pouring off HIM is too much. It dries Mydei’s eyes, singes his throat, scalds his skin, but he pushes closer, closer, splashing through simmering blood to fall to his knees at Phainon’s side.

He presses one hand to Phainon’s chest, so hot it burns away layers of his skin. Unimaginable pain screams along his nerves, but pain has never mattered much to him. He has survived worse than this.

“Phainon,” he says, leaning over HIM. “Phainon!”

HIS breath is shallow, HIS eyes are closed, HE isn’t moving, but HE is still alive. All that matters is that HE’s still alive.

“Is this what puts you in the ground?” Mydei demands, pressing his hand firmly against Phainon’s burning chest, fighting the excruciating pain of it. “Will you give up here?” Phainon’s bleeding, HIS right arm gone, HIS body bruised and battered and covered in cuts. Those cuts glitter at the ends, the skin sparkling and ragged—like the edge of the black tide, but golden instead of red-black. When HE opens HIS eyes, they don’t focus. “You have the coreflames and the black tide itself, you madman. You have all the power Amphoreus has to offer. Get up.” Phainon doesn’t move. “Get up, damn you, and live. Do not let us die.” His nails gouge into Phainon’s flesh. “Do not let me die.”

Phainon’s gaze fixes on Mydei’s, HIS eyes golden and bright. “I—”

“Save me,” Mydei says, weaponizing himself, his life, his very existence. “Love me and only me, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, Deliverer of Amphoreus.”

A horrible, steaming breath wheezes out of Phainon’s battered body, and he is a man again. An incredible man, a man who has survived thousands of years against all odds, but a man nonetheless. A man who Mydei loves—a man who loves Mydei in turn.

Phainon shoves himself up, blood dripping from his severed arm. He clutches Mydei’s wrist, gasping, shuddering, visibly steeling himself. “Bring the surviving Titans to the prison.”

“Where—” Mydei begins, but the answer is there in his mind as if he always knew, and he stares at Phainon, at the creature he’s become, until he finds the man buried beneath the veneer of godhood. “We’ll be there.” He

turns his wrist in Phainon’s hold, clutching his hand. “Don’t fucking die on me, Deliverer.”

“I love you,” Phainon says fiercely, and then HE launches HIMSELF into the air.

THEY drive THEIR essence deeper, deeper, forcing it into the core of the world, cracking it open, spilling out its essence in turn. THEY consume it, devour it, take it into THEMSELF to strengthen THEIR spirit. THEY must be the herald for THEIR siblings, leading the way into a new universe, for this one must be destroyed. The Titans have tainted it with their greed for power. And, oh, taking in the soul of a planet as it crumbles beneath THEIR hands is an ecstasy THEY had forgotten while in THEIR prison. THEY are flush with new power, growing in THEIR strength, becoming every minute more and more of what THEY were before THEY were imprisoned beneath the earth. THEY are—

Pain explodes through THEM, a blade protruding from THEIR stomach.

No. No, that isn’t possible. Not even the strange thing that emerged from THEIR prison to fight THEM could have—but it has, and it—IT?—is gowned in fiery authority, as if IT can rival THEM. Nothing has ever rivaled THEM before, not even the Titans. Twelve of them united could barely stand against THEM and THEIR siblings, but now here is this tiny creature, and IT tears ITS blade from THEIR side, ripping THEM open.

THEY tumble from the sky. Essence flows out of THEM, and there isn’t any time to gather it back up, because IT attacks again, ITS sword flashing in the light of ITS dying sun.

Barely, THEY parry the blade with another one of THEIR own.

THEY took ITS arm. THEY took ITS sword arm, and yet IT persists, screaming, launching a furious volley of attacks on THEM that THEY can only just keep up with. THEY are stronger in every way, but IT anticipates THEM as if IT understands combat better than THEY ever could, and the fear that kindled in THEIR belly previously comes roaring back.

In all the universe, nothing has compared to THEM but this thing, this ant that has become more than ITSELF, and THEY are afraid. THEY are terrified. This is not how the universe works. This is—this is an anomaly, one not even THEIR siblings could have predicted, for all of THEM knew there would come a day when THEY would break free, but none of THEM anticipated resistance. None of THEM anticipated IT.

IT is rage and violence, and ITS burning hatred is so very familiar. THEY should be able to manipulate that vehement fury, but when THEY grasp it, the emotion slips through THEIR fingers. There, burning at the heart of IT, is not hatred. ITS hatred is a mask covering an emotion that is far greater and far more terrifying.

IT isn’t rage and fury.

IT is love.

THEY stumble beneath ITS onslaught, ducking ITS blade in strategic retreat, trying to find space to put between THEMSELF and IT, but IT is relentless. IT chases THEM, hounds THEM, bullies THEM toward a crater in the center of the city, and it is with no small horror that THEY realize where that crater leads.

In vain, THEY attempt to dodge away from the crater, but golden strings capture THEIR wrists and drag THEM down as IT slams its sword into THEIR gut. THEY fall, stunned by a hit that feels like a meteor strike, plummeting deep, deep into the earth.

They are already there, the Titans. Their faces have changed, but THEY recognize THEIR children and ancient adversaries, these things THEY created with THEIR siblings. THEY climb to THEIR feet, struggling against the golden threads that bind THEM. Romance has tried this trick before, and THEY lunge for her—only for IT to crash into THEIR back and drive THEM to the ground.

“Bind him,” IT snarls.

NO, THEY shout, rattling the firmament itself, but the Titans are firm in their resolve. They take their coreflames and offer them up to the altar rising before THEM, its basin full not of water but golden blood.

THEY thrash violently beneath IT. Surely, having given up the coreflames, IT can’t stand against THEM, but IT remains strong in a way THEY cannot comprehend, powered by the strength of the love at ITS core. IT grinds THEIR face into the ground, and THEY scream.

The Titans stagger, but they aren’t defeated. Each of them presents their coreflame to the altar, and IT reaches out, giving over the final two. Symbols flare above them, ancient binding magics invoked against THEM, THEIR prison reforming. Stone crawls up from the earth, encasing THEIR hands, THEIR legs.

THEY scream again, desperately trying to roll IT off their back, but THEY can’t dislodge IT, and THEY can’t shake off the stone that closes around THEM. Fury burns within THEM, but it’s nothing like the blazing core of IT. Even now, even lacking all those coreflames, powered solely by that red-black destructive force that should be THEIRS—it should be THEIRS —IT is stronger.

Very well. If THEY cannot avoid imprisonment, THEY will take IT with them. THEY redouble THEIR efforts, forcing IT to restrain THEM, and a grim, vindictive satisfaction cuts through THEM. THEY will destroy this enemy even if that means destroying THEMSELF.

He’s burning himself out. He knows it. The coreflames rest on the altar, the black tide surges within him, and there’s nothing left within him to give. Now, at last, perhaps he can give up. Stone climbs over his fingers as he holds THEM down. Wraps around his wrists. A prison that can contain a primordial one can surely contain the black tide, too, and he will finally, finally, have his rest. Because he can’t live again.

He can’t. He will make this sacrifice, locking himself away with the primordial ones, to trap the black tide, too. For himself, yes, and for Mydei. For the somatophylakes. For everyone, for the people he has met and

known and loved along these many millennia. Mydei owns his heart, but he’s loved them all in different ways, and it is his love, now, that sustains him as rock climbs his wrists.

“You know,” a woman’s voice says.

He looks up.

There, standing above the altar in a white gown, is Cyrene with her soft, kind smile.

“You know you can depend on other people, too,” she says, and the world is still, the rock isn’t consuming him anymore, and no one is moving, not even her. “You don’t have to do all of this on your own.”

Tears burn in his eyes. “You’re gone,” he says, those tears spilling over his cheeks. “You’ve been gone so many years.”

“Silly,” she says, stepping down from the altar. Her chiton isn’t purely white, he realizes, and her hair isn’t just that familiar shade of pink. She is an iridescent rainbow, a culmination of so many things. “I’ve been hiding inside you all this time, putting myself back together. You gave me a safe place to rest.” Her hand touches his face, holding it. “You’ve been so busy saving all of us, Phainon. Why don’t you let us save you?”

His jaw works, the words stuck in his throat as he weeps. “I—I don’t know how.”

“Let us share your burdens,” she tells him, touching the wound on his chest where he took the black tide into himself. “Let it go, Phainon. Rely on us, too.”

There remain faint lines of golden light connecting him to each of the twelve coreflames where they float over the altar, lines of meaning and relationship that stretch back over tens of thousands of cycles. Some are thicker than others, Aglaea’s the thickets of them all, but there shines Mydei’s, his connection to Strife a beacon in the darkness.

He touches his chest, the stone on his hand crumbling away, and he’s not worried at all that the primordial one will escape. He flattens his palm over his sternum, over the deep gouge there, and when he withdraws his hand, something red and black and slick pools there.

“We’re with you,” Cyrene says. “Even me.” She laughs, quietly. “I never even left.”

“I didn’t know,” he says, apologetic.

She tuts. “I didn’t want you to.” Her hand falls from his cheek and curls around his. Gently, she guides his hand to the golden light rooted in his chest, the one that extends to all the others. “Let us help you for once.”

Shaking, he wraps his hand around the golden tether. The black tide surges along it, hungry to consume, to destroy, and it splits along all twelve lines of light, sinking into each of the coreflames in turn, emptying him out until he’s hollow and aching, a shell of himself.

“I…” He stares up at Cyrene. “I don’t think I have anything left,” he admits.

She huffs. “Oh, Phainon. We both know that’s a lie.” She pokes her finger against his chest. “Your greatest sin has always been that you’ve loved too much. Now why don’t you wake up?”

Phainon gasps, his eyes flying open. He lays across Mydei’s lap, and Mydei’s hands are pressed to his chest. There’s a wild look in his reddened eyes, his cheeks mottled, his lips trembling.

“Phainon,” he rasps, and then he’s clutching Phainon against him, and Phainon is clinging to him, too, clutching at his shoulder and crying and laughing at the same time. He wasn’t so hollowed out there was nothing left. Cyrene was right—she was always right. She—

He jerks away from Mydei, raking his eyes over the assembled Titans. Aglaea, Tribbie, Cipher, Amphitrite. Eunomia and Pelius are gone, replaced

with faces of Chrysos Heirs Phainon knows only vaguely. Castorice stands where Thanatos should have. Anaxagoras has survived. So has Hyacinthia. Mydei still holds him, thrumming with Strife’s power, and Worldbearing burns within Phainon’s own chest.

But there, standing before the altar in her iridescent chiton, stands Cyrene, too, and she’s smiling at him. “Thank you,” she says, and he’s weeping again, for real this time, as he turns his face into Mydei’s neck and sobs with relief.

“It’s over,” he says, clinging to Mydei, and Mydei’s clinging to him, too, the two of them wrapped around each other in the broken remains of a tomb for ancient gods.

“It’s over,” Mydei whispers back to him.

Chapter End Notes
