chapters.title: Chapter 21
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

Hyacine heals and bandages Phainon’s right arm as much as she can, but not even the Sky Titan can restore a severed limb. Phainon’s sure he’ll have a whole host of feelings about his lost arm later, but for the moment, he’s simply glad to be alive. Is glad Cyrene is alive. Is glad Mydei is alive and at his side, holding onto his remaining hand, clutching it within a bruising grip.

It’s Aglaea who calls them to order, who leads them from the mausoleum beneath the earth into the light of day. The sun above them blazes as though the primordial one never drank from it, and the rends in space are gone, but the destruction remains. The people remain.

They are everywhere in the agora, the Amphoreans who became monsters who were then returned to themselves when Phainon took in the tide. Chrysos Heirs move through their ranks, already seeing to them, offering clothes and blankets alongside cups of water.

“I don’t understand,” he says to Cyrene while leaning heavily on Mydei. “How did this happen?”

She shakes her head. “I was living inside you when you did that. How am I supposed to know?”

He gives her a half-hearted glare. “You seemed to have a whole lot of answers thirty minutes ago.”

“Well, that was thirty minutes ago. This is now. Now, I have no idea what you did,” she says, waving him off.

He looks up at Mydei.

Mydei shrugs. “Don’t expect me to know, Deliverer,” he says, his lips quirking.

Phainon tries to drag his missing right hand down his face—and a small pit forms in his stomach.

Mydei must read his sudden distress on his face. He gentles, at least as much as he ever does in public, and rests his forehead against Phainon’s. “You saved the world,” he reminds him. “You saved me.”

It takes several seconds for a faint smile to turn Phainon’s lips. “I suppose I did.”

Anaxagoras, of course, is the one who eventually proposes an explanation later that evening as the Titans gather in the Marmoreal Palace. There’s a strange pull between them, one that Phainon assumes has always been present but that Mydei explains is new. Anaxagoras has an explanation for that, too.

“Phainon undid the curse of the black tide,” he says. “By drawing it into himself, he extracted it from the land and the people.”

“We will have to explore the farms and the wilderness between the city states,” Aglaea says. “There was grass on the horizon, but we don’t know how much Phainon managed to save.”

They all look at him, and he turns away, embarrassed by the weight of their stares.

“As for the black tide itself,” Anaxagoras continues, “all of us now hold it within ourselves and our coreflames. We are its guardians.” He taps his chest. “Not only are we bound by its presence shared between us but by the weight of the cycles Phainon experienced.” He makes a thoughtful sound. “This will change what it means to be a Titan.”

“How?” Hyacine asks.

A grin splits Anaxagoras’s face. “We will have to find out, won’t we? And that will be the most exciting thing to come out of any of this.”

Phainon and Mydei share brief looks of incredulity. But of course this new mystery would please Anaxagoras.

Aglaea takes command of Okhema the following morning, martialing her Chrysos Heirs to see to those who are recovered monsters and to help rebuild. She employs the Titans, too, all except Anaxagoras and Hyacine, who disappeared in the night—presumably to return to the Grove. But when she turns to give orders to Mydei, he declines them.

“My loyalties are first to my own people,” he says, bowing politely to her. “Let me return home and assess the damage there. If it’s minimal, I will speak to my queen mother on your behalf. I will convince her to send support to rebuild Okhema.”

Aglaea studies him for a long, quiet moment, tapping her finger against her lip. “Very well,” she says at last. “You are right that I cannot keep you here. And I will, too, send messengers to the recovered army to ensure it no longer marches on your city. You are not Castrum Kremnos’s king—” And Phainon sees the relief in Mydei’s eyes at that statement. “—but I will consider you a proxy for your mother.” She extends her hand. “Let this be a tentative peace between us.”

He takes her hand. “Let it,” he agrees.

Her hand falls away, and she turns to Phainon, who lingers at Mydei’s side, not sure where he belongs in this conversation or the larger one about the world more generally. He has spent so long in his cycles that he doesn’t know where to go. What to do. But when Aglaea turns his way, fear spikes through him. How funny. He faced down a Titan’s god and he’s still afraid of Aglaea.

But her expression is soft when she regards him. “Phainon,” she says warmly, taking both his shoulders in her hands. “I should one day like very

much to hear about all the adventures we went on throughout your many lives.”

“One day?” he ventures.

“One day,” she says again. “But not this day.” Her hands fall away from him. “I release you from your service to me in light of everything you’ve done for Amphoreus. You are a free man, no longer beholden to Okhema.” She smiles, and it’s a sad thing. “Whatever debts may have existed between us in this cycle of your life are no more, and they never should have been. Live your life as you will.”

Even if she hadn’t granted him this freedom, he would have simply taken it, but her kindness is an olive branch, and he accepts it gratefully. “Thank you, Aglaea.”

Lips curling, she glances from him to Mydei. “Will the two of you travel together?”

Phainon’s face heats. It’s not as if their relationship is a secret, and they have been painfully obvious about it since arriving. He’d hoped that most people wouldn’t notice, not for any greater reason that he didn’t want to deal with external nosiness, but of course there was that kiss. And Aglaea’s not the sort to let that go. Romance sees all such relationships far more clearly than anyone else. “If he’ll have me,” Phainon says, not looking at Mydei.

Mydei makes a noise in the back of his throat that promises trouble. “If I’ll have you?” he asks. “If? And what if I won’t?”

At that, Phainon snaps back around. “What does that mean?”

“What do you think it means?” Mydei asks, one brow lifted in princely arrogance.

Phainon has no idea, but he’s not about to lose whatever this argument is that he’s stumbled into. “That you’re planning on leaving without me.”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “If I found our somatophylakes without you in tow, they’d probably string me up and leave me for dead.”

“They would not.” The thought warms his heart, but he affects a cool expression.

“Well, no,” Mydei admits, a small grin appearing on his face. “But at least one of them would probably consider it.”

“Probably?”

“Maybe.”

Aglaea makes a sound that manage to be both amused and disgusted, drawing their attention back to her. “Once you two work out precisely who’s going where and stringing up whom, Okhema will supply you with horses for your journey and whatever food and water we can afford to part with.” She places a hand on Phainon’s left arm, warm and reassuring. “And if you ever desire to return, your welcome will be a warm one.”

Mydei wants to leave immediately, but Phainon has unfinished business. He convinces Mydei to wait until after lunch, and while Mydei makes ready for their departure, Phainon goes in search of Cyrene.

She stands on a balcony near the pinnacle of the Marmoreal Palace, still in that iridescent chiton, her expression serene and inscrutable. As he approaches, she turns to him with a smile, and she hooks a lock of hair behind her ear. “I wondered when you’d come find me.”

“I thought you might be avoiding me.”

Her smile widens. “Never. I’ve just needed some time alone.” She returns her gaze to the distant horizon, green once more with the removal of the tide. There are perhaps less trees, but the world appears to be as it was before the tide. There is hope for the future of Amphoreus. A future he couldn’t have created without her help. “It’s been… a long time since I’ve been alone.”

She’s smiling, but he grimaces. “How much of my life have you seen?”

“Oh, all of it,” she replies.

He wonders if he can spill the black tide out of himself and let it destroy him. That sounds nice. “All of it?” His voice is uncomfortably high.

“Don’t worry. I closed my eyes for a lot of the more recent bits.” She winks.

He could die. “Cyrene,” he begins, strangled.

Expression softening, she beckons him closer, and he joins her against the rail, watching the sky, bright and blue and clear. “You’re going off with Mydei, aren’t you?” she asks.

He closes his eyes and nods, turning his face into the sunlight, letting it wash over him. “I am.” A part of him doesn’t want to. They’re different people, now. She’s seen all of his life, has lived all of his lives. She knows him, but he doesn’t know her. He wants to know her again. Wants to rekindle their friendship. But he suspects she’s had enough of him for many lifetimes. “You’re welcome to join us,” he says anyway. “We’re going to find his—our—somatophylakes and then head back to Castrum Kremnos. You could join us. See the world for what it really is.” Instead of what it was through the prison of his eyes. He looks at her, a little hopeful, but knowing already what she’s going to say.

“I think I want to stay.” She hops onto the railing, letting the wind catch her hair, and he wants to pull her back, but he’s not her keeper. “Aglaea’s asked me to help, and my abilities as the Time Titan are uniquely suited for fixing things, don’t you think?” She laughs, but it’s a sad sound. “I hope you understand.”

He does. That doesn’t make losing her when he’s just gotten her back hurt any less. “We’ll have to come visit you,” he says. “Mydei and I. Here, in Okhema. If Aglaea and Gorgo don’t decide that they want that war after all.”

Her eyes go vague and unfocused, and she lists to the side. He leans forward, reaching out to—but he doesn’t have his right arm anymore, and he has to awkwardly grab her with his left hand instead. She catches herself on the railing before he can. “I don’t think they will,” she says. “Go to war. I think they’re both tired. I think they both want something new.”

“That’s… good, then,” he says, resting his arm on the rail once more, trying not to worry about her balance, about her tumbling off and falling to her death. But even if she did, she could just reverse the course of time and soar back to safety. She doesn’t need him. The world doesn’t need him. Not anymore. “It’s time for something new.”

She touches his shoulder, his bad one, the one no else will go near except Mydei. “Live, Phainon,” she says. “For once in your life, be selfish, and live.”

They leave in the early afternoon, astride horses that have seen better days but that are all Okhema can bear to part with. The younger horses, the stronger horses, are needed to rebuild the city and restore the farmlands.

Mydei carries with him a papyrus from Aglaea to Gorgo and one of Aglaea’s seals—safe passage for them both, in case they come across her army. Phainon carries their supplies and the weight of something that isn’t regret but certainly feels like it. He misses his arm. He misses his sense of purpose. Another cycle would have crushed him, but without the endless churning of those cycles, he has nothing to offer the world.

“You’re upset,” Mydei observes as they make camp that first night. They tie their nags nearby and build a fire by unspoken agreement; they want the potential company. “Why?”

Phainon sits against Mydei’s side, tucking himself beneath Mydei’s arm, seeking the comfort his victory affords him. Mydei is alive, and he should be happy. “Who is Phainon of Aedes Elysiae?” he asks. “Without the cycles, who am I? What do I offer the world?”

Mydei loops an arm around Phainon’s back, settling his hand on his hip. He nuzzles into Phainon’s neck, and Phainon closes his eyes. “What do you need to offer anyone anymore, Deliverer?” Mydei asks, lightly teasing.

A frustrated sound catches in Phainon’s throat. “That’s not—I’ve had purpose for so long. And now it’s just… gone.”

Mydei’s mouth finds the curve of his jaw, not to arouse but to soothe, offering comfort and kindness. “The world is vast,” he says, “and there are paths and purposes a plenty. We will find something that fulfills you.”

He wants to believe that so very much, but he’s afraid. “And if we don’t?”

“Since when have you been a pessimist?” Mydei asks. “If you can’t find faith of your own, then trust in me. I believe there’s more for you.” There’s a tightness, a pain in Mydei’s voice, and Phainon aches.

Maybe Cyrene was right about his sins.

“Then I’ll believe in you,” Phainon says, tipping his head to the side and brushing his mouth against Mydei’s. “I’ll believe in my love for you.”

Dawn comes too early, and Phainon peels himself away from Mydei, rousing him. They break their camp after a brief meal, pack their supplies, and mount their horses. Castrum Kremnos is several days away by horse, and while they could use Mydei’s form as Strife, neither is keen on scaring the tide’s survivors with the Titan’s form.

On the second night, still camped by the side of the road, the two of them unwilling to inconvenience the villagers between Okhema and Castrum Kremnos, human figures emerge from the darkness. Mydei’s hand goes to his sword, resting at his side, and Phainon rises from where he sits. He is one-armed but ambidextrous and more than capable of helping Mydei defend their camp if needed.

“Ho, there,” a man’s voice calls. A familiar voice.

Mydei is on his feet in an instant, his expression wild, pained, hopeful. “Hephaestion?”

The shadows pause, and then they step into the circle of firelight. The somatophylakes are clothed in rags, their expressions both haggard and joyful, and they are on Phainon and Mydei before Phainon can react. Phainon finds himself enveloped in back-slapping hugs, with tears in his eyes, and he decides he doesn’t care if these men see him crying because they’re crying, too, all of them, as they grab hold of each other, as they embrace each other like they’ve just escaped the gallows.

They have, all of them.

“You fucking maniac,” Leonnius says when he finds Phainon in the fray. He grabs him in a rough embrace. “You did it. You actually fucking did it.” He shoves Phainon back, holding him at arm’s length. “Fuck me,” he breathes.

Phainon gestures to his arm. “How are those scales?”

Leonnius swats the side of his head. “Fuck the scales, you Titansdamn madman.”

And then Hephaestion is squeezing his forearm, is tugging him into another embrace. “Everything between us,” he says seriously, his hand on the back of Phainon’s neck, “is washed away. You fixed the world.”

Phainon offers him a wan smile. “I suppose I did.”

“Tell me you have wine,” Leonnius roars, throwing his arms around Perdikkas and Peucesta. “Tonight, we should drink!”

“We have travel food and water,” Mydei replies dryly. “Enough for two to reach Castrum Kremnos.”

Leonnius sighs, visibly aggrieved. “Then we will tell our stories with water and empty bellies!”

They crowd around the fire, the five bullying Mydei and Phainon until they give up the story of the Battle of Okhema. He and Mydei take turns,

interrupting each other in the retelling of events, though Mydei has to recount his combat against the primordial one. Phainon’s memories are too disjointed and surreal for him to accurately describe any of it, and he listens to his own story with wonder. He did that. He fought something stronger than a Titan—and he won.

“They’ll write songs about you,” Peucesta declares. “No. No, I will write songs about you, because no one else is going to get it right.”

“They’ll all make him too handsome,” Leonnius agrees.

Phainon scoffs, warmed not just by the fire. This easy camaraderie fills some of that gaping hole within him. “You only say that because you’re so ugly, Leonnius.”

And then they’re fighting, taking sides, arguing over who among them is the least attractive and who the most. Mydei defends him, and he defends Mydei, until the somatophylakes as a whole turn on the two of them, mocking them in the way of friendship for the love they have for each other.

Much, much later, when it’s just Hephaestion and Phainon awake, Phainon turns his face to the sky and says, “What was it like when you were one of those monsters?”

Hephaestion is silent for a long, long time, so long that Phainon thinks he’ll ignore the question entirely. But then, quietly, he replies, “Terrible. There was nothing left in me but the hunger to destroy. Even now, I still feel it, this… yawning emptiness and the need to fill it with carnage.”

Phainon leans back. He can’t bring himself to look at Hephaestion, not wanting to take away the illusion of privacy. “I think I left part of myself in those cycles. What’s left of me has…” He trails off. He doesn’t have nothing. He has Hephaestion. He has Leonnius, Perdikkas, Ptolemy, Peucesta. He has Mydei. “Everything ends.”

“Profound,” Hephaestion drawls.

“We can’t have new beginnings without endings. We’re both hollowed out now, in different ways, but we’ll find something to fill the voids within us.” He drops his hand on Hephaestion’s shoulder.

Hephaestion does the same, and they sit there, holding each other. “We will,” he says.

Castrum Kremnos is alive. Mydei could weep with relief to see the gates guarded, to see a city that lives and breathes, that pulses with energy, even if that energy is somewhat subdued. His people—but they aren’t his people anymore, not really, and that sends a pang through him. They are alive. They have survived. But they aren’t his. Not anymore. Now, all of Amphoreus must be his, and he has some obligation to its recovery from the collective trauma of the black tide.

A strange weight settles in his guts. He doesn’t know what to do with this truth, with this realization. He doesn’t know how to save people.

Subdued himself, he glances at Phainon, and Phainon catches his eye. “Excited to be home?” he asks, with the hollow expression of a man dreading his current location. Though Phainon is a free man by every measure, all the chains of his bondage broken, Mydei cannot imagine he loves Castrum Kremnos.

And Mydei, too, doesn’t love Castrum Kremnos the way he once did. He loves what it stands for. What is has been historically. What it could be again. But he doesn’t love what it became under Eurypon and what it must move away from under his mother.

“It’s a strange feeling,” Mydei admits, slipping his hand into Phainon’s. “But I’m not sure Castrum Kremons is home anymore.” Phainon looks taken aback but says nothing, and Mydei remembers what he called Phainon so many weeks ago, before his world changed so dramatically. Phainon of Nowhere. “Perhaps I’m now Mydei of Nowhere.” His lips quirk, but his smile is sad.

Phainon squeezes his hand. “The Lance of Fury. Mydei of Amphoreus.”

The titles bear a strange weight, and Mydei isn’t sure he’s ready to accept them. Not yet.

Word still travels ahead of them, reaching the palace well before they do. Gorgo waits for them in the inner courtyard, her expression cool but approving. How strange, but his mother’s approval means so little to him, now.

Still, he slides off his horse and goes to her, kneeling without hesitation. She has always been Castrum Kremnos’s queen before she was his mother. At his back, Phainon and the somatophylakes kneel, too.

“Rise,” Gorgo says. “The Strife Titan does not bend his knee to Castrum Kremnos.”

He obeys, and she offers him a small smile, the faintest indication of her approval. How strange that it means so little to him now. He helped Phainon to save the world, and his mother’s regard, which once would have made his heart soar, has become a much smaller currency.

Later, much later, when they are feted at Gorgo’s behest, Phainon leans over and says, “Tell me she’s embraced you in private.”

Mydei regards the wine in his goblet. “We have had no private moment.” Fury flickers across Phainon’s face, and Mydei touches his thigh beneath the table they share. “Put away your anger,” he says softly.

“For you,” Phainon replies, just as soft.

That Phainon is angry for him means more to him than his mother’s affection. How the world has shifted on its axis. Mydei’s heart swells. He allows himself a small smile, hidden by his goblet, and he smooths his hand higher on Phainon’s thigh.

Even later than that, when the hour is late and the sun kisses the distant horizon, when Phainon and Mydei return to Mydei’s old room, Mydei says looks around himself and feels only loathing. “I don’t want to stay here,” he says.

“I don’t, either,” Phainon says.

They look at each other and they smile and then they laugh. They cry, too, and find themselves on the floor in front of a kline, leaning against each other and once more emptied of everything they could feel.

“I don’t want to sleep in that bed with you,” Mydei says, staring at the ceiling above him. “And I don’t want to live in this palace with you. But I don’t know where we could go instead.”

Phainon tucks Mydei into his side, leaning their heads together. “The world is vast, and there are places beyond number.” His lips quirk. “Despite living for so long, I’ve barely ventured beyond our city states.”

“Then we should go to these places,” Mydei says. “Far to the east, and then to the north, where it’s so cold we can see our own breath.”

“South, too.” Phainon laces their fingers. “To sandy deserts dotted with oases.” He pauses. “Will you not miss your mother?”

Mydei lifts their fingers to his lips and kisses Phainon’s knuckles. Will he? “I will.” And he means it. His ties to her remain strong—perhaps that’s why they hurt so much. “But my presence here will only harm her. My existence will harm her, but it will be even harder for her if I remain.”

“She’s still your mother.”

“She’s the Queen of Castrum Kremnos first,” Mydei says. “She always has been. It’s why she used us so well.” He exhales, his breath shuddery, and turns into Phainon’s body. He doesn’t miss the warmth of Phainon’s lost arm but takes refuge in the strength of Phainon’s body beneath his. “Let’s leave. Let’s see the deserts and the mountains. Let’s go east and taste strange new foods.”

Phainon curls around Mydei. “You’re sure?”

“I’m sure.” They don’t belong here anymore. This isn’t home—not for him, not anymore, and never for Phainon.

“Then let’s go,” Phainon says, giving him a kiss, one that Mydei returns with fervor, with hunger.

Leaving Castrum Kremnos is as easy as entering it. While Phainon tells the somatophylakes what he and Mydei have decided, while he gives them the chance to honorably renounce their vows and stay with their families, Mydei makes his goodbyes to Gorgo. The somatophylakes, to a man, commit themselves to the unknown journey.

“We can’t trust you to survive without us,” Leonnius says.

“I should like to learn the music of these farflung places,” Peucesta says.

“And I their knowledge of numbers and the world,” Ptolemy adds.

Perdikkas smiles broadly. “It is said that eastern medicine is more advanced than our own. Can we start there?”

“Your homes,” Phainon says. “Your families…”

Hephaestion claps Phainon on his right shoulder. “Home is people,” he says. “Mydei has always been that person for us.” He sighs, a touch dramatically. “And, now, unfortunately, so are you.” He slaps Phainon on the back and goes to collect his things, but his words linger.

Home is people.

Gorgo gives them healthy horses and a cart full of supplies for their journey though she doesn’t see them off. Perhaps it’s better that she doesn’t, that she and Mydei made their farewells in private. Hephaestion brings his maps and takes charge of their journey immediately, turning them, as Perdikkas had hoped, to the east.

“There’s so much we can learn in the east,” Perdikkas says excitedly, all but vibrating in his saddle. “I’ve heard of a technique that utilizes needles to—”

“That’s not why we’re headed east,” Hephaestion says.

They all stare at him, bewildered.

“It’s not?” Mydei asks.

“It’s not,” Hephaestion confirms.

Phainon’s brows come together. “Then why?” he asks.

Hephaestion rolls up his map, tucking it into a pouch at his side. “There is a temple to Romance in the next city,” he says dryly, “and there is no better place to celebrate a union.”

Phainon sputters, but Mydei laughs. He takes Phainon’s hand in his, stretching their arms between their mounts, and grins broadly. “I hadn’t gotten around to asking you, yet,” he says. “If you’d marry a man who is no longer a prince.”

Home is people. Home is people, is a single person, and Phainon hasn’t been home in so long. He squeezes Mydei’s hand in his own, fighting back the burn of tears through a smile so broad it hurts his face. “Would you marry a one-armed madman?” he asks.

“I would have no other,” Mydei replies.

“Nor would I.”

Home is people.

“For fuck’s sake,” Leonnius barks. “Why is it always this ridiculous sentimentality with the two of you?”

Perdikkas shoves him. “Let them be in love,” he snaps back.

“Let us all have this one good thing for more than ten seconds,” Ptolemy says. “And anyway, a marriage celebration means wine for you.”

Leonnius grabs at Hephaestion. “Then we should get married, too, so there’s more wine for everyone.”

“I’d rather die,” Hephaestion replies.

“We need new friends,” Phainon says directly to Mydei, who laughs and laughs until tears stream down his cheeks.

Peucesta plucks a string of notes on his lap harp, the beginnings of a bawdy drinking song about newlyweds. Leonnius launches into the verse with too much gusto and not enough sense of pitch, and is joined shortly after by Mydei, who’s still wiping tears from his eyes. And Phainon, laughing, gives up on fighting them and lifts his voice alongside theirs.

These are his people, and they are his home.
